Laboratory studies reveal: haemoglobin 100 g/l, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 98 fl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 100 mm/hr, C reactive protein (CRP) is 59 mg/L and polymorphonuclear leucocytosis. The chest X-ray is clear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA)
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa
This patient presents with constitutional upset, abdominal pain, hypertension and mononeuritis. The raised ESR, CRP and polymorphonuclear leucocytosis support a diagnosis of vasculitis, in this case polyarteritis nodosa. The abdominal pain is highly suggestive of mesenteric ischaemia. Mononeuritis multiplex develops because of vasculitis of the vasa nervorum; it is reflected in the patient’s describing sudden loss of ability to dorsiflex his left great toe.

Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA)
Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA) is incorrect because Churg- Strauss syndrome is commonly associated with pulmonary manifestations, which are absent in this case, and the chest X-ray is normal.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
GPA is incorrect because it is commonly associated with pulmonary manifestations, which are absent in this case, and the chest X-ray is normal.

stem: A 17-year-old teenager attends the clinic with a 1-day history of pain and swelling in his left knee. He is known to have factor VIII deficiency. On examination there is restriction of joint movement. The joint is hot, swollen and extremely painful. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are normal. Test for rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Haemarthrosis
This young man has haemarthrosis or haemophilic arthritis. The pain and swelling is due to bleeding within the joint. The treatment involves replacement of factor VIII and orthopaedic assessment, with view to wash out the joint.

Juvenile chronic arthritis
Juvenile chronic arthritis is incorrect. ‘Juvenile chronic arthritis’ is the term given to a spectrum of arthritides occurring in childhood. This presentation in a haemophiliac with normal inflammatory markers and negative rheumatoid factor, does not fit. Also, the diagnosis of juvenile chronic arthritis can only be made with an onset of symptoms before the age of 16.

Pyogenic arthritis
Pyogenic arthritis is incorrect. In a pyogenic arthritis (septic arthritis), the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels would be raised.

stem: A 56-year-old patient with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to the Emergency Department with gritty, red eyes. She has rheumatoid arthritis, but this is currently controlled with methotrexate and non-steroidal anti- inflammatory agents (NSAIDs). On examination there is diffuse redness affecting both eyes and there are engorged episcleral vessels. Visual acuity is normal when corrected with spectacles, and Schirmer’s test is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Episcleritis
Episcleritis presents in this way with red, gritty eyes but preserved visual acuity. Artificial tears and NSAID drops are the mainstay of therapy, with steroid eye drops an option in more severe disease. Episcleritis is known to be associated with rheumatoid arthritis and a range of other systemic inflammatory disorders.

Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis is incorrect. Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the inside of the eyelids and covering the globe to the limbus. The cause can be infectious, due to viral or bacterial pathogens, allergic or non-allergic reactions. Conjunctivitis normally presents with redness and discharge in one eye with the patient typically complaining of the eye being stuck shut in the morning. Viral infections are associated with a prodromal illness and more of a gritty feeling, whilst in allergic reaction there is a greater association with itchiness. In bacterial conjunctivitis, treatment is generally with topical chloramphenicol. The absence of any evidence of pus, sticky eyes or itchiness makes this unlikely.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a long history of type 1 diabetes and terminal kidney disease on haemodialysis is referred from the unit with a knee problem. Over the past 24 hours, his left knee has become swollen, erythematous and extremely painful such that he is only able to flex it 30 degrees and cannot weight bear. His temperature is 39 °C. Investigations: Synovial fluid Cloudy yellow in colour White cell count (WCC) 200 × 10 9/l Gram stain negative Crystals negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Septic arthritis
Synovial fluid white cell count is unreliable in the diagnosis of septic arthritis, and Gram stain is only 60% sensitive. Given that this patient has sudden-onset monoarthritis and is pyrexial, he would be considered to have septic arthritis until proven otherwise. The effusion should be drained and the patient treated with IV antibiotics, eg flucloxacillin, until culture results are available.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative disease of joints characterised clinically by chronic pain which is worse with activity. The acute onset of symptoms, fever and inability to weight bear, and reduced range of motion makes this a very unlikely diagnosis, as does the erythematous and swollen nature of the joint.

stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the clinic complaining of pain on the lateral aspect of his elbow and on resisted dorsiflexion of the wrist. He admits to having been doing a lot of DIY around the house recently and is a keen tennis player in his spare time. Examination reveals significant tenderness over the lateral aspect of the elbow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
Lateral epicondylitis or tennis elbow occurs in response to repeated mechanical strain at the tendon insertion into the lateral epicondyle. Pain extends down the forearm and is worse on resisted dorsiflexion of the wrist. A number of treatment modalities exist, including physiotherapy, use of orthotic devices, use of non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or ultimately lateral release via surgery. The condition is generally self-limiting and resolves between 6 months and 2 years after first onset.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis is incorrect. Medial epicondylitis is also known as golfer’s elbow and leads to tendonitis affecting the flexors of the fingers and the pronators of the forearm, including pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum superficialis and palmaris longus.

Ulnar neuropathy
Ulnar neuropathy is incorrect. Ulnar neuropathy does not result from lateral epicondylitis, and leads to weakness of flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum profundus and the hypothenar eminence.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has sustained two vertebral fractures following minor trauma and is diagnosed with osteoporosis. Initially she is treated with bisphosphonate but the treatment is stopped because of side-effects. You are considering raloxifene as an alternative therapy. In your advice to the patient you should inform her that this therapy can cause which one of the following?
options: Cause vaginal bleeding at the end of each month of therapy
Improve the bone mineral density in the spine and hips
Increase the high density lipoprotein (HDL) levels
Increase the risk of breast cancer
explanation:
Increase the risk of clotting
Raloxifene is a selective oestrogen-receptor modulator that exerts both oestrogen-agonist effects on bone and lipid metabolism and oestrogen-antagonist effects on uterine endometrium and breast tissue. The most common adverse effects of raloxifene are hot flushes and leg cramps. There is also an increased risk of clots Beneficial effects: The beneficial oestrogenic activities of raloxifene include a lowering of total and low- density lipoprotein cholesterol levels and improvement of bone mineral density. Raloxifene reduces fracture risk at the spine but not at the hip. In women with a previous vertebral fracture, the magnitude of this reduction has been found to be dose-dependent and at least four times greater in women with no previous fracture. Raloxifene vs oestrogen: Raloxifene does not raise triglyceride or high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels. It does not have some of the troublesome side-effects of oestrogen, such as vaginal spotting (bleeding) or breast tenderness. Raloxifene might have fewer side-effects than are typically observed with oestrogen therapy because of its tissue selectivity.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with episodes of tingling, numbness and burning of the fingers of both hands over the past year, with colour changes, especially in the cold. Her doctor thinks it could be Raynaud’s phenomenon. With which disease is this phenomenon most often seen?
explanation:
Systemic sclerosis
Raynaud’s phenomenon is seen in almost 100% cases of systemic sclerosis and can precede the onset of the full-blown disease by many years.

Adult polymyositis
Adult polymyositis is incorrect. Although Raynaud’s may also be seen in adult polymyositis, it is not as common as in systemic sclerosis and SLE.

Cryoglobulinaemia
Cryoglobulinaemia is incorrect. Although Raynaud’s may also be seen in cryoglobulinaemia, it is not as common as in systemic sclerosis and SLE.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Although Raynaud’s may also be seen in polyarteritis nodosa, it is not as common as in systemic sclerosis and SLE.

stem: A patient complains of tenderness of the patella while walking. Which one of the following signs or investigations may be most useful in initial diagnosis of prepatellar bursitis?
explanation:
Crepitation of the knee
In prepatellar bursitis the physician might note any of the following signs and symptoms during a physical examination: Tenderness of the patella to palpation Fluctuant oedema over the lower pole of the patella Erythema of the knee Crepitus of the knee

Absent patella reflex
Absent patella reflex is incorrect. The patella reflex is not changed with bursitis.

Wasting of the quadriceps muscle
Wasting of the quadriceps muscle is incorrect. It is non-specific, but implies long-standing knee pathology causing significant pain and disuse atrophy, which is unlikely with prepatellar bursitis.

stem: A 17-year-old girl, who is otherwise fit, complains of backache and fatigue and worsening posture. Her parents have also noticed that she is increasingly becoming round-shouldered over the past few years. On examination of the back, movements are normal. There is marked kyphosis of the thoracic region. What would be the most characteristic feature of an X-ray of the thoracic spine?
options: Anterior displacement of one thoracic vertebra upon another
Irregular upper and lower vertebral endplates with loss of disc space height
Osteophyte formation on posterior facet joints
explanation:
Irregular upper and lower vertebral endplates with loss of disc space height
This girl has Scheuermann’s disease. It usually affects those between 13 and 16 years of age. The normal ossification of ring epiphyses of several thoracic vertebrae is affected. Deforming forces are greatest at the anterior border of the vertebrae so vertebrae are narrower anteriorly, resulting in kyphosis. Kyphosis, and not scoliosis, is the presenting feature of Scheuermann’s disease.

Absent neural arch
Absent neural arch is incorrect. Congenital absence of the neural arches would have presented earlier with kyphoscoliosis.

Anterior displacement of one thoracic vertebra upon another
Anterior displacement of one thoracic vertebra upon another is incorrect. Anterior displacement occurs in spondylolisthesis (a defect in the pars interarticularis of the neural arch, usually due to a fracture).

Scoliosis
Scoliosis is incorrect. This patient has kyphosis (forward curvature) not scoliosis (lateral curvature) of the spine.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with pain and marked swelling affecting her proximal interphalangeal, distal interphalangeal and carpometacarpal joints on both hands. The episodes of pain and swelling respond to non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Plain radiographs demonstrate erosions in a gull-wing pattern but no periarticular osteoporosis. A full blood count is normal, rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies are negative. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 29 mm in 1 st hour and the C-reactive protein (CRP) is 10 mg/l. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erosive osteoarthritis
This scenario describes the classic features of erosive inflammatory osteoarthritis. The gull-wing or inverted-T pattern of erosions is typical of erosive inflammatory osteoarthritis.

Polyarticular gout
Polyarticular gout is incorrect. The gull-wing pattern of erosions is characteristic of erosive osteoarthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis
Psoriatic arthritis is incorrect. There are no cutaneous features of psoriasis or nail pitting.

Seronegative arthritis
Seronegative arthritis is incorrect. Unlike in RA, in erosive there is no juxta-articular osteoporosis. Were this to be inflammatory arthritis, then it would be expected that both the ESR and the CRP would be significantly abnormal, as you can see in this case both are normal or just above the normal range.

stem: A 54-year-old woman complains of severe right shoulder pain that is localised mainly to the mid-humerus but also is felt diffusely around the anterolateral shoulder. The onset was sudden and not precipitated by trauma. Physical examination reveals limited abduction, with point tenderness over the subacromial bursa and the greater tuberosity of the humerus. A radiograph reveals a linear calcific density in the supraspinatus tendon. Which one of the following statements fits best with the underlying condition?
options: Commonest age of presentation is below 40 years
Physiotherapy is of no value in managing the condition
The calcific density is most probably calcium hydroxyapatite crystals
The calcific density is most probably calcium urate crystals
Trauma is the commonest cause of calcific tendonitis
explanation:
The calcific density is most probably calcium hydroxyapatite crystals
The clinical features and radiographic pattern are characteristic of calcific tendinitis, an extremely common rheumatic syndrome characterised by deposits of hydroxyapatite crystals within injured rotator cuff muscles near the humeral attachment region. It most commonly involves the supraspinatus tendon, but the infraspinatus and subscapularis tendons may also be involved.

Commonest age of presentation is below 40 years
Commonest age of presentation is below 40 years is incorrect. Most patients are between 40-60 years of age.

Trauma is the commonest cause of calcific tendonitis
Trauma is the commonest cause of calcific tendonitis is incorrect. Trauma is not the commonest cause – most cases are idiopathic or occur in diabetic patients.

stem: A 16-year-old school student complains of low back pain radiating to the back of his legs. There is no loss of sensation or movement. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 289 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 49 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Rheumatoid Factor Negative Lateral view X-ray spine Anterior squaring of the vertebrae What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
These radiographic findings are suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis, coupled with raised inflammatory markers and a negative rheumatoid factor. Sacroiliitis is often the first abnormality, with irregularity and loss of cortical margins, widening of the joint space and subsequently marginal sclerosis, narrowing and fusion. Lateral views of the thoracolumbar spine might show anterior squaring of the vertebrae, which is caused by erosion and sclerosis of the anterior corners and periostitis of the waist of the vertebrae.

stem: A 74-year-old man has an acutely painful, red and swollen knee. He is suffering from congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, chronic renal impairment and is currently on digoxin and furosemide. A most recent creatinine was measured at 135 μmol/l. CRP is slightly elevated and white cell count is normal. What treatment would be most appropriate for his joint pain?
explanation:
Colchicine
Given the history of congestive cardiac failure and kidney disease, it would seem most appropriate to manage his acute gout with colchicine. This is associated with less gastrointestinal irritation than NSAIDs and is not associated with fluid retention. Colchicine can be ‘renally dosed’ (ie reduced dose in renal impairment), but renal function should still be monitored.

Diclofenac
Diclofenac is incorrect. It is an NSAID, and as such may worsen heart and kidney disease.

Indometacin
Indometacin is incorrect. It is an NSAID, and as such may worsen heart and kidney disease.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Prednisolone is likely to worsen this diabetic control, which we are told is poor. If only one joint is affected, the best option in this case would be an intraarticular steroid, although that option is not given to you.

stem: A 24-year-old man has been complaining of lower back pain for over 12 months. Which one of the following features is most specific for ankylosing spondylitis?
options: Back stiffness worsening as the day wears on
Bilateral erosion of sacroiliac joints on X-ray
Limited lumbar spine motion on physical examination
Presence of human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) antigen on tissue typing
Tenderness bilaterally in the lower lumbar area
explanation:
Bilateral erosion of sacroiliac joints on X-ray
Bilateral sacroiliac erosion on X-ray is the feature most suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). Limited lumbar spine motion or tenderness can occur with other painful back conditions such as disc disease or muscle strain. The back stiffness in ankylosing spondylitis is worse in the morning and improves as the day wears on. HLA-B27 is also found in normal individuals.

Back stiffness worsening as the day wears on
Back stiffness worsening as the day wears on is incorrect. Back stiffness is worse in the morning with ankylosing spondylitis (‘morning stiffness’).

Limited lumbar spine motion on physical examination
Limited lumbar spine motion on physical examination is incorrect. Although movements are limited in AS, this on its own is non-specific.

Presence of human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) antigen on tissue typing
Presence of HLA-B27 antigen on tissue typing is incorrect. HLA-B27 positivity, although it may be helpful in diagnosis, it is not pathognomonic. 10% of asymptomatic, healthy people may be B27 positive, but never develop AS. HLAB27 also varies with ethnicity.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains of a gritty sensation in his eyes, red spots on both calves and pain in his wrists and hands. Titres of anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) are high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sjögren’s syndrome
This patient has Sjögren’s syndrome, characterized by sicca symptoms, cutaneous vasculitis and polyarthralgia and high titres of anti-Ro and La antibodies. Sjögren’s syndrome is associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca and/or xerostomia. Dysphagia, neuropathy, renal involvement, otitis media and hepatosplenomegaly are common. Anti-Ro (SS-A) and anti-La (SS-B) titres are high and are characteristic for Sjögren’s syndrome.

Avitaminosis A
Avitaminosis A is incorrect. Although xerophthalmia and keratomalacia (dry eyes, dry mouth) are manifestations of vitamin A deficiency. Other features such as arthritis and purpuric spots are not seen. The peak incidence is 2–5 years of age.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. This patient has classical signs of Sjögren’s and no feature of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) to support a primary diagnosis of SLE with secondary Sjögren’s. SLE is a non-organ-specific autoimmune disease that is nine times more common in women. The age of onset is usually 15–25 years. Conjunctivitis can occur in SLE.

stem: A 44-year-old, diabetic, obese man presents with a painful swollen ankle that has become worse over the past 2 weeks. He gives a history of recent alcohol consumption. Small rhomboid-shaped crystals are seen in the joint aspirate, along with numerous neutrophils. An X-ray shows evidence of chondrocalcinosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pseudogout
Pseudogout is true because small, rhomboid-shaped, weakly positive birefringent crystals are seen in calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy (pseudogout). Calcification of joint cartilages (chondrocalcinosis) is a feature of this disease. The joint aspirate may show numerous neutrophils.

Charcot's joint
Charcot's joint is incorrect. Charcot’s deformity arises in weight-bearing joints (mainly the ankles) and may be due to neurovascular changes rather than simple neurotrauma. It is most commonly associated with chronic sensory neuropathies, such as occur in diabetes mellitus, tertiary syphilis and syringomyelia.

Gouty arthritis
Gouty arthritis is incorrect. In gout, the crystals are needle shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis is not associated with swollen joints.

stem: Which of the following is a potentially fatal complication of microscopic polyangiitis, but not of classic PAN?
explanation:
Pulmonary haemorrhage
Pulmonary haemorrhage is not a common cause of death in classic polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), unlike in microscopic polyangiitis. Classic PAN, a necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, is felt to be less common than microscopic polyangiitis (microscopic polyarteritis), which affects capillaries, venules and arterioles. Classic PAN does not involve pulmonary arterioles and death is usually the result of kidney disease, gastrointestinal complications (infarct/perforation) and cardiovascular causes. In contrast, death in patients with microscopic polyangiitis is usually the result of kidney disease or pulmonary haemorrhage. Stroke and congestive heart failure due to intractable hypertension lead to additional late mortality and morbidity.

Bowel perforation
Bowel perforation is incorrect. It is described as a potentially life-threatening complication in PAN.

Cerebrovascular accident
Cerebrovascular accident is incorrect. It is described as a potentially life-threatening complication in PAN.

Myocardial infarction
Myocardial infarction is incorrect. It is described as a potentially life-threatening complication in PAN.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains of a gritty sensation in his eyes and a dry mouth of several months’ duration. He also has vague joint pains in his hands and feet. His wife mentions he is also dyspnoeic on exertion and cannot keep up with her during their walks. What is the cause of his eye and mouth symptoms?
explanation:
Sjögren’s syndrome
Sjögren’s syndrome is characterised by dry eyes and mouth, and may be associated with arthralgia, Raynaud’s phenomenon, dysphagia and abnormal oesophageal motility, pulmonary diffusion defects and fibrosis. Respiratory symptoms may come from a combination xerotrachea, which manifests as a dry cough, interstitial lung disease or recurrent pneumonitis. Secondary Sjögren’s may also occur in conjunction with other causes of fibrotic lung disease. This patient has no signs of any other disorder and probably has primary Sjögren’s syndrome. Anti-Ro antibodies are found in over 70% of the patients with primary Sjögren’s syndrome.

Mixed connective tissue disease
Mixed connective tissue disease is incorrect. This patient has no other features of mixed connective tissue disease, other than the symptoms described of Sjögren’s. Mixed connective tissue disease is associated with anti-RNP antibodies.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. This man has no features of polyarteritis nodosa, which is a rare multisystem vasculitis.

stem: A 73-year-old man complains of right leg pain of 2 years’ duration. There is no history of falls or injury. In the past he has been admitted to hospital for cardiac failure and takes inhaled bronchodilators and steroids for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Examination shows a healthy elderly man with mild tenderness of his right leg only. Routine blood tests show normal serum calcium and phosphate levels with a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bony metastasis from an occult malignancy
explanation:
Paget’s disease
This man has an isolated elevated ALP and bone pain suggesting Paget’s. His heart failure may be a high- output form related to Paget’s. Paget’s Disease Paget’s disease of the bone is a disorder of bone remodelling. There is uncontrolled bone turnover with excessive resorption, followed by disordered osteoblastic activity, which leads to abundant new bone formation It is common in Europe, where it affects 10% of adults by the age of 90 years. Clinical features The femur, pelvis, tibia, skull and lumbosacral spine are commonly involved It presents with bony pain, deafness due to nerve compression/loss of cochlear BMD, high-output cardiac failure and deformities The serum alkaline phosphatase level is markedly raised, with normal calcium and phosphate levels Treatment is indicated for the bone pain and can range from simple analgesics to biphosphonates and calcitonin

stem: A 57-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis, who is on rituximab and methotrexate, comes to her follow-up rheumatology clinic. She tells you that she is not feeling well within herself and for the last two months – with nausea and lethargy. She denies cough, sputum, dysuria, change in bowel habit, rashes or any wounds. On examination she looks fatigued, her blood pressure is 125/69 mmHg, pulse is 80 bpm. Examination is otherwise unremarkable – cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal systems all normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 197 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 12 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 45 mm/h 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 900 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 165 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 38 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Anti-smooth muscle antibodies Negative Anti-mitochondrial antibodies Negative Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody Negative Which one of the following is the most likely?
explanation:
Reactivation of hepatitis B
There is a risk of reactivation of hepatitis B with rituximab, and patients should be screened for previous exposure to hepatitis B prior to starting rituximab; for example, those with lone anti-hep B core antibodies should be treated with chemoprophylaxis (eg lamivudine) prior to rituximab.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis is incorrect. The association above and her anti-mitochondrial autoantibody is negative.

Auto-immune hepatitis
Auto-immune hepatitis is incorrect. Her anti-smooth muscle autoantibody is negative.

Reactivation of hepatitis C
Reactivation of hepatitis C is incorrect. Less likely given the association above.

Reactivation of TB
Reactivation of TB is incorrect. Less likely given the association above.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with bowed legs, low back pain and increasing deafness over the past 6 months. His father was similarly affected at 60 years of age and died of bone cancer. Given the likely clinical diagnosis, what would be the most characteristic finding in a blood test?
explanation:
Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase
This patient has Paget’s disease, typified by the deformity (bowed legs), deafness (due to neural foraminal narrowing causing compression of the eighth cranial nerve) and positive family history (of osteosarcoma). In Paget’s the serum alkaline phosphatase is increased (it may exceed 1000 U/l) and this reflects increased bone turnover.

Decreased 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol
Decreased 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol is incorrect. 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol levels are usually normal in this condition.

Decreased serum calcium levels
Decreased serum calcium levels is incorrect. Serum calcium levels are usually normal in this condition.

Elevated ESR
Elevated ESR is incorrect. ESR levels are usually normal in this condition.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen left knee, swollen ankles and right hallux, acutely inflamed eyes and dysuria. He was previously well, except for an episode of gastroenteritis 2 weeks previously. Clinical examination also reveals a left Achilles tendonitis and right plantar fasciitis. MRI demonstrates left sacroiliitis, with evidence of enthesopathy, erosions and fluffy periostitis. He is HLA-B27-positive and rheumatoid factor negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This clinical scenario satisfies the diagnostic criteria for reactive arthritis – arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis following an episode of infective dysentery. The radiographic findings are characteristic for a reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis occurs predominantly in men, most frequently in the third decade. There is a strong association with HLA B27 (63–96% of patients depending on case series) and ths may indicate a more chronic prognosis. Treatment in the acute stage is with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Reactive arthritis can also be associated with genitourinary infections, such as Chlamydia trachomatis and in antibiotics should be prescribed for the genitourinary (GU) infection, as well as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is incorrect. There is a clear infective precipitant

Sero-negative rheumatoid arthritis
Sero-negative rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. There is clear infective precipitant and rheumatoid arthritis is likely to be a small joint polyarthritis affecting the hands, whereas reactive arthritis is usually an oligoarthritis involving the knee.

stem: A 33-year-old Japanese man complains of recurrent oral and genital ulcers as well as painful nodules on his shins. In the past he has suffered from recurrent episodes of itchy and red eyes and thrombophlebitis in his legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behçet’s syndrome
This patient has Behçet’s syndrome. Behçet’s syndrome is more severe in males and is commonly seen in natives of Japan and East Mediterranean countries. It is characterised by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, DVTs and thrombophlebitis with rashes including erythema nodosum.

Familial Mediterranean fever
Familial Mediterranean fever is incorrect. FMF is an inherited periodic fever syndrome characterised by recurrent fevers and serositis (pleuritic chest and abdominal pain).

Palindromic rheumatism
Palindromic rheumatism is incorrect. Palindromic rheumatism (a condition where patients have recurrent episodes of joint pain followed by asymptomatic intervals) is not associated with orogenital ulcers, erythema nodosum or thrombophlebitis.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. There is no antecedent infective trigger.

stem: You are involved in reviewing a project in epigenetics where you are examining the effects of lifestyle on the prevalence of various autoimmune diseases versus the patient’s underlying human leukocyte antigen (HLA) subtype. Which of the following HLA types is most likely to be associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
explanation:
B-27
B-27 is associated with increased risk of sero-negative arthritides, including ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease. Whilst the vast majority of patients with these disorders are B-27 positive, B-27 positivity is not used as a screening test because a significant proportion of individuals who are B-27 positive are in fact disease free.

B-8
B-8 is incorrect. B-8 is associated with primary biliary cholangitis.

B-51
B-51 is incorrect. B-51 is associated with Behcet’s disease.

DR-3
DR-3 is incorrect. DR-3 is strongly associated with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.

stem: A 22-year-old coal miner presents at the Emergency Department with exertional dyspnoea and wheezing, right foot drop, weakness in his left hand, a purpuric rash over his abdomen and swollen ankles. Blood tests show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 135–175 g/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 92 fl 76–98 fl White cell count (WCC) 21.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Neutrophils 8.0 × 10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 10.2 × 10 9/l 0-0.4 × 10 9/l Lymphocytes 2.5 × 10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 10 9/l Urea 18.9 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 270 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA Negative Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA) Positive What is the most probable diagnosis?
options: Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitiis, EGPA)
explanation:
Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitiis, EGPA)
This patient has Churg–Strauss syndrome, which requires 4 of the following 6 criteria to be fulfilled.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with red scaly plaques on her elbows, knees, lower back and scalp. She also has pitting and yellow–brown discoloration of her nails and painful and swollen finger and toe joints. Blood tests show CRP 6 mg/L (normal range <5) and ESR 15mm/hr. Given the likely clinical diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Methotrexate
This patient has psoriatic arthritis with skin psoriasis, nail and joint involvement. Methotrexate is indicated to control the skin lesions and the arthritis. N.B. In psoriatic arthritis patients may have normal, slightly high or very high inflammatory markers and therefore CRP and ESR are not reliable measures of disease activity.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids is incorrect. Short-term corticosteroids, are used as bridging therapy with DMARD co- prescription to bridge the gap until DMARDs have had a chance to exert benefit, are not appropriate alone. Furthermore they may exacerbate skin lesions.

Sulfasalazine
Sulfasalazine is incorrect. Sulphasalazine is only effective for joint disease, but not skin lesions.

stem: A 61-year-old man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis over the past 8 years comes to the clinic for review. He complains of recurrent episodes of red eyes, with mild discomfort and grittiness, watering and mild photophobia. The vision is normal during these episodes. The episodes occur once every few months and last for 7–10 days each time. On this attendance at the clinic he tells you he is coming to the end of an episode. There is diffuse reddening of both eyes with engorged episcleral vessels. Visual acuity is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Episcleritis
Episcleritis carries a more benign pattern of symptoms compared with scleritis. Whilst it is less likely to be associated with systemic disease than scleritis, it is seen in patients with a history of rheumatoid arthritis. Features of episcleritis are listed below: Acute onset Mild pain/discomfort, grittiness Localised or diffuse red eye Unilateral or bilateral No associated ocular symptoms other than watering and occasional mild photophobia; vision normal

Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis is incorrect. Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the inside of eyelids and covering the glove to the limbus. The cause can be infectious due to viral or bacterial pathogens, allergic or non-allergic reactions. Conjunctivitis normally presents with redness and discharge in one eyewith the patient typically complaining of the eye being stuck shut in the morning. Viral infections are associated with a

stem: A 42-year-old obese woman with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis has been on methotrexate 25mg weekly and prednisolone 2.5mg daily for a number of years. She presents with severe hip pain of relatively sudden onset with no obvious precipitant and is now unable to walk. What is the most probable diagnosis?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Pathological fracture of the femoral neck
explanation:
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Long-term treatment with corticosteroids is a risk factor for avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

Flare of rheumatoid arthritis
Flare of rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. A rheumatoid flare is unlikely just at the hip (although possible) and she seems to have been well controlled on maximal dose methotrexate. Ideally, the prednisolone should have been stopped a number of years ago, although she may be adrenally dependent, making discontinuation difficult.

Meralgia paraesthetica
Meralgia paraesthetica is incorrect. Meralgia parasthetica (compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh) causes numbness and burning dysaesthesia over the anterolateral thigh. It may be precipitated by a sudden increase in weight. Inability to walk is not a feature of this condition, however.

Pathological fracture of the femoral neck
Pathological fracture of the femoral neck is incorrect. Atraumatic osteoporotic fractures usually cause vertebral or rib fractures. Prednisolone is a risk factor for osteoporosis, as is rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe scaly, erythematous lesions all over her body. She has also developed swelling and severe pain in her distal interphalangeal joints. Given the diagnosis of psoriasis, what treatment is likely to be most suitable for her?
options: Long-wave ultraviolet radiation (psoralen ultraviolet A; PUVA)
explanation:
Methotrexate
This lady has psoriatic arthritis with skin psoriasis and arthritis which warrants the use of methotrexate, which should exert benefit on both the skin and joints.

Coal tar
Coal tar is incorrect. Coal tar may reduce the skin lesions but will have no effect on psoriatic arthritis.

Diclofenac
Diclofenac is incorrect. Diclofenac might reduce some inflammation in her joints, it is not disease modifying and will not affect her skin significantly.

Long-wave ultraviolet radiation (psoralen ultraviolet A; PUVA)
Long-wave ultraviolet radiation (psoralen ultraviolet A;PUVA) is incorrect. PUVA may reduce the skin lesions but will have no effect on psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with lower back pain. He reports the pain is accompanied by stiffness, is worse in the morning, and improves with exercise. He denies any radiation of pain or bowel and bladder incontinence. On physical examination, there is decreased anterior flexion of the lumbar spine. Laboratory testing is positive for human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27. His spinal X-ray showed ‘bamboo spine’ deformity. He received conservative treatment in form of physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), but his symptoms continued to deteriorate. Which of the following agents are most effective for his condition?
explanation:
Adalimumab
This patient has inflammatory arthropathy with lower back pain and stiffness that improves on exercise. His X- ray showed classical bamboo spine deformity of ankylosing spondylitis. HLA-B27 is positive in more than 90% of these patients. Adalimumab is a biologic agent indicated for ankylosing spondylitis for patients who do not respond to NSAIDs and conservative treatment.

Erlotinib
Erlotinib is an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). It is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for reatment of non-small cell lung cancer.

Rituximab
Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 antigen; it depletes B cells and is used as a therapeutic biologic agent in rheumatoid arthritis, as well as other autoimmune disorders and lymphoproliferative disorders.

stem: A 40-year-old woman who is a keen gardener presents to her GP complaining of pain in her right elbow. She is right-handed and has spent the past 2 weeks planting bulbs in the garden. Her blood tests are normal. Which one of the following features would be most suggestive of a diagnosis of tennis elbow?
options: Pain on attempting the chair raise test
Pain on pressure over the medial epicondyle
Pain on wrist flexion against resistance
explanation:
Pain on attempting the chair raise test
The answer is Pain on attempting the chair raise test (Option A). This lady has tennis elbow. Tennis elbow is also known as lateral epicondylitis. Typical symptoms include pain just distal (5–10 mm) to the lateral epicondyle. Wrist extension or supination (but not flexion or pronation) against resistance with the elbow extended should provoke the patient's symptoms. The chair-raise test may also be useful in determining the diagnosis. The patient stands behind their chair and attempts to raise it by putting their hands on the top of the chair back and lifting. In patients with lateral epicondylitis, pain results over the lateral elbow. Management involves physiotherapy, wearing a band around the elbow, steroid injection or lateral release surgery.

Pain on elbow flexion
Pain on elbow flexion (Option B) is incorrect. Wrist extension or supination (but not flexion or pronation) against resistance with the elbow extended should provoke the patient's symptoms.

Pain on wrist pronation
Pain on wrist pronation (Option E) is incorrect. Wrist extension or supination (but not flexion or pronation) against resistance with the elbow extended should provoke the patient's symptoms.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with pain and stiffness of her shoulders and neck that is worse in the mornings and lasts for more than an hour. On examination active and passive movements are normal. Blood tests show a mild normocytic normochromic anaemia. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 77 mm in 1 st hour and CRP is 46mg/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
This lady has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) with proximal muscle pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and raised inflammatory markers. PMR is more common in elderly (White) females.

Frozen shoulder
Frozen shoulder is incorrect. In frozen shoulder, there is marked reduction of passive and active movement. Abduction to even 90° is impossible.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. Hypocalcaemia presents with tetany, depression, carpopedal spasm and neuromuscular excitability.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness resulting from muscle inflammation is seen in polymyositis. Pain and tenderness are uncommon features.

stem: A 27-year-old woman known to suffer from epilepsy has been admitted with a history of dizzy spells and a swollen left calf. Her blood pressure recordings confirm a postural drop in her systolic reading of over 20 mmHg. Her biochemistry shows a sodium concentration of 126 mmol/l and a potassium concentration of 6.1 mmol/l. Her blood count is normal apart from a low platelet count. She has no past history of any surgical procedure but has a history of three spontaneous miscarriages. The nurse has noticed that at times she makes jerky explosive movements of her limbs. What is the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Antiphospholipid syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome is characterised by the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies, which cause thrombosis through an effect on platelet membranes, endothelial cells and on prothrombin, protein C and protein S. It is characterised by recurrent thromboses (DVT, PE, strokes), pregnancy related complications (premature labour, miscarriage), neurological involvement (epilepsy, chorea, migraine) and rash (livedo reticularis), thrombocytopenia and prolonged clotting times. The low sodium and elevated potassium and postural drop in BP seen here raises the possibility of adrenal involvement leading to Addison’s.

Dehydration
Dehydration is incorrect. Her postural drop is due to cortisol insufficiency (probably becauseChat of an adrenal with infarct).

Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) secretion
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) secretion is incorrect. Her low sodium and high potassium is due to cortisol insufficiency (probably because of an adrenal infarct).

stem: A 65-year-old woman being treated for epilepsy presents with bone pain and muscle weakness. Blood tests show increased serum alkaline phosphatase, plasma calcium at the lower limit of the normal range, and low serum phosphate levels. An X-ray of the femur reveals linear areas of low density surrounded by sclerotic borders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteomalacia
This lady has osteomalacia. Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin and phenobarbital can induce liver enzymes that lead to an increased breakdown of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol, and this causes osteomalacia. The X-ray shows evidence of the Looser’s zones (pseudofractures), which are typical of osteomalacia.

Osteonecrosis
Osteonecrosis is incorrect. The bone profile is usually normal in osteonecrosis (also known as avascular necrosis). This is death of subchondral bone due to a compromised arterial blood supply. Radiographic features of avascular necrosis at the hip include flattening and loss of the femoral head.

Paget’s disease
Paget’s disease is incorrect. In Paget’s disease the serum alkaline phosphatase level will be raised but serum calcium and phosphate levels will be normal. The X-ray will also show a sclerotic phase of bone expansion, thickening of trabeculae and dedifferentiation (loss of distinction between cortex and trabeculae).

stem: A 59-year-old chronic smoker with long-standing diabetes mellitus is admitted to hospital with a lung infection. He is found to have a grossly swollen and deformed right ankle with tingling and numbness in the area. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Charcot's joint
Charcot’s deformity arises in weight-bearing joints (mainly the ankles) associated with a chronic sensory neuropathy, such as those found in diabetes mellitus, tertiary syphilis and syringomyelia.

Candidiasis
Candidiasis is incorrect. This condition does not cause joint deformity and is unlikely to cause the clinical scenario here.

Mononeuritis multiplex
Mononeuritis multiplex is incorrect. This is a multifocal mononeuropathy that does not cause joint deformity.

Thromboangiitis obliterans
Thromboangiitis obliterans is incorrect. Also known as Beurger’s disease, it is an inflammatory process of medium and small arteries and veins associated with smoking. It does not cause joint deformity, so is unlikely to be the answer here.

stem: You are asked to see a 65-year-old Asian woman who is complaining of generalised body aches. Her daughter also mentions that for the last few months her mother has found it difficult to get up from a chair. She suffers from diet-controlled diabetes mellitus and her blood glucose level is well controlled. Her full blood count is normal. She has low serum phosphate, plasma calcium at the lower end of the normal range and raised alkaline phosphatase levels. Which one of the following would you expect her X-rays to show?
explanation:
Linear areas of low density
This woman has generalised body aches and also has features suggestive of proximal myopathy. The bone biochemistry is in keeping with a diagnosis of osteomalacia. X-rays will typically show defective mineralisation, especially in the pelvis, long bones and ribs. Areas of low density – Looser’s zones (pseudofractures) – are characteristic of the condition.

Areas of sclerosis
Areas of sclerosis is incorrect. Osteosclerosis is usually associated with hypercalcaemia.

Brodie’s abscess
Brodie’s abscess is incorrect. Brodie’s abscess is a sign of subacute osteomyelitis, which the history does not suggest.

Osteolytic areas with bone destruction
Osteolytic areas with bone destruction is incorrect. Osteolysis is usually associated with hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with malaise, fever, backache and joint pains of one week’s duration. On examination, arthritis is present asymmetrically in the lower limbs, involving the knees, one ankle, and some metatarsophalangeal and toe joints. An eye examination reveals conjunctival congestion and there is a vesicular crusting lesion on the left sole of his foot. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 60 mm in 1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 50 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Rheumatoid factor Negative HLA B27 Positive Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This man has a reactive arthritis. Patients with reactive arthritis may have had a prodromal infection 1–4 weeks before its onset, usually with Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter or Chlamydia spp. Constitutional symptoms and asymmetric lower limb arthritis are characteristic. Conjunctivitis is common. Skin lesions include vesicular keratoderma blennorrhagica (usually on the palms and soles) and circinate balanitis on the glans penis. HLA B27 positivity is associate with a more chronic duration. The spondyloarthropathies share common clinical features and HLA B27 positivity association. Rheumatoid factor is usually negative.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presented complaining of pain in her legs. A dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan revealed osteoporosis. Her doctor prescribed 400 IU of vitamin D along with calcium supplements. Which is the most active metabolite of vitamin D involved in calcium homeostasis?
explanation:
1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol
The primary source of vitamin D in humans is photoactivation (in the skin) of 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol. This is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and further converted by the kidney enzyme 1α-hydroxylase to the active metabolite 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. N.B. A less active metabolite (24,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol) is formed if vitamin D supplies are adequate.

24,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol
24,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol is incorrect. 24,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol is a less active metabolite formed if vitamin D supplies are adequate.

25-Hydroxycholecalciferol
25-Hydroxycholecalciferol is incorrect. 25-Hydroxycholecalciferol is converted by the kidney enzyme 1α- hydroxylase to the active metabolite 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol.

Cholecaliferol
Cholecaliferol is incorrect. Cholecaliferol is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a 1-month history of left-sided headache and increased malaise which has not subsided despite regular analgesia. There is no history of trauma. She denies nausea, vomiting and dizziness; however, she does report some double vision in her left eye. Her past medical history includes hypertension and emphysema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s visual changes?
explanation:
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
This patient has a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis, given the history of headache, constitutional upset and visual disturbance. Additional symptoms include scalp tenderness, skin necrosis, jaw pain while talking or chewing, tongue pain and claudication, as well as face and neck pain with nerve damage. Visual manifestations, which include blurred vision, amaurosis fugax, transient and permanent blindness, diplopia and visual hallucinations, are caused by ischaemic changes in the ciliary arteries, causing anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion is the second most common cause of visual disturbance in giant cell arteritis, after anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Although posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy can cause visual loss in giant cell arteritis, it is much less common.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner for review. He has a history of congestive cardiac failure and ischaemic heart disease. He reports experiencing severe joint pain in his feet two weeks previously where his skin became hot, swollen and red. He is taking bumetanide 2 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg od. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 204 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 6.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Urate 595 mmol/l 0.1–0.4 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate step with respect to reducing the risk of further attacks of the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Allopurinol
This patient has signs and symptoms of gout, ie swelling and pain in joints and hot and red skin. Allopurinol ChatThe 100mg OD, to be taken after a meal, should be prescribed to reduce the risk of further attacks. withpatient should also be given analgesia such as Colchicine for the acute gout.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops pain in her left knee. What is the earliest radiological evidence of rheumatoid arthritis of the knee?
explanation:
Signs of an effusion
Massive synovitis and knee effusions are often the first evidence of rheumatoid arthritis of the knees. Erosion of cartilage and bone, loss of joint space, osteophyte formation and varus/valgus deformity are incorrect. These are considered later features. Erosion of cartilage and bone and loss of joint space may lead to a valgus or varus deformity. Osteophyte formation is a late occurrence and is caused by secondary osteoarthritis, which is secondary to the inflammatory arthritis.

Erosion of cartilage and bone
Erosion of cartilage and bone is incorrect. The erosion of cartilage and bone is considered a later feature, and may lead to a valgus or varus deformity.

Loss of joint space
Loss of joint space is incorrect. A loss of joint space is considered a later feature, and may lead to a valgus or varus deformity.

Osteophyte formation
Osteophyte formation is incorrect. Osteophyte formation is a late occurrence and is caused by secondary osteoarthritis, which is secondary to the inflammatory arthritis.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) on the basis of polyarthralgia, mouth ulcers and antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-Ro antibody positivity. The urea and electrolytes are normal, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 90 mm in 1 st hour and urinalysis is normal. How would you manage her?
options: Six monthly pulses of cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg)
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/day
Simple arthralgia and fatigue appear to respond well to hydroxychloroquine.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate is used in SLE if there is arthritis (synovitis), but it is not used for arthralgia (joint pains without swelling).

Prednisolone 10 mg/day
Prednisolone 10 mg/day is incorrect. because in the absence of serious internal organ involvement (renal, neurological, eye or lung) there is no indication for prednisolone.

Six monthly pulses of cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg)
Six monthly pulses of cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg) is incorrect. In the absence of serious internal organ involvement (renal, neurological, eye or lung) there is no indication for cyclophosphamide.

stem: A 22-year-old man complains of an acute onset of pain in his right elbow and both Achilles tendons. He also gives a history of dysuria, conjunctivitis and fever. He returned from holiday in the Far East 3 weeks ago, where he had unprotected sex. He has developed macules and pustules on his hands and feet. Investigations: ESR 42 mm/h and CRP 30 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This patient has a reactive arthritis with a triad of non-specific urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis. It may follow bacterial dysentery or exposure to sexually transmitted infection. In addition, patients may have Achilles tendonitis or plantar fasciitis. Other features are circinate balanitis and keratoderma blennorrhagica (macules, vesicles or pustules on the hands and feet). The CRP and ESR can be non-specifically elevated in all conditions.

Gonococcal arthritis
Gonococcal arthritis is incorrect. Gonococcal arthritis is usually associated with a migratory (not a fixed) arthritis and/or a tenosynovitis.

Syphilitic arthritis
Syphilitic arthritis is incorrect. The timing is too short for a syphilitic arthritis. A rash usually develops in the second stage of syphilis. The earliest feature is the primary chancre (painless ulcer).

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine insurance medical. He is concerned about osteoporosis as he has read about it online, and his mother suffered both a right hip and vertebral fractures. He demands a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan, which shows a T-score of –2.1 at the left hip and –2.6 at the lumbar spine. Which one of the following is true?
options: He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and osteoporosis at the left hip
He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and the left hip
He has osteoporosis at the lumbar spine and at the left hip
He has osteoporosis at the lumbar spine and osteopaenia at the left hip
His bone mineral density is normal
explanation:
He has osteoporosis at the lumbar spine and osteopaenia at the left hip
His T-score at the hip of −2.1 is osteopenic (between −1 and −2.5) and his T-score at the lumbar spine of −2.6 is in the osteoporotic range (<−2.5). For the purposes of diagnosing osteoporosis, a T-score between +1 and −1 (ie within one standard deviation of the young adult reference mean) is defined as normal. Osteopenia is defined as a T-score between −1 and −2.5, with osteoporosis defined as a T-score below −2.5. Osteoporosis itself is rarer in men than in women, affecting only 1 in 12 men above the age of 50 years.

He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and osteoporosis at the left hip
He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and osteoporosis at the left hip is incorrect. The T-score of 2.1 at the hip shows osteopenia.

He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and the left hip
He has osteopenia at the lumbar spine and the left hip is incorrect. To have osteopenia at both sites the T-score should be between -1 and -2.5.

stem: A 45-year-old woman complains of feeling tired, she also notices she has dysphagia, a dry mouth, a gritty sensation in her eyes and increased photosensitivity. Which would be the most definitive test for the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
Labial gland biopsy
This lady has Sjögren’s syndrome, and biopsy and histology of the labial glands from behind the lower lip provides the most definitive diagnostic test of Sjögren’s syndrome. The area is anaesthetised with lidocaine containing adrenaline, and an incision 1.5 cm long allows access to five to ten glands (2–4 mm in diameter) that are removed by simple blunt dissection. A diagnosis of Sjögren’s syndrome depends on finding foci of periductular infiltrates of at least 50 lymphocytes and/or plasma cells at a density of more than one focus per 4 mm 2.

Antinuclear antibodies
Antinuclear antibodies is incorrect. Although ANA may be positive in Sjögren’s syndrome, it is non-specific and non-diagnostic.

Oesophagogastroscopy
Oesophagogastroscopy is incorrect. In Sjögren’s OGD appearances are likely to be normal.

Serum iron level
Serum iron level is incorrect. Iron levels are unaffected in Sjögren’s.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of Raynaud’s phenomenon and progressive skin tightness - thickness of the fingers and hands, front of the chest and on her face. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Diffuse cutaneous scleroderma
The classification between limited and diffuse forms, depends on the areas of skin distribution. Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is limited to below the elbows and below the knees, but the face can be involved in both types. The key to this question is the skin thickness on the front of her chest (trunk) which indicates diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (therefore limited cutaneous scleroderma is incorrect.). Diffuse scleroderma starts with swelling and stiffness of the fingers and is followed by the development of extensive sclerosis. Heartburn, reflux or dysphagia are common. Raynaud’s phenomenon usually starts just before or at the onset of the disease, in contrast to limited cutaneous scleroderma, in which Raynaud’s phenomenon usually precedes the disease by many years. Renal involvement can be acute or chronic and can lead to hypertension. Lung disease, both fibrosis and pulmonary hypertension, contribute significantly to mortality.

Limited cutaneous scleroderma
Limited cutaneous scleroderma is incorrect. The key to this question is the skin thickness onChat the front with AIofTutor her chest (trunk) which indicates diffuse (not limited) cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. Progressive skin tightness and dysphagia are not seen in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLE is a non-organ-specific autoimmune disease characterised by antinuclear antibodies and vasculitis. It usually presents earlier, in the younger woman.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of persistent malaise, anorexia, shoulder and hip pain and a weight loss of 7 kg. On examination there is mild painful limitation of the hip and shoulder movements, but no weakness and only minor muscle pain on palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) occurs characteristically in elderly women and presents as aching and morning stiffness in the proximal muscles. Frank pain however is only seen in 1/3rd of patients. Minor tenderness is seen in the muscles rather than in the joints, PMR is on the spectrum of giant-cell arteritis. The diagnosis is made on the basis of the history and symptoms. The CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are almost always high.

Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is incorrect. Fibromyalgia classically presents with diffuse pain and multiple tender spots all over the body that may be unrelated to the affected muscles. Also this lady has significant constitutional upset – malaise, anorexia and weight loss, which does not occur in fibromyalgia.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis presents classically as bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. In a third of cases it presents with cough, fever, arthralgia, malaise or erythema nodosum. These are painful erythematous nodular lesions on the anterior aspect of the shins

stem: You are explaining the common manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus to a 32-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with the disease. Which one of the following tissues are most commonly affected in this condition?
explanation:
Joints
Joint involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the most common clinical feature (> 80%). Small joints are usually involved in a symmetrical fashion. Patients usually have arthralgia, but may have arthritis.

Heart and blood vessels
Heart and blood vessels is incorrect. The heart and vascular system are affected in 25% of cases.

Kidneys
Kidneys is incorrect. Clinical renal involvement occurs in approximately 30% of cases.

Lungs
Lungs is incorrect. Up to 60% of patients have lung involvement.

Skin
Skin is incorrect. The skin is affected in 75% of cases and erythema in a butterfly distribution on the cheeks and across the bridge of the nose is characteristic.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with early morning stiffness and pain in both shoulders and hips. On examination, active movements in these joints are restricted due to pain, but passive movements are preserved. She has no other symptoms. Blood tests are normal, except for an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 115 mm in 1st hour and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 39 mg/l. Her bone densitometry T-score value is –1.5. What are her symptoms due to?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
This lady has polymyalgia rheumatica, which is associated with proximal muscle pain (shoulders and hips) and stiffness, with raised inflammatory markers. It is not a true vasculitis, but is closely associated with giant-cell arteritis. Women are more commonly affected than men (the ratio of women to men affected is 2:1). The muscle stiffness affects the proximal muscles of the neck, upper arms and, less commonly, the buttocks and thighs. There is marked early morning stiffness. The C-reactive protein (CRP) may be elevated prior to the ESR.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis usually affects weight bearing joints and is not associated with raised inflammatory markers.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis is associated with muscle weakness polymyositis is common at a younger age (40–60 years) and is typically gradual. Systemic features of fever, weight loss and fatigue are common. There may be respiratory or pharyngeal muscle involvement leading to ventilatory failure or aspiration. The creatine kinase is usually elevated in this condition.

stem: A 58-year-old woman complains of severe unilateral temporal headaches and jaw pain when eating. A provisional diagnosis of giant-cell arteritis is made. Which one of the following is a characteristic clinical feature of this condition?
options: It does not occur in the absence of polymyalgia rheumatica
Negative temporal artery biopsy excludes the disorder
NSAID treatment is an effective first line of management
Treatment can be monitored by measuring ESR levels
explanation:
Treatment can be monitored by measuring ESR levels
Treatment of giant cell arteritis (GCA) can be monitored by measuring ESR and CRP levels.

All peripheral arteries are involved
All peripheral arteries are involved is incorrect. Giant-cell arteritis involves the cranial arteries. The superficial temporal artery is involved in most patients, providing a convenient biopsy site, but this is only the ‘tip of the iceberg’. The topographic distribution of GCA, which reflects its predilection for the internal elastic lamina, includes the aortic arch and its branches. GCA does not cause a widespread intracranial cerebral vasculitis, because intracranial arteries lack an internal elastic lamina. GCA does involve cervicocephalic arteries, including the carotid and vertebral arteries.

It does not occur in the absence of polymyalgia rheumatica
It does not occur in the absence of polymyalgia rheumatica is incorrect. An association with polymyalgia rheumatica is well known, with PMR being present in about 60% of cases of GCA.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic. She has been suffering from Raynaud’s phenomenon and reflux oesophagitis for the past 18 months and has now begun to develop subcutaneous calcinosis affecting the fingers of both hands. She has a past history of mild asthma, for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler, but is otherwise well. On examination her blood pressure (BP) is 152/82 mmHg, with pulse is 78 bpm and regular. You notice multiple telangiectasiae on examination of the face and hands. She has peripheral calcinosis affecting her fingers. Lung function is normal. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be found?
explanation:
Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with the development of CREST (the limited scleroderma picture seen here) and are present in up to 96% of individuals with CREST. Limited systemic sclerosis, another term for CREST, is characterised by Calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia. Treatment is with sildenafil and bosentan, and associated hypertension should be excluded.

Anti-Scl70
Anti-Scl70 is incorrect. Anti-Scl70 is strongly associated with the development of pulmonary fibrosis and renal disease in scleroderma. Anti-Scl70 is specifically associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis.Chat Diffuse with systemic sclerosis is a combination of skin fibrosis and organ involvement with fibrosis of the pulmonary, cardiac, GI and

c-ANCA
c-ANCA is incorrect. C-ANCA is associated with the development of granulomatosis with polyangiitis. It is a type of small vessel vasculitis commonly associated with glomerulonephritis, upper airway disease and pulmonary nodules.

stem: A 49-year-old woman is referred to clinic by her General Practitioner with fatigue, worsened by exercise and unrefreshing sleep. Chronic fatigue syndrome is suspected. Which one of the following features would suggest an alternative diagnosis?
explanation:
Significant weight loss
Chronic fatigue syndrome is characterised by fatigue – which is particularly marked after exertion – and can be associated with a variety of other symptoms, including disturbed sleep which is not refreshing and cognitive problems. Diagnosis depends on the duration of symptoms (adults require the presence of symptoms for at least 6 months) and that all other possible diagnoses are excluded. Significant weight loss would not be expected in chronic fatigue syndrome and other causes of this patient’s symptoms should be carefully investigated before a diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome is made.

Memory impairment
Memory impairment and other cognitive impairment such as poor concentration, word finding difficulties, slowed mental processing speed, poor learning abilities, impaired processing of new information, decreased attention span and poor multitasking ability can be seen in chronic fatigue syndrome. Whilst they can be features of many other conditions, they can be commonly seen in chronic fatigue syndrome.

Recurrent headaches
Recurrent headaches, which could be chronic with varied fluctuations, can be a part of chronic fatigue syndrome. Headaches without other red flag features which could suggest another diagnosis (eg focal neurologic deficit (including decreased consciousness), waking from sleep, autonomic features Chatand withsystemic symptoms including fever), are consistent with this diagnosis.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has psoriatic arthritis. Which of the following hand presentations is the most common for psoriatic arthritis?
explanation:
Nail dystrophy
Nail lesions occur in 80 to 90 percent of patients with PsA, compared with 46 percent of those with psoriasis uncomplicated by arthritis. Nail changes include: Pits, which are sharply defined depressions in the plate caused by shedding of nail plate cells. They look as if someone has taken a pin and pricked the nail several times. Pits usually occur in large numbers and involve several nails. Onycholysis, separation of the nail from its bed, which may involve the whole or only part of the nail. This change occasionally has to be differentiated from a fungal infection by sending nail scrapings for fungal cultures. Other lesions, which include leukonychia, red spots in the lunula, and nail plate crumbling.

Arthritis mutilans
Arthritis mutilans is incorrect. Arthritis mutilans affects about 5% of patients with this disease.

Cutaneous lesions
Cutaneous lesions is incorrect. Cutaneous lesions are variable or may even develop after the arthritis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is being treated for a pathological fracture of her right femur. An X-ray of the femur shows patchy sclerosis, thickening of the trabeculae and dedifferentiation. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for her?
explanation:
Pamidronate
This woman has Paget’s disease. Radiographic features in the mixed lytic and sclerotic phase of Paget's disease include bone expansion, cortical thickening and trabecular bone thickening. Bisphosphonates are the mainstay of treatment. These analogues of normal bone pyrophosphate adhere to hydroxyapatite and inhibit osteoclasts from binding. New bone formed after treatment is lamellar and not woven. This reflects a normalisation of bone turnover rather than a direct effect on osteoclasts. Pamidronate is a bisphosphonate.

Calcitonin
Calcitonin is incorrect. Calcitonin might be useful if she had postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Calcium supplements
Calcium supplements is incorrect. Calcium supplements might be useful if she had postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Raloxifene
Raloxifene is incorrect. Raloxifene might be useful if she had postmenopausal osteoporosis.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with pain over her left hip, which occurred suddenly with no history of trauma. Past history of note includes severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), for which she is managed with multiple medications, including combination steroid and long-acting β-agonist inhaler and chronically prescribed oral corticosteroids. On examination she looks cushingoid in appearance, there is pain over the hip and clicking on movement. Flexion, abduction and internal rotation are limited and she walks with a marked limp. An X-ray has excluded a fracture. Blood tests including inflammatory markers are normal. Which one of the following is the most sensitive examination to support early diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI
This patient is cushingoid and has sudden onset pain over her left hip. Without a history of trauma this raises the possibility of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the hip. MRI is the investigation of choice,with sensitivity that exceeds 90%.

Ultrasound
Ultrasound is incorrect. Ultrasound scan of the hip would not be sensitive enough to detect early AVN.

Bone scan
Bone scan is incorrect. During the early stages of AVN of the hip, a bone scan is particularly sensitive at detecting the abnormality. Although changes can be seen early on radionuclide scanning, it is MRI that is seen as the investigation of choice.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred by her GP because she has been feeling unwell and has pain, stiffness and tenderness in her joints which have gradually worsened over the last 6 months. She has a detectable rheumatoid factor. What is the most likely structure against which these antibodies are targeted?
explanation:
Fc portion of IgG1
Rheumatoid factor is an autoantibody directed against epitopes on the constant domains of the Fc portion of IgG1. In the case of patients with active rheumatoid arthritis, rheumatoid factor complexes are present in synovial fluids, and IgG-producing B cells, whose rearranged immunoglobulin gene sequences implicate antigen stimulation, are present in inflamed synovium. B cells in rheumatoid joints also synthesise antibodies to some cartilage components such as collagen type II, although these are not disease-specific. Anti-CCP antibodies are also described in the context of rheumatoid arthritis and are associated with more rapid disease progression.

Complement
Complement is incorrect. Complement activation is associated with tissue inflammation, but is not primarily associated with rheumatoid factor.

Tumour necrosis factor-alpha
Tumour necrosis factor-alpha is incorrect. Tumour necrosis factor-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine associated with rheumatoid arthritis, although rheumatoid factor is not directed against it.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with longstanding Raynaud’s phenomenon develops tightness and swelling of her fingers associated with tightness around her mouth and reflux symptoms. Blood tests show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 115–155 g/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 87 fl 76–98 fl Anticentromere antibodies are positive. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Limited systemic sclerosis
This woman has limited systemic sclerosis characterised by Raynaud’s, sclerodactyly, microstoma, impaired gastrointestinal peristalsis and likely pulmonary hypertension, associated with anti-centromere autoantibodies.

Diffuse systemic sclerosis
Diffuse systemic sclerosis is incorrect. Diffuse systemic sclerosis is associated with anti-Scl antibodies. Patients with diffuse systemic sclerosis are more likely to have interstitial lung disease and renal crisis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. SLE is not associated with tight skin, reflux or anti-centromere antibodies. It is associated with anti-dsDNA antibodies.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He says that his right shoulder has become very stiff and painful with severe limitation of movement over the past 2–3 days. He has restriction of all movements of the shoulder due to pain, but particularly external rotation and abduction. X-Ray of the right shoulder appears entirely normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 181 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c 54.1 mmol/mol (7.1%) <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adhesive capsulitis
Adhesive capsulitis, also known as frozen shoulder, can occur spontaneously after a rotator cuff injury or as a result of immobilisation, for instance after a fracture or a stroke. It is more common in patients who have a history of diabetes mellitus. There is restriction of the range of shoulder movements, includingChatactive with AIand Tutor

stem: A 75-year-old woman complains of increasing pain and swelling in both ankles, with stiffness and decreased mobility, worse in the last few months. On examination she also has painful finger joints with nodules at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints. Over the past 2 weeks she has had increasing difficulty in passing urine and dysuria. What is the most likely cause of her joint symptoms?
explanation:
Osteoarthritis
This lady has osteoarthritis of the ankles and hands. The nodules (bony outgrowths) at the proximal interphalangeal joints are called Bouchard’s nodes and those at the distal interphalangeal joints are called Heberden’s nodes. Note the timing of her articular symptoms – which are long standing. The two week history of dysuria and difficulty passing urine are unrelated to the osteoarthritis and could be due to a urinary tract infection, which is common in elderly ladies.

Behçet’s syndrome
Behçet’s syndrome is incorrect. Behçet’s syndrome does not present like this.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis is not associated with bony nodules.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. The bony nodules are associated with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis does not commonly present at this age.

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic woman with a history of osteoarthritis of her knees suddenly develops pain and swelling in her right knee. On examination the knee is red, hot, swollen and very tender. Which investigation would be most helpful in the management of this case?
options: Joint aspiration and culture, start antibiotics when 48 hour culture available
Joint aspiration, gram stain and culture, blood culture and start antibiotics
explanation:
Joint aspiration, gram stain and culture, blood culture and start antibiotics
