If a septic arthritis is suspected (which is likely in a case of monoarthritis), the joint should be aspirated and synovial fluid sent for an urgent gram stain and culture and broad spectrum antibiotics started, until the culture results are back to guide more specific antibiotic choice.

Blood culture and start antibiotics
Blood culture and start antibiotics is incorrect. Starting antibiotics should be started after the septic screen is taken (including synovial fluid and peripheral blood cultures) but should not be delayed until the results of blood culture and joint aspirate culture are back.

Joint fluid microscopy
Joint fluid microscopy is incorrect. Joint fluid microscopy is useful in crystal arthritides, such as acute gouty arthritis. In gout this would show the characteristic long needle-shaped uric acid crystals in the fluid as well as in neutrophils. A joint already damaged due to osteoarthritis is more likely to become septic. The features in this case are more in favour of septic arthritis than acute gouty arthritis.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology clinic with chronic lower back pain which is much worse in the morning. There is no history of bowel symptoms. Occasionally the pain seems to radiate to involve the buttocks and the back of his thighs. On examination, he appears to have some loss of lateral flexion. Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) testing for B27
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the SI joints
explanation:
X-ray of the sacroiliac (SI) joints
X-ray of the sacroiliac (SI) joints is correct. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is suspected, given the early morning lower back pain with loss of lateral flexion in a young man. Patients should have an anterior–posterior (AP) plain radiograph of the pelvis to visualize the SI joints. Plain film radiography is frequently sufficient to identify sacroiliitis, and this is also advocated because of its lower radiation exposure, compared to conventional CT, and as a cost-effective approach that reduces the need for expensive imaging studies. Patients with a contraindication to radiation exposure or normal X-rays with a clinical suspicion of AS instead should undergo MRI.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the SI joints
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the SI joints is incorrect. MRI of the SI joints is usually indicated only in patients without evidence of sacroiliitis on plain radiographs in whom AS is suspected based upon other symptoms and findings characteristic of AS. Of note, positive MRI findings by themselves are not sufficient to make a diagnosis of AS in the absence of other features of AS. Therefore, an MRI scan should only be ordered if there is a reasonable degree of suspicion of AS and a negative plain radiograph.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, photosensitivity and arthralgia. On examination she has oral ulcers and her urine dipstick shows haematuria and proteinuria. Given the suspected diagnosis, which antibody would be particularly specific for the disease?
explanation:
Anti-dsDNA antibody
This lady has suspected lupus and antibodies to double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) are very useful for diagnosis. This test is virtually specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, especially if the immunoglobulins are of the IgG isotype. However, while it has a high specificity it has a variable sensitivity. The anti-dsDNA result is usually quantified and this value can be a measure of the activity of the disease, as well as providing prognostication information as patients with anti-dsDNA antibodies are more likely to have complications such as renal or neurological involvement.

Antimitochondrial antibody
Antimitochondrial antibody is incorrect. Antimitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cholangitis.

Nuclear U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP)
Nuclear U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is incorrect. Anti-U1 RNP antibodies are associated with mixed connective tissue disease.

stem: A 35-year-old patient was referred by her General Practitioner (GP) because she says that for the last six months, she has felt unwell and has suffered gradually worsening pain, stiffness, swelling and tenderness of multiple small joints, including the elbows, wrists, small joints of her fingers and ankles. On examination, these joints are swollen and tender. Her GP has performed some blood tests, and her rheumatoid factor is negative. Which of the following is the most important laboratory examination to confirm a diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (also known as ACPA) are more sensitive and more specific for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis than rheumatoid factor, and in this scenario, this patient has tested negative for rheumatoid factor.

Anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid
Anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid is used in the investigation of systemic lupus erythematosus. While symptoms also include arthritis and arthralgia, extra-articular symptoms, including cutaneous manifestations, are also likely to be present.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Raised inflammatory markers are non-specific and do not help to confirm a diagnosis. While most patients with inflammatory arthritides, such as rheumatoid arthritis, have raised inflammatory markers, these can be normal.

stem: A 44-year-old woman is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic. She has been treated for many years for brittle asthma and takes a number of courses of inhalational corticosteroids each year. Her GP has arranged a DEXA scan which reveals a T score of -1.3. Her calcium is 2.05 mmol/l, and alkaline phosphatase is elevated at 180 U/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Calcium and vitamin D
The low calcium and elevated alkaline phosphatase is consistent with osteomalacia. As such, calcium and vitamin D replacement are the interventions of choice. In osteomalacia there is a normal amount of bone but the mineral content is low. This can happen due to vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D resistance, renal osteodystrophy, liver disease and in oncogenic hypophosphataemia. Presentation can be with fracture or bone pain and tenderness. Blood tests show low calcium and low phosphate and PTH can be high.

Alendronate
Alendronate is incorrect. Alendronate is a treatment option for osteoporosis, which is not the correct diagnosis. Osteoporosis implies reduced bone mass. This puts patients at risk of fractures. It can be primary or secondary. Primary osteoporosis occurs with family history, increased age, female, low BMI, prolonged immobility and untreated menopause. Secondary osteoporosis occurs with many causes, commonly: steroidChat use,with hyperthyroidism, kidney disease and liver failure. Calcium and phosphate levels are normal and diagnosis is

Teriparatide
Teriparatide is incorrect. PTH is likely to be elevated and therefore teriparatide is not indicated here. Teriparatide is a recombinant form of PTH and is therefore inappropriate in osteomalacia.

stem: A 40-year-old woman attends the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of marked intermittent pain in her right hand, particularly during the early hours of the morning. Physical examination reveals a loss of pinprick sensation in the lateral part of the hand. There is tingling and numbness involving the thumb, index and middle fingers. Which one of the following clinical features is most likely to also be associated with this condition?
options: Pain aggravated if the wrist is pronated for 2 minutes
Pain also occurring during the day if the arm is rested
Pain relieved by repetitive actions of the hand
Tingling and pain in the medial half of the palm
Weakness of the muscles of the thenar eminence
explanation:
Weakness of the muscles of the thenar eminence
This presentation is typical of carpal tunnel syndrome. The sensory changes affecting the lateral side here fit better with a diagnosis of median nerve compression. Sensory supply over the thenar eminence is preserved because this branches before the flexor retinaculum.

Pain aggravated if the wrist is pronated for 2 minutes
Pain aggravated if the wrist is pronated for 2 minutes is incorrect. Phalen’s test consists of holding the wrist hyperflexed for 1–2 minutes (the inverse prayer position), which reproduces the symptoms.

Pain also occurring during the day if the arm is rested
Pain also occurring during the day if the arm is rested is incorrect. Pain due to carpal tunnel syndrome is especially common at night.

Pain relieved by repetitive actions of the hand
Pain relieved by repetitive actions of the hand is incorrect. Pain due to carpal tunnel syndrome is especially common after repetitive actions.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with severe unrelenting pain affecting the left leg. Three months earlier he had an arthroscopic wash-out for septic arthritis affecting his left knee caused by a penetrating injury, and this is when his symptoms began. He has no other medical history of note and is a non-smoker. The patient frequently ran long distance races before the leg injury. Examination reveals a markedly reduced range of movement of the left knee with diffuse swelling of the left leg and overlying cool dry scaly skin. Examination of the right leg reveals no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are present bilaterally. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reflex sympathetic dystrophy
The description here is compatible with a diagnosis of reflex sympathetic dystrophy (complex regional pain syndrome, previously known as Sudek’s atrophy) that has developed following the previous injury. The pain is often severe and disproportionate to the signs and follows a non-anatomical distribution. The skin changes are caused by the associated autonomic dysfunction.

Ongoing septic arthritis
Ongoing septic arthritis is incorrect. He has a diffuse swelling of the left leg (rather than just the knee joint) with skin changes, making a reflex sympathetic dystrophy more common.

Underlying deep venous thrombosis
Underlying deep venous thrombosis is incorrect. A DVT usually causes a painful warm calf, and this gentleman has a cool temperature to the skin.

stem: A 49-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner, complaining of difficulty swallowing solids and liquids. She notices occasional episodes of indigestion and denies weight loss. Her past medical history of note includes intermittent joint pains, for which she self-medicates with ibuprofen. On examination, she has a pulse of 88 bpm and a BP of 135/82 mmHg. On auscultation, there is good air entry and normal heart sounds. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is no nail clubbing, although her fingers appear pale, with taut skin. There are multiple firm, white nodules on her fingertips. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 120 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 180 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 140 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation:
Anti-centromere
This patient has features of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis: Calcinosis (eg firm, white skin deposits), Raynaud’s disease, oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia (CREST syndrome). CREST syndrome is associated with anti-centromere antibodies in about 90% of cases. The goal of pharmacotherapy is to reduce morbidity and prevent complications where possible. Raynaud’s disease is typically managed with

stem: In a population of 20 000, how many people would have rheumatoid arthritis in the western world?
explanation:
200
The prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis has been consistently assessed as being between 0.8% and 1.1% of the adult population in cross-sectional studies in the United States and Western Europe, and translates into a higher prevalence in the elderly female population, hence 1% of 20,000 is 200. Lower rates of 0.2–0.3% have been reported in China and Japan.

50
50 is incorrect. The prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis is approximately 1% in the western world. In China and Japan lower rates of between 0.2% and 0.3% have been reported and the prevalence of 50 would be more relevant here.

100
100 is incorrect. The prevalence of Rheumatoid disease is higher in females than males by a ratio of approximately 3:1, however the total prevalence in general western population is approximately 1%.

1400
1400 is incorrect. Approximately 20% of the population in the western world will have arthritis of any form, of which the majority (around 15% of the population) will have osteoarthritis. This would correlate to approximately 4000 people in a population of (CDC statistics).

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with fever, sweats and malaise. Past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis which is well controlled on methotrexate, asthma (controlled on inhalers) and hayfever. She is normally fit and well, but had a urinary tract infection a few weeks ago. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 70 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Neutrophils 0.2 × 10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l Platelets 68 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l What is the most likely cause of her presentation?
explanation:
Trimethoprim
This lady has pancytopenia, probably due to the interaction between trimethoprim (for the urinary tract infection) and methotrexate, both of which are folate antagonists and have led to methotrexate toxicity. The treatment of methotrexate toxicity is folinic acid rescue and of course treating her neutropenic sepsis. Co- trimoxazole (septrin) is another folate antagonist that should not be prescribed in combination with methotrexate.

Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is incorrect. Nitrofurantoin does not commonly cause pancytopenia.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with arthralgia affecting multiple small joints. She also has night sweats, lethargy, and a rash affecting her face, particularly after she goes out in the sun for a prolonged period. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg and her pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has an active small-joint polyarthritis and a malar rash over her face. Which one of the following full blood counts would be most typical of the likely underlying diagnosis (WCC = white cell count)?
options: Hb 156 g/l, WCC 8.9 x10 9/l, PLT 420 x10 9/l
Hb 92 g/l, WCC 7.6 x10 9/l, PLT 142 x10 9/l
Hb 131 g/l, WCC 8.2 x10 9/l, PLT 540 x10 9/l
Hb 129 g/l, WCC 5.4 x10 9/l, PLT 310 x10 9/l
Hb 124 g/l, WCC 8.2 x10 9/l, PLT 95 x10 9/l
explanation:
Hb 92 g/l, WCC 7.6 x10 9/l, PLT 142 x10 9/l
This woman has a history which is entirely consistent with systemic lupus erythematous (SLE). Mild normochromic normocytic anaemia, coupled with decreases in either the white blood cell count, the platelet count, or both, fits with this underlying diagnosis. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or viscosity can be elevated, but the C-reactive protein (CRP) is often normal unless there is underlying infection or severe serositis. Anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibody titres are performed in an attempt to confirm the diagnosis.

Hb 156 g/l, WCC 8.9 x10 9/l, PLT 420 x10 9/l
Hb 156 g/l, WCC 8.9 × 10 9/l, PLT 420 × 10 9/l is incorrect. This FBC is normal, if not slightly polycythaemic.

Hb 124 g/l, WCC 8.2 x10 9/l, PLT 95 x10 9/l
Hb 124 g/l, WCC 8.2 × 10 9/l, PLT 95 × 10 9/l is incorrect. The degree of thrombocytopaenia is too severe.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with left inguinal and groin pain of 1 week’s duration that is worse with weight bearing and ambulation. Physical examination reveals a full range of motion of the left hip. She walks with a limp. She has previously been treated with aggressive chemotherapy for Hodgkin’s disease. An anteroposterior film of the pelvis demonstrates no osseous abnormality. Which one of the following tests would be most useful in making the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hip
explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hip
Magnetic resonance imaging has been shown to be extremely valuable in evaluating high-risk patients for avascular necrosis who are symptomatic but radiographically normal. Osteonecrosis / Avascular necrosis is one of the most common causes of hip pain and incapacity in patients with a variety of diseases who have been treated with corticosteroids. Risk factors for AVN Apart from corticosteroid use, other risk factors for avascular necrosis include prolonged heparin treatment, exposure to high barometric pressures (diving), excessive alcohol intake and sickle cell disease.

Arthrogram of the left hip
Arthrogram of the left hip is incorrect. An arthrogram is invasive and may be risky.

Serum rheumatoid factor
Serum rheumatoid factor is incorrect. The rheumatoid factor is likely to be negative and is non-diagnostic.

stem: You review a 21-year-old man who suffered from Still's disease as a child. Which one of the following is a common feature of Still's disease?
explanation:
Negative rheumatoid factor
Still’s disease is classically autoantibody negative. Still’s disease (which accounts for 10% of cases of juvenile idiopathic arthritis or JIA) affects boys and girls equally up to the age of 5 years; after this point, girls are more commonly affected. Adult-onset Still’s disease is rare. Clinical features include fever, maculopapular rash, myalgia and generalised lymphadenopathy. Hepatosplenomegaly, pericarditis and pleurisy also occur. Laboratory tests reveal raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), neutrophilia and thrombocytosis, though autoantibodies are negative.

Normal C-reactive protein (CRP)
Normal C-reactive protein (CRP) is incorrect. The CRP is usually very high.

Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is incorrect. The ESR is usually very high.

Splenic atrophy
Splenic atrophy is incorrect. Patients can get splenomegaly.

stem: A 20-year-old college student complains of increasing back pain and early morning stiffness. An X-ray of his lower back shows erosion of the apophyseal joints and obliteration of the sacroiliac junction. Investigations show a CRP of 19mg/l and ESR 30mm/hr. Given the most likely clinical diagnosis from these findings, what treatment would be most suitable for him?
explanation:
Oral NSAIDs
NSAIDS, such as naproxen, are the preferred analgesic for back pain in ankylosing spondylitis. Patients with ankylosing spondylitis should be encouraged to remain active and follow their normal pursuits as far as possible. Spinal extension exercises and regular physiotherapy are most useful.

Bedrest and immobilisation
Bedrest and immobilisation is incorrect. Rest and immobilisation are contraindicated as they may lead to muscle wasting, osteoporosis and ankylosis.

Colchicine
Colchicine is incorrect. Colchicine is usually used for gout.

Intra-articular steroid injections
Intra-articular steroid injections is incorrect. Intra-articular steroid injections are not helpful.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, muscle and joint pains and fatigue. Erythema in a butterfly distribution is seen on her cheeks and across the bridge of her nose. What is the most common finding that you would expect to see on investigation of her joints?
explanation:
Soft tissue swelling
This patient has features suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The joints may appear clinically normal, although sometimes there is soft-tissue swelling surrounding the joint.

Aseptic necrosis
Aseptic necrosis is incorrect. Aseptic necrosis affecting the hip or knee is a rare complication of the disease.

Bony erosions
Bony erosions is incorrect. Bony erosions are rare.

Tendon contraction
Tendon contraction is incorrect. Deformity because of tendon contraction is rare.

Thickening of joint capsule
Thickening of joint capsule is incorrect. Deformity because of joint capsule thickening is less common that soft tissue swelling.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with cough and haemoptysis. On examination, he is found to have a nasal mucosal ulceration. The doctor suspects that this patient may be suffering from granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Which tissues are most commonly involved in this condition?
explanation:
Respiratory tract
The respiratory tract is the most commonly involved tissue in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), affecting approximately 90% of cases. This condition frequently starts with symptoms in the upper respiratory tract, such as rhinorrhoea and nasal mucosal ulceration. As the disease progresses, it can involve the lungs, leading to cough, haemoptysis, and pleuritic pain. The high prevalence and characteristic presentation in the respiratory tract underscore its primary involvement in GPA, distinguishing it from other organs and systems.

Gastrointestinal tract
The gastrointestinal tract can be involved in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), but it is not the most commonly affected tissue. Gastrointestinal involvement occurs in approximately 50% of cases. Symptoms can include abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, or perforation. Although significant, this involvement is secondary to the more prominent respiratory and renal manifestations.

Kidneys
Kidney involvement is a major feature of GPA, affecting around 80% of patients. Renal manifestations typically include glomerulonephritis, which can lead to proteinuria and haematuria. However, while the kidneys are commonly affected and critical to disease prognosis, they are not as universally involved as the respiratory tract. Consequently, the kidneys are not the primary tissues most commonly affected in GPA.

stem: A 75-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is being treated with methotrexate. She presents with malaise, temperature of 37.4°C, erythema, swelling and pain of her right wrist. She cannot move her wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Joint sepsis
This patient probably has joint sepsis. Whenever a monoarthritis (one joint) is encountered, you must consider a septic arthritis first, even if a patient has a known rheumatological disease, like rheumatoid arthritis. In fact, joints that are damaged by rheumatoid arthritis are at higher risk of sepsis. Methotrexate also increases her risk of infection. This could be a flare of rheumatoid arthritis, however rheumatoid joints are very unlikely to become erythematous, and therefore joint sepsis is more likely. Fever can be absent in 50% of cases of septic arthritis and her methotrexate may make the presentation more atypical.

Flare of rheumatoid arthritis
Flare of rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. It is true, however, that osteoarthritis is the commonest joint condition in people of this age. Pain on movement, worse at the beginning of the day, and joint stiffness are characteristic features. Whenever a monoarthritis (one joint) is encountered, you must consider a septic arthritis first, even if a patient has a known rheumatological disease, like rheumatoid arthritis.

Gout
Gout is incorrect. Gout can occur in peripheral joints, causing redness and swelling, but sepsis is more likely here because she is immunosuppressed (at risk of infection) and has severe restriction in range of movement.

stem: An 87-year-old woman presents to the clinic with six weeks of bilateral knee pain which has been exacerbated by a fall in the local supermarket. She has a history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease and an inferior myocardial infarction some five years earlier. On examination, her blood pressure is 155/85 mmHg, pulse is 80 beats per minute, atrial fibrillation. Her BMI is 33 kg/m 2. There is osteoarthritis in both knees with limited flexion and patellar crepitus. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 197 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 210 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilateral knee joint osteoarthritis Which one of the following is the most appropriate option for managing her pain?
explanation:
Paracetamol
This woman has osteoarthritis against a background of obesity, hypertension, atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease. In the first instance, she should be managed with regular paracetamol, according to the WHO analgesic ladder.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is found to have anaemia. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 115–155 g/l Mean cell haemoglobin (MCH) 30 pg 27–33 pg Mean cell haemoglobin concentration (MCHC) 34 g/dl 33.4–35.5 g/dl Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 94 fl 76–98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 7.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 175 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l What is the most common cause for this condition?
explanation:
Chronic disease
Anaemia in patients with rheumatoid arthritis is usually the normocytic normochromic anaemia of chronic disease.

Haemolytic anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. A haemolytic anaemia usually has a raised MCV due to a reticulocytosis. Occasionally, iron deficiency may result as well, causing microcytosis. There may be a dimorphic picture, resulting in a normal MCV.

stem: You are asked to see a 50-year-old man in the surgical ward at 0600 h who underwent an uncomplicated cholecystectomy for gallstones the day before. He has developed excruciating pain in his right ankle joint. He has a history of angina and hypertension, for which he takes bendroflumethiazide (bendrofluazide) and aspirin. Examination of his cardiovascular and respiratory system is unremarkable, as is his abdomen. His right ankle is red, warm, swollen and tender. He can move the ankle. Routine blood tests show mildly impaired renal function with a CRP of 58mg/l. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gout
Gout usually occurs in men, in peripheral joints (such as the ankle) and an acute attack may be provoked by surgery, starvation (being nil by mouth for the operation), impaired renal function, diuretics and low-dose aspirin. Inflammatory markers are usually elevated – as in this case, although the urate level can be normal in the acute attack (and rise when the attack settles). Gout is an abnormality of uric acid metabolism that results in the deposition of sodium urate crystals in joints, soft tissue and urinary tract. It is due to hyperuricaemia resulting from the overproduction or under-excretion of uric acid. It mainly affects men and an acute attack usually begins suddenly in the early hours of the morning. Attacks may be precipitated by: Surgical operations Starvation Dietary or alcoholic excess Drugs (e.g. diuretics)

stem: A female patient has been complaining of a facial rash and arthralgia for the past 6 months. She is hypertensive and has proteinuria. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lupus nephritis
This lady, with a facial (malar) rash, arthralgia and hypertension, has SLE; in this question, the facial rash is highly suggestive of SLE. Of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, 10–20% have evidence of renal involvement, which typically develops during the first 5 years after diagnosis in about 40–50% of patients. While renal disease is a major complication of systemic lupus erythematosus, it is always important to recognise that lupus is a systemic disease and that nephritis typically occurs in patients with extrarenal symptoms such as a rash, arthralgia, Raynaud’s phenomenon and pleuropericarditis. Other major organ systems may be involved, including the central nervous system, heart and lungs

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy usually shows haematuria post respiratory illness

Rapid progressive glomerulonephritis
Rapid progressive glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Rapid progressive glomerulonephritis is characterised by a rapid loss in renal function (usually a 50% decline in the glomerular filtration rate [GFR] within 3 months), with glomerular crescent formation seen in at least 50% or 75% of glomeruli on kidney biopsies, and this question does not indicate these indices being present.

stem: A 66-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for assessment of osteoporosis, having suffered a left Colles’ fracture some 3 months earlier. Her T score is measured at -2.8. Past history of note includes an inferior myocardial infarction, some 10 years earlier, and a right leg deep vein thrombosis (DVT) some 5 years ago. Examination confirms that the Colles’ fracture has healed. Her BMI is 26 kg/m 2. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.3 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Alkaline Phosphatase 48 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Alendronate
Alendronate is the most appropriate answer. This woman in all likelihood has idiopathic osteoporosis, for which bisphosphonates (either weekly or monthly preparations) are the intervention of choice. Bisphosphonates inhibit bone resorption by attaching to hydroxyapatite sites on bony surfaces which inhibits osteoclastic action. This

stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus complains of loss of vision. On examination she is found to have multiple opacities in the lenses of both eyes. What is the most appropriate treatment in this case?
explanation:
Extracapsular lens extraction
This lady with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) has cataracts. Cataracts may occur earlier than normally expected for age, in SLE. The treatment is surgical removal of the lens. Extracapsular extraction with a posterior-chamber lens implant is the usual treatment of choice.

Intraocular steroids
Intraocular steroids is incorrect. This lady has cataracts, and intraocular steroids might be employed in an instance of Cystoid Macular Oedema, not in the treatment of cataracts.

Laser treatment
Laser treatment is incorrect. This lady has cataracts, and laser treatment is not used in the treatment of cataracts, but in other procedures such as the correction of short- or long-sightedness or mild astigmatism.

Vitrectomy
Vitrectomy is incorrect. This lady has cataracts, and vitrectomy may be performed when there is a risk of retinal detachment, not in the case of cataracts.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with a 4-day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He is now struggling to weight-bear and is having to use his father’s walking stick to help him around the house. There is no history of trauma. He has multiple sexual partners and describes recovering from urethritis approximately two weeks ago but is otherwise well. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. He has a moderate effusion around his left knee. It is warm and tender to touch. He is noted to have a rash on the glans penis. His eyes are red and he complains of pain and blurred vision. An aspiration of his knee effusion is taken. Given the likely diagnosis which of the following is most likely to be seen on Gram staining of the aspiration fluid?
explanation:
No growth
This man has arthritis, urethritis and uveitis – reactive arthritis. It often occurs with mucocutaneous lesions. Uveitis or episcleritis may also occur as ocular findings. A similar spectrum of clinical manifestations can be triggered by enteric infection with any of several Shigella, Salmonella, Yersiniaand Campylobacterspecies and by genital infection with C. trachomatis (an organism particularly associated with reactive arthritis). Reactive arthritis is associated with HLA-B27 and is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy (rheumatoid factor-negative). The arthritis is usually asymmetrical and additive. There is no sepsis and joint aspirates are sterile.

Staphylococcus aureus
S. aureus is the most common isolated organism in septic arthritis. This patient, however, is more likely to be presenting with reactive arthritis, given the onset of symptoms.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with increasingly severe back pain, which began as lumbar spine pain, spread to involve both buttocks and now affects the tops of his legs. The pain is worst on walking, and he actually feels like his legs are going to give way unless he sits town to rest, when it becomes really bad. It is relieved when he sits, particularly when he leans forward as well. He is able to cycle without pain. There is a history of smoking 10 cigarettes per day and he has mild hypertension. There is some loss of lumbar lordosis although neurological examination of both lower limbs, including power, tone and reflexes, appears unremarkable. All peripheral pulses are palpable in both lower limbs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lumbar spinal stenosis
The picture of pain on exercise, relieved by sitting forward and resting, is typical of lumbar spinal stenosis. A major difference versus vascular claudication is that sitting aerobic exercise (e.g. cycling) can take place without any pain at all. Lumbar spine X-ray and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are mainly indicated for ruling out other potential conditions. Evidence for surgical intervention is only present in those patients who have degenerative lumbar spine disease, which has precipitated the stenosis symptoms.

Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is incorrect. Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the spine and sacroiliac joint, typically presenting in young men under 30 years of age. There is unknown aetiology, but association with HLA-B27 in 88% of cases. Presentation is normally with morning spinal stiffness, which improves with activity and progressively there is loss of spinal movement. Diagnosis is clinical but can be supported by sacroiliitis on pelvic X-ray. Management is with exercise and tumour necrosis factor (TNF) alpha- blockers in severe disease. The radiation of pain, the absence of stiffness and the fact that pain worsens with activity, as well as age of presentation, all make this very unlikely here.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents to the clinic with dry eyes, a dry mouth, an erythematous rash and polyarthralgia. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Immunoglobulin G (IgG) 45 g/l < 15 g/l Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) Strongly positive Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies Strongly positive Rheumatoid factor Positive IgM Normal IgA Normal Kappa/Lambda Ratio Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with secondary Sjögren syndrome
explanation:
Primary Sjögren syndrome
The clinical features and the serology are typical of primary Sjögren syndrome (occurs alone and more likely to have positive anti-Ro antibodies than secondary Sjögren's).

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with an acutely painful and red right big toe. His uric acid level is 0.6 mmol/l (0.23–0.46). What is the most common cause of hyperuricaemia in gout?
options: Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid
Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver
Impaired renal excretion of uric acid
explanation:
Impaired renal excretion of uric acid
Approximately 90% of patients with gout have impaired renal excretion of urate.

Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid
Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid is incorrect. Faecal removal is not associated with hyperuricaemia, although one third of uric acid is removed in the faeces.

Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver
Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver is incorrect. The liver is not involved in urate removal.

Inborn error of metabolism
Chat Inborn error of metabolism is incorrect. Less than 1% have an inborn error of metabolism that with to leads purine overproduction.

Increased production of uric acid
Increased production of uric acid is incorrect. 10% exhibit increased production.

stem: A 31-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome complains of a 2-month history of pain in his right hip joint. The movements of the hip are free but painful. An X-ray provides evidence of a completely destroyed femoral head. What is the most probable diagnosis?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Pathological fracture of the femoral neck
explanation:
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
This patient is likely to have avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are at risk of AVN because the nephrotic syndrome is a prothrombotic state (due to loss of protein S and anti- thrombin III in urine) and they may be on long-term steroids. Initially, movements are restricted, particularly abduction and internal rotation. Subsequently the movements become free when the femoral head is completely destroyed.

Gouty arthritis
Gouty arthritis is incorrect. Gout usually affects the small joints of the feet or hands. There is no association with nephrotic syndrome or its management.

Pathological fracture of the femoral neck
Pathological fracture of the femoral neck is incorrect. A pathological fracture would be evident on X-ray.

Septic arthritis
Septic arthritis is incorrect. Septic arthritis would be much more acute in presentation, and movements would be limited, if not impossible, due to pain in the initial stages and ankylosis later on.

stem: A 25-year-old man is referred from his General Practitioner to the Medical Admissions Unit, complaining of joint pain for three weeks, which mainly affects the joints of his lower limbs, and lower backache for the last two weeks. During a holiday in Spain six weeks ago, he had a mild self-limiting gastrointestinal upset. He also noted that his eyes had been irritated, but this had now settled. On examination he is pyrexial, with a temperature of 37.5 °C. Investigations show a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 49 mm/hour and a normal white cell count. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the next step in this patient’s management?
explanation:
Non-steroidal analgesics
Non-steroidal analgesics is correct. This patient has reactive arthritis, suggested by the history of joint pain following a gastrointestinal upset and irritation of the eyes (suggestive of sterile conjunctivitis). This usually follows either a gastrointestinal infection or non-specific urethritis. It is characterised by seronegative arthritis and conjunctivitis, and up to 10% of patients may develop keratoderma blennorrhagica (extensive skin scaling on the sole of the feet). The diagnosis is clinical. The clinical course is usually self-limiting (around six months), and treatment is initially with anti-inflammatory drugs. Gastroprotection should be offered to patients.

X-rays of the affected joints
X-rays of the affected joints is incorrect. Joint X-rays are usually unremarkable in reactive arthritis and in most patients, there is no evidence of joint destruction. Unnecessary ionising radiation in patients should be avoided. Examples of when X-rays can be useful include osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis) and ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with swollen and painful finger joints in both hands. You suspect rheumatoid arthritis and want to test for the presence of rheumatoid factor. Which immunoglobulin is most commonly detected by routine testing?
explanation:
IgM
Rheumatoid factor is present in 70% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis. This may be of any immunoglobulin class (IgM, IgG or IgA, and less commonly Ig E and IgD). The most common tests employed clinically detect IgM rheumatoid factor (directed against the Fc portion of an IgG). Around 70% of patients with polyarticular rheumatoid arthritis have IgM rheumatoid factor in their serum. This is not diagnostic of rheumatoid arthritis, nor does its absence rule the disease out but it is a useful predictor of prognosis. Solid-phase RIA and ELISA (Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) testing to detect Rheumatoid Factor of all major immunoglobulins sensitively and in a reproducible manner may have a role in the early detection, accurate diagnosis, measure disease severity and prognosis.

IgA
IgA is incorrect. Rheumatoid factor can be of any isotype of immunoglobulins including Ig A, however IgM is present in up to 70% of patients with Rheumatoid arthritis and this is what is routinely tested for. Studies suggest that IgA measuring may have an important role in early diagnosis and predicting disease severity, and research into this area along with design of feasible universal testing methods is ongoing.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has been taking long-standing naproxen therapy for osteoarthritis. She has a history of diabetes mellitus type I and routine blood test which reveals evidence of chronic kidney disease, hyperkalaemia and hyperchloraemia. What is the most likely underlying cause of her biochemical abnormalities?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis
Type 4 renal tubular acidosis can all result as a consequence of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) administration.

Acute interstitial nephritis
Acute interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Acute interstitial nephritis is usually due to drug hypersensitivity and presents as acute kidney disease, fever, arthralgia and eosinophilia. Hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis is not a feature of this condition.

Diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy is incorrect. Diabetic nephropathy characteristically presents with proteinuria. It is a gradually declining process that leads to kidney disease after many years.

Minimal-change nephropathy
Minimal-change nephropathy is incorrect. Minimal-change nephropathy is typically seen in children and presents with nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains that she has had a relapsing pain in her left ankle for the last 4–5 weeks. She also complains of a painful rash on the soles of her feet, and pain and swelling in her right toes. Over the last 2 weeks she has also developed low back pain. On further questioning she mentions that for the last few days she has noticed painless oral ulcers, which heal spontaneously. She also has a recent history of chlamydial urethritis about a month ago. Her full blood count and kidney and liver function tests are all normal. An autoimmune screen is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This woman is likely to have a reactive arthritis. She has a recent history of chlamydial urethritis and now presents with arthritis. The painful sole is most likely due to plantar fasciitis, with the rash most likely to be keratoderma blenorrhagica, and fleeting and painless oral ulcers are well described in reactive arthritis. Conjunctivitis is part of the classic triad of reactive arthritis, and this can occur before or at the onset of arthritis. However, other eye signs such as iritis can also occur. Asymmetric sacroiliitis presenting as backache occurs in about 20% of patients with reactive arthritis.

Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is incorrect. There is a clear recent genitourinary (GU) infection, which makes Chat reactive with arthritis far more likely.

Behçet's syndrome
Behçet's syndrome is incorrect. Although this lady has oral ulcers, she has no other features of Behçet's syndrome.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis. One year ago her gold therapy was discontinued because it was found to be ineffective in controlling her arthritis. She was started and then maintained on d-penicillamine (375 mg). Two weeks ago she noticed increased difficulty in climbing stairs. Her husband, who accompanied her, added that he had to wash her hair in the last 4 days. On examination, she has synovial swelling at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands as well as both knees. Neck and shoulder movements are very restricted. Neurological assessment reveals: grade 3/5 weakness in both upper and lower muscle groups. There is patchy loss of fine touch and pinprick sensation impaired to the abdomen without a clear sensory level being obtained. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk throughout, including upper limbs. The Babinski sign is extensor bilaterally. The most probable cause of her recent weakness is which of the following?
options: Generalised weakness due to disuse muscle atrophy secondary to chronic arthritis
Spinal cord compression due to cervical myelopathy from atlanto-axial subluxation
explanation:
Spinal cord compression due to cervical myelopathy from atlanto-axial subluxation
This patient exhibits features of upper motor neurone signs affecting the upper and lower limbs. The most probable diagnosis is cervical myelopathy secondary to her rheumatoid arthritis. The hallmark symptom of cervical myelopathy is weakness or stiffness in the legs and weakness or clumsiness of the hands. Loss of sphincter control or frank incontinence is rare, but some patients may complain of slight hesitancy on urination. A characteristic physical finding of cervical myelopathy is hyperreflexia. Ankle clonus and Babinski’s sign (pathological extension of the great toe elicited by stroking the foot) in the feet may also be revealed. Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine is the procedure of choice during the initial screening process of patients with suspected cervical myelopathy.

Generalised weakness due to disuse muscle atrophy secondary to chronic arthritis
Generalised weakness due to disuse muscle atrophy secondary to chronic arthritis is incorrect. In disuse muscle atrophy Babinski’s sign is negative.

stem: A 35-year-old ship’s steward is started on a new drug for rheumatoid arthritis before leaving for Africa. He returns after four months, complaining of hair loss and blurring of vision. It is found that he has misread the prescription and is taking triple the prescribed dose daily. Which drug is most likely to cause these symptoms?
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinopathy, although this is a relatively rare side effect. The increased dose taken by the patient will contribute to the development of symptoms in this case.

D-Penicillamine
D-Penicillamine is incorrect. D-Penicillamine may cause pancytopenia, and also needs close monitoring. It does not, however, cause hair loss and blurring of vision.

Diclofenac
Diclofenac is incorrect. Diclofenac is not associated with hair loss and visual symptoms.

Gold
Gold is incorrect. Gold is given by deep intramuscular injection, with close monitoring of the full blood count and urinalysis for protein prior to each injection. It would not be an appropriate medication for this patient.

stem: An obese 50-year-old man presents in the middle of the night to the Emergency Department with pain and swelling of his first, second, third and fourth metatarsophalangeal joint, left ankle and right knee. On examination the joints are swollen, red, hot and tender. His CRP is 61mg/L, ESR 45mm/hr and urate is 3.0 (normal range 3.4-7.0 mg/dL). Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Naproxen
This patient has gout, which is treated with quick-acting non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), such as naproxen, unless there is a contraindication. Naproxen is the commonly used due to its infrequent renal, gut and nervous system side-effects. Long term therapy would be with allopurinol. If NSAIDs are contraindicated, such as in renal impairment, colchicine may be used. The dose of colchicine may be lowered, depending on the degree of renal dysfunction. Colchicine can cause significant diarrhea and abdominal pain and can be nephrotoxic. Do not be dissuaded by the normal serum urate as 40% of acute gout cases show a normal urate, which usually rises when the attack has settled. Normal Uric acid levels are 2.4-6.0 mg/dL(female) and 3.4-7.0 mg/dL (male). The CRP and ESR can be non-specifically elevated and does not differentiate between inflammation or infection.

Codeine
Codeine is incorrect because codeine, although a good analgesic agent, is not an anti-inflammatory medication.

Erythromycin
Erythromycin is incorrect because erythromycin is an antibiotic.

stem: A 23-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is planning to start a family. Which one of the following drugs would be safest to prescribe?
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is considered safe pre-conception, during pregnancy and breast-feeding in women, and does not seem to increase the risk of adverse outcomes in paternally exposed children. Other drugs that may be safely used in man with rheumatioid arthritis considering having children in the near future include NSAIDs and TNF-α inhibitors.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide may irreversibly affect male fertility.

Leflunomide
Leflunomide is incorrect. Leflunomide can inhibit purine/pyrimidine synthesis and is contraindicated in pregnancy or while trying to conceive. A 2 year washout is required prior to conception, which may be accelerated with cholestyramine or charcoal.

Sulfasalazine
Sulfasalazine is incorrect. Sulfasalazine can drop the sperm count and therefore may be reduce chances of conception.

stem: A 30-year-old woman undergoes arthroscopy and joint fluid aspiration for suspected rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following findings would best confirm the diagnosis?
options: Marked vascular proliferation on the synovial membrane
Neutrophils in the aspirate on microscopy
explanation:
Marked vascular proliferation on the synovial membrane
The synovial membrane is almost always involved in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). There is marked vascular proliferation with increased permeability of blood vessels on the synovial membrane that is typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Thickening of the synovial membrane and proliferation into folds and fronds may also be seen.

Clear synovial fluid
Clear synovial fluid is incorrect. The synovial fluid is turbid, with neutrophils, in earlier phases of RA, but this is not a diagnostic feature.

Increased viscosity of synovial fluid
Increased viscosity of synovial fluid is incorrect. The viscosity of synovial fluid is decreased in RA, unlike in osteoarthritis where it is increased.

Normal-looking synovial membrane
Normal-looking synovial membrane is incorrect. We would expect synovitic changes above in RA, not a normal synovial membrane.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is sent to you for review. There is a history of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis for which she takes NSAIDs and sulfasalazine. Examination reveals changes consistent with rheumatoid arthritis and a palpable spleen. Her blood picture reveals mild anaemia, neutropaenia and a platelet count of 74 × 10 9/L (150–400 × 10 9/L). Bone marrow biopsy reveals an excess of immature granulocyte precursors. Autoimmune screen reveals a raised ESR, positive rheumatoid factor, positive ANA and antihistone antibody. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Felty syndrome
Felty syndrome is defined as the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly and a low white cell count. This is the clinical picture presented here.

Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is incorrect. Clinical symptoms of amyloidosis include diarrhoea, heart failure and other symptoms that may be associated with an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia such as bone pain. None of these features is present in this lady.

Portal hypertension with splenomegaly
Portal hypertension with splenomegaly is incorrect. Portal hypertension with splenomegaly would not tie in with the long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis, and there is no other reason why this lady may have developed portal hypertension.

stem: A 43-year-old man with a past history of hypothyroidism presents with a 3-month history of pain and stiffness in the joints of his hands and feet. He also gives a history of dyspnoea, which started 6 weeks ago. Examination shows swollen hand joints and signs of a right pleural effusion. A diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is made, based on the history examination and blood tests which showed a positive anti-CCP antibody and CRP of 46mg/L. Which one of the following is characteristic of a rheumatoid pleural effusion?
options: It has a low glucose level
It should be treated by decortication
Long-standing rheumatoid effusions have low cholesterol levels
explanation:
It has a low glucose level
Up to 5% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis develop pleural effusions at some stage. Pleural effusions are more common in men. These effusions are exudates and typically have a low pH (< 7.2), a high lactic acid dehydrogenase (LDH) level and a low glucose level. Rheumatoid arthritis is unlikely to be the cause of an effusion if the glucose level in the fluid is over 1.6 mmol/l. Large amounts of cholesterol can accumulate in long-standing rheumatoid pleural effusions.

It has a high pH
It has a high pH is incorrect. The rheumatoid effusion has a low pH (acidic).

Long-standing rheumatoid effusions have low cholesterol levels
Long-standing rheumatoid effusions have low cholesterol levels is incorrect. Long-standing rheumatoid effusions can contain cholesterol.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is attending the Rheumatology Clinic. She complains of shortness of breath. Assuming that this is due to respiratory involvement by SLE, what would be the most common pulmonary manifestation?
explanation:
Pleural effusion
Pleurisy and pleural effusions are the most common pulmonary manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and are often bilateral. These pleural effusions are exudates

Atelectasis
Atelectasis is incorrect. Atelectasis may be seen, but is less common than pleural effusion.

Pneumonitis
Pneumonitis is incorrect. Pneumonitis may be seen, but is less common than pleural effusion.

Restrictive lung disease
Restrictive lung disease is incorrect. Restrictive lung disease may be seen, but is less common than pleural effusion.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the General practitioner with a throbbing joint pain in her hands which keeps her up at night. She complains of a stiff neck which can be incredibly painful. On examination there are swan- neck deformities of her fingers and Z-deformity of her thumbs. Which of the following is closely involved in the pathology of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tumour necrosis factor alpha-α
Elevated levels of tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 1 (IL-1), interleukin 6 (IL-6), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), fibroblast growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor have all been demonstrated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Elevated levels of TNF-α in particular have been demonstrated within the joint spaces of patients with active rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-TNF-α agents have shown impressive results in rheumatoid arthritis and are prescribed for patients who have continued active disease despite two disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.

Interleukin-2
This cytokine is closely implicated with both helper and killer T cells to regulate immunity. It has been used as a pharmacological agent in the treatment of cancers such as malignant melanoma. It does not appear to have a central role in the mode of pathogenesis of Rheumatoid arthritis.

Interleukin-10
Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is am immunoregulatory cytokine implicated in various inflammatory and auto immune conditions such as Graves disease and Sjögren syndrome, and Il-10 therapy in the treatment of Crohn’s disease is an area of ongoing research. It is not thought to be central to the pathogenesis of rheumatoid Chat arthritis. with

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, malaise, weight loss and myalgia over the past month. You suspect polyarteritis nodosa and arrange to perform some blood tests. Which abnormality would you be most likely to find?
explanation:
Elevated creatinine
Raised creatinine is often present and is included in the list of diagnostic criteria. Diagnostic criteria from the American College of Rheumatology (1990) (which do not differentiate between PAN and microscopic polyangitis): 3 of the following 10 criteria must be present to classify a vasculitis as PAN: Weight loss of 4 kg or more Livedo reticularis Testicular pain/tenderness Myalgia or leg weakness/tenderness Mononeuropathy or polyneuropathy Diastolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg Elevated urea and creatinine levels Infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) Abnormality on arteriography Biopsy of small- or medium-sized artery containing polymorphonuclear neutrophils

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with an eight week history of chest pain. She describes the pain as a burning sensation that is worse when lying flat. Over the past two weeks, she reports feeling more fatigued with frequent dizzy spells. Her past medical history includes severe rheumatoid arthritis that is poorly controlled with medical therapy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 70 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 295 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 62 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 15 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s presentation?
explanation:
Piroxicam
This woman has an upper gastrointestinal bleed, given the history of dyspepsia and increased fatigue and dizzy spells, coupled with anaemia and raised urea levels on her blood tests. Common pharmacological causes include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as piroxicam. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs work

stem: A 35-year-old computer operator with rheumatoid arthritis comes to see you with an upper respiratory tract infection and malaise. He has a purpuric rash all over his body and, on examination, a mass is felt in the left upper quadrant of his abdomen. A full blood count shows: haemoglobin 73 g/l, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 79 fl, white cell count (WCC) 2.5 × 10 9/l, platelets 47 × 10 9/l. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Felty syndrome
Felty syndrome is the association of long-standing (> 10 years) rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly, neutropenia (or pancytopenia). Recurrent infections, weight loss, a vasculitic rash and leg ulceration can also occur.

Caplan syndrome
Caplan syndrome is incorrect. The combination of rheumatoid nodules and pneumoconiosis is known as Caplan syndrome.

Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules
Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules is incorrect. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules do not usually cause any symptoms.

stem: A 30-year-old man who is being managed by the ophthalmologists for anterior uveitis is referred to you for an opinion. He is now suffering from painful genital ulcers and a rash which resembles erythema nodosum. On examination he has oral aphthous ulcers and ulcers on his scrotum. Other history of note includes diarrhoea, which his General Practitioner thought was due to irritable bowel syndrome. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 231 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 65 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behcet’s disease
This presentation is highly suggestive of Behçet’s disease – orogenital ulceration, uveitis, erythema nodosum, diarrhoea (intestinal involvement with Behçet’s) and raised inflammatory markers. This is mainly a clinical diagnosis, as there is no single diagnostic test.

stem: A 35-year-old man patient was referred from his GP to the sexual health clinic because of recurrent genital ulcers with four recurrences in the last year. Last year he had a painful red eye and was diagnosed with panuveitis. On examination the patient has scrotal ulcers, also has mouth ulcers. You request some blood tests in clinic, 24 hours later the patient phones your secretary complaining of a pustule at the site of blood taking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behçet’s disease
This patient has Behcet’s syndrome characterized by orogenital ulceration, uveitis and pathergy. The pathergy is a hypersensitivity reaction to the intradermal penetration of the venipuncture needle with the development of a sterile pustule at the site of blood taking. The diagnostic criteria of Behcet’s syndrome require the presence of recurrent oral ulcers and any two of the following: genital ulcers, defined eye lesions, defined skin lesions, a positive skin pathergy test.

Familial Mediterranean Fever
Familial Mediterranean Fever is incorrect because Familial Mediterranean fever is a periodic fever syndrome in patients with recurrent fevers. There is usually a family history, patients are usually of Mediterranean descent and complain of pleuritic chest and abdominal pain (serositis).

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is incorrect because there is no history of bloody diarrhea and genital ulcers and the pathergy are not common in ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman is taking etanercept for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism of action of etanercept?
explanation:
Binds to TNF-alpha
The mechanism of action of etanercept is thought to be its inhibition of TNF (alpha and beta both), functioning as a decoy receptor, preventing the binding to the cell surface tumour necrosis factor receptor (TNFR), preventing TNF-mediated cellular responses by rendering TNF biologically inactive. Etanercept mimics the inhibitory effects of naturally occurring soluble TNF receptors, the difference being that etanercept, because it is a fusion protein rather than a simple TNF receptor, has a greatly extended half-life in the bloodstream, and therefore a more profound and long-lasting biologic effect than a naturally occurring soluble TNF receptor.

Binds to TNF-alpha receptors
Binds to TNF-alpha receptors is incorrect. Currently, the TNA-alpha receptor is not used as a pharmacological target.

Binds to CD52 receptors
Binds to CD52 receptors is incorrect. Alemtuzumab is an anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of weakness, especially on walking up stairs or rising from a chair. She has had a dry cough and shortness of breath. On examination bibasilar crepitations. Investigations reveal: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 74 mm in 1 st hour, C-reactive protein (CRP) 32 mg/l. The creatine kinase is 5742 U/l, creatinine 231 µmol/. Urine dipstick shows +++ blood. What is the likely cause of her kidney disease?
explanation:
Acute tubular necrosis
This woman has the anti-Jo-1 syndrome (which is characterised by polymyositis and lung fibrosis) and rhabdoymyolysis. Her creatine kinase level is very high and she has myoglobinuria (+++ blood on dipstick). Above levels of about 5000 U/l there is a risk of myoglobin crystallisation in the kidneys, which causes an acute tubular necrosis. The immediate management is to force a diuresis. It may be necessary to alkalinise the urine.

Acute glomerulonephritis
Acute glomerulonephritis is incorrect. With glomerulonephritis there is usually blood and protein in the urine.

Amyloid
Amyloid is incorrect. Amyloidosis is usually associated with heavy proteinuria (nephrotic syndrome).

NSAID nephropathy
NSAID nephropathy is incorrect. The best fit is rhabdomylosis from the Jo-1 syndrome.

stem: An elderly man complains of an acutely swollen left knee. An X-ray shows intra-articular calcification. Joint aspiration reveals small, rhomboid-shaped crystals. These signs occur in which of the following?
explanation:
Pyrophosphate arthritis
Pseudogout (pyrophosphate arthritis) occurs as a result of the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals (chondrocalcinosis) in the large joints, particularly the knees. Small, rhomboid-shaped crystals are seen which show weakly positive birefringence on polarized light microscopy. Pseudogout is associated with osteoarthritis (which is more common in the elderly) and metabolic disorders (such as hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis). The X-ray shows calcified cartilage called chondrocalcinosis, which is associated with pseudogout.

Acute gouty arthritis
Acute gouty arthritis is incorrect. In gouty arthritis the crystals are long and needle shaped.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Crystals are not seen in the synovial fluid in osteoarthritis.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Crystals are not seen in the synovial fluid in rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has been visiting her GP for a while, complaining of recurrent nosebleeds. She has also consulted for cosmetic surgery advice about the shape of her nose as it seems to be dipping, and presents for examination under anaesthesia to a private surgeon. Preoperative blood testing reveals anaemia with Hb of 105 g/l (11.5–15.5), and urinalysis reveals haematuria, red blood cell casts and proteinuria. Her surgery is cancelled, and further testing reveals a serum creatinine concentration of 195 μmol/l (60–110). Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
The mean onset of GPA is 40 years of age, with an incidence of 0.5/100 000 individuals. Classically, it is said to consist of necrotising granulomatous lesions in the upper or lower respiratory tracts, a focal necrotising vasculitis involving both arteries and veins, and a focal glomerulonephritis of the kidneys. Individual manifestations with differing severity in certain organ systems may occur. Laboratory screening involves testing of c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody). Patients are often anaemic with a leukocytosis, and there are urine changes similar to those described above, which represent a glomerulonephritis-type picture. Lung involvement causes chest X-ray changes: these may be bilateral multiple nodules, cavitated mass lesions or pleural effusion in 20% of cases. Pulmonary function testing may reveal a restrictive lung defect. Treatment of choice is cyclophosphamide and steroid therapy. The 5-year survival rate with aggressive treatment is around 80%.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss)
This is a vasculitis of the small and medium-sized blood vessels, often in patients with asthma and/or allergic rhinitis. Similar to GPA, there would be haematoproteinuria; however, there are typically no recurrent nosebleeds or nose-saddling.

stem: A 30-year-old man has erythrodermic psoriasis and arthritis mutilans involving several digits in both hands. He is currently taking methotrexate and sulphasalazine. He has several tender and swollen joints. Blood including CRP and ESR are normal. What would be the most logical next step treatment for him?
explanation:
Adalimumab
Anti-tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) agents (e.g. adalimumab) have been found to be highly effective in the treatment of severe skin and joint disease due to psoriasis. He would probably continue methotrexate, add in adalimumab and stop sulphasalazine.

Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. He is already on two DMARDs and therefore should be escalated to biologic therapy, as per NICE guidelines, rather than adding in another DMARD like hydroxychloroquine. N.B. hydroxychloroquine can cause flaring of skin psoriasis

Leflunomide
Leflunomide is incorrect. He is already on two DMARDs and therefore should be escalated to biologic therapy, as per NICE guidelines, rather than adding in another DMARD like leflunomide.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Oral corticosteroids are not going to be effective enough to control his disease. N.B. oral steroids can destabilise the skin disease and cause skin flares.

stem: A 24-year-old Nigerian complains of right hip pain. Blood tests show a haemoglobin level of 80 g/l and the blood film shows target cells, sickle cells and reticulocytes. An X-ray shows loss of the right femoral head with periarticular sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Avascular necrosis
Flattening and loss of the right femoral head on X-ray is consistent with avascular necrosis. This is a known complication of sickle cell disease, which is consistent with this patient’s anaemia and blood film. This condition results from a single glutamic acid to valine substitution at position 6 of the ß-globin polypeptide chain. The greatest prevalence is in Africa, where the heterozygote frequency is over 20%. It may lead on to secondary osteoarthritis.

Osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis is incorrect. In osteomyelitis there is usually periosteal reaction seen on the plain film.

Septic arthritis
Septic arthritis is incorrect. Clinically the patient may have a peripheral source of sepsis and systemic upset such as fever. The X-ray may be normal in the very early stage of the disease, joint effusion may be seen. There may be juxta-articular osteoporosis due to hyperaemia, narrowing of the joint space due cartilage destruction in the acute phase, destruction of the subchondral bone on both sides of a joint. If left untreated, reactive juxta- articular sclerosis and, in severe cases and ankyloses (fusion) will develop.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of difficulty walking, particularly upstairs and or getting up from a chair. On examination there is wasting of the pelvic girdle muscles. She has also developed a purple discoloration of the eyelids. Which one of the following investigations will be most helpful in the diagnosis and management of this condition?
options: Raised serum creatine phosphokinase / creatinine kinase (CPK/CK)
explanation:
Raised serum creatine phosphokinase / creatinine kinase (CPK/CK)
This lady has dermatomyositis (proximal weakness and heliotrope rash). Serum creatine phosphokinase / kinase (CPK or CK), aminotransferases and aldolase are usually raised and are useful guides to the activity of the disease.

A raised ESR
A raised ESR is incorrect. A raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is a response to any inflammatory reaction in the body. In this condition, the ESR is raised in about 5% of cases.

Myositis-specific antibodies
Myositis-specific antibodies is incorrect. Myositis-specific antibodies are not present in all cases of dermatomyositis and so are not helpful in the diagnosis or management of this condition. N.B. myositis-specific antibodies are only positive in 20% of cases.

stem: A young man presents to the Emergency Department with an acutely swollen and painful right knee, associated with red gritty eyes. He has recently returned from Thailand, where he had diarrhoea and vomiting for several days. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 301 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 41 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) 1:40 Giant macrophages. No organisms Joint are seen on Gram staining. What could the diagnosis be?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This patient has the classic triad of reactive arthritis: arthritis, conjunctivitis and bacterial dysentery (although the condition of course also occurs after non-specific urethritis. Reactive arthritis is usually associated with HLA B27 and occurs after bacterial dysentery caused by Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia spp. or may follow sexually acquired infection with HIV, gonorrhoea and Chlamydia spp. Joint aspiration shows the presence of giant macrophages. N.B. inflammatory markers can be non-specifically elevated.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with a 6-week history of pain in her fingers that is exacerbated by the cold. On further questioning, she says that she has difficulty swallowing from having a constant dry mouth despite drinking plenty of water. She complains of a gritty sensation in her eyes. There is no other past medical history of note and she takes no regular medication. On examination, her observations are within normal limits. There are no remarkable abnormalities detected on respiratory, cardiovascular or abdominal examination. Which of the following investigations will confirm the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-Ro
This patient has Sjögren syndrome, characterised by inflammation and destruction of the exocrine glands. Patients may have dry/gritty eyes, with intolerance to contact lenses, dry mouth, photosensitivity, fatigue and joint pain. In early disease, excessive watering or deposits of dried mucus in the corner of the eye and recurrent attacks of conjunctivitis can occur. Dry mouth often manifests as the ‘cream cracker’ sign, an inability to swallow dry food without fluid or waking up in the night to take sips of water. On examination, xerostomia can be detected as a diminished salivary pool, a dried fissured tongue, often complicated by angular stomatitis, and chronic oral candidiasis. The eyes may be reddened and roughened due to shallow erosions in the conjunctivae. Multiple auto-antibodies may be present, including rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti-La and anti-Ro. Of the antibodies listed in the question, however, anti-Ro is the most specific for Sjögren syndrome.

Double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (ds-DNA)
Double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (ds-DNA) antibodies are used in the detection of systemic lupus erythematosus, a multisystem autoimmune disease causing a variety of symptoms, including malar Chat rash, with arthralgia and Raynaud’s disease. Systemic lupus erythematosus is not responsible for this patient’s symptoms

stem: You review a 48-year-old woman who presents complaining of joint pains and who has suffered recurrent infections over the past few months. Blood tests are positive for rheumatoid factor on blood testing and her WCC is low. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following features is most likely to be found in her case?
explanation:
Splenomegaly
Felty syndrome is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and consists of splenomegaly and neutropenia in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Leg ulcers or sepsis are associated complications.

Distal interphalangeal joint involvement
Distal interphalangeal joint involvement is incorrect. The hands are commonly involved in rheumatoid arthritis, but it is more usual for the proximal interphalangeal joints to be involved.

Flexural surface rheumatoid nodules
Flexural surface rheumatoid nodules is incorrect. Rheumatoid nodules are found in a high percentage of patients and occur most commonly on the extensor surfaces of joints such as the elbows.

HLA-DR2 tissue type
HLA-DR2 tissue type is incorrect. HLA-DR4 is associated with Felty syndrome.

stem: A 70-year-old woman who lives alone complains of increasing pain in her left knee and episodes of the joint ‘giving way’. She is no longer able to climb stairs. Valgus deformity with instability is also noted. She currently takes 6-8 Co-codamol 30/500 tablets per day. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for her?
explanation:
Joint replacement
Disabling osteoarthritis in the elderly who live alone requires definitive treatment so that their independence is not curtailed. Joint replacement would be the best choice in this case.

Hormone replacement therapy
Hormone replacement therapy is incorrect. HRT is not a treatment for osteoarthritis. It may help with osteoporosis.

Intraarticular steroid injections
Intraarticular steroid injections is incorrect. Intraarticular steroids in osteoarthritis often only give short-term symptomatic relief, and often do not help at all.

Physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is incorrect. Her arthritis seems so severe that physio is unlikely to help.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents for review. She has recently suffered a viral upper respiratory tract infection, diagnosed by her general practitioner (GP) as glandular fever. Progressive tiredness has followed and she presents to the Emergency Department for review. On further questioning she admits to haemoptysis but her GP put this down to the infection. Urine examination reveals the presence of blood and protein, and an admission creatinine is 342 µmol/l. She is admitted to the renal ward, and renal biopsy and staining reveals a linear pattern of immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposition against the glomerular basement membrane. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Goodpasture’s syndrome
The microscopy and staining here reveals the presence of linear immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposition (anti- glomerular basement membrane or anti-GBM antibody). Goodpasture’s syndrome can present with asymptomatic proteinuria or non-visible haematuria, acute nephritic syndrome, nephrotic syndrome or chronic kidney disease. Management of Goodpasture’s syndrome involves the use of combination cytotoxic therapy and corticosteroids. Severe pulmonary haemorrhage responds to plasma exchange, which can be performed in a number of specialist immunology units. Recurrent Goodpasture’s syndrome can occur in response to repeated viral infections.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura
This condition is not associated with anti-GBM antibodies.

Membranous nephropathy
This condition is not associated with anti-GBM antibodies.

stem: A 32-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis presents with left-sided chest pain. On examination, he is febrile. The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Pericarditis
This patient has acute pericarditis, as suggested by the electrocardiography (ECG) tracing. Classical ECG findings in the acute period is diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation and depression of the PR segment. It is a known extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis. Diagnosis is made when at least two from the following criteria are met: characteristic chest pain – pleuritic pain eased by leaning forwards pericardial friction rub classical ECG changes pericardial effusion (new or worsening).

Pulmonary fibrosis
Pulmonary fibrosis is incorrect. Fibrosing alveolitis is the most common pulmonary manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis. ECG changes that may be seen would be those of right heart strain due to secondary pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of tiredness, fever, weight loss and pain and stiffness in her shoulders and neck. She has now developed a severe headache. She does not have any visual symptoms or jaw claudication. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the temporal region. Blood tests show: haemoglobin 105 g/l (normal range 115–165 g/l), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 80 mm in 1 st hour (normal range 0–30) and CRP 54mg/L. She is 60kg in weight. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Prednisolone 60mg
