This patient most probably has giant-cell arteritis (GCA), which is an inflammatory granulomatous arteritis of large arteries that occurs in association with polymyalgia rheumatic. It affects people over the age of 50 years. A raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is a hallmark of this condition. The CRP is usually elevated as well. There can also be a mild normocytic normochromic anaemia. A dose of 1mg/kg of prednisolone is usually recommended. A temporal artery biopsy should be scheduled for within two weeks of starting steroids.

Aspirin 300mg
Aspirin 300mg is incorrect. 300mg of aspirin is given to patients with an ischaemic stroke. In Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), aspirin 75mg is given alongside prednisolone for vascular prophylaxis.

Prednisolone 120mg
Prednisolone 120mg is incorrect. 120mg of prednisolone risks significantly more steroid-related adverse events versus 60mg, with little or no added efficacy brought by the higher dose.

stem: A 57-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. She has trouble with Raynaud’s phenomenon, for which she wears gloves all the time and takes amlodipine. She also has a history of reflux oesophagitis, for which she takes regular omeprazole. On examination she looks thin and tired, her body mass index (BMI) is 18 kg/m 2 and her blood pressure is 162/89 mmHg. There is calcinosis on examination of the fingers. She has an elevated respiratory rate at rest. On auscultation you can hear crackles at both lung bases. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 111 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 187 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 148 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following investigations is likely to contribute most to the diagnosis of her underlying respiratory problem?
explanation:
High resolution CT
This patient has systemic sclerosis with symptoms of Raynaud’s, oesophageal dysmotility and calcinosis on examination of the fingers. Her shortness of breath with crackles is therefore suggestive of the possibility of pulmonary fibrosis. The most accurate way to evaluate this is ultimately with high-resolution computed tomography (CT), and this would be the investigation of choice.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of episodic finger discolouration triggered by cold exposure and emotional stress. She describes her fingers turning white, then blue, and finally red upon rewarming. Her past medical history is unremarkable, and she denies any other systemic symptoms. What is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
CREST syndrome
CREST syndrome is a subtype of limited scleroderma characterised by calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. The patient's episodic finger discolouration in response to cold or stress strongly suggests Raynaud's phenomenon, which is a hallmark of CREST syndrome. Although she has no other systemic symptoms at present, early-stage CREST can predominantly present with Raynaud’s phenomenon before other features develop.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are connective tissue disorders that primarily affect the skin, joints, and blood vessel walls, leading to joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility. While vascular Ehlers-Danlos Chatcan withinvolve vascular abnormalities, including possible digital ischemia similar to Raynaud’s phenomenon, it does not

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Due to its multi-system involvement, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) typically presents with a wide range of symptoms, such as a characteristic malar rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, serositis, renal disorders, and neurological symptoms. While Raynaud's phenomenon can be associated with SLE, it is generally not the sole presenting symptom. The absence of these additional features makes isolated Raynaud's phenomenon less likely to be due to SLE in this patient.

stem: You review a 78-year-old woman who complains of severe proximal muscle pain and stiffness, which is worst in the early morning on rising from bed. Which one of the following features would suggest a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica?
options: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) just above the normal range
Mild response to corticosteroid therapy after 4 weeks treatment
Pain and muscle stiffness worst in the mornings
explanation:
Pain and muscle stiffness worst in the mornings
Polymyalgia rheumatica is a common clinical syndrome in patients over the age of 55 years and is characterised by stiffness and soreness in the shoulder- and hip-girdle areas. It is sometimes associated with mild joint swelling.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) just above the normal range
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) just above the normal range is incorrect. The ESR is usually markedly elevated. Laboratory findings include normocytic/normochromic anaemia and markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). Serum alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase can also be elevated.

Painless muscle weakness
Painless muscle weakness is incorrect. In PMR, pain is the prominent feature. These patients may have ‘power limited by pain’ on neurological testing, but do not have a proximal myopathy true weakness.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of arthritis of many years’ duration that has deformed her hands presents with pain and colour changes in the fingers of both hands on exposure to cold, dryness in her mouth and a gritty sensation in her eyes. Her GP is concerned because her immunoglobulin profile is abnormal. IgG: 45 (5-16g/L) IgA: 2.4 (1.0-4.0g/L) IgM: 1.3 (0.5-2.0g/L) From what complication is she suffering?
explanation:
Sjögren’s syndrome
This lady has Sjögren’s syndrome (dry eyes, dry mouth and Raynaud’s syndrome), which is probably secondary to rheumatoid arthritis. Sjögren’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder of unknown aetiology, characterised by lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to glandular fibrosis and exocrine failure. The age of onset is usually in the fourth and fifth decades, with a female to male ratio of 9:1. The disease may be primary or secondary in association with other autoimmune diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroiditis or primary biliary cholangitis). Dryness of the eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) may be demonstrated by Schirmer’s test. Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor and Ro and La antibodies are present in most cases.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. This condition does not explain her ocular symptoms. Secondary Sjögren’s is recognized in this condition.

stem: A 70-year-old man with a long history of cervical spondylosis presents with pain, tingling and numbness in both arms. He has increased tone, hyper-reflexia and upgoing plantars on examination of the lower limbs. What would the most appropriate treatment be in his case?
explanation:
Neurosurgical referral
Bilateral root pain with paraesthesiae in patients with cervical spondylosis, accompanied by lower limb upper motor neurone signs, is a neurosurgical emergency because a central disc prolapse may compress the cervical spinal cord.

Analgesia and sedation
Analgesia and sedation is incorrect. An urgent neurosurgical referral is essential in this case.

Bedrest
Bedrest is incorrect. An urgent neurosurgical referral is essential in this case.

Cervical root block
Cervical root block is incorrect. An urgent neurosurgical referral is essential in this case.

Soft support collar
Soft support collar is incorrect. An urgent neurosurgical referral is essential in this case.

stem: A 54-year-old right-handed man with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic complaining of left shoulder pain and stiffness. He says this pain came on gradually over the past few months then gradually began to ease, although now the joint is very stiff. He tells you that his movement is now severely limited on that side such that he can’t continue his hobby of woodworking anymore. There is no point tenderness on palpation of the joint, although all movements are severely restricted due to stiffness, including passive external rotation. X-ray of the shoulder is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Referral for physiotherapy
This patient has adhesive capsulitis, which is more commonly seen in patients with underlying diabetes or thyroid disease. The diagnosis is made clinically, and radiology is only usually performed if there is any doubt as to the underlying cause of shoulder pain. Three phases of disease are commonly seen: initial, severe pain; this is then replaced by a predominant picture of stiffness then gradual recovery, which may take as long as 1–3 years. In the early stage of adhesive capsulitis, intra-articular steroids may help. This patient is outside of that period, and therefore analgesia and physiotherapy are the most appropriate courses of management.

Intra-articular steroid injection
Intra-articular steroid injection is incorrect. Some studies suggest that intra-articular steroids may be useful in the early stages of the disease but this man has clearly passed the window where they might be useful.

stem: A 37-year-old gym instructor gives a 2-year history of numbness and burning of his fingers precipitated by cold. He now feels tightness in his fingers and is unable to extend them completely. He also complains of a progressive difficulty in swallowing food. Which one of the following blood investigations would most aid in the diagnosis?
explanation:
Anticentromere antibodies
This patient has limited cutaneous scleroderma, which usually starts with Raynaud’s phenomenon many years before the appearance of any skin changes. He has Raynaud’s, sclerodactyly and oesophageal dysmotility. In limited scleroderma the skin involvement is limited to the hands, face, feet and forearms. The skin is tight over the fingers and often produces flexion deformities of the fingers. Anticentromere antibodies occur in 70–80% of cases.

Antinuclear antibodies
Antinuclear antibodies is incorrect. ANAs, although likely to be positive, are non-specific and non-diagnostic.

Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. Haemolytic anaemia is not specific for this condition.

Normocytic normochromic anaemia
Normocytic normochromic anaemia is incorrect. Normochromic anaemia is not specific for this condition.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with increasing headache, nausea, vertigo, decreasing vision in both eyes and persistent fever. She also complains of pain in her legs when she goes jogging. Her blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg and her femoral pulses are weak, with a radio–femoral delay. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Takayasu’s arteritis
This patient has classic symptoms of Takayasu’s arteritis. She is a young female, with headache, vertigo (likely due to poor posterior territory circulation), systemic upset (fever), claudication, hypertension and weak pulses. Takayasu’s arteritis is a chronic inflammatory granulomatous panarteritis of the major arteries – the carotid, innominate and subclavian arteries and the ascending arch of the aorta. The brachial, radial and ulnar arteries can also be involved. It most commonly affects women (the ratio of women to men is 8:1), with a typical age onset of 25–30 years. Although it has a worldwide distribution, it is most common in Asia. The usual presentation is with claudication and systemic symptoms of fever, arthralgia and weight loss.

Coarctation of aorta
Coarctation of aorta is incorrect. She has many features not seen with coarctation (eg systemic symptoms). Coarctation of the aorta most commonly occurs in the region where the ductus arteriosus joins Chatthe withaorta, i.e. at the isthmus, just below the origin of the left subclavian artery. The other features that this patient demonstrates

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis commonly presents with upper airway involvement (typically epistaxis, nasal crusting and sinusitis), lower airways involvement (haemoptysis, dyspnoea) with kidney disease.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a symmetrical polyarthritis comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has been taking regular paracetamol and diclofenac but is still suffering from significant joint pains. On examination she has valgus deformity of both elbows and evidence of active synovitis affecting her wrists, hands, knees and ankles. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 500 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Rheumatoid factor + Which one of the following is the most appropriate additional management?
explanation:
Methotrexate
This woman has rheumatoid arthritis – as evidenced by small joint polyarthritis, with raised inflammatory markers and positive rheumatoid factor. She has a reactive thrombocytosis, as platelets may rise as an acute phase marker, secondary to inflammation. Methotrexate is the first-line disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD). It is usually given as a single once-weekly dose with additional folic acid.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the Respiratory Clinic with increased shortness of breath. She has suffered from Raynaud’s syndrome for some time, and around 6–9 months ago began treatment for gastro-oesophageal reﬂux. Other past history of note includes smoking of 10 cigarettes per day. On examination, her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg, with a pulse of 83 bpm. Auscultation of the chest reveals ﬁne inspiratory crackles throughout both lung ﬁelds. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 135 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l FEV1 2.1 FVC 2.3 Adjusted KCO Low Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Systemic sclerosis The constellation of symptoms and signs seen here, with Raynaud’s, gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease, dyspnoea and a restrictive pattern of spirometry, is highly suggestive of systemic sclerosis with pulmonary ﬁbrosis. Antinuclear antibody testing is usually positive, high-resolution CT scanning reveals changes characteristic of interstitial lung disease: pulmonary ﬁbrosis. Calcium channel blockers, prostaglandins and cyclophosphamide have all been used in the treatment of systemic sclerosis related lung disease, and PDE5 inhibitors are now used extensively for control of pulmonary hypertension. A Asthma One would expect an obstructive pattern of spirometry, and onset of asthma at this age would be unusual. Polyphonic wheezes are more RHEUMATO likely to be heard, as crackles may signify infection. B Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) An obstructive spirometry pattern would be found and the extrapulmonary features are not associated with COPD. D Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Although the features could be consistent with SLE, the absence of any rashes or cytopaenias make SLE less likely than systemic sclerosis. E Idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis The most striking feature dissuading you from the diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary ﬁbrosis is Raynaud’s phenomenon, which is strongly linked to connective tissue disease.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with an acutely painful and red right big toe. His uric acid level is 0.4 mmol/l (normal range 0.23–0.46 mmol/l). What is the most common cause of hyperuricaemia in gout?
options: Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid
Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver
Impaired renal excretion of uric acid
explanation:
Impaired renal excretion of uric acid
Around 90% of patients with gout have impaired renal excretion of urate. N.B. 40% of cases of acute gout have a normal serum urate, as with this patient.

Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid
Decreased faecal excretion of uric acid is incorrect. Although one-third of uric acid is removed in the faeces, faecal removal is not associated with hyperuricaemia.

Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver
Decreased removal of uric acid by the liver is incorrect. The liver is not involved in urate removal.

Increased production of uric acid
Increased production of uric acid is incorrect. 10% exhibit increased production of urate.

stem: A 66-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with a 2-week history of progressive shoulder pain. She ﬁnds it particularly difﬁcult to get dressed in the morning when her pain is at its worst. She feels generally weak and fatigued and has lost approximately 2 kg in weight. She has no past medical history of note. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 90 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 127/77 mmHg. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal, with vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen, with no palpable organomegaly. There is bilateral proximal muscle stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inﬂammatory condition that more commonly presents in women over the age of 60 years. It has similarities with the large vessel vasculitis temporal or giant cell arteritis (GCA), and if visual symptoms are present, GCA should be considered, along with urgent referral to Ophthalmology. PMR tends to have a rapid onset and is characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness which is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy which causes proximal muscle weakness. The treatment of choice is long-term steroidal therapy. A Adhesive capsulitis Adhesive capsulitis, or ‘frozen shoulder’, is the gradual onset of pain and stiffness of the shoulder joint. It is more common in middle-aged women. However, usually, only one shoulder is affected. Bilateral shoulder pain and stiffness should raise suspicion of an alternative diagnosis. B Fibromyalgia Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome that more commonly affects women. It is characterised by widespread pain that can frequently fail to improve with regular analgesia. Other illnesses often coexist with ﬁbromyalgia such as irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache and atypical chest pain. Unlike PMR, ﬁbromyalgia is not an inﬂammatory disease and the intensity of the symptoms in the morning that improve throughout the day suggests an alternative diagnosis. C Hyperthyroidism Hyperthyroidism and other endocrine diseases such as Cushing’s disease can cause proximal myopathy. This patient presents with additional symptoms which could indicate hyperthyroidism, including weight loss. However, proximal muscle pain and stiffness indicate an inﬂammatory cause of this patient’s symptoms, in contrast to myopathy that typically causes muscle weakness, but less likely pain or stiffness. E Polymyositis Polymyositis is an inﬂammatory muscle disease associated with inﬂammation and weakness of proximal muscles. Proximal muscle RHEUMATO ache may also be a symptom. However, morning stiffness is not a feature of polymyositis and is more suggestive of PMR.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has been recently diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. She wants to know more about the possible symptoms that she may experience in the future. What is the most common gastrointestinal complication seen in this condition?
explanation:
Mouth ulcers
Mouth ulcers are the most common gastrointestinal problem in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and may be a presenting feature.

Autoimmune hepatitis
Autoimmune hepatitis is incorrect. Liver involvement is unusual, though lupoid antibodies have been noted in patients with autoimmune hepatitis.

Intestinal infarction
Intestinal infarction is incorrect. Intestinal infarction may result from a hernia.

Mesenteric vasculitis
Mesenteric vasculitis is incorrect. Mesenteric vasculitis is more common in polyarteritis nodosa.

Pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is incorrect. Pancreatitis is rare in SLE.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with three weeks history of daily fevers, an erythematous rash which appears to get worse with the spikes of fever, joint pains affecting both knees, his right elbow and his left ankle, and extreme fatigue. He is unable to hold down his job as a builder because of these symptoms. On examination, his temperature is 37.3°C, heart rate is 68/min and regular. There is a pericardial rub, the chest is clear. You conﬁrm evidence of oligoarthritis. Investigation Results Normal Value Hb 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 12.8 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 149 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 micromol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 75 mm/1st hour 0–10 mm/ 1st hour CRP 210 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Ferritin 590 microg/l 20–250 µg/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Adult onset Juvenile Chronic Arthritis The answer is Adult onset juvenile chronic arthritis (JCA) - The fevers lasting for more than 2 weeks, coupled with oligoarthritis, an erythematous rash and pericarditis ﬁts with systemic JCA. The fever seen with JCA exhibits periodicity, and occurs once or twice per day. Autoantibodies are generally unhelpful, with ANA and rheumatoid factor positivity being seen in approximately 10% of patients. NSAIDs form the basis of symptom relief, and a short course of systemic corticosteroids can be considered to gain disease control. Second-line agents include both methotrexate and anti-TNF based therapies. D Septic arthritis Septic arthritis is incorrect, it is a possible differential for the oligoarthritis seen here, but is less likely given the 3 week history of fevers, suggesting a subacute presentation. B Haemochromatosis Haemochromatosis is incorrect, because although the ferritin is elevated, this is because ferritin is an acute phase protein, rather than representing iron overload. C Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect, it is usually associated with a symmetrical small joint polyarthritis, and is therefore unlikely here. E Seronegative arthritis Seronegative arthritis, is incorrect, it is often associated with lower back pain / sacroilitis, or enthesopathies such as plantar fasciitis. None of those features are seen here.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with early-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She has suffered from a number of infections as a child and you wonder about inherited complement deficiency. Deficiency of which one of the following complement factors is most associated with early onset SLE?
explanation:
C4
C4 deficiency is associated with SLE. Deficiencies of early parts of the classical pathway increase the risk of SLE. Early onset SLE is most associated with C1q deficiency, although it also occurs with increased frequency in those individuals with C4 deficiency, C1 r/s deficiency and C2 deficiency. For C1 or C4 deficiency there is equal sex incidence. In C2 deficiency the sex distribution reflects non-complement associated SLE and occurs slightly later.

C3
C3 is incorrect. C3 deficiency increases the risk of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS).

C5
C5 is incorrect. Deficiency of C5 is associated with severe recurrent infections including meningitis.

C7
C7 is incorrect. Deficiencies of late parts of the classical pathway (C5–C9) increase the risk of recurrent meningitis.

stem: A 55-year-old man attends the clinic complaining of increasing pain and weakness of his lower limbs which is preventing him from getting up from a chair easily and from climbing the stairs. Blood tests show a creatine kinase level of 14,500 IU/l. A chest X-ray reveals a large shadow in the right mid-zone and pulmonary function tests reveal evidence of pulmonary fibrosis. Which antibody is most strongly associated with this underlying disease?
explanation:
Anti-Jo-1
This patient has polymyositis, which is often associated with an increased risk of malignancy (threefold). The typical presentation is with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, usually affecting the lower extremities first. Creatine kinase is usually elevated and is a guide to disease activity. Antisynthetase (Anti-Jo-1) antibodies are strongly associated with polymyositis and interstitial lung disease (the Jo1 syndrome).

Anti-centromere
Anti-centromere is incorrect. Anti-centromere antibodies are found in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Anti-dsDNA
Anti-dsDNA is incorrect. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are found in SLE.

Anti-Scl-70
Anti-Scl-70 is incorrect. Anti-Scl-70 antibodies are found in diffuse systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 57-year-old man on ciclosporin following a renal transplant suddenly develops severe pain, swelling and redness in his left knee. Which one of the following investigations would be most helpful in providing a diagnosis?
options: Joint fluid microscopy and Gram stain
explanation:
Joint fluid microscopy and Gram stain
This patient most probably has septic arthritis as a consequence of his immunosuppressive therapy with ciclosporin. Joint fluid microscopy and Gram staining would establish the diagnosis.

Blood culture
Blood cultures may not be positive in up to one-third of cases, but should be done.

CRP
The CRP is likely to be non-specifically elevated.

Serum creatinine
The creatinine is not likely to be affected.

X-ray of the knee joint
X-ray of the joint would not reveal any abnormality (unless a fracture is suspected, but thereis nil to suggest this).

stem: A 47-year-old personal assistant attends the outpatient clinic with a six-month history of malaise and joint pains. She has had to quit her job. She is also complaining of difﬁculty sleeping at night and urinary frequency. She complains of still being tired on waking up. On examination, palpation of her muscles appears to cause pain in several different regions, especially around the shoulders and neck. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 126 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 198 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.9 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 2.8 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 11 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 2.0 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 28 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 101 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 25 IU/l 5–30 IU/l (Anti-CCP) Negative Rheumatoid factor (RF) Negative Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Fibromyalgia Fibromyalgia is said to occur in between 1 and 2% of the general population and has a female to male ratio of 9:1, presenting most often in the 30–50-year age group. It presents with musculoskeletal pain that often has multiple trigger points and may be poorly deﬁned. The 1990 ACR classiﬁcation criteria for FM include (1) the presence of widespread pain for more than 3 months and (2) pain, not just tenderness, that can be elicited by manual pressure of approximately 4 kg/cm2 at 11 or more deﬁned tender points. The number of painful tender points is correlated strongly with psychologic distress, not only in patients with FM but also in the general population. (These criteria are classiﬁcation criteria for the selection of subjects for research studies, not diagnostic criteria.) At a clinical level, ﬁbromyalgia is much more than widespread pain. Substantial overlap exists in major depressive disorder, various anxiety disorders and chronic fatigue syndrome, and in multiple regional pain syndromes, such as headache, atypical chest pain (chest pain with normal cardiac evaluation ﬁndings), irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pelvic pain, temporomandibular joint pain ( jaw pain with no underlying pathologic condition) and others. The EULAR 2016 management guidelines suggested that initial management should involve patient education and focus on nonpharmacological therapies. In case of non-response, further therapies should be tailored to the speciﬁc needs of the individual and RHEUMATO may involve psychological therapies (for mood disorders and unhelpful coping strategies), pharmacotherapy (for severe pain or sleep disturbance, such as tricyclic antidepressents) and/or a multimodal rehabilitation programme, such as graded exercise programmes. B Depression However, this lady may have depression as well as ﬁbromyalgia; there is association and overlap. C Rheumatoid arthritis The normal autoimmune screen and inﬂammatory markers make RA unlikely. D Polymyalgia rheumatic This patient has a normal ESR. Patients with polymyalgia rheumatic usually have elevated inﬂammatory markers – ESR and CRP. Additionally she is slightly too young for PMR, which is very rare in patients under 50 years of age. E Systemic lupus erythematosus The normal autoimmune screen and ESR make SLE very unlikely – 95% of patients with SLE have a positive ANA. This lady has a negative ANA, effectively excluding SLE.

stem: You are asked by the obstetricians to review a 28-year-old woman who has had three previous miscarriages. Each of her miscarriages occurred at around the 14th week of pregnancy. Blood testing showed positive antiphospholipid antibodies. Further questioning into her medical history revealed a history of venous thrombosis after a plane ﬂight. She is 8 weeks’ pregnant. She is commenced on low-dose aspirin. Which further intervention would you implement?
explanation: B Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin daily This patient has evidence of the antiphospholipid syndrome (APLS). This is characterised by recurrent miscarriage with three unexplained mid-trimester fetal losses and a venous thrombosis, albeit somewhat ‘provoked’. She likely has antiphospholipid antibodies. Standard therapy where there is recurrent miscarriage and a diagnosis of APLS is low-molecular-weight heparin and lowdose aspirin during pregnancy and approximately 6 weeks postpartum, which is also a prothrombotic state. APLS is thought to be the cause of complications in around 45/100 000 pregnancies. E IV immunoglobulin therapy There is no indication for immunomodulation with IV immunoglobulin therapy. She needs vascular prophylaxis and anticoagulation. A Warfarin therapy Warfarin is teratogenic and contra-indicated in pregnancy, particu- RHEUMATO larly in the ﬁrst and third trimesters. Outside pregnancy, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, patients with a history of thrombosis are usually managed with warfarin therapy. C Prednisolone 40 mg daily There is no indication for prednisolone, unless there are features of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (multi-organ involvement), which this lady does not have. D Azathioprine therapy There is no indication for immunosuppression with azathioprine. She needs vascular prophylaxis and anticoagulation.

stem: A 58-year-old male patient with well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis reminds you of his scheduled right knee replacement surgery in 6 weeks’ time. His medications include etanercept 50 mg subcutaneously weekly, prednisolone 5 mg per day and co-codamol tablets. What advice regarding his medication should be given prior to surgery?
options: Stop etanercept 4–6 weeks prior to surgery
Stop etanercept 2–4 weeks prior to surgery
Stop both etanercept and prednisolone 2–4 weeks prior to surgery
explanation:
B Stop etanercept 2–4 weeks prior to surgery The British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) guidelines (January

2005) for prescribing tumour necrosis factor (TNF-α) blockers in adults with RA recommend withholding etanercept and other TNFblockers (inﬂiximab and adalimumab) for 2–4 weeks prior to a major surgical procedure. Stopping earlier may lead to disease ﬂareup and thus interfere with the surgery. Treatment may be restarted postoperatively if there is no evidence of infection and once wound healing is satisfactory. Small-dose prednisolone is safe – it doesn’t increase the risk of infection or interfere with wound healing and therefore need not be stopped. However, care must be taken to administer 50–100 mg hydrocortisone perioperatively in order to meet with increased demands during the stress of major surgery. C Stop both etanercept and prednisolone 2–4 weeks prior to surgery This may increase the risk of an addisonian crisis. A Stop etanercept 4–6 weeks prior to surgery This may increase the risk of RA disease ﬂare-up. D Keep the medications unchanged This may increase the risk of infection. E Double the dose of etanercept This may increase the risk of infection and is not a licensed dose regimen for etanercept, which could have potentially dangerous effects.

stem: A 19-year-old man was referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with a long history of pain in the back and knee joints. The initial problem started with recurrent back and wrist pain when he was 6 years old. He was treated for possible juvenile arthritis, which often responded to analgesia. Over the year the disease has been relapsing and remitting, but since last year the back pain has been constant all over the spine and has not responded to analgesia. Several investigations in the past include X-ray of the spine and knee, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody and autoimmune proﬁle. All these investigations were reported as normal. He had a normal childhood with no illness and there is no family history of note. He has seen the dermatologists for an abnormal dark-brown pigmentation in his ears and sclera, but no cause was found. On examination, his knees are swollen and painful. He also has tenderness all over his spine. Both sclera and ears show an abnormal dark brown pigmentation. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 103 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 9.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 250 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.6 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 0.9 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l Glucose 4.2 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l ALP 110 u/l 30 - 150 u/l X-ray spine Calciﬁcation of intervertebral disc X-ray knees Soft tissue swelling with meniscal calciﬁcation Urinalysis: Colour Dark Glucose +++ Blood - What is the probable underlying diagnosis?
explanation: D Alkaptonuria Alkaptonuria is a hereditary disease characterised by a deﬁciency of the enzyme homogentisic oxidase, which is responsible for the degradation of homogentisic acid produced from phenylalanine and tyrosine. Accumulation of homogentisic acid causes pigmentation of the urine, sclera and connective tissues. Deposition in the joints causes cartilage pigmentation (ochronosis) and degeneration. Homogentisic acid is a reducing agent, and therefore it gives an incorrect positive Glucostix test but normal Clinitest. Urine, after standing, becomes dark in colour due to oxidation of the product. The knees and spine are commonly affected. The sacroiliac joint may be spared. No curative treatment is yet available. C Phenylketonuria Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism that results in decreased metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine. Untreated PKU can lead to intellectual disability, seizures, behavioural problems and mental disorder. It may also result in a musty smell and lighter skin. A Osteogenesis imperfecta In osteogenesis imperfecta the X-rays are likely to be abnormal and blue sclerae are often observed. B Ankylosing spondylitis X-rays would show changes in the sacroiliac joints (erosions, sclerosis, fusion) and there are no pigmentary problems. E Polyarticular Still’s disease Still’s disease is not associated with urinary problems or ocular pigmentation.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted via the Emergency Department after suffering acute lower back pain. X-ray in the department revealed two compression fractures suspicious of osteoporosis. Past medical history of note includes depression and anxiety. On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 16 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 125/72 mmHg, with a pulse of 55/min and regular. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 112 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 202 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 102 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.2 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l ALP 115 u/l 30 - 150 u/l T-score –3.1 Which of the following is likely to be the most important contributory factor to her condition?
options: Low BMI leading to secondary ovarian failure
explanation:
A Low BMI leading to secondary ovarian failure This patient has a very low BMI (and is slightly bradycardic), and further questioning may reveal that she is not currently menstruating and may not have been for some time. This leads to a lack of oestrogenisation and consequent negative effects on bone mineral density. Increased BMI in contrast is associated with increased bone mineral density up to the point of development of type 2 diabetes, when a fall in BMD and increased risk of fracture is seen. C Hyperthyroidism Hyperthyroidism is another possibility, but we are given no information that she has symptoms or signs of this and indeed she is bradycardic, not tachycardic. B Genetic predisposition to osteoporosis Clearly a genetic predisposition to osteoporosis might also increase the risk of fracture at an early age, but BMI is almost certainly the greatest contributor to risk here. D Hypovitaminosis D

Although a risk factor for demineralisation of bone, her biggest risk factor is low BMI. E Calcium deﬁciency Her calcium is in the normal range.

stem: A 34-year-old, right-handed woman complains of pain in her right wrist which has been evident for 3 months. Recently she has also noted some pain in her left wrist, although of much less severity. She works at a till in a superstore and has been ﬁnding it difﬁcult to continue with her job. The examination reveals a localised swelling and tenderness over the lateral, dorsal aspect of the right wrist and mild tenderness in the left wrist, particularly over the radial aspect. The haematology and biochemistry blood test results are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A De Quervain’s tenosynovitis This lady has tenderness at the thumb-sided tendons – at the radial side of the wrist and at the base of the thumb – and probably has an occupational aetiology given her job as checkout cashier. De Quervain’s tenosynovitis refers to inﬂammation of the abductor pollicis longus tendon at the wrist joint. It is best diagnosed by inspecting the wrist from the radial side, with the palms together. It is then seen as a unilateral swelling, extending from the ﬁrst carpometacarpal joint proximally. The diagnosis is conﬁrmed by Finkelstein’s test. In this test, the patient is asked to bring the thumb across the palm and clasp the ﬁngers around it. The examiner then pulls it in the ulnar direction, which elicits a sharp pain. This condition is commonly caused by occupational or avocational repetitive movement of the thumb, but has also been associated with RA, psoriatic arthritis, direct trauma, pregnancy and the post-partum period. Treatment options include splinting, steroid injections into the joint and surgical decompression of the tendon tunnel. C Wrist synovitis This lady has localised swelling at the radial side (not the whole wrist). Wrist synovitis is inﬂammation of the wrist joint and therefore the whole wrist would be swollen diffusely. RHEUMATO B Intersection syndrome This lady has irritation at the ﬁrst dorsal compartment. Intersection syndrome is a painful condition that affects the thumb side of the forearm when inﬂammation occurs at the intersection of the muscle bellies of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis crossing over the extensor carpi radialis longus and the extensor carpi radialis brevis. These 1st and 2nd dorsal muscle compartments intersect at this location, hence the name. The mechanism of injury is usually repetitive resisted extension, as with rowing, weight-lifting or pulling. D Ganglion A ganglion is a discrete, palpable lump. E Trigger thumb A trigger digit is a common disorder characterised by catching, snapping or locking of the involved ﬁnger ﬂexor tendon, associated with dysfunction and pain.

stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a second episode of acute gout over the past four months. He was given a short course of ibuprofen, and his symptoms settled over the course of a few days. Medications include ramipril, amlodipine and bendroﬂumethiazide. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 134/72 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m2. There is clear acute gout affecting the right great toe. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 130 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 189 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urate 630 mmol/l 0.1–0.4 mmol/l CRP 195 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Glucose 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to reducing the chance of further gout episodes?
explanation: D Stop Bendroﬂumethiazide Thiazides are known to increase the risk for acute gout because they reduce renal clearance of uric acid. As such, they increase the propensity for acute attacks of gout. It is thought that attacks of gout are triggered by a twin rise in triglyceride and uric acid levels; hence the RHEUMATO negative impact of bendroﬂumethiazide on triglycerides may further increase the risk for acute episodes. A Allopurinol Given this patient is taking a thiazide diuretic, stopping the diuretic is the most appropriate ﬁrst-line intervention. In the event that the urate level is still raised after cessation of the thiazide, allopurinol would be the next step for long-term prophylaxis. B Benzbromarone Benzbromarone is available in the United Kingdom on a named patient basis, and it is a uricosuric that is usually added in to allopurinol therapy. C Ibuprofen While long-term ibuprofen would likely keep the patient’s symptoms at bay, it is likely to carry signiﬁcant risks, given his coexisting hypertension, and should be avoided. E Stop Ramipril Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are associated with an increased risk for gout, though not to the same degree as thiazide diuretics. It is therefore appropriate to ﬁrst stop bendroﬂumethiazide and then consider stopping ramipril if symptoms persist.

stem: A 45-year old woman presented with 4-month history of an erythematous rash over her cheeks, her anterior upper chest and the backs of her hands. Over the same period she had become short of breath on exertion. In the last month, she had also complained of difﬁculty walking up the stairs at home. General examination revealed a rash as noted above and dilated capillaries at the base of some of the ﬁngernails. On examination of the chest, there were a few bibasal crepitations. Neurological examination revealed mild weakness of hip ﬂexion but it was an otherwise normal exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Dermatomyositis

This patient has a rash which is typical for dermatomyositis. The rash over the chest probably represents the ‘V- sign’ and the rash on the back of the hands is likely to be Gottron’s papules. Proximal weakness is manifest as difﬁculty walking upstairs. The shortness of breath and bi-basal crepitation are likely to represent complicating interstitial lung disease. B Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) E-GPA is a systemic vasculitis of small vessels and is associated with p-ANCA. It usually occurs in persons with a history of airway allergic hypersensitivity. Eosinophilia occurs in association with systemic features such as weight loss and night sweats. Vasculitis, particularly of the peritoneal vasculature, usually occurs in the ﬁnal stages of evolution of the illness. C Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) This case description is not at all typical of RA, which is primarily an inﬂammatory disease of the joints. Skin manifestations can occur occasionally in RA, including nodules, pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum and palmar erythema. Pulmonary ﬁbrosis can also occur as a complication of RA. However, the lack of joint involvement in this case makes RA extremely unlikely. D Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) This case description is not at all typical for AIP, in which the most common manifestations are abdominal pain and psychiatric disturbances. E Systemic lupus erythematosus Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can have a rash similar to that seen in dermatomyositis. The rash in SLE is photosensitive and most commonly seen in sun-exposed areas – the cheeks (i.e. a malar distribution), upper anterior and posterior chest and over the backs of the hands. Whilst not really described clearly in this case, a heliotrope (i.e. peri-orbital ring) rash, rather than a malar rash, is more typical of dermatomyositis. Despite the potential similarity of the rash, dermatomyositis is a more likely answer in this case because of the co-existing muscle weakness and suggestion of interstitial lung disease.

stem: A 64-year-old man is referred to you by the Emergency Department. He presents with a diffusely warm, swollen ankle joint although he does not seem in particular pain.The swelling has been worsening gradually over the past 12 weeks. Medications include gliclazide 160 mg/day. Examination in the Emergency Department reveals a grossly deformed red, swollen right ankle. RHEUMATO Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 122 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.5 × 10 /l 4.0 - 11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 186 × 10 /l 150 - 400 × 10 /l CRP 12 mg/l < 10 mg/l Ankle x-ray Loss of joint margin, significant bone destruction and joint remodelling Which one of the following interventions is most appropriate in this case?
explanation:
C Immobilisation in a plaster cast This patient has Charcot arthropathy, the clue being that he is not in any pain (it is an anaesthetic joint), the foot is grossly deformed and he likely has underlying type 2 diabetes, indicated by the prescription of gliclazide. Immobilisation in a cast for 3–6 months is the treatment of choice; this is thought to be complemented by use of bisphosphonates: the reduction in bone reabsorption associated with bisphosphonates is thought to accelerate healing. Good control of blood glucose to reduce the risk of microvascular complications is associated with a decreased incidence in Charcot arthropathy, although once established it cannot be reversed. B IV Flucloxacillin While the joint is hot and swollen, the normal C-reactive protein and white blood cell count make it unlikely that this is due to osteomyelitis, and therefore antibiotics are not indicated. A Calcium and vitamin D Although one facet of treatment is to ensure he is vitamin D replete, the most important part of managing a Charcot joint is to immobilise it and allow healing. D Surgical drainage Although the joint appears ‘swollen’, it is actually grossly deformed due to underlying bone and the CRP is normal, making infection very unlikely, and there is no effusion to drain. E Ibuprofen 400 mg po tds A Charcot joint is anaesthetic and therefore not painful, as given to

you in the question, and therefore neither analgesia nor anti-inﬂammatories is indicated.

stem: You review a 42-year-old woman who is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic because blood tests have shown a positive CCP antibody at > 200. Her rheumatoid factor is negative. She denies any joint pains or stiffness and examination is normal, with no evidence of synovitis. The blood test was performed as part of a health check. Her great-grandmother had rheumatoid arthritis with signiﬁcant deformities at a time that unfortunately, biological therapy was not available. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 137 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/ Platelets (PLT) 188 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/ Neutrophils 2.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/ Lymphocytes 1.8 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/ ESR 10 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 2 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 28 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 101 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 15 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Glucose 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Anti-CCP RF Negative ANA Negative What is the best management plan?
options: Nothing: reassure and discharge her from clinic
explanation: B Advise her to stop smoking There is evidence that stopping smoking and delaying the onset of the development of arthritis in patients at risk of developing RA (such as this lady, with positive anti-CCP antibodies) can ameliorate the prognosis of patients in whom arthritic symptoms have already developed (e.g. reduce the burden of joint damage). C Start hydroxychloroquine Although hydroxychloroquine is the best-tolerated and least toxic DMARD, there is no evidence that patients at risk of developing RA (asymptomatic, anti-CCP positive) have any better prognosis when treated before symptoms develop. A Start methotrexate This lady has anti-CCP antibodies and a family history of rheumatoid arthritis. She does have a higher risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, although she does not have any synovitis currently and therefore the beneﬁts of starting methotrexate do not outweigh the risk. D Nothing: reassure and discharge her from clinic This lady is asymptomatic and could be discharged from the clinic. However, she should be informed about the effects of smoking on her joints, advised to stop smoking and to seek medical advice if she develops any symptoms of joint pains, stiffness, swelling etc. E Work her up for anti-TNF This lady does not fulﬁl criteria for a diagnosis of RA, and is certainly not eligible for biologic therapy. There is no evidence that starting therapy before the onset of symptoms changes the prognosis or course of disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man from West Africa comes to the clinic for review. He had been to the Heart Failure Clinic for review some three to four weeks earlier and had been started on some new medication. He RHEUMATO tells you that he was unable to tolerate a drug called ramipril before this because it led to ‘problems with his kidneys’. Over the past two to three weeks, he has suffered increasing fatigue, night sweats and generalised joint pains. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 112/72 mmHg and a pulse of 85 bpm and regular. Despite the joint pains, there are no signs of active synovitis. There are bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.8 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 174 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 119 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ANA Positive Anti-histone antibody: Positive Anti-Ro: Negative Rheumatoid factor: Negative Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
explanation:
D Hydralazine The pattern of symptoms, coupled with the autoantibody screen seen here, is suggestive of drug-induced lupus. Patients with heart failure who cannot tolerate angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition are recommended to trial hydralazine and nitrate as alternatives, which leaves hydralazine as the most likely cause of drug-induced lupus here. Withdrawal of the drug is likely to lead to resolution of symptoms over the course of a few weeks. Other causes of drug-induced lupus include thiazides, although anti-Ro antibodies will be positive, and procainamide, isoniazid, timolol and phenytoin. A Bendroﬂumethiazide Anti-Ro antibodies are often positive in drug-induced lupus related to thiazide diuretics, and so the fact that anti-Ro is negative here makes bendroﬂumethiazide less likely as the underlying cause. B Bisoprolol

There are case reports of drug-induced lupus in association with beta-blocker therapy, although they would not be considered a likely cause here. The main concern is, of course, bronchospasm and worsening of asthma in association with their use. C Furosemide Like bisoprolol, furosemide is more rarely described as a cause of drug-induced lupus, compared to hydralazine. It is most often described as an exacerbating factor, alongside other drugs known to cause lupus themselves. E Isosorbide mononitrate Nitrates are not described as a cause of drug-induced lupus and are effective in reducing preload in patients with cardiac failure.

stem: A 51-year-old man, who owns a bar in Tenerife, comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has suffered increasingly severe knee pains and is now unable to bend his right knee due to pain and swelling. He admits to drinking up to 10 units of alcohol per day and has recently been recommended to follow a diabetic diet by his Spanish general practitioner. Examination reveals a blood pressure RHEUMATO of 155/95 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. He is tanned, in keeping with living in Spain. There is truncal obesity, with a body mass index (BMI) of 33 kg/m2. Both knees are swollen, the right more so than the left, and ﬂexion of the right knee is limited to around 30 degrees. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal values Hb 134 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CRP 42 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 10.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l ALT 122 IU/l 7–55 IU/l ALP 95 IU/l 30–150 IU/l Ferritin 630 µg/l 24–355 µg/l (male) Urate 0.43 mmol/l 0.1–0.4 mmol/l (male) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Pseudogout This patient presents with oligoarthritis and has evidence of chronic liver disease with abnormal liver function tests and elevated ferritin and blood glucose levels. This constellation of features supports an underlying diagnosis of haemochromatosis, which is associated with pseudogout or pyrophosphate arthropathy. A Gout While uric acid levels are commonly measured in patients with suspected gout, it is not very sensitive or speciﬁc, as 15% of patients with gout have normal serum uric acid levels while 25% of the normal population have hyperuricaemia. Given the other features present, pseudogout is the more likely underlying diagnosis, as opposed to gout. B Osteoarthritis There are multiple features in the history which point towards a diagnosis of pseudogout over osteoarthritis, though it is an important differential. The joint X-ray would help distinguish between the two diagnoses. Pseudogout has the classical chondrocalcinosis appearance,

whereas in osteoarthritis, patients have loss of joint space, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts on X-ray. D Septic arthritis Given the WCC is normal and CRP level is only 42, septic arthritis seems very unlikely. The chronic nature of this patient’s condition also makes septic arthritis less likely in this scenario. E Seronegative arthritis The lack of involvement of joints other than the knees makes the diagnosis of seronegative arthritis less likely.

stem: A 34-year-old sales representative presents with severe pain going down her neck and right arm. She admits that this pain is worse on sitting in her car while driving for long periods. Past history includes two previous road trafﬁc accidents, but nil else of note. On examination, there is weakness and sensory loss over a C5/C6 nerve distribution and pain with neck movement, particularly extension. An MRI of the spinal cord is arranged. Which other investigation would be most useful in this case?
options: Plain X-rays of the right elbow
explanation: A Nerve conduction studies This patient has symptoms of cervical radiculopathy, resulting from disc degeneration due either to herniation or degenerative change (spondylosis). When there are posterior osteophytes leading to anterior spinal cord compression, as is likely here, patients present with chronic radicular arm pain, numbness and tingling sensations. The investigation of choice is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning to assess spinal cord encroachment, and nerve conduction studies to assess the degree of nerve damage. Treatment is with physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents. Patients will usually improve with time, and surgical intervention is needed in less than 5% of patients. C Autoimmune proﬁle This lady has a likely mechanical problem, with no features to suggest an autoimmune/inﬂammatory cause. RHEUMATO B Myelogram Myelography uses a real-time form of X-ray called ﬂuoroscopy and an injection of contrast material to evaluate the spinal cord, nerve roots and spinal lining (meninges). It is particularly useful for assessing the spine following surgery, and also for assessing disc abnormalities in patients who cannot undergo MRI. A myelogram is not appropriate here as it is invasive and expensive, and there are no contraindications to an MRI in this case. D Arthroscopy of the right shoulder This lady has a cervical radiculopathy, i.e. nerves emanating from the cervical spine, and therefore a shoulder arthroscopy is unlikely to help. E Plain X-rays of the right elbow The C5/C6 radiculopathy is not related to her elbow. The ulnar nerve is often compressed at the elbow, however.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining that he is unable to get up off his low sofa. There is also a history of pain and tenderness particularly over the thigh muscles and the shoulder girdle. On further questioning, he admits to shortness of breath on exercise and chronic cough. Examination reveals an obese man with obvious proximal muscle weakness and evidence of interstitial lung disease. CK level is 1050 U/l (24–195), ESR is raised and anti-Jo-1 antibodies are positive. What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Polymyositis Patients with polymyositis commonly present after 3–6 months of symptoms with painful proximal muscle weakness. CK levels may be elevated to 5–50 times the upper limit of normal. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with coexistent interstitial lung disease, Raynaud’s phenomenon and peripheral arthritis. Prednisolone is the mainstay of treatment, at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg/day. In patients who fail to show improvement, disease-

modifying steroid-sparing agents may be added. A high-protein diet and supervised exercise may further improve symptoms. Most patients have a favourable response to corticosteroid therapy, and 5year survival rates approach 80%. Women are more frequently affected than men, with a female:male ratio of 3:1. There is an association with malignancy in a signiﬁcant minority of patients, including adenocarcinomas of the cervix, lung, ovaries, pancreas, bladder and stomach. D Giant cell arteritis The lack of unilateral headache/scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and the rise in CK make GCA unlikely. A Polymyalgia rheumatica PMR is characterised by bilateral aching and morning stiffness in at least two areas (neck or torso, shoulders or proximal arms, hips or thighs). There is elevated ESR and a prompt response to low-dose glucocorticoids. The history of pain and tenderness and the additional symptoms are not consistent with PMR. B Dermatomyositis Dermatomyositis and polymyositis are both idiopathic inﬂammatory myopathies, but the former is distinguished by the presence of cutaneous lesions such as Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash or the shawl sign. E Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism should always be ruled out in patients presenting with a possible myopathy, but hypothyroid- related myopathy is not associated with a high rise in CK or anti-Jo antibodies.

stem: A-40-year old man presents to the Emergency Department with digital ulceration and areas of gangrene affecting the ﬁngers and toes. The problem started a few months back with insidious tingling, numbness and discolouration of his ﬁngers associated with pain. Gradually, the symptoms progressed with more severe discolouration and the appearance of ulcers on the tip of his ﬁngers associated with a constant burning sensation. He noticed that on walking he would experience severe pain in the instep of his foot and the calves. There is no history of angina or exertional dyspnoea. He is a heavy smoker but has no medical history. Examination revealed cold hands and feet with extensive cyanosis, ulceration and gangrene of the ﬁngers and toes. There are absent pulses in the radial, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibia arteries. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 126 g/l 135–175 g/l RHEUMATO WCC 12.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT 240 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l ESR Rheumatoid factor (RF) 20 mm/hour Negative 1–20 mm/hour ANA Absent What is the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: D Buerger’s disease This heavy smoker has critical digital ischaemia with absent pulses and negative autoantibodies. Thrombangiitis obliterans (Buerger’s disease) is a disease of small and medium-sized arteries and veins resulting in inﬂammation and ulceration. There is no excessive atheroma and it does not involve the coronary arteries like atherosclerosis. The disease occurs mainly in cigarette smokers. The patient presents with symptoms of arterial ischaemia. Migratory phlebitis in the superﬁcial vein is present in 40% of cases. The disease progresses proximally, resulting in gangrene of the digits. Diagnosis is usually clinical. Arteriogram is also of beneﬁt and will show occlusion of distal arteries of the hands and feet. Treatment is supportive and patients should stop smoking. A Takayasu’s arteritis There is no constitutional upset, or signs of large vessel and aortic involvement, inﬂammatory markers are normal and Takayasu’s usually occurs in females. B Disseminated atherosclerosis There is no history of angina or exertional dyspnoea. C Systemic sclerosis The patient has negative autoantibodies and has no other features of systemic sclerosis. E Acrocyanosis Acrocyanosis is persistent blue or cyanotic discoloration of the extremities, most commonly occurring in the hands, although it also occurs in the feet and distal parts of face. Acrocyanosis is not painful, nor is it associated with digital ulceration.

stem: A 43-year-old man attends for review. His past medical history includes renal stones treated by lithotripsy, and he also has type 2 diabetes. He is taking treatment for high cholesterol. He has been attending the clinic for a number of months with long-standing pain and swelling in his ﬁngers. This is the clinical appearance of his hands: Picture courtesy of Charlie Goldberg, M.D., UCSD School of Medicine and VA Medical Center, San Diego, CA What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Gout This is chronic gout with tophi (uric acid crystals in the soft tissues), indicating long-standing hyperuricaemia. Untreated chronic tophaceous gout can develop and lead to severe joint destruction. Men are affected twice as commonly as women, and it tends to be a disease of middle to older age; as a general rule, uric acid levels are elevated for 20 years before the onset of gout. Hyperuricaemia is associated with an increase in all-cause mortality. Patients with gout are often clustered within the metabolic syndrome: diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia and low high-density lipoproteins, though no evidence indicates that either gout or hyperuricaemia causes any of these other disorders. The relationship between serum uric acid and cardiovascular disease remains controversial, but raised uric acid may be an independent risk factor for vascular disease in some RHEUMATO individuals with other risk factors. A Calcinosis Calcinosis cutis is the deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin and subcutaneous tissue. White calcium deposits can be seen in nodules, unlike the picture shown here. C Pseudo-gout The clinical manifestations of the crystal arthropathies can be difﬁcult to distinguish. However, pseudo-gout tends to occur in older patients and risk factors include hypothyroidism, haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and Wilson’s disease. Furthermore, there are risk factors for gout in this patient. D Psoriatic arthropathy Psoriatic arthropathy most commonly presents as a poly- or oligoarthritis. There are ﬁve patterns of involvement: distal arthritis (DIP joint involvement), asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans and spondyloarthritis. This is not the description provided for this patient. E Rheumatoid arthritis The swelling is more extensive than would be expected for RA, and there is no history of joint stiffness in the history, which makes RA unlikely.

stem: A 40-year-old woman reports intermittent joint pains affecting her wrists, ankles and knees for the last six months. She describes each episode as involving pain, swelling and erythema in one of the above joints, which usually resolves with anti-inﬂammatory drugs over one to two days. Recently, the frequency of attacks has increased to two to three times per week from the previous two to three attacks every month. The last episode, involving the right knee, occurred three days ago. Examination in clinic was unremarkable for synovitis in any of the joints. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial step?
options: Give the patient open access to the rheumatology clinic when they have the next attack
explanation: A Give the patient open access to the rheumatology clinic when they have the next attack The patient is suffering from palindromic rheumatism, affecting mostly large joints. This is characterised by one or more features of inﬂammation, such as pain, swelling and erythema affecting an articular or periarticular site which lasts less than 72 hours before recovering completely. Any of the joints may be affected. In approximately 50% of patients, this may progress to rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The factors suggesting progression are small joint involvement, and a positive RFor anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP). The most common cause of recurrent or relapsing arthritis, however, is crystal arthritis. It is therefore important to ask the patient to report to clinic in the event of a future attack for synovial ﬂuid aspiration and examination for urate and calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate (CPPD) crystals. Hyperuricaemia may be present but is not diagnostic and so testing for serum uric acid is not the correct answer here. Other diseases, such as systemic autoinﬂammatory disorders (periodic fever syndromes), Whipple’s disease, arthritis associated with hyperlipidaemia and intermittent hydrarthrosis, should be taken into account in the differential diagnosis of patients with recurrent arthritis. C Bone scan A bone scan would confer a lot of radiation for this young woman which is not justiﬁed by her symptoms. B X-ray of hands This lady has a 6-month history and therefore X-rays are unlikely to be abnormal. An ultrasound (or MRI) to look for subclinical synovitis would be far more helpful than X-rays. D Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing An ANA test is non-speciﬁc and unlikely to be helpful if positive. A far more useful test would be an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide RHEUMATO (CCP) antibody, which is more sensitive and more speciﬁc for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) than rheumatoid factor, and can predate the clinical onset of RA. E Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing This presentation does not sound like vasculitis at all, and therefore ANCA testing is incorrect.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with arthritis affecting his wrists, knees, ankles and some of his ﬁnger joints. He also has marked morning stiffness and a rash which affects his trunk and extremities. You understand from his mother that he has little interest in sport. You also notice a pericardial rub. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 102 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 145 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l ESR 58 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h (MCV) 79 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ ANA + at 1:160 MRI of both knees is suggestive of synovitis; echocardiogram is suggestive of pericarditis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Whilst juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Still’s disease) normally occurs in younger children, it may occasionally present in adolescents or young adults. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and RFare almost always negative in sJIA. Their presence should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses. A positive RF, for example, may be associated with RF-positive polyarticular JIA, Sjögren's syndrome, or the early onset of adult- type rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in teenagers (although these disorders are not associated with high fevers and other sJIA features). Both RF and ANA may be present in children with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). However, these conditions rarely mimic sJIA. False-positive results may be seen in some

patients. Some chronic infectious processes, such as subacute bacterial endocarditis, can cause unexplained fevers and a positive RF. A microcytic anaemia, which tends to be resistant to iron replacement and pericarditis, is often found. Patients may also present with symptoms consistent with uveitis. Options for pharmacotherapy include NSAIDs, corticosteroids, methotrexate and anti-TNF biologicals. C Rheumatoid arthritis A diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is reserved for adult patients, whereas this patient is an adolescent. A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Multi-system rheumatologic disease may be distinguished from juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) by clinical features and laboratory ﬁndings. SLE often presents in adolescence with fever, rash and non-erosive arthritis. The ANA is positive in SLE but also may be present in oligoarticular and RF positive polyarticular JIA. Both SLE and systemic-onset JIA may manifest as fever and serositis, but the skin ﬁndings are different. In addition, malar rash, nephritis, cytopenia, hypocomplementaemia and anti-double-stranded DNA and other autoantibodies are seen only in SLE. D Sarcoidosis Most of the reported cases of childhood sarcoidosis are accompanied by non-speciﬁc constitutional symptoms, such as fever, fatigue, malaise and weight loss, as well as symptoms from particular organs, such as the lungs, eyes, skin and lymph nodes. The joints tend not to be affected in children. E Kawasaki disease Kawasaki syndrome is a vasculitis in children, with prominent features including cervical lymphadenopathy and ‘strawberry red’ lips, palms and soles of feet. In some children coronary artery aneurysms may form.

stem: A 61-year-old man who has a long history of rheumatoid arthritis, currently treated with methotrexate, presents to the Emergency Department with an acute arthritis affecting his right elbow. He tells you he was pruning roses a few days earlier in the garden and wonders whether something may have got into the joint. His rheumatoid disease has been stable for some time on methotrexate, and he takes lisinopril in addition for hypertension. His BP is 142/72 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular and he is pyrexial (38.6 °C). The elbow is erythematous and hot, there is a signiﬁcant effusion and he is holding the joint in ﬂexion because of pain on minimal movement. RHEUMATO Investigation Result Normal values Hb 111 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 15.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 115 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l CRP 205 mg/l < 10 mg/l X-ray elbow Changes consistent with rheumatoid arthritis Which of the following is the most important next step?
explanation: A Aspiration of joint This patient has septic arthritis until proven otherwise. As such, it is essential that the diagnosis and likely pathogen are conﬁrmed by joint aspiration. B IV Flucloxacillin Blind antibiotic use in a patient taking immunosuppression is ill advised. The joint should be aspirated and then broad-spectrum antibiotics started, pending sensitivities. C Serum urate testing Serum urate may be elevated, but it would not divert you from joint aspiration to rule out septic arthritis. D Oral naproxen Of course this patient needs analgesia, but the most important part of management is to aspirate the joint for a diagnosis. E IV Co-amoxiclav After joint aspiration, broad-spectrum antibiotics (usually benzylpenicillin and ﬂucloxacillin) are started to cover joint sepsis.

stem: A 62-year-old man attends for review. He has evidence of arthritis affecting the shoulder, elbow, radiocarpal and knee joints bilaterally, with pain also in the left ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint. An X-ray of the knee is shown below. Aspiration of the left knee reveals calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Serum uric acid level is slightly above the upper limit of normal. Other medical history of note is ulcerative colitis. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation: B Pseudogout The clinical picture of joint involvement, coupled with X-ray evidence of chondrocalcinosis and synovial ﬂuid pyrophosphate crystals, is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of pseudogout. The slightly elevated uric acid level and a history of ulcerative colitis are ‘red herrings’ in this case. Chondrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals within the hyaline and ﬁbrous cartilage. On X-ray, this is seen as a calciﬁc appearance within the joint line (as shown above). Management involves use of simple painkillers and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents, coupled with physiotherapy where appropriate. Associated conditions include haemochromatosis and Wilson’s disease where there are other symptoms and signs, and it may be worth screening for these concomitant illnesses. Pseudogout has an equal male : female ratio, with the frequency increasing with advancing age; it is said to affect around 5% of subjects above the age of 30 years. RHEUMATO E Septic arthritis Acute monoarticular gout can be indistinguishable from septic arthritis in the history and clinical examination, and in some cases, these coexist. However, the identiﬁcation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals and no mention of inﬂammatory cells in the synovial ﬂuid make this answer incorrect. A Gout Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals, which are ﬁne, needlelike and negatively birefringent under polarised light. C Primary osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis has a predilection for the knees, hips, interphalangeal joints, ﬁrst carpometacarpal joints, ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joints and apophyseal (facet) joints of the lower cervical and lower lumbar spine. It is not associated with calcium pyrophosphate crystals. D Rheumatoid arthritis There is no suggestion of morning stiffness in this case history, and the distribution of affected joints and presence of calcium pyrophosphate crystals make rheumatoid arthritis unlikely.

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP), complaining of dry eyes, dry mouth and vaginal dryness on sexual intercourse. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history; speciﬁcally, there is no history of rheumatoid arthritis or connective tissue disease. Which of the following is a likely clinical feature in this case?
options: 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing
explanation:
A 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing The answer is 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing (Option A). This woman has Sjögren syndrome, as evidenced by her symptoms of dry mouth and dry eyes and the fact that other mucosal surfaces are affected. It may be primary or secondary (related to other autoimmune conditions). There is plasma cell inﬁltration of salivary and lacrimal glands with positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, and a

deﬁnitive positive Schirmer’s test is deﬁned as <5 mm wetting per 5 minutes. Treatment involves use of artiﬁcial tears and screening for ophthalmic (corneal dryness and ulceration) and dental (caries) complications. C Negative anti-Ro antibodies Negative anti-Ro antibodies (Option C) is incorrect. This woman with Sjögren may have anti-Ro (or anti-La) antibodies. Anti-Ro antibodies have been detected in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (32%), Sjögren syndrome (59%), idiopathic inﬂammatory myopathies (19%), systemic sclerosis (21%) and mixed connective tissue disease (29%). B Hypersalivation Hypersalivation (Option B) is incorrect. This lady with Sjögren is likely to have decreased (not increased) parotid salivary gland ﬂow. Increased salivation is a common problem secondary to antipsychotic medications such as clozapine. In such patients, glycopyrrolate can be useful, as it is an anticholinergic which does not cross the blood–brain barrier. D Negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA) Negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA) (Option D) is incorrect. This lady with Sjögren may have a positive ANA. ANA occurs in SLE (98%), scleroderma (95%), mixed connective tissue disease (100%), drug-induced lupus erythematosus (95%), Sjögren (60%), rheumatoid arthritis (45%), Raynaud’s phenomenon (40%) and polymyositis/dermatomyositis (35%). It can also occur in organspeciﬁc autoimmune conditions such as autoimmune hepatitis (70%), primary biliary cholangitis (70%), Hashimoto’s (50%) and Grave’s disease (50%). E Low oestrogen levels Low oestrogen levels (Option E) is incorrect. Her oestrogen levels are likely to be normal. She has dyspareunia because of Sjögren exocrinopathy, not related to her oestrogen levels. Oestrogen levels can become chronically low in post-menopausal women, primary ovarian pathology or suppression of the hypothalamus–pituitary–gonadal axis. In patients symptomatic of low oestrogen, hormone replacement therapy is an option.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic following a referral from his Dentist. She had been seeing the Hygienist after experiencing recurrent mouth ulcers. She has a past medical history of uveitis, after presenting with pain and redness of the eye and irritable bowel syndrome and was seen RHEUMATO in the Sexual Health Clinic six months ago with vulval ulceration. Examination reveals multiple shallow ulcers in the mouth but no cutaneous lesions elsewhere. Cardiorespiratory examination is normal. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 122 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 219 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Creatinine 71 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 32 mm/hour < 29 mm/hour What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Behçet syndrome Behçet’s syndrome is a rare multisystem disease which classically presents with recurrent oral aphthous ulceration alongside systemic features. These include other cutaneous ulcers, genital ulcers, ocular symptoms (usually uveitis), GI symptoms, arthritis and nervous system disease.
