It is felt to be an autoimmune-driven vasculitis and is more common in East Asia and the Mediterranean. Patients usually present in early adulthood. E Reactive arthritis Reactive arthritis occurs after enteric or genitourinary infections. Neither appears to have occurred here. Additionally, ocular symptoms tend to be conjunctivitis and arthritis is absent. B HIV infection HIV infection can result in ulceration in the oral cavity and genital region. Where it causes uveitis, it more commonly does so in the posterior, rather than the anterior, segment, as with this patient. Therefore, it is less likely to present with the features noted in this case but should, of course, be considered and tested for. C Herpes simplex Herpes simplex may refer to either type 1 or type 2. Type 1 classically causes oral ulcers, whereas type 2 causes genital herpes. Type 1 can additionally result in ocular disease, but it would be unusual for the ulceration to occur in both regions and in eye disease, all disseminated in time. D Crohn’s disease Crohn’s disease can result in oral ulceration and symptoms outside

the GI tract, including uveitis, although the combination of oral and genital ulceration is more suspicious of Behçet’s syndrome.

stem: A 69-year-old woman attends the Rheumatology Clinic with progressive right knee pain affecting her ability to walk to the shops. The pain is constant throughout the day and is worsened by movement and weight-bearing. She denies fever and has been well with no recent illnesses. Her past medical history includes hypertension and type II diabetes. On examination, her temperature is 36.1 °C. She has a heart rate of 77 bpm, with a blood pressure of 146/92 mmHg. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal and vesicular chest sounds are heard throughout, with oxygen saturations of 97% on room air. Her right knee is mildly swollen and tender to touch; it feels warm but is not erythematous. There is palpable crepitus on movement and a small prepatellar effusion is noted. Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes are seen. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: D Paracetamol and topical ibuprofen This patient has osteoarthritis (OA), a degenerative arthritis capable of affecting multiple joints. OA of weight- bearing joints such as the hips and knees is very common. In OA, bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden’s nodes) and proximal interphalangeal joints (Bouchard’s nodes) are often seen, as described in this question. Unlike inﬂammatory arthritis, OA does not have a typical pattern of early morning joint stiffness that improves throughout the day and pain is often constant and worsened with movement. Restricted movement, joint effusions and crepitus are all signs of OA. The ﬁrst-line treatment for OA is oral paracetamol and topical non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as topical ibuprofen. C Oral non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs If oral paracetamol and topical NSAIDs fail to treat the pain associated with OA, oral NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, can be trialled, provided there are no contraindications. RHEUMATO A Colchicine Colchicine is used in the treatment of gout. Gout is a crystal arthropathy associated with hyperuricaemia secondary to chronic kidney disease, a purine-rich diet or drug therapy, including thiazide diuretics. Gout presents as an acutely painful joint, typically in the ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint. It is uncommon for gout to present as progressive knee degeneration and gout does not account for this patient’s Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes. B Intra-articular corticosteroids The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that intra-articular corticosteroid injections be considered as an adjunct to treatment for osteoarthritis, but it should not be the mainstay of treatment. First-line agents such as paracetamol and topical ibuprofen should be tried ﬁrst. E Prednisolone and methotrexate The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that intra-articular corticosteroid injections be considered as an adjunct to treatment for osteoarthritis, but it should not be the mainstay of treatment. First-line agents such as paracetamol and topical ibuprofen should be tried ﬁrst.

stem: A 65-year-old Asian woman was referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with long-standing joint problems. She described initial involvement of the small joints of the hands, which resolved after a few weeks. Now the main joints involved are the wrists, elbows and knees. Before she migrated to the UK from Pakistan 2 years ago, she had suffered recurrent ear infections and a few episodes of nasal septum inﬂammation. On each episode, she was treated with antibiotics and analgesia. She has a family history of systemic lupus erythematosus and she is on amlodipine for hypertension. On examination, the wrists and the knees are swollen and tender with reduced active and passive movement. The nose is saddle-shaped RHEUMATO and the right upper ear cartilage is red and tender. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 95 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l ESR 86 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 146 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) Rheumatoid factor (RF) 120 μmol/l Negative 50–120 µmol/l ANA Negative Urine dipstick Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Relapsing polychondritis This lady has inﬂammation of the outer ear, nasal septum and relapsing remitting arthralgia/arthritis consistent with relapsing polychondritis. Relapsing polychondritis is a disorder that affects, cartilaginous and connective tissues causing episodic inﬂammation and destruction. Onset is typically in middle age and it occurs in equal frequency in men and women. The most common symptom is inﬂammation of the external ear and nasal cartilage. It is often associated with arthritis involving both small and large joints. Characteristic of the disease are bouts of inﬂammation that heal over weeks. Recurrent inﬂammation results in destruction of cartilaginous tissue resulting in ﬂoppy ears and a saddle nose. Biopsy of affected cartilaginous tissue will conﬁrm the diagnosis. C Mixed connective tissue disorder The ANA is negative and she has no features of connective tissue disease. A Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) This lady has outer ear inﬂammation, ie of the cartilaginous pinna, and relapsing arthritis which are key differentiators from GPA. Although we are not given an ANCA result (expecting a cANCA with GPA), the renal function is normal and urine dipstick is inactive. D Systemic sclerosis In systemic sclerosis, ear and nose involvement is not common and Raynaud’s is almost universal.

E Polymyalgia rheumatica The lady has a negative ANA.

stem: A 56-year-old woman who suffered a road trafﬁc accident some years ago presents to the clinic for review. She has been complaining of increasing pain and weakness in her right arm over the past few months and is now unable to work. Past history of note includes osteoarthritis. On examination, there is weakness and wasting of the triceps, wrist and ﬁnger extensors, loss of the triceps jerk and sensory loss over the middle ﬁngers of the hand. Prolapse of which intervertebral disc is most likely to be responsible for her symptoms and signs?
explanation:
C C6–7 A lateral cervical disc protrusion at the C6–7 level (i.e. the disc between the 6th and 7th cervical vertebrae) compresses the exiting C7 nerve and thus causes pain and weakness over the C7 myotome (triceps, wrist and ﬁnger extensors), loss of the triceps jerk and loss of sensation over the C7 dermatome. Pain relief and immobilisation may be appropriate for initial management, although in those who fail to respond, MRI and assessment for surgical decompression are recommended. A C4–5 C4–5 (C5 nerve root): A herniation at this level can cause shoulder

pain and weakness in the deltoid muscle at the top of the upper arm, and does not usually cause numbness or tingling. B C5–6 C5–6 (C6 nerve root): A C5–6 disc herniation can cause weakness of the biceps (muscles in the front of the upper arms) and wrist extensor muscles. Numbness and tingling along with pain can radiate to the thumb side of the hand. This is one of the most common levels for a cervical disc herniation to occur. D C7–T1 C7–T1 (C8 nerve root): This level is located at the very bottom of the neck, where the cervical spine meets the thoracic, or upper, back. A herniation here can cause weakness with handgrip, along with numbness and tingling and pain that radiates down the arm to the little ﬁnger side of hand. E T1–2 T1–2 disc protrusion speciﬁcally refers to the deterioration of one or more of the intervertebral discs in the thoracic (middle) segment of the spine. The protrusion of a disc between any of the 12 vertebrae in the thoracic spine (T1–12) can cause severe pain and other symptoms if nerve compression is present. Disc protrusion in the thoracic spine, however, is somewhat rare because the thoracic spinal segment is attached directly to the ribcage, keeping the 12 thoracic vertebrae relatively stable and stationary. Lumbar disc protrusion (in the lower back) and cervical disc protrusion (in the neck) are much more common. The cervical spine is constructed around the vertebrae, or the seven stacked bony building blocks in the spine. They are numbered from top to bottom as C1 to C7. The nerve that is affected by the cervical disc herniation is the one exiting the spine at that level, so at the C5–6 level it is the C6 nerve root that is affected.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a 2-month history of arthralgia and lethargy. She also complains of grittiness in her eyes and a dry mouth. There is no past medical history of note and she takes no regular medications. Investigations reveal a positive Schirmer’s test. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Anti-Ro
This patient has (primary) Sjögren syndrome clinically with arthritis, dry eyes and mouth. Conjunctival dryness can be quantified by Schirmer’s test, in which a strip of filter paper is placed under the lower lid and the distance along the paper that tears are absorbed is measured – a distance of < 10 mm in five minutes is positive. Pathologically, secretory glands are infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid
Anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid is highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus. It is not seen in Sjögren syndrome.

Anti-La
Anti-La antibodies are positive in 30% of cases of Sjögren syndrome. It is not the most common antibody seen.

Anti-Jo-1
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are seen in polymyositis. They are not present in Sjögren syndrome.

stem: A 30-year-old woman visits your clinic with a 2-month history of pain in both her hands. Which characteristic symptom in her clinical history would you be most likely to see that would reflect an inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Inability to extend and flex her fingers fully
Inability to knit because of pain in her fingers
Marked stiffness for more than an hour in the mornings
Presence of firm non-tender nodules in the fingers and on the elbows
explanation:
Marked stiffness for more than an hour in the mornings
Morning stiffness is a classic feature of inflammation, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Morning stiffness is significant when it lasts for one hour or longer. Morning stiffness may also be seen in other disorders such as polymyalgia rheumatic (proximal muscles) and ankylosing spondylitis (back).

Feels tired and unwell
Feels tired and unwell is incorrect. Constitutional upset is not specific for RA.

Inability to extend and flex her fingers fully
Inability to extend and flex her fingers fully is incorrect. Limitation of mobility is not specific for RA.

Presence of firm non-tender nodules in the fingers and on the elbows
Presence of firm non-tender nodules in the fingers and on the elbows is incorrect. Subcutaneous nodule occur in 25% of RA cases and only in seropositive (rheumatoid factor) positive patients.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of fever (38 °C), sweats and a cough. She is on 7.5 mg prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 80 mm in 1 sthour 0–10 mm in the 1 sthour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 46 mg/l 0–10 mg/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.4×10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Neutrophils 4.5×10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l Lymphocytes 0.5×10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 10 9/l Platelets 100×10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l What is your management?
explanation:
Antibiotics and increase prednisolone
The question to consider in this case is whether this woman has an exacerbation of her lupus or an infection, or both. Evidence for infection comes from her history and the elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). Supporting a diagnosis of lupus flare is the fever, high ESR, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia. She is therefore likely to have a chest infection that has precipitated a flare in disease and should be treated with both steroids and antibiotics. Also increasing the dose of steroids may provide adrenal support, as she was already on steroids prior to the infection.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with pain in her shoulders, inability to lift her arms fully and pain in the joints of both wrists and fingers for the past 2 months. There is a history of morning stiffness that lasts for more than an hour. On examination she has a swelling of proximal interphalangeal joints. ESR 78mm/hr CRP 56mg/L Rheumatoid Factor 1:1280 Anti –CCP antibody level positive 1000 U/ml (normal <100) What clinical conclusion can be best drawn from the available information?
options: Based on the symptoms and results of the blood test, a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis can be
Complement levels should be measured to rule out systemic lupus erythematosus
Radiographs of the affected joints are necessary to confirm the diagnosis
She must be suffering from rheumatoid arthritis as rheumatoid factor is specific for this condition
The rheumatoid factor may be a false-positive reaction
explanation:
Based on the symptoms and results of the blood test, a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis can be
made This lady fulfils the classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis were updated in 2010 with ≥6 fulfilled criteria indicating a definite diagnosis of RA. Four areas are covered in the diagnosis: Joint involvement: 1. Small joints: the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, second through fifth metatarsophalangeal joint and wrist as small joints 2. Large joints: shoulders, elbows, hip joints, knees, and ankles as large joints: Involvement of 1 large joint gives 0 points

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of progressive breathlessness, swelling of his ankles, painful joints and earache. An X-ray of his chest shows multiple nodules scattered throughout both lung fields. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria and non-visible haematuria. What is the most probable diagnosis?
options: Churg–Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA)
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
GPA is a potentially fatal disease caused by a generalised vasculitis that has a predisposition for the upper respiratory tract, lungs and kidneys, which is clear in this patient. There can be nasal ulceration, rhinitis, otitis media, pulmonary symptoms and variable shadows on the chest X-ray (particularly multiple nodules), hypertension and glomerulonephritis.

Berger's disease
Berger's disease is incorrect. Berger’s disease is an IgA nephropathy that causes repeated episodes of glomerulonephritis and haematuria associated with viral infections. Pulmonary symptoms, arthralgia and otitis media do not occur in this condition.

Churg–Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA)
Churg–Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA) is incorrect. Churg–Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA) is a vasculitis with significant pulmonary involvement, and features that may be consistent with severe asthma.

stem: A 20-year-old Italian waiter has painful mouth and genital ulcers associated with arthralgia of his elbows and knees. On examination, tender, red, raised lesions are seen on both legs. He has had two such attacks in the past. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behçet’s disease
This young man from Italy has classical symptoms of Behçet’s syndrome – orogenital ulceration, polyarthalgia and erythema nodosum. Behçet’s disease is a vasculitis of unknown aetiology that characteristically targets venules. It is common in the Mediterranean region and in Japan, where there is a strong association with HLA B51. Oral ulcers occur in almost all cases. Genital ulcers are less common (60–80%). The usual skin lesions are erythema nodosum or acneiform lesions, but migratory thrombophlebitis and vasculitis also occur.

Enteropathic arthritis
Enteropathic arthritis is incorrect. There is no history to suggest inflammatory bowel disease. Enteropathic arthritis is an acute inflammatory oligoarthritis that occurs in 12% of people with ulcerative colitis and in 20% of people with Crohn’s disease. Mouth ulcers, erythema nodosum and iritis can occur. Treatment of the underlying condition relieves the symptoms.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. There is no history of antecedent infection. Reactive arthritis is a triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis or uveitis and non-specific urethritis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of polyarthralgia, dry eyes and a low-grade fever (up to 37.8 °C). She has tender joints with no demonstrable synovitis. Investigations show: antinuclear antibodies (ANA) 1:640, rheumatoid factor 1:320, antibodies to double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) and anti-Ro antibodies are present. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient because there are antibodies against double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA). SLE shows a female predominance (7:1) and the typical age range at presentation is 20–45 years. In addition, she has the symptoms of secondary Sjögren's syndrome, with the corresponding anti-Ro and rheumatoid factor antibodies. Primary Sjögren's syndrome serology usually includes a positive rheumatoid factor test (90%), positive antinuclear antibody (90%), anti-Ro (85%), anti-La (60%) and hypergammaglobulinaemia.

Mixed connective tissue disease
Mixed connective tissue disease is incorrect. Mixed connective tissue disease is characterised by antibodies against ribonucleoprotein (RNP).

Systemic sclerosis
Systemic sclerosis is incorrect. She has no features of systemic sclerosis, such as skin thickening.

stem: A 65 year old woman has back pain radiating down both legs. The pain is aggravated by walking and is relieved on rest and when she walks uphill. On examination, the straight leg-raising test is negative. Ankle jerks are absent. What is the most probable cause of her pain?
explanation:
Spinal stenosis
Spinal stenosis occurs in elderly patients and presents with pseudoclaudication, i.e. discomfort or pain in the legs on walking that is relieved by rest and by bending forwards. Symptoms of spinal stenosis occur as a result of limitation of space in the vertebral canal. Patients are able to walk further when leaning on a shopping trolley or walking uphill because spinal flexion increases the space available for the cauda equina and unfolds the ligamentum flavum. The diagnosis is confirmed by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Decompression is indicated if mobility or quality of life is significantly impaired.

Disc prolapse
Disc prolapse is incorrect. She does not have any radicular or sciatica like symptoms (pain radiating down one leg below the knee) and straight leg raise is negative.

Vertebral fracture
Vertebral fracture is incorrect. A vertebral fracture is likely to cause severe focal tenderness at the vertebral body affected and the pain would not improve on walking uphill.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is 16 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. She has suffered from a facial rash consistent with lupus, and has had blood and protein found on dipstick testing over the past 18 months. Which one of the following antibodies, if found positive, is thought to be most associated with increased risk of complete heart block in the newborn infant?
explanation:
Anti-Ro
IgG antibodies to Ro and La are known to be associated with neonatal complete heart block (CHB), and can occur alone or in combination, but anti-Ro are found in around 95% of cases. They recognise the cardiac 5HT-4 serotoninergic receptor, and inhibit serotonin-activated calcium L channels. There is an associated lupus-type rash, but this disappears by month 6 as the maternal antibodies are gradually cleared. Unfortunately, congenital heart block carries a poor prognosis.

Anti-dsDNA antibodies
Anti-dsDNA antibodies is incorrect. Although they are highly specific for SLE, these antibodies do not cross the placenta and therefore cannot cause neonatal lupus or congenital heart block.

Anti-centromere
Anti-centromere is incorrect. This antibody is not commonly associated with SLE or neonatal complete heart block as it does not cross the placenta.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Currently she is maintained on 25 mg of prednisolone per day and you are considering introducing azathioprine as a second-line agent. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 130 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l The levels of which one of the following can be easily measured to assess the risk of azathioprine toxicity?
explanation:
Thiopurine S-methyltransferase activity
TPMT mutations lead to elevated levels of 6-mercaptopurine. 6-Mercaptopurine is associated with excessive bone marrow suppression. Over the past few years a TPMT assay has been developed which is available in most tertiary centres to assess potential risk and therefore if a patient’s TPMT is low, azathioprine is contraindicated (or used with extreme caution at low doses).

stem: A 49-year-old man who works in a plant assembling small- to medium-sized machine tools presents to the clinic complaining of pain on wrist extension. He says that the problem is getting worse at work and he is unable to grip well and carry the pieces of machinery he has assembled. On examination his blood pressure is 142/83 mmHg and his body mass index(BMI) is 26kg/m 2. General physical examination is unremarkable. The lateral elbow and forearm pain is reproduced when you ask him to perform resisted wrist extension. The maximal point of pain is about 0.5 to 1 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
This man’s symptoms are typical of lateral epicondylitis, also known as tennis elbow. Work-related lateral epicondylitis risk factors were identified in a systematic review, including the handling of tools greater in weight than 1 kg, regularly lifting loads greater than 20 kg a number of times in the day, and doing more than 2 hours of repetitive movements during any 1 day’s work. Physiotherapy with the wearing of an elbow strap orthosis and local corticosteroid injections are effective treatment, as is a lateral release procedure in resistant cases.

Medial epicondylitis
Medial epicondylitis is incorrect. Medial epicondylitis (golfer’s elbow) pain is felt at the medial Chatelbow. with

De Quervain’s tenosinovitis
De Quervain’s tenosynovitis is incorrect. In de Quervain’s tenosynovitis, Finkelstein’s test would be positive – when pain is felt at the lateral wrist when the thumb is placed across the palm and wrist forcibly medially deviated.

stem: A 40-year-old woman complains of pain and stiffness in the small joints of her hands, especially in the mornings. An X-ray shows only soft-tissue swelling, but magnetic resonance imaging reveals erosions at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which one of the following indicates a worse than average prognosis?
options: Anaemia occurring a year after onset
Gradual onset over a few months
explanation:
Gradual onset over a few months
This patient most probably has rheumatoid arthritis. A gradual insidious onset over a few months indicates a worse prognosis. A worse than average prognosis (with a predictive accuracy of 80%) is indicated by: Female sex Gradual onset over a few months Positive IgM rheumatoid factor Anaemia developing within 3 months of onset Anti-CCP antibody positivity (associated with more aggressive joint disease)

Anaemia occurring a year after onset
Anaemia occurring a year after onset is incorrect. Anaemia within 3 months indicates a worse prognosis.

Negative IgM rheumatoid factor
Negative IgM rheumatoid factor is incorrect. A positive rheumatoid factor indicates a worse prognosis.

stem: A 60-year-old woman complains of feelings of aching and heaviness in both legs on walking that causes her to stop walking and bend or sit down. Extending the back aggravates the symptoms. An X-ray of the spine is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Crush fracture of the lumbar vertebrae due to osteoporosis
explanation:
Spinal stenosis
This patient has spinal stenosis with pseudoclaudication after walking, which is relieved with rest or leaning forwards. Reduction in spinal canal diameter usually due to osteoarthritis may cause spinal claudication while walking. Root compression symptoms may occur. The straight leg-raising test is negative in spinal stenosis.

Crush fracture of the lumbar vertebrae due to osteoporosis
Crush fracture of the lumbar vertebrae due to osteoporosis is incorrect. Vertebral fracture due to osteoporosis would be evident on X-ray.

Lumbar disc prolapse
Lumbar disc prolapse is incorrect. Restricted forward flexion with pain radiating into the buttocks or down the legs (sciatica) characterises lumbar disc prolapse. Extension of the back usually relieves the symptoms.

Lumbar spondylolisthesis
Lumbar spondylolisthesis is incorrect. Displacement (usually forward) of one lumbar vertebra upon another is seen in spondylolisthesis. The X-ray picture is diagnostic.

stem: In monosodium urate monohydrate arthropathy, what is the most characteristic feature seen on examination of the synovial fluid?
options: Positive birefringence of the crystals when seen under polarised light
explanation:
Presence of long needle-shaped crystals
Needle-shaped crystals are found in the synovial fluid in gout.

Orange colour of synovial fluid
Orange colour of synovial fluid is incorrect. A high concentration of monosodium urate monohydrate (MSUM) crystals in chronic gout can make the synovial fluid appear white.

Positive birefringence of the crystals when seen under polarised light
Positive birefringence of the crystals when seen under polarised light is incorrect. MSUM crystals are typically long and needle-shaped and show negative birefringence.

Rhomboid shape of the crystals
Rhomboid shape of the crystals is incorrect. MSUM crystals are typically long and needle-shaped and show negative birefringence. N.B. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are small and rhomboid in shape, and are positively birefringent under polarised light

stem: A 42-year-old alcoholic man is admitted with pain, swelling and redness over the first metacarpophalangeal joint. On examination he has a number of tophi, and this is diagnosed as gout. He is started on allopurinol and discharged. Two days later he returns complaining of pain and inflammation over the small joints of his hands, wrists, ankles and knees. On examination, his temperature is 38.5 °C. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 145 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Allopurinol treatment
Allopurinol may precipitate a severe acute attack of gout, including pyrexia and should not be given during an acute attack, but rather 4-6 weeks after the attack has settled with NSAID / colchicine cover. Given that this patient was an alcoholic, however, the risks of using a NSAID might have been deemed too great in this case, but an alternative should have been chosen, such as colchicine (which may cause diarrhea) or prednisolone Chatbe (which has a myriad of risks, including precipitating upper GI bleeds, which, therefore, may not with here). suitable N.B. Allopurinol can precipitate Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so rashes should be taken very seriously.

stem: A 55-year-old obese patient complains of a 4-month history of moderate pain in her finger joints, mainly at the end of the day, which improves with rest. She has also noticed some swelling. On examination there is tenderness to palpation and enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints. Her GP has kindly performed some blood tests and her rheumatoid factor is 1:80 and ANA is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteoarthritis
This lady’s pain increases with joint use and at the end of the day and improves with rest and examination confirms bony outgrowths (not true joint ‘swelling’ or synovitis) at the DIPs, Heberden’s nodes. Pain is the key symptom in osteoarthritis and is usually mild, improving with rest and moderation of activity. Severe disease can cause pain at rest or at night. The source of pain can be underlying bone, the joint capsule or surrounding structures. Physical examination reveals tenderness to palpation, bony thickening (osteophyte formation), small effusions and crepitus. Specific joint findings also occur: Typical findings in the hand are bony enlargement of the proximal interphalangeal joints (Bouchard’s nodes) and the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden’s nodes). The first carpometacarpal joint may be involved, causing a squared appearance of the lateral aspect of the hand. Involvement of the foot leads to bunions. In the knee there can be pronounced valgus and varus deformities, Baker’s cyst or locking (suggesting meniscal damage). Early hip findings include limited internal and external rotation. Back findings include pain; true osteoarthritis occurs at the apophyseal joints; degenerative disc disease and diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis are distinct entities.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of right knee pain, swelling and erythema. She has no past history of note apart from hypertension, for which she takes bendroflumethiazide. On examination, her blood pressure is well controlled at 128/82 mmHg and she has a body mass index (BMI) of 27 kg/m 2. Her right knee is swollen and erythematous. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 12 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l You suspect that she may have pseudogout. What type of crystals are you expecting to find on joint aspiration?
explanation:
Rhomboid shaped positive birefringence
Pseudogout is caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals, which are rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent. It is important to remember that, although pseudogout is not infective, it may be associated with both raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and raised white blood cell count. Patients

stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He has left-sided posterior pelvic, hip and back pain which has persisted over the last 4 months. Past medical history of note includes gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) for which he takes regular omeprazole and it is well controlled. An X-ray conducted by his GP has revealed both osteolysis and new bone formation around the left hip joint and pelvis. On examination, left hip movements are severely limited by pain and stiffness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 198 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alkaline Phosphatase 528 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.56 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reduce his pain and stiffness?
explanation:
IV zolendronate
This man has Paget’s disease. Where there are symptoms of bone pain and stiffness, coupled with a raised alkaline phosphatase, bisphosphonates are the intervention of choice.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who has taken up jogging comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has pain affecting the lateral aspect of her hip and outer thigh, worse on palpation and exacerbated by walking. The pain is also made worse by lying on the affected side. Examination reveals pain and stiffness at the extremes of external and internal rotation. Hip X-ray, including frog leg views, is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Trochanteric bursitis
The lateral hip and thigh pain, worse on direct pressure, coupled with a normal plain X-ray, fit best with a diagnosis of trochanteric bursitis. Passive stretching exercises coupled with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the initial intervention of choice. Local glucocorticoid injection into the bursa can be considered for patients with severe pain and who fail to respond to conservative measures. Longitudinal release of the iliotibial band is only considered up to a year after symptoms begin, in patients who have not responded to two injections.

Proximal myopathy
Proximal myopathy is incorrect. Proximal myopathy is characterised by weakness, atrophy and reduced or normal tone and reflexes. It can be due to muscular dystrophy, metabolic myopathy, dermatomyositis or drug- induced myopathy. The presence of hip pain makes this less likely, and the absence of weakness makes it very unlikely.

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis brings some blood results to clinic to show to you: Investigation Result Normal Value Males:135–175 g/l Haemoglobin 114 g/l Females:115–155 g/l Platelets 470 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 102 fl 76–98 fl 'Abnormal. Please contact lab Haematocrit for more results' Which drug therapy is most likely to be responsible for this picture?
explanation:
Methotrexate
Methotrexate is a folate antagonist (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors) and, therefore, can cause a macrocytic anaemia – raised MCV.

Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. Hydroxychloroquine does not cause anaemia (but can provoke an oxidant haemolytic crisis in G6PD deficient patients).

stem: A 77-year-old man says he woke up in the morning with a painful, warm, red and swollen right knee. He is only taking thyroxine for hypothyroidism and says has no other medical problems apart from some “old age arthritis”. An X-ray of his knee shows calcification of the meniscus only. Blood tests show a CRP of 49 mg/l and an ESR of 45 mm/hr. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyrophosphate arthropathy
The most likely diagnosis here is pseudogout. Pyrophosphate arthropathy is characterised by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in fibrous and articular cartilage. Shedding of crystals into the joint spaces provokes an attack of pseudogout. This may present clinically as a sudden onset of pain, inflammation and swelling of the knee. Radiography may show calcification of the articular cartilage or menisci (chondrocalcinosis). Examination of the synovial fluid under polarising light microscopy allows the identification of CPPD crystals. Risk factors for pseudogout include osteoarthritis and metabolic disorders including hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, haemochromatosis and hypophosphatasia. Inflammatory markers can be elevated.

Acute gout
Acute gout is incorrect. He does not have any risk factors for gout, but does have risk factors for and radiographic features of pseudogout.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with an acutely swollen, painful right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Which one of the following features would most reliably distinguish gout from septic arthritis as the cause?
options: The presence of negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid
The presence of polymorph leucocytes in the synovial fluid
explanation:
The presence of negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid
The presence of monosodium urate crystals (which rotate the plane of polarised light) establishes the diagnosis of gout – negatively birefringent needle shaped crystals.

A polymorph leukocytosis
A polymorph leukocytosis is incorrect. A polymorph leucocytosis can occur in any acute inflammatory condition.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. Hyperuricaemia is frequently asymptomatic, and is not always present in clinical gout – 40% of acute gout cases have a normal serum urate.

The presence of polymorph leucocytes in the synovial fluid
The presence of polymorph leucocytes in the synovial is incorrect. Polymorphs are present in synovial fluid in gout and septic arthritis.

stem: You review a 59-year-old woman with a history of deteriorating vision. You diagnose the patient to have ischaemic optic atrophy. Ischaemic optic atrophy is most likely to be associated with which one of the following diseases?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
Ischaemic optic neuropathy is a prominent ophthalmic manifestation of giant cell arteritis and GPA. Ischaemic optic atrophy may be a major ophthalmic manifestation of giant-cell arteritis, GPA and, less commonly, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Other causes of optic atrophy include secondary optic atrophy after papilloedema, demyelinating optic neuritis as seen in multiple sclerosis, vitamin B 12 deficiency, quinine and methyl alcohol ingestion. The degree of visual loss depends on the underlying cause. Hereditary causes of optic atrophy include Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (a mitochondrial disorder).

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. This is not seen in rheumatoid arthritis.

Seronegative arthritis
Seronegative arthritis is incorrect. Ischaemic optic neuropathy is not seen in seronegative arthritis.

Still’s disease
Still’s disease is incorrect. Ischaemic optic neuropathy is not seen in Still’s disease.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic by her gynaecologist with a history of swelling and pain in her right big toe and left knee. The only positive finding on gynaecological examination was the presence of cervicitis. An endocervical swab tested positive for chlamydial infection. Investigation Result Normal Value White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115–155 g/l Platelets 300 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 40 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 45 mg/l 0–10 mg/l X-ray right foot Normal What is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This lady has reactive arthritis triggered by Chlamydia trachomatis, causing non-specific cervicitis. Seronegative spondyloarthritis develops in 1–2% of patients with this condition. N.B. the white cell count and inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR) can be elevated in all the conditions listed and therefore does not help differentiate between them (unless the white cell count was dramatically elevated, suggesting infection). The X-rays can be normal in all of the above, although may show erosions in rheumatoid arthritis and recurrent gout.

stem: A middle-aged woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate develops sudden swelling in one of her knees. The knee is hot and tender. She is afebrile. Blood tests show a mild anaemia, normal white cell count and CRP of 45mg/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation in her case?
explanation:
Joint fluid microscopy and culture
Septic arthritis must be excluded in this lady. Septic arthritis may occur in a joint damaged by rheumatoid arthritis. This typically presents acutely with a painful, hot, tender, swollen joint, usually monoarticular. Joint fluid culture would be the most appropriate investigation in this case. 50% septic arthritides are afebrile and Immunosuppressed patients may present atypically, e.g. with only a modest acute phase response – as in this case where her CRP is only 45mg/L. (It is very unusual to get red joints in a rheumatoid flare and with a monoarthritis, the diagnosis of septic arthritis should always be considered).

Blood culture
Blood culture is incorrect. The immediate investigation in the synovial fluid culture, however blood cultures should be done as well, to look for peripheral sources of sepsis.

Joint fluid crystal examination
Joint fluid crystal examination is incorrect. A crystal arthritis is unlikely.

Test for rheumatoid factor
Test for rheumatoid factor is incorrect. We already know that she has rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 70-year-old man has been experiencing a right-sided headache and severe temporomandibular joint pain when he eats for the past week. He now presents with a sudden loss of vision in his right eye. What treatment is required urgently to avoid vision loss in the left eye?
explanation:
Intravenous steroids
This man has giant-cell arteritis. This is an inflammatory granulomatous arteritis of large arteries, which can occur in association with polymyalgia rheumatica. Involvement of the ophthalmic arteries causes a sudden painless temporary or permanent visual loss. Corticosteroids are obligatory in this condition because they significantly reduce the risk of irreversible visual loss and other focal ischaemic lesions. Intravenous steroids are indicated when there is sudden unilateral loss of vision to avoid vision loss in the other eye.

Intraocular steroids
Intraocular steroids is incorrect. Intraocular steroids might be employed in an instance of Cystoid Macular Oedema, not in a case of visual loss with giant cell arteritis (GCA).

Oral steroids
Oral steroids is incorrect. Intravenous steroids are the correct mode of administration if someone has visual loss with GCA.

Timolol
Timolol is incorrect. This gentleman has GCA, and not glaucoma.

stem: A 50-year-old woman is concerned about osteoporosis because her mother had it. She had a premature menopause at the age of 40 but no other risk factors in her history. You decide to perform a bone mineral density (BMD) test. This comes back showing a Z-score of 0 and T-score of –0.5 SD. How do you interpret these results?
options: Patient has lower than expected BMD for her age
Patient has normal BMD for her age
Patient is at risk of fracture and should receive treatment
explanation:
Patient has normal BMD for her age
Her z score is 0 (indicating normal BMD for age) and her T score is -0.5 (i.e. > -1) which is normal. The T-score represents the bone mineral density (BMD) measurement compared with that which would be obtained from an average person at their peak bone mass. The Z-score is the BMD score compared with a normal individual but adjusted for the age of the person. A Z-score of 0 means that the individual has normal BMD for their age. The WHO definition of osteoporosis is a T-score of –2.5 standard deviations below the norm or lower. At this level the person is deemed to be at risk of fracture. Osteopenia is defined as a T-score between –1 and –2.5 SD.

Patient has lower than expected BMD for her age
Patient has lower than expected BMD for her age is incorrect. Her Z score indicated normal BMD for age and her T score is normal.

Patient is at risk of fracture and should receive treatment
Patient is at risk of fracture and should receive treatment is incorrect. Her Z score indicated normal BMD for age and her T score is normal.

stem: A 18-year-old patient presents with purpura on his back, buttocks and extensor surface of his lower limbs. He has dipstick haematuria. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Henoch–Schönlein purpura
The clinical presentation is entirely typical, with a purpuric rash on the back, buttocks and extensor surfaces of this young man’s lower limbs. The haematuria is also suggestive of this vasculitic process. It should be noted that this vasculitic process does not result in thrombocytopaenia as platelet numbers are usually normalor raised.

Haemophilia A
Haemophilia A is incorrect. This is not the correct presentation. Haemophilia results in joint and muscle bleeding, which is not the case in this situation. Also, it would not result in haematuria.

Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura
Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP) is incorrect. The presentation in this young man is entirely typical of Henoch–Schönlein purpura. It is a bit difficult to justify a diagnosis of ITP without a reduced platelet count being discussed. Also normally ITP would not result in haematuria.

Thalassaemia trait
Thalassaemia trait is incorrect. There is nothing in the history to suggest this, and this would not result in purpura. This is usually an asymptomatic state.

stem: A 35 year old patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus has been complaining of a 3-month history of right shoulder pain. She describes this as a frozen shoulder, and says it hurts to move her shoulder. Her GP has performed blood tests and her CRP is 5mg/L and ESR 10mm/hr and a shoulder X-ray is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adhesive capsulitis
Microvascular disease causes abnormal collagen repair in people with diabetes, and this predisposes to adhesive capsulitis. Occasionally, fibrous strands are seen traversing the joint space. Patients with diabetes can present with fibrosis elsewhere (e.g. Dupuytren’s contracture). Trauma, the associated transient inflammatory state with granulation tissue, and eventual fibrous adhesions and thickening of the capsule may give rise to adhesive capsulitis.

Calcific tendonitis
Calcific tendonitis is incorrect. Although calcific tendonitis is more common in diabetics, pain is usually on abduction and calcium deposits are usually seen on X-ray.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis is unlikely at this young age.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis usually presents with a small joint polyarthritis with raised inflammatory markers.

stem: A 17-year-old woman presents with red spots on her buttocks and legs, joint pains, oedema, hypertension and proteinuria. She had an upper respiratory tract infection a few days earlier. Blood results show a normal albumin level; urine dipstick reveals +3 protein +2 blood. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Henoch–Schönlein purpura
This young woman has Henoch–Schönlein purpura as evidenced by her symptoms and signs. This condition often follows an acute respiratory tract infection, and usually follows a benign course over weeks or months. A characteristic sign includes a purpuric rash over the buttocks and extensor surfaces. Joint pains and acute abdominal pain are common. Around one-third of patients have nephritis presenting with peripheral oedema, hypertension and proteinuria. Complications include massive gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and ileus and, rarely, kidney disease.

Goodpasture’s disease
Goodpasture’s disease is incorrect. Lung involvement (pulmonary haemorrhage) is seen in Goodpasture’s disease: the chest X-ray may show diffuse infiltrates in the lower zones. Goodpasture’s disease does not present with a purpuric rash.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis would have additional features such as nasal ulceration, rhinitis, otitis media and pulmonary symptoms, and variable shadows may be seen on chest X-ray, particularly multiple nodules.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has been experiencing increased pain and stiffness in her hands, wrists, upper arms, shoulders and calves for 2 years. She describes transient swelling at the wrists. She is frequently roused from sleep by pain and complains of marked fatigue with little stiffness sometimes associated with tingling in the hands, arms and feet. Review of systems reveals increasing urinary urgency and recurrent attacks of headaches. On examination there is no significant abnormality apart from multiple tender spots over the spine and limbs, corresponding to bony prominences and to muscular tissue. Blood tests reveal a white blood cell count (WCC) of 4 × 10 9/l and a platelet count of 167 × 10 9/l. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 20 mm in 1 st hour. The rheumatoid factor is negative and the antinuclear antibody (ANA) test comes back positive at 1:40. The creatine kinase and thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Fibromyalgia syndrome
This patient has fibromyalgia, a common syndrome that is characterised by diffuse persistent musculoskeletal pain, tenderness at focal trigger points, non-restorative sleep and therefore fatigue and low mood. It typically affects women predominantly between the ages of 30 and 60 years. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 1990 criteria for the classification of FMS allows positive identification of the syndrome, which include: A history of widespread pain which has been present for at least 3 months. Pain on digital palpation in at least 11 of the following 18 tender-point sites (each of which is bilateral): occiput, low cervical, trapezius, supraspinatus, second rib, lateral epicondyle, gluteal, greater trochanter, knee. On physical examination, patients with primary FMS usually appear well with no obvious systemic illness or articular abnormalities. Although this lady describes joint swelling – the swelling is transient, Chatwhich areTutor with AI unusual and is not found on clinical examination.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner complaining of rectal discharge and pain affecting his right knee. On examination, his conjunctivae are red and inflamed. His right knee is mildly swollen, warm and tender to touch. There are thickened and scaly patches of skin on his palms and soles and they appear brown in colour. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 94 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 35 mm in the first hour 0–10 mm in the first hour Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
This man has reactive arthritis that is likely triggered by a sexually transmitted disease, given the history of rectal discharge. Features of reactive arthritis include arthritis (particularly knee and ankle inflammation), conjunctivitis and keratoderma blennorrhagica (thickened yellow/brown patches of skin on the palms and soles of the feet). Reactive arthritis may occur in conjunction with a gastrointestinal or sexually transmitted infection, with symptoms beginning around 1–3 weeks after the initial period of infection.

stem: A 27-year-old man complains of low back pain for some years. He says he had an episode of severe diarrhoea 3 weeks earlier, and that he has experienced waxing and waning “stomach problems” that have gone on for a couple of years. An X-ray of the lumbosacral spine shows erosion of the lower joint margins of the vertebrae. Blood tests show a raised ESR of 47mm/hr. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
This patient has ankylosing spondylitis (AS). The main lesion is spinal ankylosis with sacroiliac joint involvement. X-ray of the sacroiliac joints might show squaring of the vertebrae, erosions of the apophyseal joints and obliteration of the sacroiliac joints. It may be precipitated by an infection (e.g. with Yersinia) in genetically predisposed individuals (HLA-B27 gene). Although he describes ‘stomach’ pain, he is talking about GI symptoms. He should be investigated for inflammatory bowel disease.

Gonococcal arthritis
Gonococcal arthritis is incorrect. Gonococcal arthritis is usually migratory and can be associated with a tenosynovitis (inflammation of the tendon sheath) and pustular skin rash.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. He has had back pain and GI symptoms for a number of years. His severe diarrhea (possible GI infection causing reactive arthritis) was only a few weeks ago.

stem: A 20-year-old man is seen in the clinic with a rash over his buttocks and lower legs and pain and swelling in both knees. Two weeks earlier, he had an upper respiratory tract infection. His blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg. Routine blood tests are unremarkable except for raised immunoglobulin A (IgA) levels and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 62 mm/1 st hour. Urinalysis shows evidence of proteinuria (2+. Blood 1+). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Henoch–Schönlein purpura
This patient has Henoch–Schönlein purpura, characterised by a rash affecting the buttocks and lower limbs with a raised IgA levels causing IgA nephropathy. It is a small-vessel vasculitis that usually occurs in children and young adults. Chronic kidney disease is rare in this condition.

Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis
Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis is incorrect. The clinical features are not suggestive of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa does not present like this.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type II diabetes presents with a history of painful hands and feet and morning stiffness for the past three months. Investigations confirm a diagnosis of sero-positive erosive rheumatoid arthritis (RA). She has some pain relief from non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). She currently takes metformin 500 mg three times daily (TDS) and has good glycaemic control as reflected by a HbA1c of 50 mmol/mol (20– 46 mmol/mol). Which of the following disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) would be the most appropriate initial treatment for her early RA?
explanation:
Methotrexate
DMARDs such as methotrexate are the mainstay of treatment for RA. Methotrexate helps in maintaining function and reducing progression of the disease. Other first-line agents include leflunomide and sulfasalazine, but most patients will receive methotrexate.

Ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is more toxic than methotrexate or sulfasalazine with nephrotoxicity and immunosuppression. It is generally reserved for RA with systemic features, such as vasculitis.

Etanercept
The tumour necrosis factor (TNF) alpha-antagonists, etanercept and infliximab, are generally reserved for patients who are unresponsive to traditional DMARDS. If the disease is severe and has not responded to with intensive therapy with a combination of DMARDs, biological agents may be offered in combination

stem: A 66-year-old woman is admitted with a left hip fracture after a fall at home. She has a history of hypothyroidism, hypertension and chronic kidney disease, with a baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 ml/min/m 2. She is post-menopausal. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scan reveals a T score at the femoral neck of -2.8 (> −1). Which treatment should be started to prevent further fractures?
explanation:
Denosumab
Denosumab can be used for secondary prevention of fractures in osteoporotic patients with any estimated glomerular filtration rate. This is given as a 60 mg subcutaneous injection every six months. It is contraindicated in hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the RANK ligand. Common side-effects are joint and muscle pains.

Alendronic acid
This patient is post-menopausal, with osteoporosis (T score < 2.5) and a fragility fracture. Alendronic acid is an appropriate treatment for secondary prevention. It is, however, contraindicated when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is < 35 ml/min/m 2.

Strontium ranelate
This patient has osteoporosis, is post-menopausal and has had a fragility fracture. Strontium ranelate can be used in these patients; however, it carries an increased risk of myocardial infarction and therefore is not first line. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease should be reassessed every 6–12 months. The patient has chronic kidney disease and hypertension. Denosumab is, therefore, a more appropriate choice.

stem: A 60-year-old patient has been complaining of a 1-month history of generalised headache, malaise and fever. He has also noticed scalp sensitivity while brushing his hair. Given the likely diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Oral corticosteroids
This patient presents with giant-cell arteritis, so corticosteroids are mandatory to reduce the risk of irreversible blindness. The starting dose is 40-60mg prednisolone and dosage reduction must be gradual and should be judged solely on clinical features as acute-phase responses are no guide. Most should have achieved a maintenance dose of 10 mg/day after 1 year. The known persistence of disease in a significant proportion of patients for 4 years or more and the possible recurrence of symptoms, including blindness, even a year after corticosteroid withdrawal, argues for a very gradual reduction of dosage.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment and anticoagulation is not recommended. Aspirin co-prescription (alongside steroids) are recommended for vascular propylaxis.

Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is incorrect. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment and anticoagulation is not recommended.

Dipyridamole
Dipyridamole is incorrect. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment and anticoagulation is not recommended.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents with swelling and pain in the proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands. Both hands show ulnar deviation with pitting of the nails and onycholysis. What could be the cause of his condition?
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
This man has psoriatic arthritis (of the rheumatoid distribution). Whilst a distal form of arthritis is most specific for psoriatic arthropathy it can present by mimicing rheumatoid arthritis clinically and may be distinguished only by the presence of scaly lesions on the skin or nail changes (such as pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis).

Dermatophyte infection
Dermatophyte infection is incorrect. Dermatophytic infections are limited to the skin, hair, nails and mucous membranes and do not cause arthritis.

Gonococcal arthritis
Gonococcal arthritis is incorrect. Nail changes do not occur in gonococcal arthritis.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. This gentleman has nail changes of psoriasis, making the diagnosis psoriatic arthritis (that resembles rheumatoid arthritis).

stem: A 45-year-old man complains of burning pain in his foot, with diminished sensation in the sole. He twisted his ankle a week earlier. Severe pain and paraesthesiae can be elicited by applying pressure behind the medial malleolus. What is the most likely cause of his presentation?
options: Injury to the common peroneal nerve
explanation:
Compression of the tibial nerve
This person has tarsal tunnel syndrome caused by entrapment of the tibial nerve.

Atherosclerosis of the popliteal arteries
Atherosclerosis of the popliteal arteries is incorrect. Burning pain is not a feature of intermittent claudication, where the pain is caused mainly by walking.

Injury to the common peroneal nerve
Injury to the common peroneal nerve is incorrect. Foot drop is seen with damage to the peroneal nerves. Sensation is lost over the front and outer half of the leg and dorsum of the foot.

Rupture of the Achilles tendon
Rupture of the Achilles tendon is incorrect. Rupture of the Achilles tendon causes sudden pain at the back of the ankle during running or jumping. Loss of sensation and burning pain do not occur in this condition.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a past medical history of osteoarthritis (only affecting her hand joints) and diet- controlled diabetes mellitus complains of a sudden onset of pain, swelling and stiffness in her right knee. Examination shows that the right knee is swollen, erythematous and tender. Her blood tests show a CRP of 41mg/L and an ESR of 52mm/hr. Which one of the following tests is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
options: Aspiration and examination of the synovial fluid
explanation:
Aspiration and examination of the synovial fluid
This woman with a monoarthritis may have a septic arthritis or pseudogout, and the inflammatory markers do not help to distinguish between the two. The most appropriate test to lead to an early diagnosis is aspiration of the joint and synovial fluid Gram stain and culture, and examination of the synovial fluid under polarised light for rhomboid crystals that exhibit weakly positive birefringence, which is typical of pseudogout. N.B. A synovial fluid white cell count greater than 50,000/mm 3 with more than 90% neutrophils is highly suggestive of bacterial infection and Gram-stain examination and culture may reveal the organism responsible.

A trial of colchicine
A trial of colchicine is incorrect. The most important diagnosis to exclude with a monoarthritis is a septic arthritis, and therefore aspiration of the joint should be the first investigation of choice. This Chat otherwith investigation would not be diagnostic.

X-ray of the knee
X-ray of the knee is incorrect. The most important diagnosis to exclude with a monoarthritis is a septic arthritis, and therefore aspiration of the joint should be the first investigation of choice. This other investigation would not be diagnostic.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome has been on oral prednisolone for 6 years. She now presents with right-sided hip pain and a limping gait. The pain was of sudden onset and has built slowly over the past week. Examination reveals limitation of abduction and internal rotation of the right thigh. She is apyrexial. Which one of the following investigations would be most useful to make a diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
MRI of the hip
This patient most probably has suffered avascular necrosis of the femoral head because of her prolonged corticosteroid treatment. N.B. the nephrotic syndrome increases the risk of thrombosis as well and therefore is a risk factor for avascular necrosis (AVN).

Blood culture
Blood culture is incorrect. Infection is not likely.

Joint fluid microscopy
Joint fluid microscopy is incorrect. There is nothing to suggest a septic arthritis (eg systemic upset, raised CRP).

Serum uric acid
Serum uric acid is incorrect. Gout is unlikely to affect the hips.

stem: A 69-year-old diabetic woman has chills and rigors and has a 1-day history of pain in her right knee. She is afebrile. Her blood tests show a CRP of 25mg/L, ESR 37mm/hr and a weakly positive rheumatoid factor. What clinical diagnosis should be considered most likely until excluded?
explanation:
Septic arthritis
Involvement of a single joint occurs in 90% of cases. The knee is most commonly affected. 50% of cases do not feature a fever. Diabetes increases her risk of infection. Her inflammatory markers are elevated, in keeping with infection.

Gouty arthritis
Gouty arthritis is incorrect. Gout is more likely to affect the first metatarsophalangeal joint (but can cause knee monoarthritis) and is also not associated with chills and rigors.

Pseudogout
Pseudogout is incorrect. Pseudogout is the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in a joint that is already affected by arthritis. These patients usually have long-standing pain and several joints may be involved.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is usually a small joint polyarthritis. A weakly positive rheumatoid factor in an elderly patient is negligible.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a 30-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with severe right sided shoulder pain and pain during the middle portion of arm abduction. She also complains of weakness when lifting or rotating the right arm. She says the pain came on suddenly whilst reaching for a heavy cooking pan. An X-ray of the shoulder is normal. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Torn rotator cuff
A torn rotator cuff can occur spontaneously in elderly patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The patient is able to abduct the arm, but the pain worsens during the middle of the range of abduction. There may also be associated weakness on lifting or rotating the affected limb.

Adhesive capsulitis
Adhesive capsulitis is incorrect. Adhesive capsulitis (true frozen shoulder) is a rare condition in which there is severe shoulder pain and complete loss of all shoulder movements.

Calcific tendonitis
Calcific tendonitis is incorrect. Calcific tendonitis is due to calcium pyrophosphate deposits in the tendon that would be apparent on X-ray. The condition is not always symptomatic.

stem: A 57-year-old obese woman presents with numbness, tingling and burning on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. On examination there is dysaesthesia (increased sensitivity to light touch) in the affected area. An X-ray of the hip joint is normal. What is the most likely possible cause of her symptoms?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
explanation:
Meralgia paraesthetica
This patient has meralgia paraesthetica. It is caused by entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament. Most patients are obese; weight reduction helps to relieve symptoms. It can also be caused by wearing very tight, low-rise trousers; looser trousers help to relieve symptoms.

Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is incorrect. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head causes severe hip pain. Again the X-ray might show a well-demarcated area of increased bone density or collapse of the affected bone. Usually there would be an associated risk factor such as corticosteroid or heparin treatment.

Trochanteric bursitis
Trochanteric bursitis is incorrect. Trochanteric bursitis occurs as a result of trauma or unaccustomed exercise in most cases. The pain over the greater trochanter is worse on going up the stairs, when abducting the hip and classically at night patients cannot sleep on the affected side. There is usually a focal area of tenderness around the greater trochanter.

stem: A middle-aged woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with right foot drop and numbness in her right hand, with thenar eminence wasting and sensory loss over the radial half of her hand. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Mononeuritis multiplex
The presence of multifocal concurrent peripheral nerve lesions in this case suggest mononeuritis multiplex as the most likely cause for her symptoms. This patient has a right median nerve and a right peroneal nerve lesion. Mononeuritis multiplex is a neuropathy of two or more peripheral nerves that are not anatomically related. Pathologically, the nerves are made susceptible to mechanical compression by ischaemia caused by vasculits of the vasa nervorum (blood supply to the nerves) or infiltration of the nerves. A number of case reports exist to suggest it is associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

Entrapment neuropathy
Entrapment neuropathy is incorrect. Entrapment neuropathies result from compression of peripheral nerves due to hypertrophied synovium or joint subluxation. Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel is the most common, and bilateral compression can be an early clinical manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis. Aching pain and paraesthesia characteristically occur in the distal affected parts, followed by sensory loss and muscle wasting.

Peripheral sensory neuropathy
Peripheral sensory neuropathy is incorrect. Motor weakness and muscle wasting do not accompany peripheral sensory neuropathy.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with cold hands. She reports that she usually struggles with this on colder days or when in cold water. Her complaint began with pale and cold digits and has now progressed to painful, purple finger tips. She has also struggled with dysphagia and heartburn for the past five years. She also reports a history of hypertension. On examination, her blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg, and her heart rate is 90 bpm. There is significant skin hardness and thickening palpable on the fingers and toes. Bilateral X-rays of the hands and feet showed cutaneous calcifications, especially near the fingertips. Which one of the following tests is likely to be correlated with the diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-centromere antibody
The limited cutaneous form of systemic scleroderma is often referred to as CREST syndrome. ‘CREST’ is an acronym for the five main features: calcinosis Raynaud's syndrome oesophageal dysmotility sclerodactyly telangiectasia. The anti-centromere antibody is more specific for the CREST syndrome than diffuse progressive systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains of back pain and tenderness in her thighs. She also mentions that she finds it difficult to climb stairs. She has never smoked and does not drink alcohol. She has well-controlled asthma and takes a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid only. Her full blood count is normal. She has an alkaline phosphatase level of 250 U/l (normal range 40–125 U/l), her plasma calcium concentration is 1.98 mmol/l (2.12–2.62 mmol/l). Her liver and kidney function tests are normal. What would you expect her pelvic radiograph to show?
options: Layers of periosteal new bone formation
explanation:
Translucent bands
This patient has osteomalacia, which is characterised by translucent bands (Looser’s zones or pseudofractures) at points of stress. Osteomalacia is characterised by back pain, muscle weakness and bone tenderness. It is due to vitamin D deficiency. Biochemical abnormalities are a raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and low calcium and phosphate levels. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) may be elevated (secondary hyperparathyroidism), leading to a phosphaturia (loss of phosphate in the urine).

Bone expansion and sun-ray appearance
Bone expansion and sun-ray appearance is incorrect. These appearances are suggestive of - A chondrosarcoma A metastatic tumor in the bone An osteogenic sarcoma

Punched-out osteolytic lesions
Punched-out osteolytic lesions is incorrect. Punched out osteolytic lesions are usually found in myeloma.

stem: A 43-year-old man who is known to be HIV positive is treated with a number of medications including didanosine. He has recently suffered a third attack of gout in the past 5 months, which was managed with a course of colchicine. His creatinine is normal, as are his ALT and alkaline phosphatase; urate is 620 mmol/l. He is currently experiencing an acute gout attack. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his gout in this situation?
explanation:
Colchicine
Colchicine is effective in both the treatment and prevention of gout attacks. In this patient's case, colchicine has already been used to manage previous gout attacks successfully, demonstrating its efficacy and tolerability. It does not have significant interactions with didanosine or other common antiretroviral medications, making it a safe option for someone on a stable HIV treatment regimen. Furthermore, colchicine can be continued at a lower dose for prophylaxis, helping to prevent future attacks without compromising his HIV management.

Allopurinol
Although allopurinol is commonly used to lower uric acid levels, it significantly increases plasma levels of didanosine by more than 100%. This interaction is likely to amplify the side effects of didanosine, which include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, fever, headache and peripheral neuropathy. Given the patient's existing HIV treatment regimen, introducing allopurinol would complicate his management and increase the risk of adverse effects.

stem: A 49-year-old man who has multiple pathologies including congestive cardiac failure, COPD and active tuberculosis comes to the Emergency department for review. He has pain in his right great toe and is diagnosed with acute gout, his urate is 530 micromol/l. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Pyrazinamide
Pyrazinamide is a strong urate retention agent, causing a greater than 80% reduction in renal clearance of uric acid at a 300-mg therapeutic daily dose.The metabolite pyrazinoic acid is oxidized by xanthine oxidase and is likely responsible for the hyperuricemic effect.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is incorrect. Beta blockers increase insulin resistance, leading to increased risk of glucose intolerance, but they are not a prominent cause of hyperuricaemia.

Ethambutol
Ethambutol is incorrect. Ethambutol does lead to a rise in uric acid, but the elevation is less marked and more variable versus that seen for pyrazinamide.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is incorrect. Rifampicin is not associated with increased serum urate, (in contrast to both pyrazinamide and ethambutol).

stem: An elderly man, who had a left hip replacement 2 years ago, now presents with right hip pain. An X-ray of the affected area shows an increased trabecular pattern and cortical thickening of the right hemipelvis, with narrowing of the joint space and osteophyte formation. Routine blood tests are normal except for serum alkaline phosphatase, which is elevated to 477 IU/l. What is the probable reason for his right hip pain?
explanation:
Paget’s disease of bone
The X-ray findings and isolated elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (with normal serum calcium and phosphate levels) are characteristic of Paget’s disease of bone. This may cause bony pain due to secondary osteoarthritis or pathological fractures.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. These X-ray features and isolated elevated ALP do not occur in osteoarthritis.

Osteoarthritis with cholelithiasis
Osteoarthritis with cholelithiasis is incorrect. The X-ray appearances do not occur in osteoarthritis and cholelithiasis (gall stones) causing a rise in ALP, would usually be associated with deranged liver function tests as well.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. These X-ray features and isolated elevated ALP do not occur in rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP for review. He has severe pain affecting the right shoulder which is worst during the middle range of abduction. He is unable to initiate abduction of his shoulder via active movement, although passive elevation is less painful. There are no other abnormal physical signs. Plain radiograph is normal What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Supraspinatus tendonitis
Supraspinatus tendonitis is one of the commonest causes of painful restriction of shoulder movement across all ages. In 30% of cases there is a definite history of trauma. Fewer than 5% of cases are bilateral. Pain radiates to the upper arm and is made worse by active abduction and elevation. Passive elevation reduces impingement of the tendon and is often less painful. Supraspinatus muscle is the main one involved in the initial range of abduction, particularly the first 15 o and deltoid then predominates increasingly for the remainder of the range. Impaired initiation of abduction is therefore typically present. Analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the treatment of choice, although some patients may require local corticosteroid injection. Around 70% of patients improve without physiotherapy over a 5–20-day period. Physiotherapy may aid mobilisation in patients with persistent stiffness.

The Milwaukee shoulder
The Milwaukee shoulder is incorrect. The Milwaukee shoulder is a severe erosive osteoarthritis of the shoulder with a haemorrhagic (bloody) effusion, usually seen in elderly ladies.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with an inability to raise her arms over her shoulders. Over the past few weeks she has also been having difficulty swallowing food. On examination there is muscle wasting and the muscles are tender, with reduced tendon reflexes. Investigation Result Normal Value White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115–155 g/l Platelets 450 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 58 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 27 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Creatinine Kinase 1800 IU/l 23–175 IU/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyositis
In polymyositis there is symmetrical proximal muscle weakness resulting from muscle inflammation. Dysphagia, dysphonia and respiratory weakness can develop. Diagnosis is by measurement of creatine kinase, electromyography (EMG) and muscle biopsy. The ESR and CRP may be elevated or normal.

stem: A 35-year-old patient complains of feeling unwell for the last 6 months. He has increased photosensitivity and a purplish-red rash around the eyes. On examination there is an erythematous scaly eruption over the extensor surfaces of his arms. Which other concurrent disease would you suspect?
explanation:
Malignancy
This patient has dermatomyositis, with a heliotrope rash that often precedes or accompanies muscle weakness. The heliotrope rash is a symmetrical, confluent, purple-red, macular eruption of the eyelids and periorbital tissue. Oedema may also be present. A significant proportion of adults with polymyositis (10%) and dermatomyositis (15%) have underlying malignancy, usually a carcinoma. The association with malignancy is stronger for adults with dermatomyositis, who die from cancer significantly more often than age-matched controls. Many types of malignancy have been reported in association with dermatomyositis, including lung, oesophageal, breast, colon and ovarian tumours. Among women with dermatomyositis, the risk of ovarian cancer is as much as 20 times greater than that of the general population. Most patients diagnosed with primary polymyositis or dermatomyositis (children excepted) should undergo some surveillance for a disease-associated malignancy.
