This screening should be based on a careful history, physical examinations and the performance of a limited number of routine tests (eg chest radiography), in addition to age-appropriate cancer screening such as mammography and flexible sigmoidoscopy.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus is not overtly directly related to dermatomyositis.

stem: A 25-year-old mechanic complains of stiffness and low back pain that is worse in the mornings. He is HLA B27-positive. A provisional diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis is made. What would be the most characteristic finding on an X-ray of the lower spine?
options: Subchondral bony sclerosis on the iliac sides of the sacro iliac joints
explanation:
Subchondral bony sclerosis on the iliac sides of the sacro iliac joints
X-rays in ankylosing spondylitis may show subchondral bony sclerosis on the iliac sides of the sacroiliac joints.

Narrowing of disc space
Narrowing of disc space is incorrect. Narrowing of the disc space is typically seen in patients with a prolapsed intervertebral disc.

Osteophyte formation
Osteophyte formation is incorrect. Syndesmophytes are seen later on X-rays and may cause bony ankylosis and permanent stiffening (bamboo spine). A syndesmophyte is a bony growth originating inside a ligament, commonly seen in the ligaments of the spine, specifically the ligaments in the intervertebral joints leading to fusion of vertebrae. Syndesmophytes are pathologically similar to osteophytes.

Osteoporosis of trabecular bone
Osteoporosis of trabecular bone is incorrect. Osteoporosis of trabecular bone is not seen in ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 62-year-old retired postman awoke with ‘darkened’, impaired vision in the upper half of the visual field of his left eye 3 days prior to evaluation. He described the onset of symptoms as ‘like a shade being pulled down’ over the visual picture. He did not complain of eye pain. He had noted a headache for 6 weeks beforehand, and had consulted his GP on three occasions about this. He was told that he was suffering from tension headache, and was prescribed simple analgesics. When questioned specifically he reports having pain at each side of his jaw when he eats, especially towards the end of the meal. He is hypertensive and on treatment with a β-blocker. He has never smoked. Which of the following diagnoses is likely?
explanation:
Arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy
Altitudinal defects (from the bottom up, or the top down) are common in vascular disorders of the optic nerve head, so this is likely to be an ischaemic optic neuropathy. The preceding headache and symptoms of jaw claudication raise the suspicion of temporal arteritis (giant cell arteritis (GCA)), the feared complication of which is arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy. This patient would likely have elevated ESR and CRP.

Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion is incorrect. Central retinal artery occlusion causes painless loss of vision in one eye and usually does not produce an altitudinal field defect. Fundoscopy reveals a pale retina with aAI cherry Tutor red spot.

Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis is incorrect. Optic neuritis presents with acute or subacute painful loss of vision in one eye and is uncommon in this age group. Altitudinal field defects are unlikely to occur.

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with progressive proximal myopathy, which has increased in severity over the past 3 months. She has a history of osteoarthritis, which is managed with regular paracetamol, and hypertension which is managed with ramipril and amlodipine. On examination, her BP is 148/72 mmHg, pulse is 80 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. There is obvious proximal myopathy. Her creatine kinase is elevated at 1780 U/l and you suspect polymyositis. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive?
explanation:
Anti-nuclear antibodies
Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) is positive in one third of patients with polymyositis. Anti-Jo antibodies are also commonly described as being positive in myositis, although they are more commonly seen in patients who also have other features such as pulmonary fibrosis, arthritis and Raynaud’s phenomenon.

Anti-smooth muscle
Anti-smooth muscle is incorrect. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are most strongly associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

pANCA
pANCA is incorrect. pANCA stands for perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and target the nuclear of neutrophils. They are a subset of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). pANCA is associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, but also primary sclerosing cholangitis, ulcerative colitis and microscopic polyangiitis.

stem: A 22-year-old student, newly diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis has increasing back pain and early morning stiffness. Blood tests (FBC, U&E, LFTs and CRP) are all normal. What treatment would you advise as a first line therapy?
explanation:
Oral NSAIDs
The answer is Oral NSAIDs (Option C). Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are often effective in relieving the symptoms of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). Physiotherapy is the mainstay of treatment and patients should be encouraged to continue exercises irrespective of the pharmaceutical options employed, including biologic agents. N.B. inflammatory markers can be normal in active ankylosing spondylitis.

Anti-TNF treatment
Anti-TNF treatment (Option A) is incorrect. This patient has not yet tried NSAIDs, which are the first line treatment and may abate his symptoms. In order to be eligible for anti-TNFs, patients should have tried at least 2 NSAIDs for at least 4 weeks.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone (Option D) is incorrect. Oral steroids should be avoided.

stem: A 62-year-old woman complains of general lethargy, morning stiffness and inability to comb her hair because of arm pain. There is no muscle tenderness although she says there is pain on movement of the shoulders and hips. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 57 mm in 1 st hour. CRP is 46mg/L. Electromyography of the deltoid muscle is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) occurs more commonly in the elderly, particularly women, and presents as aching and morning stiffness in the proximal muscles. PMR is on the spectrum of giant-cell arteritis. The diagnosis is made on the basis of the history and symptoms. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is almost always remarkably high (> 40 mm in 1 st hour), as is the CRP.

Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is incorrect. Fibromyalgia classically presents with diffuse pain and multiple tender spots all over the body that might be anatomically unrelated to the affected muscles. The ESR and CRP are normal in this condition.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness resulting from muscle inflammation is seen in polymyositis. Electromyography would show the typical triad of changes with myositis: spontaneous fibrillation potentials at rest, polyphasic or short-duration potentials on voluntary contraction, and salvos of repetitive potentials on mechanical stimulation of the nerve.

stem: A 39-year-old man with coeliac disease presents complaining of pain in both legs and difficulty walking. An X- ray shows linear areas of low density surrounded by sclerotic borders in both femurs. Given the most likely explanation for his lower-limb symptoms, which blood test would be most useful in diagnosing this condition?
explanation:
Serum alkaline phosphatase
The history and results of the investigations suggest that this patient has developed osteomalacia, which can occur due to malabsorption of vitamin D in patients with coeliac disease. In osteomalacia, blood results will show: The plasma calcium concentration is low or normal Parathyroid hormone can be elevated if there is secondary hyperparathyroidism The serum phosphate level might be low due to increased parathyroid hormone-dependent phosphaturia, though this is variable Serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is usually low (except in vitamin D-resistant rickets) Alkaline phosphatase is reliably elevated in osteomalacia, for this reason it is the preferred answer here

Urinary phosphate excretion
Urinary phosphate excretion is incorrect. Parathyroid hormone stimulates urinary phosphate excretion

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents for review. She complains of severe pain and restriction of movement affecting her right elbow, which is particularly bad on the outside of the arm. There is no past medical history of note and she is a keen gardener. The pain is reproduced on resisted wrist extension when the examiner fixes the right elbow. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical history?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis
Lateral epicondylitis (so-called tennis elbow) is caused by inflammation of the musculotendinous origin of the common extensors on the lateral side of the elbow. It is most prevalent in the 20–40-year age group and is seen in up to 10–15% of regular tennis players. On examination there is local tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and resistance against wrist extension reproduces the pain. Management involves rest, ice after exercise, stretching physiotherapy exercises, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and local steroid injections. A counterforce brace may be useful and patients resistant to conservative therapy may be referred for surgery to effect a lateral release.

Cervical radiculopathy
Cervical radiculopathy is incorrect. The pathology is at the c-spine, and therefore patients will usually have neck pain as well.

Medial collateral ligament instability
Medial collateral ligament instability is incorrect. This is a knee pathology.

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic with severe rheumatoid arthritis. She is currently taking a second-line agent, low-dose prednisolone and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Despite this she still has active disease and wants to increase her therapy if possible. You are considering using etanercept, an anti-tumour necrosis factor (anti-TNF) agent in this patient. Which one of the following interactions or previous illnesses would prompt avoidance of etanercept if possible?
options: Use in a patient with previous iron deficiency anaemia
Use in a patient with previous history of psoriasis
explanation:
Co-morbid multiple sclerosis
Co-morbid demyelination is a contraindication for anti-TNF treatment. Other cautions include its use in patients with active hepatitis B or hepatitis C or heart failure. The caution which everyone is aware of with anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agents is, of course, the risk of reactivation of tuberculosis in patients who have a previous history of the disease.

Co-morbid diabetes
Co-morbid diabetes is incorrect. TNFa is implicated in insulin resistance, and therefore theoretically anti-TNF treatment might improve this; however, this has not been confirmed clinically. Caution would be needed, however, in starting anti-TNF treatment, if a patient has recurrent infections with diabetes (e.g. ulcers).

Use in a patient with previous history of psoriasis
Use in a patient with previous history of psoriasis is incorrect. Anti-TNFs are more effective in combination with methotrexate and anti-TNFs are used for psoriasis and psoriatic arthropathy.

stem: A 25-year-old man gives a 2-week history of painful joints affecting his lower limbs. He returned from a trip to south-east Asia 3 weeks ago. During this holiday he had developed loose bowel motions followed by eye irritation. He has a psoriasiform rash on the lower limbs and soles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis usually follows a sexually transmitted infection (especially chlamydia) or gastroenteritis (e.g. due to Shigella, Salmonella or Campylobacter) It most commonly affects young men carrying the HLA-B27 antigen The arthritis can affect various joints, but typically involves the knees and ankles Enthesitis can lead to heel and foot pain Inflammatory eye disease and mucocutaneous manifestations are common Conjunctivitis may be followed by uveitis Some patients develop skin lesions: psoriasiform changes on the soles (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) present as tender, keratotic plaques; palmar involvement may be present and more typical psoriasis-like plaques may occur elsewhere An annular or serpiginous eruption known as circinate balanitis may be present on the glans penis Rare complications include heart block, aortic incompetence and pericarditis Management involves identification and treatment of precipitating infection, symptomatic treatment such as with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, injection of corticosteroids into affected joints and topical treatments akin to those used in psoriasis; prolonged disease may require disease-modifying agents

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with symptoms of Raynaud’s phenomenon, progressive thickening of the skin on her fingers and telangiectasiae on her face and upper body. A past history of reflux oesophagitis is noted and she is currently undergoing investigation for bilateral hearing loss. Examination reveals BP of 155/80 mmHg, pulse is 85 bpm and regular. You confirm the presence of sclerodactyly, calcinosis and telangiectasiae. There is loss of fine-touch sensation in the fingers. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 187 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 211 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Systemic sclerosis
The features seen here (sclerodactyly, calcinosis, telangiectasia) fit best with a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis. Reflux oesophagitis may also be seen as here, and there is often renal impairment and hypertension, for which ACE inhibition is the intervention of choice. Studies report that 20–40% of patients with systemic sclerosis have some degree of hearing loss, although the underlying mechanism for this is unclear.

stem: A 45-year-old white woman complains of sudden back pain radiating down to her ankles. Her menstrual periods are regular. On examination, there is sensory loss over the soles of her feet and calves but the right side is much worse than the left. The straight leg-raising test is positive. Her body mass index (BMI) is 34 kg/m 2. Routine blood tests are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lumbar disc prolapse
The patient has radicular symptoms and signs due to a lumbar disc prolapse. This may have occurred as a result of her obesity (a body mass index of > 30 kg/m 2 indicates obesity).

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis may cause localised back pain but there would be no radiation down to the ankles and no sensory loss.

Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is incorrect. She has radicular symptoms which are unexplained by osteomalacia. In osteomalacia the alkaline phosphatase level is raised, along with raised parathyroid hormone levels and low levels of 25- hydroxycholecalciferol.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis (causing a fracture and therefore localized and radicular symptoms) would be rare in premenopausal woman (she is continuing to have regular menstrual periods).

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with severe tiredness and lethargy. She also reports having joint pains and dry, gritty eyes. You arrange an antibody screen, which reveals positive anti-Ro antibodies and positive antinuclear antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sjögren’s syndrome
Clinically and serologically this lady has Sjögren’s. Anti-Ro antibodies are anti-extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibodies. Subtypes of ENA antibodies can be distinguished by their fluorescence pattern, as seen on enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing. Anti-Ro antibodies are particularly associated with SLE and Sjögren syndrome. Other ENA antibodies include anti-La antibodies (associated with Sjögren’s alone), anti-Sm (associated with SLE alone) and anti-U1-RNP (associated with a range of diseases including SLE and overlap syndrome).

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is incorrect. Antinuclear antibodies are found in around 95% of cases of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), but are non-specific and are found in many other autoimmune conditions. They have low specificity, but a high negative predictive value, ie if someone is ANA negative they are extremely unlikely to have SLE. This lady does not have any clinical features to suggest that she has primary SLE with secondary Sjogrens (such as malar rash) nor any laboratory features (such as low complement or anti- dsDNA).

stem: A 55-year-old woman known to suffer from severe disabling rheumatoid arthritis has a 12-month history of dyspnoea. She has also had a dry cough for that time. She has never smoked and has never been employed. Examination shows a woman of average build with severe hand deformities and nodules at the elbow. Cardiovascular examination is normal. Respiratory examination reveals a diffuse expiratory wheeze. Routine blood tests, a chest X-ray and an electrocardiogram (ECG) are all normal. What is the most likely reason for her symptoms?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans
Bronchiolitis obliterans is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, and presents with a non-productive cough and dyspnoea. Physical examination might reveal a diffuse wheeze. The chest X-ray can be normal or can show a miliary or diffuse nodular pattern. Histology will show intraluminal polyps of organising connective tissue. It is treated with corticosteroids, but the prognosis is poor. Other causes of bronchiolitis obliterans are: Toxic fume inhalation Bone marrow transplantation Post-lung or post-heart transplantation Infections (viral and Mycoplasma and Legionella spp.) Penicillamine Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Polymyositis Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can affect the lungs in many ways. It is associated with: Bronchiectasis

stem: A 70-year-old sheep farmer presents complaining of pain and restricted movements of his right groin for over a year. He also complains of early morning stiffness in the joint that lasts for about half an hour but the pain can get worse throughout the day. The stiffness and pain have been progressively increasing and now he finds it difficult to carry out his routine activities. On examination he appears physically fit. An X-ray of the hip shows some decrease in joint space and subchondral sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is the commonest joint condition in people of this age. Pain on movement, worse at the end of the day, and joint stiffness are characteristic features. Remember that hip pain presents as pain in the groin or buttock.

Brucellosis
Brucellosis is incorrect. This patient is systemically well and only one joint is affected. Brucellosis may present as pyrexia of unknown origin or with non-specific attacks of lassitude, headache, generalised myalgia and night sweats. Untreated brucellosis for a year or more can also present with bouts of depression. Splenomegaly is usually present, along with lymphadenopathy, arthritis and endocarditis. Arthralgia can occur but is not localised to a single joint and movements are not restricted.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis affects the peripheral small joints of the hands and feet and is usually symmetrical.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with rhinitis, asthma and tender subcutaneous nodules. Antibodies to MPO-ANCA are present in his blood and the eosinophil count is 1.2 × 10 9/l (normal range 0.04–0.4 × 10 9/l). A chest X-ray shows patchy pneumonitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)
This patient has the clinical triad of rhinitis, asthma and eosinophilia, along with antibodies to ANCA-MPO (pANCA), which is highly suggestive of EGPA.

Microscopic polyangiitis
Microscopic polyangiitis is incorrect. Eosinophilia is not seen in microscopic polyangiitis also involves the lungs and can result in recurrent haemoptysis. ANCA-MPO antibodies are usually found.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa is ANCA-negative and rarely involves the lungs.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. Eosinophilia does not occur in granulomatosis with polyangiitis. This usually presents with rhinorrhoea, cough, haemoptysis and pleuritic pain. Although c-ANCA is more common in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, pANCA may be seen.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of malaise, weight loss, occasional fever and progressive difficulty in climbing stairs. She also has dyspnea and a dry cough. On examination there is wasting of the pelvic girdle muscles with weakness and bibasal crepitations on chest auscultation. Electromyography (EMG) shows spontaneous fibrillation, high-frequency repetitive potentials and polyphasic potentials on voluntary movements. What is the best diagnostic test?
explanation:
Muscle biopsy
The history and findings are suggestive of adult polymyositis and the best diagnostic test is muscle biopsy. A fine-needle muscle biopsy shows fibre necrosis and regeneration in association with an inflammatory cell infiltrate with lymphocytes around the blood vessels and between muscle fibres. This condition affects women three times more often than men. The onset can be insidious over several months. The major clinical feature is proximal muscle weakness, which is progressive. Wasting of the muscles might also be noted. Respiratory muscles are affected in severe disease (especially those patients with anti-Jo-1 antibodies). N.B. in this case – all of these options are valid and will be performed, but muscle biopsy is the best answer of the list.

Pulmonary function tests
Pulmonary function tests is incorrect. Pulmonary function tests would demonstrate a restrictive pattern of spirometry, but are non-diagnostic.

stem: A college student complains of painful mouth ulcers associated with pain and swelling in both hands. She has had several episodes of vasospasm in her fingers, with pallor, cyanosis and subsequent redness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 99 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 4 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 61 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) 1:640 Anti-dsDNA positive What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus
This lady has SLE due to oral ulceration, arthritis, Raynaud’s syndrome (triphasic colour change from white to blue to red) and antinuclear (ANA) and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA antibodies), thrombocytopenia (possibly due to ITP), a raised ESR and a normal CRP. Antinuclear antibodies, although non-specific, are found in 95% of patients with SLE. Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, are highly specific for SLE, are found in approximately 50% patients and confer a worse prognosis.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents with pain in both buttocks, and redness and mild pain in his right eye. Given the most likely clinical diagnosis, which of the following clinical signs would be the earliest evidence of this condition?
options: Fixed flexion deformity of the hip
Retention of lumbar lordosis during spinal flexion
explanation:
Retention of lumbar lordosis during spinal flexion
Retention of lumbar lordosis during spinal flexion is an early sign of ankylosing spondylitis, a type of inflammatory arthritis that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. This condition is characterised by inflammation that leads to chronic pain and stiffness, particularly in the lower back and buttocks. As the disease progresses, the inflammation can cause fusion of the vertebrae, leading to a loss of the normal curvature of the spine. Early recognition of this sign is crucial for diagnosis and management, as early treatment can help prevent severe spinal deformity and improve the quality of life for affected individuals.

Fixed flexion deformity of the hip
Fixed flexion deformity of the hip is incorrect because hip joint involvement typically occurs later in the course of ankylosing spondylitis. This deformity results from prolonged inflammation and eventual joint damage, leading to a permanent bending of the hip joint. The early stages of ankylosing spondylitis are more likely to affect the spine and sacroiliac joints rather than the hips. Thus, fixed flexion deformity of the hip would not be one of the earliest signs of the condition.

Paraspinal muscle wasting
Paraspinal muscle wasting is also incorrect, as this occurs later in the progression of ankylosing spondylitis. Muscle wasting happens due to chronic inflammation and disuse atrophy from prolonged pain Chatand withstiffness. In the early stages, inflammation and pain are more prominent, and muscle wasting develops over time as the

stem: A young African-American woman is diagnosed as having systemic lupus erythematosus. What is the characteristic epidemiological feature of this condition?
options: First-degree relatives have a 25% chance of developing the disease
It is about twice as common in women than in men
It is associated with HLA-DR2 and -DR3 in White ethnicity
The age of onset is usually over 40 years
The highest incidence is amongst White women
explanation:
It is associated with HLA-DR2 and -DR3 in White ethnicity
There is an increased frequency of HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3 in white Europeans with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

First-degree relatives have a 25% chance of developing the disease
First-degree relatives have a 25% chance of developing the disease is incorrect. First-degree relatives have a 3% chance of developing the disease. There is a higher concordance rate in monozygotic twins (up to 25%).

It is about twice as common in women than in men
It is about twice as common in women than in men is incorrect. It is about nine times as common in women as in men.

The highest incidence is amongst White women
The highest incidence is amongst White women is incorrect. It is most common in African-American women, with a prevalence of 1:250.

stem: A 25-year-old man complains he has had pain in his right elbow, right wrist, left knee and left ankle for the last two weeks. He recently came back from Thailand, where he had been on a 3-week holiday with his friends. He reports that whilst on holiday he had unprotected sex. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the tendons around the involved joints but no actual joint swelling. He also has a skin rash, which is vesicopustular, but it doesn't affect his hands and feet in particular. Blood tests show CRP 35mg/l and ESR of 40mm/h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gonococcal arthritis
This patient has a gonococcal arthritis with periarthritis dermatitis syndrome. He has probably acquired a sexually transmitted infection via unprotected intercourse. Most patients exhibit migratory polyarthralgias followed by fever, tenosynovitis and dermatitis. The skin lesions can be maculopapular or vesicular, with the vesicles becoming vesiculopustular over time. The raised inflammatory markers are non-specific and can occur in any of the listed conditions.

Fungal arthritis
Fungal arthritis is incorrect. Fungal arthritis usually occurs in an immunosuppressed patient.usually Patients Tutor have systemic upset (fever, malaise, etc).

Tuberculous arthritis
Tuberculous arthritis is incorrect. Tuberculous arthritis is usually a chronic monoarthritis (one joint affected) of a peripheral joint, which is a cold synovitis (skin overlying is not red or warm) or of the spine (leading to vertebral collapse and kyphosis). Patients usually have systemic upset.

stem: A 50-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a history of general muscle weakness of 12 months’ duration. She also gives a history of pain in the small joints of her hand, which she has had for more than 18 months. In addition, there is a history of difficulty swallowing. Examination is normal except for weakness and tenderness of her upper arms; there is no obvious synovitis affecting her hands. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 60 mm in 1 st hour, her haemoglobin is 95 g/l, and her mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean cell haemoglobin concentration (MCHC) are normal. Serum antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor are positive. Creatine kinase is 1250 units/l. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyositis
This lady has muscle weakness, dysphagia (due to muscle weakness and a raised CK indicating polymyositis, which may also give rise to polyarthralgia, anaemia of chronic disease, raised inflammatory markers, positive ANA and rheumatoid factor. Polymyositis is a disorder of the muscles characterised by necrosis of muscle fibres, together with regeneration and inflammation. Dermatomyositis is the name given to the condition when a rash accompanies polymyositis. This shows an increased incidence of carcinoma (of all types).It presents with proximal muscle weakness and wasting. Muscle pain and tenderness can occur in up to 50% of patients, but weakness is the main symptom. Arthralgia affecting the small joints of the hands can occur in about half of all patients, pre-dating the muscle weakness. Dysphagia due to oesophageal muscle spasm occurs in up to 50%. Raynaud’s phenomenon is commonly seen. Muscle enzymes (creatine phosphokinase and aldolase) are raised and can be used to monitor the disease. Electromyography (EMG) shows short polyphasic motor potentials, spontaneous fibrillation and high-frequency repetitive discharges. Patients may have a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), a normocytic and normochromic anaemia, and positive rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies. Patients should be treated

stem: A 54-year-old man with a history of obesity, type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents to the clinic complaining of pain in his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He takes orlistat, ramipril, indapamide, amlodipine and metformin and has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen for intermittent bouts of the same pain that have occurred over the past 18 months. On examination he has a blood pressure of 149/90 mmHg and a body mass index (BMI) of 31 kg.m 2. He has pain, swelling and redness over the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 229 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l X-rays shows erosions with sclerotic margins and intraosseous calcifications. Which one of his drugs should be discontinued?
explanation:
Indapamide
This man has gout, a condition associated with insulin resistance, obesity and type 2 diabetes. ChatIndapamide with as a member of the thiazide class is associated with raised serum uric acid, so discontinuing indapamide and substituting another antihypertensive is the management of choice.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has just been diagnosed as having rheumatoid arthritis of her knees, hands and feet. On clinical examination, which complication would most likely be evident?
explanation:
Baker’s cysts
Popliteal cysts (‘Baker’s cysts’) may occur in rheumatoid arthritis following persistent effusion into the knee joint.

Heberden’s nodes
Heberden’s nodes is incorrect. Heberden’s nodes occur in osteoarthritis at the DIPs.

Mallet finger
Mallet finger is incorrect. The long extensors inserting into the distal phalanx are particularly prone to rupture by trauma, resulting in mallet or ‘baseball’ finger.

Telescopic fingers
Telescopic fingers is incorrect. Telescopic fingers indicate an arthritis mutilans (a rare very severe, mutilating type of arthritis associated with psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. This would be very rare in a newly diagnosed young patient.

stem: A 17-year-old girl complains of pain in her hip and knee joints, as well as fever, bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. A barium enema shows rose-thorn ulcers. What is the most characteristic feature seen on colonoscopy in this condition?
explanation:
Discrete ulcers
This girl has enteropathic arthritis secondary to Crohn’s disease. Both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis may be associated with enteropathic arthritis. Barium studies in Crohn’s disease may show strictures, rose-thorn ulcers and cobblestone mucosal surfaces. Colonoscopy may show discrete ulcers.

Colonic dilatation
Colonic dilatation is incorrect. Colonic dilatation is a feature of ulcerative colitis.

Diverticula
Diverticula is incorrect. Diverticular disease does not present with arthralgia and usually occurs in elderly people with low fibre diets.

Red-raw mucosa
Red-raw mucosa is incorrect. Red raw mucosa is a feature of ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. What is the most common finding on blood testing that would be of help in supporting a conclusion that she had active disease?
explanation:
Low complement levels
Complement levels fall in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) due to the formation of immune complexes. Disease activity is SLE is assessed clinically (worsening rashes, joint pain, etc) and also with laboratory parameters – falling complement levels, rising ant-dsDNA antibodies (found in approximately 50% patients with SLE), rising ESR levels and also falling blood counts (haemoglobin, platelets and white cells).

Anticardiolipin antibody
Anticardiolipin antibody is incorrect. Anti-cardiolipin autoantibodies are not a disease activity marker in SLE. Some patients with SLE have anticardiolipin antibody (associated with the antiphospholipid syndrome; APLS) and are prone to recurrent abortions, thrombosis and thrombocytopenia.

Antinuclear antibody (ANA) titre
Antinuclear antibody (ANA) titre is incorrect. The presence of ANA is useful for diagnosis (95% of SLE patients are ANA positive), the titre is not useful for prognosis or disease activity assessment.

VDRL-positive
VDRL-positive is incorrect. VDRL is not a marker of disease activity. The false-positive rate for syphilis serology is around 10%.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with malaise, anorexia, pain in his shoulders and hips, and a weight loss of 8.7 kg, which symptoms have developed over the past 3 months. Examination is unremarkable, except for mildly painful limitation of movement of his hips and shoulders. His ESR is elevated at 72 mm/h. C-reactive protein (CRP) is elevated at 35 mg/l. CK is in the normal range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
This elderly patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) with proximal pain, systemic upset (weight loss and anorexia) and raised ESR and CRP. Patients with PMR are at increased risk of giant cell arteritis and cerebrovascular events, and should be treated with prednisolone.

Gout
Gout is incorrect. Gout usually presents with a monoarthritis.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis is associated with a rise in CK and proximal muscle weakness (myopathy).

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with symmetrical small joint polyarthritis.

stem: A 41-year-old man presents to the clinic with recurrent oral and genital ulceration. You suspect that he has Behçet's disease. Which one of the following HLA antigens is thought to be most strongly associated with the development of Behçet's?
explanation:
HLA-B51
Human leucocyte-associated (HLA) antigen HLA-B51 is known to be associated with Behçet’s disease.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is incorrect. HLA-B27 is associated with seronegative arthritides and conditions such as psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.

HLA-DR2
HLA-DR2 is incorrect. HLA-DR2 is associated with rheumatic fever (but protective against rheumatoid arthritis).

HLA-DR3
HLA-DR3 is incorrect. HLA-DR3 is associated with anti-CCP negative rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.

HLA-DR4
HLA-DR4 is incorrect. HLA-DR4 is associated with type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 51-year-old patient of northern European ethnic origin presents to the clinic with a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. She is concerned as two other first-degree relatives have been diagnosed with the condition. Which HLA subtype is found most commonly in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
DR4
Genetic factors account for 50% of rheumatoid arthritis risk, and in northern Europeans this is due to an epitope of DR4.

DR3
DR3 is incorrect. HLA DR3 is associated with type 1 diabetes, Graves’ disease and myasthenia gravis.

DR1
DR1 is incorrect. DR1 is associated with increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis in patients of southern European origin.

B5
B5 is incorrect. B5 is associated with Behçet’s disease.

B27
B27 is incorrect. HLA B27 is associated with seronegative arthritides and inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling in both knees. An X-ray shows a rim of calcification of the lateral meniscus in both knees. What will be the characteristic finding in the joint aspirate?
explanation:
Positively birefringent crystals
This lady has pseudogout, which is caused by calcium pyrophosphate deposition and is associated with calcification of joint cartilage (chondrocalcinosis). The diagnosis is made by finding weakly positive birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the synovial fluid.

Needle-shaped crystals
Needle-shaped crystals is incorrect. Needle shaped crystals are seen in gout.

Neutrophils
Neutrophils is incorrect. Many neutrophils are also seen in the joint aspirate of pseudogout; hence, pseudogout is often misdiagnosed as septic arthritis.

No abnormality
No abnormality is incorrect. The synovial fluid microscopy is diagnostic in pseudogout.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with left knee pain. She has a history of hypertension which is treated with indapamide 1.5 mg daily and is obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 31 kg/m 2. She looks well and her blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg. On examination, the knee is unremarkable, but internal rotation of the left hip is limited by pain. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 192 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 10 mm in 1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
X-ray left hip and pelvis
Pain can be referred from the joint above or below and in this case the pathology, likely osteoarthritis, is likely to be at her hip (causing referred knee pain). The white count is normal, as is erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), so that there is nothing to indicate an infective or inflammatory cause here.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis, currently treated with methotrexate, comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has significant arthritis affecting both knees, and tells you that she has had pain in the right knee with a posterior swelling for some months. Most recently, after a sponsored walk, she tells you the swelling began to decrease in size slightly, but the pain in her knee got worse and she has developed swelling and pain affecting the calf. On examination, her BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular and her temperature is 37.7°C. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. There is pain on palpation behind the right knee, extending down into the upper portion of the calf. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 137 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate 0–10 mm in the 1 st 34 mm/1 sthour (ESR) hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 42 mg/l 0–10 mg/l D-dimer 268 Significant degeneration due to rheumatoid Plain x-ray right knee arthritis Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ruptured popliteal cyst
The history of posterior knee swelling that decreases in size after exercise, coupled with increased pain and calf swelling, is typical of a ruptured popliteal cyst. Such cysts can occur in patients with rheumatoid arthritis due to synovial fluid accumulation. Upon rupture, the fluid can track down into the calf muscles, causing pain and swelling mimicking DVT. The physical findings and the modest elevation in inflammatory markers support this diagnosis rather than an acute infection or thrombosis. Management typically involves NSAIDs to reduce pain and inflammation, emphasizing the non-emergency nature of the condition.

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
While DVT can present with pain and swelling in the calf, this patient lacks typical risk factors such as immobility, recent surgery, or malignancy. The onset after physical exertion is not characteristic of DVT, which usually occurs spontaneously or after immobilisation. Additionally, the clinical picture includes a history of posterior knee swelling and pain, which aligns more closely with a ruptured cyst rather than a thrombotic event.

Osteomyelitis
This condition involves infection of the bone, which typically presents with systemic symptoms such as fever and elevated white cell count. The patient's lack of fever lowers the suspicion for osteomyelitis significantly. Moreover, osteomyelitis frequently requires a clear source of infection or trauma for it to occur. Given the patient's history and normal WCC, the diagnosis of osteomyelitis is unlikely.

Ruptured gastrocnemius muscle
Muscle ruptures are often accompanied by immediate and severe pain, as well as loss of function, particularly in activities involving plantarflexion of the ankle. These injuries are more likely to occur in the lower portion of the calf. The patient’s history of the popliteal swelling, along with new calf symptoms after exercise, does not correlate with a muscle rupture which frequently occurs abruptly and is not associated with knee swelling.

Septic arthritis
Infection within a joint manifests with severe pain, joint immobility, significant systemic symptoms such as fever, and a high CRP. This patient does not present with high fever or severe systemic symptoms, which are hallmarks of septic arthritis. The slightly elevated CRP and normal WCC do not support an infectious process within the joint. Furthermore, knee degeneration noted on X-ray aligns more with chronic rheumatoid arthritis rather than an acute septic joint.

stem: A 28-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis presents with blood ++ and protein + in the urine. An ultrasound scan shows normal-sized kidneys. A renal biopsy might reveal which one of the following features?
explanation:
IgA deposition
IgA deposition is most likely in this patient due to the presence of blood and protein in the urine, which are hallmark features of IgA nephropathy. IgA nephropathy is commonly associated with ankylosing spondylitis, particularly in young men. The condition is characterized by the deposition of IgA in the glomeruli, leading to episodes of visible or microscopic haematuria and proteinuria. The normal-sized kidneys observed on ultrasound further support this diagnosis, as significant structural changes are not typically seen in IgA nephropathy in its early stages.

Apple-green birefringence in polarised light
Apple-green birefringence in polarised light is indicative of amyloidosis, where amyloid deposits are detected using Congo red staining. In cases of amyloidosis, one would expect significant proteinuria and often enlarged kidneys on imaging. This patient's presentation does not fit with amyloidosis as there is no mention of prolonged disease duration or heavy proteinuria. Additionally, the kidney size is normal, which is less typical for amyloidosis, where kidneys may be enlarged due to amyloid deposits.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is a type of glomerular disease that often presents with nephritic and nephrotic syndrome features. It is characterised by the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane Chat and with mesangial cell proliferation. stem: A 44-year-old man presents with pain in his hips and lower back. Blood tests are unremarkable except for serum alkaline phosphatase, which is 1200 IU/l (normal range 45–105 IU/l). A plain X-ray shows osteolytic and osteosclerotic lesions. What is the most common site of occurrence of this disease?
explanation:
Lumbar spine
This patient has Paget’s disease, as suggested by the results of the investigations – the isolated elevated ALP and lytic and sclerotic radiographic changes. Between 60% and 80% of patients with radiologically identified Paget’s disease are entirely asymptomatic. The disease may involve one bone or many. The condition commonly affects the spine, especially lumbar spine (with a frequency of 30-75%).

Femur
Femur is incorrect. The proximal long bones, especially the femur, are also affected frequently (25-35% of cases). Involvement of the shoulder girdle and proximal humerus is not uncommon.

Fibula
Fibula is incorrect. Although any bone may be affected, the fibula, ribs, and bones in the hands and feet are involved infrequently.

Skull
Skull is incorrect. The skull is affected in 25-65% of cases.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents with a 4 month history of swollen painful joints has been partially responsive to various non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). You diagnose her with rheumatoid arthritis and decide to treat her active arthritis with methotrexate, the first line DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following features is typical of methotrexate therapy?
options: Birth control measures must be in use before methotrexate is started
Bone marrow suppression is not seen with low-dose methotrexate therapy
Clinical improvements are usually seen within the first week of therapy initiation
Hepatic fibrosis is common in relation to prolonged use of the drug
Yearly full blood count and liver function test monitoring is necessary
explanation:
Birth control measures must be in use before methotrexate is started
Methotrexate is known to be teratogenic and women with childbearing potential should use an adequate method of birth control. Men and women should discontinue methotrexate 3–6 months before attempting conception.

Bone marrow suppression is not seen with low-dose methotrexate therapy
Bone marrow suppression is not seen with low-dose methotrexate therapy is incorrect. Myelosuppression can occur at any dose and at any time during therapy

Clinical improvements are usually seen within the first week of therapy initiation
Clinical improvements are usually seen within the first week of therapy initiation is incorrect. Initial improvement seen in 3–6 weeks and peak efficacy in 4–6 months of starting methotrexate.

Yearly full blood count and liver function test monitoring is necessary
Yearly full blood count and liver function test monitoring is necessary is incorrect. Initially, blood tests are performed every 2 weeks for 6 weeks, then monthly thereafter.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with leg ulcers and swollen neck glands. A diagnosis of Felty’s syndrome is made. Which typical finding on blood testing would you expect to find in her case?
explanation:
Normocytic normochromic anaemia
Felty’s syndrome is the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly and neutropenia. Lymphadenopathy and leg ulceration may also occur. In Felty’s syndrome there is reticuloendothelial stimulation leading to hypersplenism. The blood shows normocytic normochromic or hypochromic anaemia with neutropenia. Pancytopenia may occur. The marrow shows erythroid hyperplasia with precursors arrested at the metamyelocyte stage.

High platelet count
High platelet count is incorrect. A high platelet count occurs with active disease.

Lymphocytosis
Lymphocytosis is incorrect. Lymphocytosis is not common in Felty’s syndrome.

Positive HLA B51
Positive HLA B51 is incorrect. HLA B51 is associated with Behcet’s syndrome.

stem: A 65-year-old woman who is known to suffer from chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is brought to the Emergency Department by her partner. For the past few weeks she has been suffering increasing proximal myopathy and bony pain, predominantly affecting the long bones of the arms and legs. Blood testing reveals profoundly low phosphate levels. Urine testing reveals the presence of glycosuria, although serum glucose is unremarkable. What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
D Oncogenic osteomalacia Certain tumours, including mesenchymal tumours, adenocarcinomas (e.g. prostatic carcinoma) and haematological malignancies such as myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, appear to produce a phosphaturic substance. They secrete ﬁbroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) and other phosphaturic proteins. Most affected patients have increased circulating FGF23 levels. The primary transport protein responsible for phosphate reabsorption in the kidney is the type II sodium-phosphate co-transporters (NaPiIIa and NaPi-IIc) localised in the proximal tubule. FGF23 decreases reabsorption of phosphate and production of 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D by the kidney, acting via FGF receptor 1

(FGFR1) signaling. The resulting hypophosphatemia causes rickets, osteomalacia, bone pain, muscle weakness, and fractures, usually accompanied by a marked reduction in concentration of 1,25OH vitamin D. Other abnormalities of renal function such as glycosuria and aminoaciduria may also be present occasionally . Treatment with vitamin D metabolites and phosphate supplements may result in some resolution of skeletal symptoms. In the case of solid tumours, removal of the primary tumour also results in improvement of symptoms. C Hypoparathyroidism Hypoparathyroidism is associated with hypocalcaemia and increased phosphate, and is unlikely here given there has been no surgery that could have led to secondary hypoparathyroidism. A X-linked hypophosphataemia X-linked hypophosphataemia presents with symptoms of rickets in childhood. It is X-linked dominant, with more severe symptoms in boys and is treated with calcitriol and phosphate supplementation. B Tumour lysis syndrome Tumour lysis syndrome is associated with induction chemotherapy, and is primarily manifest by hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function. E Hyperparathyroidism Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with hypercalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism with renal impairment, neither of which are reported here on blood testing.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis complains of breathlessness, mouth ulcers, weakness and malaise. There are inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Blood testing shows the following results: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 90 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 75 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Which one of her medications is most likely to be responsible for these findings?
explanation:
Gold
Gold can cause pancytopenia and pulmonary fibrosis. Both may result in breathlessness. N.B. methotrexate (not included in the options) would also be a fitting answer.

Naproxen
Naproxen is incorrect. Naproxen may be associated with gastrointestinal bleeding and anaemia, but not with pancytopenia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) gives birth to her first child. The nurses are concerned because the newborn infant looks as if she has an SLE-like skin rash. Which maternal autoantibody is most associated with the development of neonatal lupus?
explanation:
Anti-Ro antibodies
Neonatal lupus is highly associated with anti-Ro antibodies, although there can also be an association with anti-La antibodies. The rash usually fades and regresses by 6–8 months of age. Note: These babies are also at risk of congenital heart block.

Anti-cardiolipin antibodies
Anti-cardiolipin antibodies is incorrect. Although it is found in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), it does not cross the placenta to cause neonatal lupus.

Anti-ds DNA antibodies
Anti-ds DNA antibodies is incorrect. Although they are highly specific for SLE, these antibodies do not cross the placenta and therefore cannot cause neonatal lupus.

Anti-La antibodies
Anti-La antibodies is incorrect. Nonatal lupus is more highly associated with anti-Ro antibodies, although there can also be an association with Anti-La antibodies.

stem: A 47-year-old woman complains of exertional dyspnoea associated with a dry cough and bloody discharge from her nose. Her ankles, fingers and toes are swollen. Blood tests for antibodies are positive for cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitiis, EGPA)
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
GPA is a small-vessel necrotising vasculitis and commonly presents with upper airway involvement (typically epistaxis, nasal crusting and sinusitis), lower respiratory tract involvement (haemoptysis, dyspnoea), kidney disease and mucosal ulceration and deafness due to serous otitis media. The characteristic immune marker is the cytoplasmic (sometimes called ‘classic’) antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (cANCA). The principal antigen in the cytoplasm has now been identified as being proteinase 3.

Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitiis, EGPA)
Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitiis, EGPA) is incorrect. There is no mention of eosinophilia or asthma. Churg-Strauss is associated with pANCA (directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO)).

Goodpasture’s syndrome
Goodpasture’s syndrome is incorrect. Goodpastures is associated with kidney disease and anti- glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM).

stem: Which one of the following statements best describes a patient with primary Raynaud’s phenomenon?
options: Anti-nuclear antibody is positive in 70% of cases
Digital gangrene is a frequent complication
Fingers are usually symmetrically involved during an attack
More common in middle aged females (40-60 years)
Nail fold capillary scope shows dilated vessels
explanation:
Fingers are usually symmetrically involved during an attack
In primary Raynaud’s fingers are symmetrically involved. Primary Raynaud’s Secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon phenomenon Age (average) 30 years > 50 years Sex Female Male Tissue damage Absent Digital ulcers, gangrene Symmetry Symmetrical attacks Asymmetrical attacks Capillary scope Negative Positive Autoantibodies Negative Positive Associated Scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, other None diseases connective tissue diseases

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a purpuric rash affecting his legs and buttocks. He also complains of joint pains, especially affecting his knees and ankles, abdominal pain and vomiting. You understand that he suffered an upper respiratory tract infection a few days before presenting to the GP. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 234 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 35 mm/hr 0–10 mm in 1 st h Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood+, protein+ Given the suspected diagnosis which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Glomerular IgA deposition
This boy has Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP). Features seen in HSP on renal biopsy are similar to those seen in IgA nephropathy, with increased presences of inflammatory cells within the mesangium, Chatcrescent formation with and IgA deposition. stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic. She complains of arthritis affecting her knees, elbows, wrists, ankles and the small joints of her fingers. She has also had very high fevers, spiking at night, and weight loss of 4 kg over the past 5 months. On examination, she has generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and arthritis over a joint distribution that is consistent with rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following investigations would be most indicative of a diagnosis of adult-onset Still’s disease?
explanation:
Very raised ferritin
A markedly high ferritin is more specifically associated with Still’s. Still’s is a rare inflammatory arthritis characterised by high spiking fevers, joint inflammation, and an erythematous rash. Although there is cross over with other arthritides, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are usually negative.

Positive anti-CCP antibodies
Positive anti-CCP antibodies is incorrect. Anti-CCP antibodies are found in rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP antibodies are more sensitive and more specific for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis than rheumatoid factor.

Positive anti-nuclear antibody
Positive anti-nuclear antibody is incorrect. Still’s is classically autoantibody negative

Positive rheumatoid factor
Positive rheumatoid factor is incorrect. Still’s is classically autoantibody negative

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a six-week history of tiredness, cough and shortness of breath. He mentions that he has also had episodes of haematuria. Blood tests are positive for pANCA and negative for anti-GBM antibody. The eosinophil count is 0.3 × 10 9/l (normal range 0.04–0.4 × 10 9/l). What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Microscopic polyangiitis
Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) commonly causes fatigue, fever, weight loss, arthralgias, cough, shortness of breath and renal impairment. Whilst rhinosinusitis can occur in both EGPA and MPA its absence, along with a normal eosinophil count and negative anti-GBM antibody, are pointers towards MPA.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formally known as Churg–Strauss syndrome) is incorrect. Although pANCA antibodies can be found in Churg–Strauss (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, EGPA), eosinophilia is a characteristic feature of Churg–Strauss syndrome while the eosinophil count in this patient is normal.

Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis
Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis is incorrect. ANCA antibodies are not present in cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. In granulomatosis with polyangiitis, cANCA is found.

stem: A 50-year-old obese patient presents in the middle of the night to the Emergency Department with pain and swelling of his first, second, third and fourth metatarsophalangeal joint, left ankle and right knee. On examination the joints are swollen, red, hot and tender. Investigation Result Normal Value White Cell Count (WCC) 5.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Urate 3.2 mg/dl 3.4–7.0 mg/dl Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 25 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 5 mg/l 0–10 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gout
This patient has an acute polyarthritis of peripheral joints with red joints suggestive of gout, a condition well associated with obesity and recognised as a feature of the metabolic syndrome. A septic polyarthritis should be excluded with synovial fluid analysis – the knee is the most accessible site. Do not be dissuaded by the normal serum urate as 40% of acute gout cases show a normal urate, which usually rises when the attack has settled. Normal Uric acid levels are 2.4-6.0 mg/dL(female) and 3.4-7.0 mg/dL (male) In gout the first metatarsophalangeal joint (‘podagra’) is affected in 50% of first attacks and in 70% of all attacks. Other common sites are the knees, ankles, mid-tarsal joints, small hand joints, wrists and elbows. The axial skeleton and large central joints are rarely involved. Attacks often wake the patient in the early morning with localised irritation and aching. Within a few hours the joint and surrounding tissues are swollen, hot, red, shiny and extremely painful.
