stem: A 38-year-old man complains of increasing exertional dyspnoea. On examination, he has severe thoracic kyphosis. Fine inspiratory crepitations at the apices are heard on auscultation of the chest. X-ray of the spine shows ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament and facet joint fusion. There is also significant calcification and arthritic changes around both SI joints. What is the condition?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
The clinical picture and X-ray findings are characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis. Associated apical fibrosis of the lungs may occur in only 1% of cases, but respiratory problems are more commonly due to severe kyphosis.

Fibrosing alveolitis
Fibrosing alveolitis is incorrect. This patient has apical fibrosis as an extra-articular feature of ankylosing spondylitis.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. These changes are not seen in a reactive arthritis and there is no precipitating infection history given.

Scheuermann’s disease
Scheuermann’s disease is incorrect. Scheuermann’s disease is a self-limiting condition of childhood with uneven wedging of vertebral bodies leading to significant kyphosis.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of high spiking pyrexia, arthralgia and widespread rash. On examination his distal interphalangeal joints are swollen and hepatosplenomegaly is present. Despite a thorough examination you cannot detect a rash, despite the patient adamantly telling you that he has seen a widespread pink rash over the last four evenings. Blood tests show a CRP of 78mg/l. ESR was not performed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Adult Still’s disease
This patient has adult-onset Still’s disease due to the high spiking fever, swollen DIPs, hepatosplenomegaly and transient rash, which is usually maculopapular, salmon-pink rash on his trunk and arms, which occurs during the fever and usually subsides when the fever defervesces. The ESR and CRP can be elevated in all of the listed conditions and is non-differentiating. Adult onset Still’s disease is found worldwide, with an incidence of 1–3 per million, most commonly in the age range 16–35 years and affecting males and females equally in most populations. There is no consistent human leucocyte antigen (HLA) association. The fever typically appears in the evening. Spikes in excess of 39 °C are typical, though a return to a normal temperature does not occur in 20% of cases. Arthralgia is almost universal and can intensify during the febrile episodes. Distal interphalangeal joint involvement, seen in one in five patients, is useful to distinguish it from other inflammatory arthropathies. The classic Still’s rash is a maculopapular, salmon-pink rash on the trunk, thighs and arms or axillae, which appears during the temperature spike and can disappear when the fever subsides. The rash can also appear on the face, palms and soles and at sites of skin trauma (the Koebner phenomenon) in a third of adults. A severe sore throat (culture-negative) is relatively common in adults. Other common manifestations are hepatosplenomegaly, with or without generalised lymphadenopathy, and polyserositis, of which pericarditis (in a third of cases) and pleuritis are the most common. Rare features include sicca symptoms (dry eyes, mouth), myocarditis, restrictive lung disease, liver or kidney disease, panophthalmitis or inflammatory orbital pseudotumour, epilepsy, intravascular coagulopathy or haemophagocytic syndrome, and amyloidosis.

stem: A 27-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency presents with a painful, red and swollen, first metatarsophalangeal joint of the left foot. Which of the following is the most common cause of acute gout in association with G-6P deficiency?
explanation:
Increased production of pentose sugars
This patient most probably has acute gout. Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6PD) converts glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) to glucose. Deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of G6P. The accumulated G6P enters the hexose monophosphate shunt and leads to increased production of pentose sugars. These act as a substrate for phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) synthetase and result in increased production of purines that are catabolised to uric acid. Hypoglycaemia in G6P deficiency also increases catecholamine levels, which increase glycogenolysis in muscles. This causes lactic acidosis. The increased lactic acid competes with uric acid for excretion, thus decreasing urate excretion.

Decreased glucose levels in blood
Decreased glucose levels in blood is incorrect. Although glucose is decreased in this condition, it is not responsible for the symptoms seen.

Impaired degradation of free radicals
Impaired degradation of free radicals is incorrect. Although these oxidative free radicals can contribute, they are not directly responsible.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with severe pain and stiffness in her shoulder muscles and pelvis for the past 3 weeks that is worse in the mornings. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is raised 52mm/hr and CRP is 45mg/L . What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Stiffness, aching and pain in the muscles of the neck, shoulders, back, hips and thighs characterise the polymyalgia rheumatica syndrome. It is on the spectrum of giant-cell arteritis. The diagnosis is made from the history and symptoms. The ESR and CRP are elevated.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness resulting from muscle inflammation is seen in polymyositis, but pain is usually not a feature. The CK is elevated.

Pseudogout
Pseudogout is incorrect. Pseudogout is the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in a joint. The muscles are unaffected. Shoulder and pelvic involvement is rare.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis commonly affects the small joints of the wrist, hands and feet. Shoulder and pelvic involvement is rare and muscle weakness and tenderness is not seen.

stem: A 35-year-old woman, who has two children, and has had one stillbirth and one miscarriage, now presents with 8 weeks’ amenorrhoea. There is a history of Raynaud’s phenomenon and dysphagia. On examination her blood pressure is 170/120 mmHg. Ulcers are noted on the index and middle fingers of both hands. The doctor advises her not to continue with the pregnancy. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diffuse systemic sclerosis
Diffuse systemic sclerosis is associated with maternal deaths. Reactivation of quiescent scleroderma can occur during pregnancy and increased frequency of small and pre-term babies as well as renal and cardiac complications for the mother. Therapeutic abortion must be considered in these patients in cases of rapid worsening of disease activity. The worst life-threatening complication in pregnancy is scleroderma renal crisis. There may also be serious cardiopulmonary problems.

Antiphospholipid syndrome
Antiphospholipid syndrome is incorrect. This may cause recurrent miscarriage but is not an indication for termination of pregnancy.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. The prognosis is most favourable in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) if the disease has been in remission for at least 6 months before conception.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of acute gout affecting his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. This is his third attack over the past six months, and he usually takes ibuprofen for a few days over the acute period. He has a history of hypertension and takes ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 143 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 232 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 99 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urate 610 mmol/l 0.1–0.4 mmol/l Which of the following is the underlying mechanism of action of the prophylactic therapy this patient requires?
explanation:
Xanthine oxidase inhibitor
In this situation, after the acute flare has settled, allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor which reduces uric acid production, is indicated to prevent further episodes. Allopurinol should not be started during an acute attack, as it may worsen acute gout, even though in the long term, it prevents gout attacks. It would usually be started at least two weeks later. Febuxostat is another example of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

stem: A 38-year-old male postgraduate student from Hong Kong presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of sudden-onset left ear pain, and with an inability to sleep on the affected side. He reports that he is feeling very low because he has had a number of health problems since coming to this country 6 months ago. On further questioning, he admits to having general aches and pains, including pains in various joints over this time. He reports that both his eyes are red all the time but that anti-allergy drops bought from the chemist have had no effect. He has also had a couple of nose bleeds, which is a ﬁrst for him and which he blames on the increased pollution in the air, which he also feels is responsible for the hoarseness in his voice. He denies any known medical problems and, apart from analgesics, he is not on any regular medication. Positive ﬁndings on clinical examination include left auricular chondritis, bilateral eyelid oedema and bilateral mild episcleritis, tenderness to palpation over the anterior trachea and pain on palpation over the costochondral joints. The GP orders some blood tests and X-rays, including rheumatoid factor, which is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Relapsing polychondritis This young man has inﬂammation of cartilaginous structures – the pinna (red, painful ear), nasal septum (epistaxis) and larynx (hoarse voice), as well as chostochondritis and the C-rings of the trachea, consistent with relapsing polychondritis (RP). There is no gender difference in the distribution of the disease, and although it can occur at any age it is most common in the ﬁfth decade. The patient’s reported symptoms depend on the area of the body affected. General symptoms include intermittent fever and weight loss, but other more speciﬁc symptoms include sudden onset of ear pain with an inability to sleep on the affected side, diminished hearing, mono- or polyarthritis, back pain, myalgias, mild epistaxis, saddle-shaped nose, redness of the eyes indicative of conjunctivitis, episcleritis and/or scleritis, hoarseness of the voice and recurrent respiratory infections. There are no speciﬁc diagnostic laboratory ﬁndings in patients with RP, but the nonspeciﬁc indicators of inﬂammation (ESR, CRP) are often elevated. No speciﬁc therapy exists for RP, but the goal of treatment is to control the patient’s symptoms and to preserve the integrity of the affected cartilaginous structures. The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids. It is important in these patients to investigate for the presence of other concurrent autoimmune diseases. C Granulomatosis with polyangitis (GPA) This condition should, however, be considered in the differential. Ear pain and chostochondritis do not occur with GPA. GPA is a rare multi-system autoimmune condition with a wide spectrum of symptoms including lethargy, ongoing rhinitis and sinusitis, arthritis, lung, eye and ENT manifestations. Hallmark histological features are a necrotising granulomatous inﬂammation and pauci-immune vasculitis in small and medium-sized vessels. B Reactive arthritis Ear pain, epistaxis and hoarse voice are not features of reactive ar- RHEUMATO thritis. Reactive arthritis is a systemic inﬂammatory disorder characterised by an aseptic oligoarthritis, triggered by infections arising most commonly from the genitourinary and gastrointestinal systems. A history of urethritis/dysuria and conjunctivitis completes the reactive arthritis triad. D Cogan’s syndrome Cogan syndrome is a rare chronic inﬂammatory autoimmune-mediated disorder characterised by inﬂammation of the ears and eyes. The pathophysiology is poorly understood, but the immunological theory is based on the release of auto-antibodies against corneal, inner ear and endothelial antigens, and of anti-nuclear cytoplasmic autoantibodies (ANCA). Preceding infection may also be implicated but again the exact mechanism is unclear. Cogan syndrome can lead to vision difﬁculty, hearing loss and dizziness. The inner ear is affected, leading to hearing loss in Cogan syndrome, whereas in this case the cartilaginous pinna is affected resulting in a red, swollen, painful ear. E Polyarteritis nodosa This is a rare medium-sized vessel vasculitis, usually leading to mesenteric ischaemia and mononeuritis multiplex. Its presentation is usually of acute onset, with non-speciﬁc symptoms including fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia and fever. Multi-system involvement may occur with wide and varied symptoms. However, the symptoms described in this patient are more consistent with relapsing polychondritis.

stem: A 65-year-old white male, who is a chronic smoker, presents with low back and hip pain. His serum alkaline phosphatase level is 1000 IU/l, calcium 2.25 mmol/l and phosphate 1.2 mmol/l. ESR is 15mm/hr. Other liver function tests are normal. He also complains of difficulty in hearing. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Paget’s disease of bone
This man has Paget’s disease of bone, which commonly occurs after the age of 40 years. The classic presentation is with bone pain, bone deformity, deafness and pathological fractures. The diagnosis is established by the finding of a raised serum alkaline phosphatase level but normal liver function tests and bone profile. N.B. the calcium can become elevated with immobility. Deafness can occur as the VIII cranial nerve becomes compressed due to bony overgrowth causing neural foraminal narrowing.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. Myeloma is not associated with deafness and bone pain from osteolytic lesions causes hypercalcaemia and the ESR is elevated due to paraprotein.

Squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung
Squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung is incorrect. The patient is male and a heavy smoker which are risk factors for squamous-cell carcinoma, however alkaline phosphatase raised with a normal bone profile and liver function is likely be caused by Paget’s disease rather than metastases to the bone from the lung primary. Deafness is not a feature of bone metastases but is a known complication of Paget’s disease of the bone.

stem: A 57-year-old man with long-standing osteoarthritis of his right hip is seen in the clinic prior to admission for hip replacement. He has a history of peptic ulcer and is on lansoprazole. Which anticoagulant formulation would offer him the best protection against postoperative thrombosis?
explanation:
Subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin
Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is preferable to unfractionated heparin in major orthopaedic surgery because it causes less bleeding, a lower incidence of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and offers the convenience of a once-daily subcutaneous administration.

Intravenous heparin
Intravenous heparin is incorrect. Intravenous routes would involve staying in hospital and reduce mobility (being attached to the iv drip).

Low-dose aspirin
Low-dose aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin would provide inadequate thromboembolic prophylactic cover.

Warfarin
Warfarin is incorrect. Warfarin would have to be converted to heparin prior to surgery and then back to warfarin post-operatively, and is more difficult to achieve a therapeutic dose (with INR measurements, monitoring and dose titrations) than a single subcutaneous injection and there is a higher risk of bleeding.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of pain and swelling of the proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands. A clinical diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is suspected. Which one of the following findings on blood testing is most likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation:
Normochromic normocytic anaemia
Anaemia of chronic disease may be seen in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) this can be due to chronic inflammatory disease, or it can also be seen for example in chronic kidney disease due to long-term NSAID use.

High antinuclear antibody levels
High antinuclear antibody levels is incorrect. Although a quarter-a third of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have low titres of antinuclear antibody (ANA), it is non-specific and is not part of the classification criteria.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is incorrect. HLA-B27 is not known to be associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

Neutropenia
Neutropenia usually occurs in RA due to myelosuppression related to medications, but may also occur in Felty’s syndrome (the triad of RA, neutropenia and splenomegaly).

stem: You are seeing a 21-year-old man with a 3-year history of inﬂammatory back pain. You make a presumptive diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). You order X-rays of the lumbosacral spine, sacroiliac joints and HLA B27. Which of the following statements is correct with regard to HLA B27?
options: It can be used as screening test for AS in the general population
The likelihood of a positive test depends on the racial and ethnic background of the patient
The test helps distinguish AS from other spondyloarthropathies
HLA B27 is essential for the diagnosis of AS
Acute anterior uveitis is relatively more common in B27-negative than –positive patients
explanation:
B The likelihood of a positive test depends on the racial and ethnic background of the patient The sensitivity and speciﬁcity of the test depend on the racial and ethnic background of the patient. The prevalence of HLA B27 varies among ethnic groups and races. Inuits have been shown to have the highest frequency of the gene (25–40%), with an overall prevalence of spondyloarthropathies between 2 and 4%. HLA B27 frequency is only 8–9% in people from Holland and Germany. Accordingly, the prevalence of spondyloarthropathies (2%) is lower than in Inuit. D HLA B27 is essential for the diagnosis of AS Most AS patients do not need HLA B 27 testing if they have certain clinical and radiological features. Patients can fulﬁl the criteria for AS without testing positive for HLA B27. A It can be used as screening test for AS in the general population Although HLA B27 may be helpful in diagnosis, 10% of the asymptomatic healthy normal population may be HLA B27 positive and therefore it cannot be used as a screening test. C The test helps distinguish AS from other spondyloarthropathies HLA B27 positivity does not distinguish between the axial spondyloarthropathies.

E Acute anterior uveitis is relatively more common in B27-negative than –positive patients Acute anterior uveitis is more common in B27-positive than -negative patients.

stem: A 24-year-old Japanese city banker presents with recurrent mouth ulcers. He was seen by the oral surgeons, who prescribed chlorhexidine mouthwashes and oral aciclovir. He has used prednisolone lozenges in the past with good effect. More recently, the ulcers have been occurring more frequently. In the last two days, he has felt pain at the tip of his penis, particularly when having sexual intercourse. He has also felt increasingly tired recently, to the point that he has given up playing football. He denies any weight loss and his appetite is unchanged. He has a history of irritable bowel disease. He also remembers treating an eye condition with steroid drops a year or two previously. He is currently taking oxytetracycline prescribed by his general practitioner (GP) for acne. On examination, there are multiple aphthous ulcers in the oral cavity. There is also a small aphthous ulcer on the tip of the penis. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations are unremarkable. Abdominal examination reveals mild, diffuse tenderness but no masses. Rectal examination reveals no abnormality. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 120 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 400 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 20 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour ANA - AdsDNAA - What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Behçet’s syndrome This is a chronic multi-system disease, most prevalent in the Mediterranean, Middle East and Japan. It has been associated with various HLA types including B12, -B51 and -B5. There is no speciﬁc diagnostic test, making it a diagnosis of exclusion. Its features can overlap with those of Crohn’s disease, and therefore the latter must be excluded. It is a systemic vasculitic disorder involving arteries and veins, with a tendency to thrombosis. In over 90% of cases there are painful oral aphthous ulcers, in over 70% genital aphthous ulcers and in over 50% ocular inﬂammation occurs. Other features include arthritis, central nervous system involvement, skin lesions (e.g. erythema nodosum, folliculitis and acneiform lesions) and pathergy (abnormal response to tissue injury, e.g. skin ulceration following trauma or venepuncture). It commonly runs a relapsing and remitting course. Treatment is largely symptomatic in mild cases, but systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants may be required by some. E Systemic lupus erythematosus Oral ulceration is a common feature of SLE, but genital ulcers are not. Lupus antibodies are negative and Behçet’s disease is a much more likely explanation for the multiple features described. A Crohn’s disease Oral aphthous ulceration is a feature of Crohn’s, but genital ulcers are not. Uveitis, which is suggested in the scenario, can be associated with a wide variety of conditions including Crohn’s, but is one of the commoner features of Behçet’s disease. Acne, whilst extremely common, is another feature supportive of Behçet’s. Overall, the constellation of ﬁndings in a Japanese patient, with no speciﬁc features of inﬂammatory bowel disease, make Behçet’s disease the best answer. C Reactive arthritis Reactive arthritis usually follows a sexually transmitted infection (especially chlamydia) or gastroenteritis; arthritis is a key feature which is lacking here; otherwise, there may be urethritis (rather than discrete genital ulcers) and conjunctivitis. D Herpes simplex type I infection This tends to cause peri-oral rather than genital disease. Steroid treatment is likely to worsen it. Whilst it can be recurrent as in this scenario, there are many features here which it would not explain.

stem: A 66-year-old retired labourer presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of an acutely swollen and red ankle. The attack started the night before with swelling and pain, and despite taking various analgesics, the pain intensiﬁed. He is a known hypertensive and suffers from congestive cardiac failure and osteoarthritis. He had previous similar episodes a few years ago. His current medications include bendroﬂumethiazide, lisinopril and amlodipine. On examination, the patient is apyrexial. There is a small, hard lump on his ear and he has a red, swollen and exquisitely painful right ankle, but he has full range of movement. Based on this patient’s history and clinical examination, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Gout He has had previous episodes or attacks before and has risk factors for gout, e.g. diuretic use, and has a tophus on clinical examination. Given that he has tophaceous gout, he should be started on allopurinol, when the acute attack has settled. Losartan could be started, in place of one of the other antihypertensives, the former having uricosuric action. Gout and pseudo-gout are conditions caused by the accumulation of crystals in the joint space resulting in pain, redness and swelling in the affected joints. Both conditions are more prevalent in males, gout more markedly so, and usually affect patients in the age range 30–60 years. Gout is caused by the accumulation of monosodium urate monohydrate crystals, whilst pseudo-gout is caused by the accumulation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals. In gout, the ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe is the site most commonly affected (the condition is known as ‘podagra’), with other common sites being the ankle, wrist and knee. The condition results from overproduction or reduced secretion of uric acid, with thiazide diuretics and foods that are rich in purines increasing the frequency of attacks. D Pseudo-gout Although it is difﬁcult to reliably distinguish gout and pseudo-gout on clinical grounds, a tendency exists for gout symptoms to develop rapidly over a few hours, whereas the onset of symptoms in pseudogout tends to be more insidious and may occur over a period of several days. The joints affected by pseudo-gout usually include the knee, wrist and shoulder. A Septic arthritis Septic arthritis should, however, always be considered in a mono- RHEUMATO arthritis. Patients with crystal-induced arthritis may also present with fever and malaise, but he has no risk factors for septic arthritis such as recent penetrating injury or gonorrhoea, and the previous similar episodes suggest gout. B Reactive arthritis There is no infective precipitant – gastrointestinal or genitourinary. Reactive arthritis is usually an oligoarthritis (2–4 joints affected). E Fracture of the ankle A fracture without a history of trauma or injury and in the absence of osteoporosis is very unlikely.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has mixed connective tissue disease, which has responded initially to corticosteroids, and he is present to discuss potential second-line therapies. He attends with his partner, as they are trying to start a family and want to discuss if any of the medications will affect his fertility. Which of the following is the best intervention for the connective tissue disease which also preserves his fertility?
explanation:
Azathioprine
Azathioprine is most appropriate because although it may cause a small reduction in sperm count, it is not associated with birth defects.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide causes a decreased sperm count in male patients. In higher doses and prolonged treatment, this can lead to irreversible azoospermia, resulting in irreversible infertility. In women, it is also teratogenic and associated with congenital malformation, especially in the first 10 weeks of gestation.

Leflunomide
Leflunomide is incorrect. Leflunomide is teratogenic and it is therefore not recommended during periods of attempted conception.

stem: A 62-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with worsening shoulder pain and stiffness. Her symptoms are more pronounced in the morning and improve as the day continues. She has been trialling ibuprofen for the pain which has provided some relief. There is no history of headache or visual symptoms and she denies recent injury. Her past medical history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 10 mg daily. Her observations are recorded to be within normal limits. On auscultation, her chest sounds are clear and her heart sounds are normal. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen. There is bilateral shoulder and hip pain, with a reduced range of movement. Examination of her skin reveals no rashes or discolouration. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following features will most likely be present?
explanation:
A C-reactive protein > 10 mg/l This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). PMR is an inﬂammatory condition that more commonly presents in women over the age of 60 years. It has similarities with the large vessel vasculitis, temporal or giant cell arteritis (GCA), and if visual symptoms are present, GCA should be considered, along with urgent referral to ophthalmology. PMR tends to have a rapid onset (< 2 months) and is characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness, which is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy, which is associated with proximal muscle weakness.

Laboratory investigations show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. D Positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) Antinuclear antibodies are markers used to assess for underlying autoimmune diseases. A positive ANA may or may not be seen in PMR and its presence is not speciﬁc to the disease, making it an unreliable diagnostic test. B Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint stiffness Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint stiffness is not a feature of PMR. PMR is predominantly characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles. Distal joint stiffness is not seen and is usually a sign of a different inﬂammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). MCP joint stiffness is a common presenting feature of RA. C Onset > 8 weeks polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) typically has an acute onset of symptoms over a period of four weeks. A more delayed presentation suggests an alternative diagnosis such as degenerative arthritis. E Proximal muscle weakness Proximal muscle weakness is not a symptom of PMR. Rather, proximal pain and stiffness are seen. Proximal muscle weakness suggests a different underlying disease such as polymyositis or myopathy.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with an acute myocardial infarction. He has been resuscitated and thrombolysed. He now mentions he has been feeling unwell for the last 2 months with dyspnoea, malaise, joint pains, weight loss and intermittent fever. His doctor has recently started him on an antihypertensive drug and he has recently experienced palpitations. He also gives a history of patchy numbness over his lower limbs and arms. His blood tests reveal that he has a mildly raised urea and creatinine levels; his erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 88 mm in 1 h and CRP is 35 mg/l. There is no past history of intravenous drug abuse or of unprotected sex. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
This patient has multisystem involvement. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a vasculitis secondary to the deposition of immune complexes. Renal impairment, hypertension, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, heart failure and polyneuropathy are all known to occur. The diagnosis can be confirmed by histological examination of biopsy material from an affected organ, or by angiographic demonstration of microaneurysms in hepatic, intestinal or renal vessels. There can be an acute phase response (raised CRP and ESR), and for unknown reasons PAN may be associated with hepatitis B antigenaemia.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is incorrect. Patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis usually have upper and lower respiratory tract involvement (sinuses and lungs).

stem: A young man who works as a clown in a circus attends the Rheumatology Clinic with a history of recurrent dislocation of his right shoulder. He also complains of increasing pain and stiffness in his left hip. On examination, his height is 150 cm and there is evidence of skin laxity and bruising. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is characterised by generalised hypermobility (with recurrent dislocations), skin laxity (and easy bruising), short stature with scoliosis and ocular fragility. It is a congenital disorder of collagen synthesis in which the capillaries are poorly supported by subcutaneous collagen.

Acromegaly
Acromegaly is incorrect. Acromegaly does not present with these features, but has features of growth hormone excess and pituitary mass effect.

Homocystinuria
Homocystinuria is incorrect. In homocystinuria osteoporosis and a marfanoid are seen, which is due to deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine synthetase. Intellectual disability and thrombosis are the presenting features. Patients have downward lens dislocation.

stem: A 73-year-old woman complains of dry, gritty eyes, a constant sensation of mouth dryness and swollen parotid glands. You suspect that she has Sjögren’s syndrome. Which one of the following tests is NOT likely to help in establishing the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the parotid gland
explanation:
Lymph node biopsy
This patient has Sjögren's syndrome and a lymph node biopsy will not help in establishing a diagnosis. A lymph node biopsy may be helpful in a patient with Sjögren's syndrome if lymphoma is being considered, as patients with Sjögren's have an increased risk of lymphoma. Sjögren’s syndrome is characterised by dry mouth and dry eyes, with variable lacrimal or salivary gland enlargement. N.B. Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination with fluorescein or Rose Bengal staining might reveal the punctate staining of keratoconjunctivitis.

Oral labial biopsy
Oral labial biopsy is incorrect. Oral labial biopsy can show characteristic lymphocytic infiltration of the minor salivary glands.

Serum antibody to Ro antigen
Serum antibody to Ro antigen is incorrect. Around 70% of patients with Sjögren’s syndrome have raised serum antibodies to the Ro antigen.

stem: A 35-year-old woman complains of bilateral stiff and painful joints in her hands and feet for the past 3 months. The stiffness lasts for more than an hour in the mornings. On examination, her fingers are swollen and stiff. Movement is painful. Which of the following tests has the greatest specificity for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis?
options: X-ray of the hands and feet
explanation:
Anti-CCP antibodies
This lady has features of an inflammatory arthritis, of which rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely. Anti-CCP (or ACPA) antibodies are more sensitive and more specific for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, than rheumatoid factor.

X-ray of the hands and feet
X-ray of the hands and feet is incorrect. Only soft tissue swelling may be visible on X-ray in early disease.

Joint aspirate for crystals
Joint aspirate for crystals is incorrect. Gout is unlikely in a young female.

Plasma rheumatoid factor
Plasma rheumatoid factor is incorrect. This lady has features of inflammatory arthritis, of which rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely. Anti-CCP antibodies are more specific for a diagnosis rather than rheumatoid factor.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of pain, swelling and redness of his left big toe. The results of his blood tests are as follows: Investigation Result Normal value Urea 8.4 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 156 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urate 0.625 mmol/l 0.1 - 0.4 mmol/l What would be the drug of choice in this case?
explanation:
Colchicine
Colchicine is correct. Colchicine is most effective during the first 12–24 hours of an attack, but its effectiveness declines with the duration of inflammation. A reduced dosing schedule is recommended for patients with renal impairment, and at high dose it causes adverse GI effects, particularly diarrhoea and vomiting.

Allopurinol
Allopurinol is incorrect. Allopurinol should not be started in an acute attack. It is indicated only under cover of a course of an NSAID or colchicine, and never within a month of an acute attack.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of intermittent fever accompanied by chest pain, which is worse on lying down. He has recently also noticed pain in the joints of his hands and feet. He is febrile, with a temperature of 39 °C. His pulse is 98/min and his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. The positive ﬁndings on examination are enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes, pericardial rub, mild hepatomegaly and synovitis of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and wrist joints. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 105 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 20 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 540 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 110 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 246 mg/l < 10 mg/l ALT 69 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 246 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Ferritin 4567 μg/l 20–250 µg/l Chest X-Ray (CXR) Cardiomegaly 2-D echocardiogram MSU and blood culture Pericardial effusion - ANA, RF, ANCA, anti CCP All - Computed tomography (CT) abdomen Hepatosplenomegaly Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Adult-onset Still’s disease This man has a long history of fever, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, serositis and hepatosplenomegaly consistent with Still’s disease. Clinical features of adult-onset Still’s disease include arthralgia or arthritis; a high fever (>39oC), especially in the afternoon and evening; ﬂeeting salmon-pink maculopapular rash which is most prominent with fever; serositis; anaemia; elevated acute phase reactants; and evidence of reticuloendothelial activation. In between the febrile episodes the patient feels rather well. The laboratory investigations commonly reveal leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, markedly raised serum ferritin and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Autoantibodies are negative. C Undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) A very high fever, raised CRP, organomegaly and negative ANA make connective tissue disease very unlikely. The term UCTD is used to describe patients who have symptoms of autoimmune disorders or connective tissue disease with particular laboratory ﬁndings to match, but who do not meet all the diagnostic criteria for the more well-deﬁned conditions. UCTD symptoms are similar to those of MCTD, but there are no antibodies to snRNP present. A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) A very high fever, raised CRP, organomegaly and negative ANA make SLE very unlikely. SLE is associated with a normal CRP and an elevated ESR. The presenting symptoms in SLE can be very variable due to the condition having multi-system effects ranging from indolent to fulminant, but the classic presentation is of the triad of arthralgia, fever and malar rash in a woman of child-bearing age. RHEUMATO B Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) A very high fever, raised CRP, organomegaly and negative ANA make MCTD very unlikely. MCTD is a term used to describe a condition that features overlap of autoimmune connective tissue disorders with certain laboratory ﬁndings to match. It is recognised to consist of the following core features: • Raynauds • Sclerodactily • Arthritis/arthralgia • Acrosclerosis • Myositis • Oesophageal dysmotility • Pulmonary hypertension • Lung ﬁbrosis • Raised anti–U1-RNP antibodies • Antibodies against U1-70 kd small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP). D Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) This patient has a very high fever and his RF and CCP are negative, making RA very unlikely. Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetrical autoimmune polyarthropathy causing pain, swelling and joint deformity. The patient may complain of morning stiffness and generalised malaise and will have raised inﬂammatory markers; rheumatoid factor is positive in around 70% of sufferers.

stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department for review. She tells you that she has recently commenced methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis but has realised that she should have been taking 5 mg weekly, and by mistake, she has been taking this as a daily dose. Consequently, she has run out of three months’ medication in only 12 days and has most recently developed a sore throat. She looks well, and her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. General physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most important investigation here?
explanation: B Full blood count Myelosuppression is the most likely consequence of methotrexate toxicity and puts the patient at risk of a catastrophic infection. As such, in this case, the most appropriate initial test is a full blood count. Where acute toxicity exists (as here), calcium folinate (calcium leucovorin) is a potent agent for neutralising the immediate toxic effects of methotrexate. Where large doses or overdoses are given, calcium folinate may be administered by intravenous infusion in doses of up to 75 mg within 12 hours, followed by 12 mg intramuscularly every six hours for four doses. C Liver function testing Hepatic ﬁbrosis is associated with chronic use of methotrexate. Although this patient’s dose will have reached toxic levels, it is haematological toxicity which is the main concern here. A Folic acid level Although folate is given together with methotrexate to prevent toxicity, the level of methotrexate this patient has taken means that folic acid will not be protective, however much she has consumed. D Methotrexate level This patient is a reliable historian and has almost certainly taken the methotrexate. A plasma level for methotrexate will not signiﬁcantly add to the information we have already or change the management of this patient. E Urea and electrolytes Nephrotoxicity is not a prominent feature of methotrexate overdose. Measuring the full blood count is much more crucial in this case in establishing the risks of infection associated with bone marrow toxicity in methotrexate overdose.

stem: A 26-year-old woman known to have lupus since the age of 19 years presents in the clinic with right groin pain. This started 4 months ago and has been progressively getting worse. The pain is present all the time and increases further on weight-bearing. She walks with a limp. The range of movements at both hips is painful and restricted, the right much more than the left. Her medications include prednisolone 5 mg daily, azathioprine 125 mg daily, Adcal-D3® 1 tab twice daily and co-codamol. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 102 g/l 115–155 g/l RHEUMATO WCC 4.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 123 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.8 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.9 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 4.5 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 4 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 33 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Creatinine (Cr) 84 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine dipstick All normal You order an urgent X-ray of the hips. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Avascular necrosis of the hips Deprivation of blood supply to the cortex and medulla results in marrow cell death and causes AVN. The common causes are lupus, high-dose corticosteroid therapy, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, sickle cell disease, alcoholism, Caisson’s disease and Gaucher’s disease. In lupus, femoral head involvement is the most common and in 90% of cases progresses to involve the opposite side after 12 months. The pain is often most severe and recalcitrant, with poor response to analgesic and anti-inﬂammatory medications. CRP and ESR may show mild/moderate elevation in this condition, or may be normal. Indeed no particular blood parameter is useful for diagnosis or assessing prognosis of this condition. Plain X-ray characteristically shows irregular contouring of the femoral head, although it may appear normal in the early phase. MRI is the most sensitive modality of imaging for AVN of the hip, and is the investigation of choice in patients where AVN is suspected but radiography is normal. Conservative treatment involves non-weight bearing to prevent the collapse of the femoral head and secondary osteoarthritis. Depending on the stage of the disease, surgical options include core decompression or replacement of the femoral head. A Osteoarthritis of the hips She is far too young to have osteoarthritis of her hips. B Trochanteric bursitis Trochanteric bursitis is characterised by lateral thigh pain and is worse on lying on the affected side. D Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) of the hips This woman has known SLE, and her inﬂammatory markers are normal.

E Sacroilitis Sacroiliits does not occur with SLE (it occurs with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, enteropathic arthritis and reactive arthritis) and is usually characterised by buttock pain, whereas buttock or groin pain can be associated with hip pathology.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with an 8-month history of severe joint pain and stiffness. Her sister has similar symptoms. There is no past medical history of note and she takes no regular medication. stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with a photosensitivity and polyarthralgia of her hands. On examination she has oral ulcers and nil else and her urine dipstick shows haematuria and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus
This lady has SLE characterized by photosensitivity (probably causing a photosensitive rash), arthralgia, oral ulceration and likely renal involvement (highly suggested by the urine dipstick positive for blood and protein) – although a renal biopsy is required to confirm this. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic condition in which a low level of baseline activity is punctuated by flares of higher activity. The overall severity of the disease in an individual patient depends on the nature and frequency of these flares. The diverse clinical features of SLE mean that the disease may present to any of a number of different specialists, SLE may be diagnosed if a patient meets at least four of the following 11 criteria: Malar rash Discoid rash Photosensitivity Oral ulcers Arthritis Serositis (pleuritis or pericarditis) Renal disorder (proteinuria > 0.5 g/24 hours, or +++ persistently or cellular casts) Neurological disorder (seizures or psychosis) Haematological disorder (haemolytic anaemia or leukopenia of 4.0 × 10 9/l on two or more occasions, or lymphopenia of 1.5 × 10 9/l on two or more occasions, or thrombocytopenia of 100 × 10 9/l)

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the Rheumatology Clinic. He has a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis for which he has received regular ibuprofen and, because of a poor response to therapy, a course of diclofenac. On review, he tells you there has been no significant improvement in his symptoms and he has prolonged morning stiffness affecting his lower back and severe limitation of movement. explanation:
Adalimumab
Failure to control symptoms after two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is an indication for intervention with a biological agent in ankylosing spondylitis. stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with chronic back pain. An X-ray of the spine shows vertebral crush fractures and evidence of osteoporosis. Which of the following blood results would be most in keeping with this diagnosis?
options: Normal or high alkaline phosphatase levels
explanation:
Normal or high alkaline phosphatase levels
This lady has osteoporosis, which is usually associated with a normal bone profile, although alkaline phosphatase can be elevated for several months following a fracture. Osteoporosis implies a reduction in the amount of bone mineral per unit volume of anatomical bone (exceeding the natural decline with age).

Low parathyroid hormone levels
In osteoporosis levels of parathyroid hormone are typically normal.

Elevated phosphate levels
Elevated phosphate levels is incorrect. In osteoporosis levels of serum phosphate are normal.

Low calcium levels
Low calcium levels is incorrect. In osteoporosis serum calcium levels are normal.

Raised parathyroid hormone levels
Raised parathyroid hormone levels is incorrect. In osteoporosis parathyroid hormone levels are normal.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a rash around her eyes and over her hands. She also complains of difﬁculty brushing her hair. Which of the following results is associated with this condition?
options: Giant cell identiﬁcation on biopsy of the temporal artery
explanation: E Anti-Jo antibodies A heliotrope rash around the eyes and violaceous papules (Gottron’s papules) over the hands is characteristic of dermatomyositis. The disorder is associated with the development of anti-Jo antibodies in roughly 30% of patients, and can also commonly cause polymyositis that affects proximal muscles (e.g. causing difﬁculties in brushing hair, standing up from a chair). There are two peaks of onset, one in childhood and the other between the ages of 40 and 60 years. Dermatomyositis occurs twice as frequently in women as it does in men. There is an association with malignancy, commonly of the lung, breast, female genital tract, stomach and rectum. Dermatomyositis precedes neoplasm occurrence in 40% of cases, both conditions occur together in 26%, and in 30% the neoplasm occurs ﬁrst. RHEUMATO C Giant cell identiﬁcation on biopsy of the temporal artery Temporal (also known as giant cell) arteritis is an inﬂammatory condition of blood vessels that can cause malaise, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and loss of vision. The gold standard for diagnosing the condition is biopsy of the temporal artery. However, a negative result does not deﬁnitively rule out the diagnosis as blood vessels are often involved in a patchy pattern with skip lesions. Unilateral biopsy of a 1.5–3 cm length is 85- 90% sensitive. A Raised angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels Raised ACE levels are associated with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Cutaneous ﬁndings include erythema nodosum, and indurated purple-red plaques (theplaques are termed lupus pernio when affecting the nose, ears, and cheeks). B Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLE is also associated with a facial rash, in a pathognomonic butterﬂy distribution, but not with the development of Gottron’s papules. D Anti-centromere antibodies Anti-centromere antibodies are found in patients with the CREST syndrome (a limited form of systemic sclerosis in which there is Calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oEsophageal involvement, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia). Additional cutaneous features of the CREST syndrome include skin thickening, hyper and hypo-pigmentation in a ‘salt and pepper’ appearance, nail fragility, and ulcer formation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent miscarriages, the most recent of which occurred at 16 weeks' gestation. She reports a previous DVT two years ago but has no other signiﬁcant medical history. Physical examination is unremarkable. The patient’s obstetric and thrombotic history prompts further testing for possible antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Which of the following laboratory investigations is most appropriate to conﬁrm a diagnosis of APS in this patient?
explanation: C Lupus anticoagulant The lupus anticoagulant test, along with anticardiolipin antibodies and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies, is part of the diagnostic criteria for APS. A positive lupus anticoagulant test, combined with this patient’s clinical history of recurrent miscarriages and previous thrombosis, supports a diagnosis of APS. A Antinuclear antibodies While antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are associated with autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, they are not diagnostic for APS. ANA testing would not help to conﬁrm APS in this patient. B Rheumatoid factor Rheumatoid factor is commonly used in diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis. It is unrelated to APS and would not be helpful in this case. D C-reactive protein C-reactive protein is a marker of inﬂammation and is not speciﬁc for APS. Its level is typically elevated in infections or inﬂammatory conditions, but it does not play a role in the diagnosis of APS. E Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) is a marker for rheumatoid arthritis, not for APS. Testing for anti-CCP would not be relevant in this case.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has been losing weight over the past few months, suffering from night sweats and has multiple joint pains. Her other concerns are that she has signiﬁcant hair loss with scarring around the patches where the hair is lost. Other problems include sensitivity to the sun, particularly on her face, which has resulted in needing to wear factor 50 sun screen. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/82 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has a ﬂushed facial appearance. There is obvious small joint polyarthropathy, particularly affecting her ﬁngers, toes, ankles and wrists. She is slim with a body mass index (BMI) of 21 kg/m2. You note scarring alopecia on examination of her scalp. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 101 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l RHEUMATO Platelets (PLT) 178 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 70 mm/1st h 0–10 mm/1st h Urine Blood +, Protein ++ Which of the following tests is most likely to be positive?
explanation: A Anti-nuclear antibody Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) is associated with a range of autoantibodies Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) is present in virtually all patients with SLE. Should ANA be positive, then antibodies to dsDNA, complement, ANA subtypes and anti-Ro/La be sent in attempt to inform about prognosis and potential organ involvement. B Anti-smooth muscle antibody Anti-smooth muscle antibody may be positive in autoimmune hepatitis rather than SLE. ANA is positive in virtually all patients with SLE. C Anti-CCP antibody Anti-CCP is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) rather than SLE. It is present in around 75% of patients with RA and has a speciﬁcity of around 95%. D c-ANCA c-ANCA is associated with granulomatous polyangiitis and not SLE. E Rheumatoid factor Rheumatoid factor is associated with RA where it is present in around 75% of patients; however, it is rather less speciﬁc. It is present in up to 30% of patients with SLE; however, the question here asks for the most likely positive test. ANA is positive in virtually all patients with SLE.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with increasing lower back pain, which is also affecting the posterior pelvis. He says this is worst in the morning, responds poorly to regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, and only really gets slightly better after he starts to move about. It has been present for the past 4 months. He has no past history of note apart from mild asthma, which is managed with a salbutamol inhaler. On examination, his BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 72 bpm and regular. There is bilateral pain over the sacroiliac joints, with forward and lateral lumbar flexion limited by pain. Which of the following is required to confirm a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis?
explanation:
Sacroilitis on X-ray
Sacroilitis on a pelvic X-ray is consistent and specific to ankylosing spondylitis and should be considered as a first-line imaging investigation. The British Society for Rheumatology recommends the following criteria for diagnosis of AS: Clinical criteria: Low back pain, for more than 3 months; improved by exercise, not relieved by rest Limitation of lumbar spine motion in both the sagittal and the frontal planes Limitation of chest expansion relative to normal values for age and sex. Radiological criterion: Sacroiliitis on X-ray. Definite AS is diagnosed if the radiological criterion is present plus at least one clinical criterion, and probable AS if three clinical criteria are present, or if the radiological criterion is present but absent the clinical Chat criteria. with

stem: A woman who was given a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis 4 years ago presents for review. She has been suffering signiﬁcantly increased shortness of breath over the past few months. Respiratory function testing reveals evidence of pulmonary ﬁbrosis, and echocardiography suggests elevated right heart pressures. You arrange for iloprost infusion treatment. Which one of the following pharmacological interventions is most likely to provide additional beneﬁt in reducing pulmonary artery pressure?
explanation: D Sildenaﬁl Sildenaﬁl has positive effects in reducing pulmonary arterial pressure. Ghofrani published evidence (in Annals of Internal Medicine) in 2002 from a study in 30 patients with pulmonary hypertension; six of these patients had evidence of systemic sclerosis. Severe pulmonary hypertension was deﬁned as pulmonary artery pressure >40 mmHg. Patients were randomised to receive between 12.5 and 50 mg of sildenaﬁl in addition to iloprost infusion. The study showed a dose-dependent beneﬁt of sildenaﬁl on pulmonary artery pressure. Unfortunately, pulmonary hypertension is still a signiﬁcant contributor to mortality in systemic sclerosis. C Atenolol Although blood pressure control may reduce pulmonary artery pressure by a small degree, sildenaﬁl is the best ﬁt here. Beta blockers are best avoided in patients with systemic sclerosis, as non-cardioselective beta blockers (and cardioselective beta blockers to a certain extent) may cause peripheral vasoconstriction and worsen the symptoms of Raynaud’s. A Ramipril Although blood pressure control may reduce pulmonary artery pressure to a small degree, sildenaﬁl is the best ﬁt here. ACE inhibitors are the treatment of choice for renal disease associated with systemic sclerosis, in which the ACE inhibitor may halt or even reverse the decline in renal function in certain cases. B Amlodipine Although blood pressure control may reduce pulmonary artery pressure by a small degree, sildenaﬁl is the best ﬁt here, and calcium channel blockers are not usually indicated for patients with pulmonary hypertension associated with systemic sclerosis. A small proportion of patients may beneﬁt from a reduction in pulmonary blood pressure associated with their use, and this is indicated by RHEUMATO acute vasoreactivity testing. Calcium channel blockers are useful in the non-urgent management of Raynaud’s phenomenon that does not respond adequately to general measures, and therefore many patients with systemic sclerosis may be prescribed amlodipine for this reason. E Prednisolone Steroids do not improve pulmonary artery pressure and are a risk factor for scleroderma renal crisis, and should therefore be used sparingly in patients with scleroderma. High-dose steroids may, however, be useful in patients with pleurisy, pericarditis or other severe systemic manifestations of systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 32-year-old man is referred with lower back pain which wakes him at night for about 6 months. The pain is localised to the lower lumbar region and the buttock. He has changed his job from working in a warehouse doing heavy lifting to clerical tasks. He has to wake himself an hour or two earlier in the mornings than he used to in order to loosen up so that he can get to work on time. His past medical history revealed a malignant skin melanoma that was surgically removed 2 years earlier. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 90 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 295 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 25 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 5 mg/l 0–10 mg/l What is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
options: Melanoma recurrence and spread to vertebrae
Osteomyelitis of the lower lumbar vertebra
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
The character of the back pain implies inflammatory disease. Pain has persisted for over 3 months. He has noticed increasing back stiffness in the morning that improves during the day; and the pain is probably so severe at night that it prompts him to get up and become mobile to reduce the symptoms. It is important to note that the question does NOT say the pain is worse at night (which would make one think of malignant cause). The above features suggest an inflammatory nature of the pain, most probably ankylosing spondylitis. stem: A 32-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis complicated by deforming arthritis comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. His arthritis is very poorly controlled, and he has recently failed to gain signiﬁcant beneﬁt from methotrexate. You elect to institute therapy with tocilizumab. The patient asks you about potential adverse events. Which side-effect would be the most important to counsel him RHEUMATO about?
explanation: D Neutropenia The answer is Neutropenia (Option D). Neutropenia and neutropenic infections may be seen with tocilizumab therapy. A Depression Depression (Option A) is incorrect. Depression is not an observed side-effect of tocilizumab therapy. B Diabetes Diabetes (Option B) is incorrect. Diabetes would not be expected with tocilizumab. Diabetes is a common complication of corticosteroid-based therapy and may need treatment to control blood sugars. C Folate deﬁciency Folate deﬁciency (Option C) is incorrect. Folate deﬁciency is a common side-effect of methotrexate use, not tocilizumab. E Lung ﬁbrosis Lung ﬁbrosis (Option E) is incorrect. Lung ﬁbrosis is a side-effect of many medications, but not tocilizumab. Possible causes include methotrexate, bleomycin, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and cyclophosphamide.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with progressively worsening muscle weakness over the course of the past 4 months. In particular she says she has had problems getting out of a chair and climbing the stairs. She also has slight pain over her shoulder muscles and occasional difficulty swallowing. Her BP is 135/72 mmHg, with pulse 78/min and regular. There is grade 4/5 weakness affecting the proximal muscles of both arms and legs, but no evidence of a skin rash. explanation:
Prednisolone
This patient has polymyositis, for which corticosteroids are the initial treatment of choice. Polymyositis is an autoimmune-mediated striated muscle inflammation associated with progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness with myalgia and arthralgia. stem: A 32-year-old man is referred as an emergency by his general practitioner (GP). He presents with a history of haemoptysis over the past few days, with cough, fevers, nausea and vomiting. The GP had diagnosed ﬂu, but the patient re-presented a few days later, and routine bloods revealed Hb 92 g/l and a creatinine of 385 µmol/l. On examination, he is severely short of breath and has bilateral basal inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the lung ﬁelds. Urgent renal biopsy the day after admission reveals a necrotising glomerulonephritis with linear immunoglobulin and complement deposits on the basement membrane. While being in this non specialist hospital, he suffers a large haemoptysis, (20–30 ml of blood). Given the likeliest diagnosis, which step would be most appropriate in his initial management?
explanation:
D Commence IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide This patient has strong evidence of Goodpasture’s syndrome. Goodpasture’s syndrome is an uncommon condition with an incidence of 0.5/1 000 000 per year. There is a male predominance, and age at presentation follows a bimodal distribution: young men presenting with a pulmonary–renal picture in the 20–30-year age group, and elderly women presenting with a predominantly renal picture. The

safest way to secure a diagnosis is by renal biopsy, and the typical picture demonstrated is a necrotising glomerulonephritis, with positive staining for both immunoglobulin and complement. Where there is severe haemoptysis, rapid removal of anti- GBM antibody is indicated, and the best way to do this is by plasmapheresis at a specialist centre. This is usually accompanied by pulsed therapy with IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. Prognosis is dependent on presenting renal function; a high percentage of patients who have lost more than 50% of their renal function at diagnosis unfortunately progress to long-term renal replacement therapy. E Commence IV furosemide therapy This patient needs immunosuppression for Goodpasture’s disease. The haemoptysis is due to pulmonary haemorrhage secondary to vasculitis, not pulmonary oedema. A diuretic would be the wrong therapy. A Plasmapheresis This patient has Goodpasture’s syndrome with a pulmonary–renal syndrome. The best initial management would be intravenous methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide and then plasmapheresis, which is usually only available in specialist centres While plasmapheresis is being arranged, the patient should be given IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. B Commence oral prednisolone This patient has life-threatening pulmonary–renal syndrome and needs rapid induction of remission; oral prednisolone would be too slow to achieve the best possible outcome. C Commence oral cyclophosphamide This patient has life-threatening pulmonary–renal syndrome and needs rapid induction of remission; Treatment is tailored according to severity and extent of disease. The level of immunosuppression should reﬂect the severity of vasculitis. Cyclophosphamide can be given orally daily or pulsed intravenously at 2–3-week intervals. There has been a move towards using intravenous therapy in recent times.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has progressive swelling and pain in both wrists. It started in the right hand four months ago and in the left hand one month ago. She is a contract cleaner. On examination, there is pain on telescoping both thumbs, palpating the scaphoid tubercle and palpating the anatomical snuffbox bilaterally. There is pain on ulnar deviation of the wrist. There is no erythema and the joints do not feel warm to touch. Finkelstein test is negative. A bilateral hand X-ray is requested. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Preiser's disease
Preiser’s disease is bilateral idiopathic avascular necrosis of the scaphoid bone. The scaphoid bone is at high risk of avascular necrosis, as its blood supply enters proximally before traversing the bone. It may be due to repetitive trauma, such as from this patient’s occupation, or due to drug side-effect. Options for management include conservative analgesia and physiotherapy or surgical intervention.

Carpel tunnel syndrome
Carpel tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the median nerve, leading to pain and paraesthesiae of the hand. Paraesthesiae is in the distribution of the median nerve: thumb, index finger, middle finger and radial side of the ring finger. This may lead to reduced grip strength. The patient does not display symptoms Chat consistent with AI with Tutor carpel tunnel syndrome.

Psoriatic arthritis
Although psoriatic arthritis is typically oligoarthritic at presentation, there are no other factors consistent with this diagnosis. Psoriatic arthritis typically affects interphalangeal joints: 30% present with dactylitis, psoriasis is seen in 80% and nail disease in 60%. Axial involvement is common in psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman complains of a loss of appetite, low-grade fever, pain in the shoulders and buttocks and severe cramping pain in her arms and hands during an aerobics class. On examination, the radial pulse is weak in both arms. The blood pressure is 85/60 mmHg in her right arm, 60/40 mmHg in her left arm and 130/80 mmHg in both legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Takayasu’s disease
This lady has Takayasu’s – she is of the right age and gender (the typical patient is a woman aged 20–40 years), with upper limb claudication, constitutional upset (fevers, anorexia), weak/absent pulses and a discrepancy in blood pressure between the two arms. Bruits are common. Takayasu’s disease is an idiopathic arteritis that affects the first few centimetres of the innominate, carotid and subclavian arteries, together with the adjacent portion of the aorta.

Cervical rib syndrome
Cervical rib syndrome is incorrect. This patient has systemic symptoms. Congenital development of the costal process of the C7 vertebra (cervical rib) can cause thoracic outlet compression. This involves the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery. Pain and numbness may be felt in the hand. The radial pulse may be weak and the forearm cyanosed.

Churg–Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss syndrome is incorrect. She does not have any features associated with Churg–Strauss syndrome, such as asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, pulmonary infiltrates.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with bone pain. She has progressively become weaker, and she now ﬁnds it RHEUMATO difﬁcult to get up. Social history reveals her diet has a high content of minimally processed seeds and beans. On examination, she has 3/5 power in shoulder abduction and adduction but 5/5 power in all other muscle groups in the arms. In the legs, she has 3/5 power in hip ﬂexion and extension but normal power in the rest of the legs. Her plantar reﬂexes are ﬂexor. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 130 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 150 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.9 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 96 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 45 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Chloride (Cl-) 109 mmol/l 98–106 mmol/l Bilirubin 17 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALP 590 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 36 g/l 35–55 g/l Phosphate (PO43-) 0.6 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 19.0 mmol/l 24 - 30 mmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.02 mmol/l 2.20 - 2.60 mmol/l What is the most likely underlying cause of her clinical picture?
explanation:
C Osteomalacia The clinical picture is one of bone pain and proximal myopathy. The blood tests show a mild hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia associated with a high alkaline phosphatase, which is typical of osteomalacia. There is also an acidosis, which is caused by the inhibition of phosphate, bicarbonate and sodium reabsorption by parathyroid hormone (PTH). Osteomalacia is more common in ethnic groups who are dark-skinned, or in those who wear extensive skin coverings. This does not allow for cholesterol to be converted to vitamin D in the skin. Patients who’s diet contains large amounts of minimally processed whole nuts, seeds and beans are also at high riskas the phytic acid in these foods chelates vitamin D and calcium. X-rays may show Looser’s zones, which are areas of decalciﬁcation. D Hypothyroidism Although hypothyroidism is associated with proximal myopathy, it

is not associated with the low serum calcium and elevated alkaline phosphatase seen here. A Type 1 renal tubular acidosis Type 1 renal tubular acidosis is associated with hypokalaemia, which is not seen here. B Hypoparathyroidism Hypoparathyroidism is associated with elevated levels of phosphate, which doesn’t ﬁt the biochemical picture seen here. E Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) PMR is associated with proximal muscle pain and weakness, but not with the abnormalities in calcium metabolism seen here.

stem: You review a 62-year-old man in the Cardiology Clinic, some 6 weeks after his admission for acute myocardial infarction. He was commenced on lipid-lowering therapy with simvastatin after his myocardial infarction, in addition to other medications including ramipril 10 mg daily and aspirin 75 mg, which he has taken for several years. Since his myocardial infarction he has been increasing his exercise, but is complaining of pains in the joints and muscles, general malaise and a skin rash. Blood testing reveals the following: Investigation Result Anti ds-DNA antibodies Negative Anti-histone antibodies Positive C3/C4 levels Normal You suspect a diagnosis of lupus. Which of the following represents the most appropriate course of action?
options: Start prednisolone 30mg PO daily for 6 weeks
Observe for resolution of symptoms over time
explanation: B Withdraw his simvastatin This man has just been started on many medications and has positive anti-histone antibodies. There is a suspicion that this man has druginduced lupus. Generally symptoms are said to appear some 3 weeks to 2 years after the onset of therapy, making his simvastatin the most likely culprit in this case. Drug-induced lupus is said to affect the 50– 70 year age group most commonly, has a male:female ratio of 1:1 and affects Caucasians more commonly than other populations. Skin rash is RHEUMATO seen in around 25% of sufferers, joint pains and malaise are more common, and Raynaud’s is seen in around 25%. Anti-histone antibodies are more likely to be positive in drug-induced lupus versus non-drug-induced lupus; anti-ds DNA antibodies are less likely to be positive. C3/C4 levels are usually normal. Drugs which may directly cause lupus include simvastatin, captopril, valproate, penicillamine, carbamazepine, methyldopa, procainamide, minocycline, griseofulvin and a host of other agents. Treatment is withdrawal of the offending medication, with rapid clinical resolution normally apparent. D Start prednisolone 30mg PO daily for 6 weeks The patient’s symptoms are likely to resolve with withdrawal of the culprit drug, without the need for such high-dose steroids. A Withdraw his ramipril Ramipril does not commonly cause a drug-induced lupus. C Withdraw his aspirin Aspirin is not commonly associated with drug-induced lupus. E Observe for resolution of symptoms over time The patient’s symptoms are likely to continue if the offending drug is continued.

stem: A 67-year-old man attends the Rheumatology Clinic during an episode of gout. He has a past medical history of mild renal impairment and hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. His current medications for gout include allopurinol 100 mg daily and colchicine 500 μg daily. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 118 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 202 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 157 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: course of prednisolone 30 mg daily for one week
explanation:
E Increase the dose of colchicine

Increasing the colchicine to 500 μg 2–4 times a day until symptoms are relieved (maximum 6 mg per course) should be sufﬁcient to get on top of this patient’s acute exacerbation. The original dose of 500 μg was acting as a prophylactic agent and is useful when allopurinol is started, as well as in patients who are unresponsive to allopurinol. The BNF states colchicine can be used in caution down to an eGFR of 10. Expert evidence suggests this can be the standard dose. D Increase the dose of allopurinol Increasing the dose of allopurinol may make matters worse, as allopurinol can trigger a worsening of gout. Allopurinol should not be started in an acute attack, nor should the dose be increased in an acute attack. A A course of prednisolone 30 mg daily for one week A short course of corticosteroids is a possibility if the patient fails to respond to the increased dose of colchicine, but increasing the dose of colchicine would still be the most effective here. B Add diclofenac to his regime Adding diclofenac may worsen both the renal function and BP in this patient and should be avoided in this case. Full-dose colchicine is the ﬁrst-line treatment for acute gout. C Halve the dose of allopurinol Halving the dose of allopurinol is unlikely to be helpful in the acute setting and may actually risk further future attacks when the dose is returned to normal.

stem: A 54-year-old man comes to the clinic. He is concerned as he plays the piano in a local hotel and is not able to manage this at the moment. On further questioning, he admits to 2 h of morning stiffness, and pain affecting the hips, knees and elbows. On examination, he has nodules over his elbows and pain over the PIP joints of the ﬁngers. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 45 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial therapy in this man with respect to his long term ability to play the piano?
explanation: B Prednisolone 20 mg PO This man is likely to have seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RF positive, as he has nodules) and needs early intensive intervention to reduce joint damage and disability, to allow him to maintain function. Steroids should be started concomittently with DMARDs, such as methotrexate. Steroids have a rapid onset of action and bridge the gap before methotrexate exerts its effects (up to 12 weeks). D Surgical tendon release We are told that this man plays the piano, and as such surgical tendon release would be best avoided if possible due to the period of time involved in recovery. A Diclofenac 50 mg tds Although he may gain some symptomatic relief from diclofenac, it does not have any disease modiﬁcation and therefore does little to reduce joint damage. C Splinting of his ﬁngers Although he does need to rest his ﬁngers while the inﬂammation is controlled, splinting will not signiﬁcantly reduce pain or inﬂammation or damage. E Joint fusion We are told that this man plays the piano, and as such joint fusion would be best avoided if possible due to the period of time involved in recovery.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. She attends the clinic with her mother, who has a severe form of the disease. She is considering having children but is worried that they too might inherit the condition. They have a number of questions about heritability, including about HLA associations with rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following HLA antigens is known to be associated with the development of rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
HLA DR4
HLA antigens DR1 and DR4 are associated with rheumatoid arthritis and primary sclerosing cholangitis.

HLA B5
HLA B5 is incorrect. HLA B5 is thought to be associated with an increased risk of Behçet’s disease.

HLA B27
HLA B27 is incorrect. HLA B27 is associated with increased risk of seronegative arthritides and inflammatory bowel disease.

HLA B8
HLA B8 is incorrect. HLA B8 and HLA DR3 are associated with an increased risk of Graves’ disease.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of painful hands and fingers. On examination he has bilateral sausage-shaped fingers and pain over the distal interphalangeal joints. His nails are also pitted. There is no other past medical history of note. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 140 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets 180 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 46 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Rheumatoid factor negative Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriatic arthritis
The picture of symmetrical DIPJ polyarthritis, dactylitis and nail pitting is very typical of psoriatic arthritis. Nail pitting may be the only visible sign of psoriasis and frank skin plaques do not necessarily have to be present. Most patients are rheumatoid factor-negative, although case series report positive rheumatoid factor in 5–9% of

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a history of pain and swelling accompanied by early morning stiffness of 30 min affecting her hands and feet.
