She had been ﬁt and healthy until the onset of joint symptoms 10 weeks ago. The ﬁndings of examination of her hands are shown in the image below. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value (Hb) 121 g/l 115–155 g/l (WCC) 10.5 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l (PLT) 450 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l ESR 67 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 45 mg/l < 10 mg/l (AST) 33 IU/l 10–40 IU/l (ALP) 313 IU/l 30–130 IU/l You order an autoantibody screen and X-ray of the hands and feet. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrent symmetrical seronegative arthritis with pitting oedema (RSSPE)
explanation: A Early rheumatoid arthritis (RA) Symmetric involvement of the hands is the hallmark of RA. In early disease, there may be swelling of the wrists, MCP or PIP joints, but no deformity. The above symptoms and signs, in association with an acute phase response, are strongly suggestive of early RA in this patient. Treatment includes early aggressive DMARD therapy, analgesics and anti-inﬂammatories, a physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessment, and education on RA as well as on the side effects and monitoring of disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs). D Osteoarthritis The patient’s age and degree of morning stiffness are not consistent with osteoarthritis. B Recurrent symmetrical seronegative arthritis with pitting oedema (RSSPE) RSSPE presents with oedema of the hands and feet, along with synovitis, and it most commonly occurs in older adults. There is coexistent malignancy in 16–30% of patients, including from haematological (leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and lymphoma) and solid tumours (prostate, breast, gastrointestinal, lung, ovarian, bladder and endometrial). C Early scleroderma There are no reported skin changes in keeping with scleroderma. E Reﬂex sympathetic dystrophy syndrome (RSDS) This syndrome usually only affects one extremity and describes a continuing (spontaneous and/or evoked) regional pain that is disproportionate in time or degree to the usual course of any known trauma or other lesion. The pain is regional (not in a speciﬁc nerve territory or dermatome) and usually has a distal predominance of abnormal sensory, motor, sudomotor, vasomotor and/or trophic ﬁndings.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a long history of diabetes mellitus, which is now managed with insulin, presents for review. She has acute pain and swelling over the ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint of her left foot and there are rounded, calcium-like deposits in her ear cartilage. Investigation Result Normal values HbA1c 72.68 mmol/mol (8.8%) 9.29 - 53.0 mmol/mol (3 - 7 %) WCC 6.8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
explanation: B Colchicine This patient has chronic kidney disease, probably as a result of longstanding poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and has developed gout. As such, colchicine would be the initial treatment of choice. The creatinine is a little high, although the eGFR is likely to be over 30 and therefore colchicine could be ‘renally dosed’ at 500 mcg bd. The incidence of renal stones is increased in patients with gout: 80% of these are uric acid stones. D Paracetamol Paracetamol is not likely to be sufﬁciently effective enough for the acute pain and inﬂammation of gout. A Diclofenac 50 mg po tds Non-steroidals in this case may exacerbate salt and water retention and worsen renal function. C Allopurinol 100 mg po daily Allopurinol should not be started during an acute attack, but could be started at least four weeks after the attack has settled. If ﬂares are more frequent, it can be started during a ﬂare. The contraindication to allopurinol in renal impairment is relative, and this drug can be used even in moderate–severe kidney disease providing dose reduction is employed. E Prednisolone 40 mg po daily Corticosteroids are reserved for those patients in whom non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents and colchicine are either contraindicated or there is patient intolerance.

stem: A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 4-month history of facial rash. It started at the bridge of the nose and slowly spread to the face. She has just returned from Nigeria and the rash ﬂared up while she was there. The rash is non-itchy and not painful. She has tried various cosmetic products, but none have worked. She also complained that her hair has started falling out. She has no past medical history and is not on any medication. On examination, she has a well-deﬁned erythematous scaly rash, with an area of scarring over the face, ear and scalp. She has patchy hair loss over her scalp. Other examinations are completely normal. Investigations reveal the following Investigation Result Normal value Hb 136 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 150 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 50 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 98 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l RHEUMATO (Ca2+) Anti-ds DNA Anti-nuclear antibody Not detected Not detected What the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Discoid lupus This lady has a scaly rash localised to her face with scarring alopecia, with no systemic manifestations and negative anti-nuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA. Discoid lupus primarily affects the skin and is characterised by a well-demarcated macular rash with erythema, scales, plaques and atrophy. It is a variant of SLE, in which skin involvement is the main feature. It is more common in African–Caribbean women. Photosensitivity is a feature as well as scarring alopecia of the scalp. Very rarely patients may develop systemic features, but these are usually mild. Diagnosis is made by biopsy of the lesion. E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) This lady has a scaly rash localised to her face with scarring alopecia, with no systemic manifestations and negative anti-nuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA, making systemic lupus very unlikely. A Lupus pernio Lupus pernio is a cutaneous form of sarcoidosis with dusky-purple inﬁltration of the nose. B Dermatomyositis The facial rash of dermatomyositis is around the eyelids. D Morphoea Morphoea is a localised form of scleroderma, characterised by dermal sclerosis with pigmentation. The skin appears thickened, rather than scaly.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with pain, swelling and stiffness in the small joints of her hands and wrists for 2 weeks. On further questioning, she says she has been feeling more tired over the past 3 months and has given up her dance class because of aching joints in her feet. She has been previously ﬁt and healthy. Her mother-in-law suffers from rheumatoid arthritis. She works as school teacher, smokes four cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol on occasions. Which one of the following is the strongest risk factor for developing rheumatoid arthritis in this case?
explanation: A Smoking This lady has rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA commonly presents as a symmetrical arthritis affecting the small joints of the hands and wrists. Smoking is the strongest environmental risk factor for developing RA, especially in those that are anti- cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) positive. Smoking may contribute to citrullination (post- translational modiﬁcation of arginine residues) in the lungs. This lady should be encouraged to stop smoking, which will help her joints, as well as her general health. D Family history This lady’s mother in law (not a blood relative) has rheumatoid arthritis, and therefore does not contribute to her genetic risk. B Alcohol Alcohol is not a risk factor for developing rheumatoid arthritis, and in fact may lower the risk. C Exercise (dance classes) Exercise is not a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis. Overuse of a joint may increase the risk of osteoarthritis. E Occupation There has been interest in occupational risk factors for rheumatoid arthritis, although nil conclusive identiﬁed. This patient as a teacher does not put her at an increased risk.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic after suffering her second Colles’ fracture. Dual- energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scanning reveals a T-score of -2.8, conﬁrming osteoporosis. The patient is keen to start preventive therapy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value RHEUMATO Phosphate (PO43-) 0.9 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.27 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l ALP 180 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Urea 3.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l What is the best choice for initial therapy in this patient?
explanation:
E Bisphosphonate therapy Osteoporosis is deﬁned by a T-score of –2.5 SD or below on DXA scanning NICE guidelines TA160/161 state that alendronate is recommended as a treatment option for the secondary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in postmenopausal women (such as the patient in this scenario) who are conﬁrmed to have osteoporosis. In women aged 75 years or older, a DXA scan may not be required if the responsible clinician considers it to be clinically inappropriate or unfeasible. Alendronate is also recommended as a treatment option for the primary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in the following groups (see links below for full guidance): a) Women aged 70 years or older who have an independent clinical risk factor for fracture or an indicator of low BMD and who are conﬁrmed to have osteoporosis. In women aged 75 years or older who have two or more independent clinical risk factors for fracture or indicators of low BMD, a DXA scan may not be required. b) Women aged 65–69 years who have an independent clinical risk factor for fracture and who are conﬁrmed to have osteoporosis. c) Postmenopausal women younger than 65 years who have an independent clinical risk factor for fracture and at least one additional indicator of low BMD, and who are conﬁrmed to have osteoporosis. Risedronate and etidronate are recommended as alternative treatment options for the primary and secondary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in postmenopausal women who are unable to comply with the special instructions for the administra-

tion of alendronate, or have a contraindication to or are intolerant of alendronate. Oral bisphosphonates are relatively contraindicated with dyspepsia, but IV bisphosphonates are associated with a higher increased risk of avascular necrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures. Another rare complication of long-term bisphosphonate therapy is the risk of long bone mid-shaft fractures, possibly due to prolonged suppression of bone turnover. The International Osteoporosis Foundation and the European Society on Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis (ESCEO) conclude that the risk of these rare (<1 in 1000) atypical fractures is outweighed by the beneﬁt of prevention of other osteoporotic fractures. A Hormone-replacement therapy> HRT has been proven to reduce loss of bone mineral density and fracture risk at vertebral and other sites in postmenopausal women. In recent years, however, the risks of thrombosis, cardiovascular disease and cancers have thrown into question the risk-beneﬁt ratio of HRT. B Calcitonin therapy Calcitonin is rarely used as a treatment for osteoporosis now because of the risks of osteosarcoma associated with its use over the longer term and the availability of alternatives. C Calcium and vitamin D supplementation Calcium and vitamin D are insufﬁcient alone, but may be used alongside bisphosphonates. NICE osteoporosis guidelines state that unless clinicians are conﬁdent that women who receive treatment for osteoporosis have an adequate calcium intake and are vitamin D replete, calcium and/or vitamin D supplementation should be considered. D Raloxifene Raloxifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modiﬁer that appears to be associated with a reduction in the risk of oestrogen receptor-positive breast carcinomas, as well as positive effects on bone mineral density. Raloxifene is not recommended by NICE as a treatment option for the primary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in postmenopausal women, but recommends that it should be considered for the secondary prevention of osteoporotic fragility fractures in postmenopausal women who: • are unable to comply with the special instructions for the administration of alendronate and either risedronate or etidronate, or have a contraindication to or are intolerant of alendronate and either risedronate or etidronate; and • who also have a combination of T-score, age and number of independent clinical risk factors for fracture (see guidelines below). RHEUMATO

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of bilateral knee and left middle ﬁnger pain and swelling. She has no previous history of joint problems. On systematic enquiry, she denies any recent infection. She has recently returned from a holiday with four friends to Spain. On examination, she is pyrexial, with a temperature of 38.7 °C, and a tachycardia of 110 beats/min. She is noted to have small pustules on the sides of some ﬁngers, and a diffusely red, swollen, painful middle ﬁnger that she cannot ﬂex. She also has pitting in some nails with hypertrophic plaques of scaling skin on both knees. She has a similar lesion in her scalp behind the right ear. Her right knee is red and hot and very painful, and held in slight ﬂexion. She resists any movement of it. General medical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Gonococcal arthritis Disseminated gonococcal infection is caused by the bacteraemic spread of the sexually transmitted bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The best-ﬁt syndrome described in this patient is the dermatitis– polyarthritis– tenosynovitis syndrome, symptoms including fever, symmetrical polyarthralgia (small or large joints), tenosynovitis and dermatitis (painless vesiculopustular lesions). Diagnosis is made by culture of synovial ﬂuid, skin lesions and specimens from urethral swabs. Treatment includes symptomatic relief with NSAIDs, and ceftriaxone and azithromycin. E Mixed connective tissue disease Mixed connective tissue disease is an overlap syndrome including features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis and polymyositis. High titres of anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) are seen. It is not consistent with this patient’s history and examination. A Psoriatic arthritis Some of the signs described in this patient are consistent with psoriatic arthritis (scaling skin on her knees and nail pitting), but the onset is too rapid and the single joint disease is more severe than expected. B Reactive arthritis

Reactive arthritis would be in the differential diagnosis. Reactive arthritis also typically presents with the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis, and is an inﬂammatory response to a distant gastrointestinal or urogenital infection. C Rheumatoid arthritis The pattern of joint involvement and additional signs are not consistent with RA.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to the General Medical Clinic. She has been suffering from long-standing problems with her joints. The joints have become progressively stiffer and her hand has slowly changed shape. Both of her hands are affected. She has not seen any doctors for the last ten years because her husband died due to medical errors. Her daughter has brought her in at this point as she is concerned about difﬁculty coping with manual dexterity in activities, such as cooking. There is a past medical history of appendicectomy and humeral fracture, but no regular medications. There is palpable swelling of the joints. Her hand is shown below. What investigation is most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: E Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) Anti-CCP is a useful investigation with greater speciﬁcity than RHEUMATO rheumatoid factor for rheumatoid arthritis. It isn’t an initial investigation and is usually requested when the index of clinical suspicion is high, yet RF testing is negative. C Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) ANA is a non-speciﬁc marker associated with several rheumatological autoimmune conditions. 30% of people with rheumatoid arthritis have positive ANA and therefore it is not a particularly useful marker for this patient. This test would be more useful had the patient a presentation more consistent with systemic lupus erythematous (SLE), such as a facial butterﬂy rash, psychosis with symmetrical polyarthritis. A CRP CRP is an acute-phase reactant which can be useful in monitoring levels of inﬂammation. It is a non-speciﬁc test and would not be helpful in diagnosis. B Joint aspiration and light microscopy Aspiration would be a more appropriate investigation in patients with acute monoarthritis with effusion to differentiate between septic arthritis, gout and pseudogout, especially if the patient was unstable. In this patient, joint aspiration would be unlikely to yield a diagnosis as the long, progressive, deforming and symmetrical disease seen is not consistent with an acute monoarthritis. D Rheumatoid factor Although rheumatoid factor is an appropriate investigation as this patient clinically has symptoms and signs of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) including symmetrical polyarthritis with synovitis and deformity, it doesn’t conﬁrm the diagnosis as it is only positive in 6070% of those with RA.

stem: A 30-year-old woman, being followed up for well-controlled systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and on prednisolone 5 mg/day, was noted to have a slightly elevated creatinine by her GP. Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 20 mm in 1 st hour, antibodies to double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) –ve, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) titre 1:320. Subsequent investigations, including a kidney biopsy, revealed World Health Organisation (WHO) class II disease (mesangial lupus nephritis). Which one of the following would be the ideal treatment in this case?
options: High-dose glucocorticoid pulses + intravenous cyclophosphamide + Hydroxychloroquine
High-dose glucocorticoid pulses + intravenous cyclophosphamide + azathioprine +
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine alone
This patient has Class II lupus nephritis, which has a good prognosis and does not require immunosuppression unless there is significant proteinuria, but all patients should have hydroxychloroquine (unless contraindicated). Furthermore, a low erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and negative dsDNA (double-stranded DNA) antibodies suggest inactive disease. Treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) nephritis is based on the class of disease determined by renal biopsy and on disease activity. World Health Organisation (WHO) disease classification: I Minimal change (normal on light microscopy) II Mesangial III Focal segmental proliferative IV Diffuse proliferative V Membranous VI Glomerulosclerosis

stem: A 59-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with a 3-week history of progressive shoulder pain and stiffness. Her symptoms improve throughout the day. She has noticed that in the last 2–3 days, she has lost 1 kg in weight. She denies previous injuries or trauma. Over-the-counter paracetamol and ibuprofen provide some relief for her symptoms. She has a past medical history of irritable bowel syndrome and depression. On examination, she is afebrile. Her heart rate is 80 bpm, with a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg. She has a respiratory rate of 15 breaths/minute, with saturations of 99% on room air. There is palpable shoulder pain bilaterally. Her power and sensation are equal and normal throughout. Which of the following investigations will most likely suggest the diagnosis?
explanation: D ESR This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). PMR is an inﬂammatory condition that more commonly presents in women over the age of 60 years. It has similarities with the large vessel vasculitis temporal or giant cell arteritis (GCA) and if visual symptoms are present, GCA should be considered, along with urgent referral to ophthalmology. PMR tends to have a rapid onset (< 2 months) and is characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness which is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy which causes proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory investigations show elevated ESR and C-reactive protein. A raised ESR > 40 mm/hour, together with the clinical history and examination, is characteristic of the disease. A Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are positive in a number of diseases, particularly types of small vessel vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). PMR is a type of large vessel vasculitis and is typically diagnosed with a raised ESR level. ANCA is commonly negative in PMR. B Creatine kinase (CK) Creatine kinase (CK) would be a useful investigation to request to diagnose myositis such as polymyositis and dermatomyositis. Symptoms of polymyositis include general malaise, weight loss and proximal muscle weakness. A raised CK reﬂects muscle damage and breakdown. It is not elevated in PMR. C Electromyography (EMG) studies Electromyography (EMG) studies are also used to aid the diagnosis of myositis or neuropathy. Although if CK is signiﬁcantly raised (ie > 2000 units/litre), an EMG may not be necessary for making the diagnosis of myositis. In myositis, EMG studies demonstrate various characteristic signs, including spontaneous ﬁbrillation potentials at rest. However, EMG studies are normal in PMR and do not play a role in the diagnosis. E Muscle biopsy RHEUMATO A muscle biopsy is not used in the diagnosis of PMR. It is considered in myopathic disorders such as polymyositis or dermatomyositis where a biopsy shows muscle ﬁbre necrosis and a lymphocytic inﬁltrate.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital sores, and a history of uveitis. She also reports joint pain in the knees and ankles. On examination, there is evidence of swollen and tender joints. What is the best initial treatment for this patient's condition?
explanation:
Colchicine
Colchicine is considered the best initial treatment for Behcet Syndrome due to its efficacy in controlling mucocutaneous manifestations such as oral ulcers and erythema nodosum. It also helps in reducing inflammation in joints, providing relief from arthralgia which is common in Behcet Syndrome patients. Studies have shown that colchicine can significantly decrease the frequency and severity of mucocutaneous symptoms when compared to placebo. This makes it a suitable first-line therapy before considering more aggressive treatments.

Sulfasalazine
Sulfasalazine has some utility, particularly where GI ulceration predominates. However, it does not have strong evidence supporting its use specifically targeting mucocutaneous lesions prevalent in Behçet's syndrome compared with colchicine’s well-documented benefits on these manifestations. Additionally, gastrointestinal disturbances are common adverse effects associated with sulfasalazine usage, making patient compliance challenging.

stem: A 60-year-old patient has been complaining of a 1-month history of generalised headache, malaise and fever. He has also noticed scalp sensitivity while brushing his hair. What is the most appropriate test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
Temporal artery biopsy
Temporal artery biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test for giant-cell arteritis. A 2-cm segment of a tender artery will provide positive histology in 70% of cases. The diagnostic rate may be enhanced by taking longer segments or by the biopsy. While biopsy confirmation of the diagnosis is important, it should not be a reason for withholding steroids because the patient is at risk of irreversible blindness without treatment.

Antinuclear antibody test
Antinuclear antibody test is incorrect. Antibody tests are likely to be negative in GCA.

CT scan of head
CT scan of head is incorrect. Intracranial imaging is likely to be normal in GCA.

ESR
ESR is incorrect. An elevated ESR is not sensitive.

stem: A 50-year-old Asian woman, who has been living in the United Kingdom (UK) for 5 years, presents complaining of bone pain, especially in the lower back and both legs. She also describes difﬁculty walking upstairs and standing from a sitting position. The patient is a lifelong vegetarian but does eat small amounts of dairy products. On examination, there is mild proximal muscle weakness. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Phosphate (PO43-) 0.7 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.1 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l ALP 180 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Urea 3.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l What would be the most likely radiographic ﬁnding on Xray of this patient’s hip?
options: Low-density bands extending from the cortex
explanation:
B Low-density bands extending from the cortex This woman’s ethnic origin and her history are suggestive of osteomalacia. In fact, vitamin D deﬁciency is very common in the UK, even in white patients, due to the climatic conditions. The diagnosis would be conﬁrmed by blood results and X-ray ﬁndings. Looser’s zones occur in this condition and are characterised by low-density bands extending from the cortex inwards. Osteomalacia is associated with vitamin D deﬁciency, which leads to hypocalcaemia, phosphate levels at the lower end of the normal range and elevated ALP levels. Bone pain and proximal myopathy are well-recognised sequelae. C Osteopenia Osteopenia and osteoporosis are usually associated with normal bone proﬁles/biochemistry. Risk factors for osteopenia include past history of smoking, early menopause, below-normal body weight and type 2 diabetes. A Normal bones This is a possibility, even in osteomalacia, but given her symptoms, clinical ﬁndings of myopathy and abnormal biochemistry, there is likely to be evidence of osteomalacia on imaging. D Subperiosteal erosions Subperiosteal erosions can be seen in hyperparathyroidism, which would be associated usually with hypercalcaemia and low serum phosphate levels. E Sclerotic bone Sclerotic and lytic bones may be seen in Paget’s disease, in which one would see an isolated elevated ALP level and normal serum calcium levels.

DR Ankylosing Spondylitis Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of disorders characterised by seronegative inflammatory arthritis or spondylitis.  Overview Key Facts  Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of disorders characterised by seronegative inflammatory arthritis or spondylitis and they include:  ankylosing spondylitis (AS)  reactive arthritis (RA)  psoriatic arthritis (PA).  Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is axial spondyloarthritis characterised by sacroiliitis on X-ray.  Axial spondyloarthritis can also occur in the absence of X-ray changes and this is classified as non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis.  Arthritis is typically symmetrical, involves larger joints and especially affects the knees and ankles.  Presentation typically includes musculoskeletal features of spondylitis, arthritis and enthesitis, but also has extra-articular features such as uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).  In ankylosing spondylitis, patients typically present with back pain and stiffness, which often improves with exercise.  There is a strong genetic association with HLA-B27. Epidemiology  There is a strong genetic association with HLA-B27, found in up to 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis.  Most seronegative spondyloarthropathies present between 15 and 40 years of age and are more common in men.  Ankylosing spondylitis has a prevalence of 0.1%. Aetiology The aetiology of seronegative spondyloarthropathies is poorly understood, but it is thought to have a strong association with the presence of the HLA-B27 genotype. Pathophysiology  Exposure of the immune system to microorganisms (eg from barrier damage to the skin in psoriasis or bowel in IBD) may be of relevance for the pathogenesis of axial spondyloarthritis.  It is thought that cytokines enhance the inflammatory process, including tumour necrosis factor (TNF); this is targeted by TNF-α monoclonal antibodies in the management of Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI seronegative spondyloarthropathy, which is refractory to disease-modifying drugs and steroid management.  There is a growing body of thought that ‘microtrauma’ from bodily stress may cause inflammation at the site of enthesitis, leading to bony changes and pathological new bone formation.  Clinical Presentation  Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) typically presents with lower back pain and stiffness in a young man, with inflammatory aspects to the back pain and associated anterior chest pain:  AS usually onsets between 15 and 40 years with a higher incidence in men (5 : 1).  Pain is usually worse in the morning and relieved by movement.  There may also be associated buttock pain.  Sacroiliitis is the main feature along with spondylitis; however, there is also peripheral arthritis in approximately 35% of cases.  The sacroiliitis typically improves with exercise and is worse on rest, and may present with insidious onset – typically as pain may have a nocturnal element to it.  Extra-articular features include anterior uveitis and aortic incompetence.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  other seronegative spondyloarthropathies  rheumatoid arthritis  osteoarthritis  lupus (SLE)  gout  inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  infection, eg tuberculosis.  malignancy, such as metastasis or lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Some investigations are commonly done for all seronegative spondyloarthropathies, these include blood tests such as:  inflammatory markers  full blood count (FBC) for anaemia  alkaline phosphatase (ALP), which may be elevated.  An initial set of investigations would also include blood tests for rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibodies.  HLA-B27 testing is not a reliable diagnostic method when used alone, but it increases the suspicion of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy if positive.

DR  Diagnosis of AS requires radiological evidence of sacroiliitis, inflammatory spinal pain (lasting more than 3 months) and limited spinal movement or chest expansion.  Diagnosis requires referral to a rheumatologist for confirmation.  Radiological changes include:  blurred joint margins  subchondral erosion  sclerosis or fusion of the sacroiliac joint  loss of lumbar lordosis  bamboo spine.  As these changes may take many years to become evident on Xray, MRI may be useful in the early stages of presentation.  Plain film X-ray in psoriatic arthritis may show osteolysis around joints.  Management Non-pharmacological  Generally, physiotherapy is likely to be helpful and regular exercise helps maintain dependence and improves symptoms in the long term. Pharmacological  Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a good analgesic for symptomatic pain relief for AS.  If disease is refractory to NSAIDs, disease-modifying drugs or steroids can be used.  Sulfasalazine or methotrexate may help peripheral arthritis but have no impact on spinal disease.  Anti-TNF-α therapy is very effective and requires a high disease activity index score among other criteria for a prescription. Surgical  End-stage disease necessitates surgical treatments such as joint replacement and spinal straightening.  Prognosis  The course of the condition is variable but is generally progressive and irreversible.  Quality of life is often affected due to pain, reduced mobility and a resultant loss of function.  Prognosis is also dependent on the patient's age at presentation, and treatment methods used.  Complications include:  anterior uveitis  osteoporosis  spinal fractures and spinal cord injury  hip involvement Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cardiac complications – such as aortic and nonaortic valve disease, congestive heart failure and arrhythmias. Antiphospholipid Syndrome Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune disease which produces a hypercoagulable state.  Overview Key Facts  Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune disease which produces a hypercoagulable state.  Primary antiphospholipid syndrome occurs in the absence of any other related disease.  Secondary antiphospholipid syndrome occurs with other autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  Patients often present with a combination of recurrent pregnancy loss and/or thrombosis of arteries, veins or the microvasculature.  Antiphospholipid syndrome puts a patient at risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, as well as pregnancy-related complications such as miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery and preeclampsia.  Diagnosis is made via blood tests demonstrating lupus or anticardiolipin anticoagulation.  Treatment is with anticoagulation, which is often required lifelong. Epidemiology  30% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus have positive antiphospholipid antibodies.  The condition is most commonly found in younger women of childbearing age  The male:female ratio is 1:3.5.  The prevalence is higher in the black population. Aetiology  The cause of antiphospholipid syndrome is unknown.  APL antibodies are clinically linked to the condition, however, it is not known whether they are involved in pathogenesis and up to 5% of the healthy populations will also have these antibodies present.  Antiphospholipid syndrome may be present secondary to inflammatory or autoimmune conditions such as:  Systemic Lupus Erythematosus  Rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis  Systemic sclerosis.

DR  Bechet's disease  Giant cell arthritides  Sjogren's syndrome. Pathophysiology  Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune disease which produces a hypercoagulable state caused by antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin antibodies and lupus anticoagulant).  Antibodies react against proteins that bind to phospholipids on the plasma membranes.  Clinical Presentation  Antiphospholipid syndrome is defined by thrombosis formation and/or recurrent pregnancy loss  Thrombosis may be:  arterial (eg ischaemic stroke)  venous (eg deep vein thrombosis)  microvascular (in which case it may cause end-organ dysfunction).  A blotchy reddish patch of discoloured skin, described as livedo reticularis, may occur. In some cases, ulcers may form on the legs. An example of livedo reticularis and a clinical presentation of antiphospholipid syndrome:  Differential Diagnosis  Antiphospholipid syndrome needs to be differentiated from conditions which can also cause microvascular thrombosis, such as:  hemolytic uremic syndrome  thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (HUS-TTP)  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  vasculitis. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  A diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome can be made if:  one clinical event occurs (ie thrombosis or pregnancy complication)  two positive blood test results spaced at least three months apart detect lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin antibodies.  Management  The mainstay of treatment for antiphospholipid syndrome is anticoagulation.  In people without symptoms, no treatment is required.  In people with antiphospholipid antibody-associated thrombosis, anticoagulants such as warfarin are used to prevent further thrombosis, with a target international normalised ratio (INR) of 2.0–3.0.  Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) may be used as an alternative to warfarin, but not in people who are triple positive with all three types of antiphospholipid antibody (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibody).  Non-pregnant patients are usually anticoagulated with heparin or warfarin.  Low-dose aspirin is used in pregnancy. Low-molecular-weight heparin can be used as an alternative if aspirin is not tolerated.  In an attempt to prevent recurrent miscarriages, women with previous recurrent miscarriages and a diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome are often advised to take aspirin and to start low-molecular-weight heparin treatment after missing a menstrual cycle.  In surgical patients, there should be a heightened awareness for venous thromboembolic disease prophylaxis.  Prognosis  As there is no cure for antiphopholipid syndrome, most patients with APS need to take anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication daily lifelong.  Healthy pregnancy can be achieved with the use of anticoagulants. Avascular Necrosis Avascular necrosis occurs when the blood supply to the end of a bone is disrupted – this can be temporary or permanent. This causes osseous cell death (death of bone tissue).

DR  Overview Key Facts  Avascular necrosis (AVN) occurs when the blood supply to the end of a bone is disrupted – this can be temporary or permanent. This causes osseous cell death (death of bone tissue).  Risk factors of AVN include bone fractures, joint dislocations, excess alcohol consumption and use of high-dose steroids.  The most common site of AVN is the femoral head.  Early stages of AVN are asymptomatic.  Symptoms include joint pain and a limited range of motion.  Diagnosis is typically by radiographic imaging, eg X-ray, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  Treatments include pharmacological therapy and surgery. Epidemiology  Anyone can be affected by AVN, but it is most common in people between the ages of 30 and 50. Aetiology  AVN occurs when blood flow to the bone is disrupted or reduced; this can be caused by:  joint or bone trauma – dislocated joint and fracture may damage nearby blood vessels; radiation used in cancer treatments can harm blood vessels  medical conditions, eg sickle cell anaemia, Gaucher’s disease, coagulopathies, vasculopathies  fatty deposits in blood vessels – lipids can block small blood vessels.  Risk factors for the development of avascular necrosis:  trauma  systemic corticosteroid use (use of high-dose corticosteroids) or Cushing syndrome  excessive alcohol use  bisphosphonate use  certain medical treatments, eg radiation therapy for cancer, chemotherapy and immunosuppressant medication  high levels of blood triglycerides, total cholesterol, lowdensity lipoprotein cholesterol and non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol  heavy smoking. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology of AVN is not fully understood.  The final common pathway of the pathophysiology is the interruption of blood flow to the bone. This causes necrosis of marrow, medullary bone and cortex.  AVN commonly affects bones with a single terminal blood supply, eg femoral head, carpals, talus and humerus.  Osteocyte necrosis occurs after approximately three hours of anoxia.  The pathogenesis of AVN is multifactorial, it can be due to: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  vascular occlusion, eg due to trauma (fracture, dislocation), non-traumatic stress and stress fractures  altered lipid metabolism  coagulopathy  abnormal joint remodelling – necrosis of bone triggers osteoclasts, osteoblasts, histiocytes for the repair process; osteoblasts form new bone on top of the dead bone; this can cause a thick scar, preventing revascularisation of necrotic bone.  Subchondral bone subsequently collapses, which can lead to progressive secondary arthritis.  Clinical Presentation  Early stages of avascular necrosis may be asymptomatic. Symptoms depend on the affected joint.  Pain in the affected joint.  Avascular necrosis of the femoral head may cause:  pain in groin, thigh or buttock  pain lasting longer than 6 weeks  pain worse on weight-bearing and movement  gradual onset of pain, progressively worsening over time and subsequently may be present at rest  usually no history of trauma.  Physical examination:  early stages may produce no physical examination findings  patient may walk with a limp  may have tenderness around the affected bone  active and passive joint movements may be restricted and painful  hip rotation to elicit pain with the patient sitting or lying supine may reproduce pain in the groin, thigh and anterior aspect of the knee; this will help differentiate hip pain from pain originating from the spine and knee  a neurological deficit may occur if a nerve is compressed due to necrosis  advanced AVN may cause joint deformity and muscle wasting.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  osteoarthritis  osteoporosis  osteomyelitis  soft tissue trauma  inflammatory synovitis  complex regional pain syndrome  neoplastic bone conditions.

DR  Diagnosis/Investigation  Radiography:  X-ray – may reveal bone changes that occur in the later stages of AVN; early AVN is not apparent on plain radiographs; avascular bone may appear dense (whiter)  MRI – the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for AVN diagnosis  Blood tests – if high suspicion of rheumatological disease or infection.  Management Non-pharmacological  Refer to an orthopaedic surgeon if the patient has signs of AVN of the femoral hip on MRI of the hip.  Rest – reducing weight and stress on the affected bone. May need to use crutches to keep weight off the joint for a period of time.  Exercises – musculoskeletal physiotherapists can provide exercises to help maintain or improve range of motion in the affected joint:  exercises cannot cure AVN but can slow down disease progression and associated pain. Pharmacological  NSAIDs, eg ibuprofen, to help relieve the pain associated with AVN.  Bisphosphonates and prostacyclin analogues for pre-collapse disease.  Statins may be offered to reduce the amount of cholesterol. Surgical  Treatment depends on the site, age of the patient and required function of the joint.  Core decompression surgery with or without adjunctive pharmacological therapy for pain reduction and potential prevention of the need for total hip replacement:  core decompression involves relieving internal bone pressure through drilling a hole into the bone; the extra space within the bone stimulates new vascular growth and new bone formation.  Arthroplasty is indicated in older, immobile patients presenting with AVN of the femoral head.  Realignment osteotomy or arthrodesis is indicated in younger patients presenting with AVN of the femoral head.  Specialist tertiary centres may offer bone grafting to encourage vascular regrowth and osteotomies to unload damaged hip articular surface. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Prognosis depends on disease stage, bone affected and presence of any underlying conditions.  Post-operative recovery involves non-weight bearing for 12 months and gradual return to work and driving at 8 weeks.  Poor prognostic factors include:  age older than 50 years  advanced stage of AVN at time of diagnosis  necrosis of greater than one-third of the weight-bearing area of the femoral head on MRI  non-modifiable risk factors, eg corticosteroid-induced AVN.  Other  Natural history of AVN comprises subchondral necrosis, subchondral fracture and collapse of the bone, deformity of the articular surface and osteoarthritis. Later stages of AVN include sclerosis and total joint destruction. Behçet Syndrome Behçet syndrome is a vasculitis that manifests with a variety of mucocutaneous, vascular, gastrointestinal, ophthalmological and central nervous system symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Behçet syndrome is a vasculitis that manifests with a variety of mucocutaneous, vascular, gastrointestinal, ophthalmological and central nervous system (CNS) symptoms.  There are no specific investigative tests but pathergy testing, as well as autoimmune screening, can help to rule out other diagnoses.  The mainstay of treatment for severe disease is corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapies, eg azathioprine.  Symptoms usually improve with time and treatment over a course of 1–2 years. Epidemiology  It is often seen in patients from Turkish, Israeli and East-Asian backgrounds.  It is most common in young adults aged between 20 and 30 years.  Symptoms tend to be more severe in men.

DR Aetiology  Aetiology is unclear, with studies showing possible genetic predisposition, with increased inflammation and immunological activity.  Distinction between whether it is an auto-inflammatory or autoimmune disorder is not well established. Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology is unclear, with theories suggesting the presence of neutrophil hyper-reactivity.  Clinical Presentation  Diagnosis based on clinical criteria of:  recurrent oral ulcers  plus two other clinical manifestations of:  recurrent genital ulcers around the scrotum or labia  skin manifestations such as erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions or papulopustular and/or nodular lesions  eye involvement, eg uveitis, hypopyon  positive pathergy test which involves the formation of a pustule/papule 48 hours after the skin is pricked with a sterile needle  gastrointestinal involvement, eg crampy abdominal pain, diarrhoea  blood vessel involvement (rare), eg deep vein thrombosis, thrombophlebitis  CNS involvement, eg seizures, cranial nerve palsies, dizziness, memory impairment.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  aphthous stomatitis  Crohn’s disease/ulcerative colitis  herpes simplex  necrotising vasculitis  seronegative spondyloarthropathies  acne vulgaris  erythema nodosum  superficial thrombophlebitis  rheumatoid arthritis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There are no specific diagnostic tests for Behçet syndrome, but tests are performed to rule out alternative diagnoses.  Pathergy testing:  subcutaneous skin prick forms an induration in the skin within 48 hours that may be present with a papule/pustule  positive in Behçet syndrome. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Rheumatoid factor:  to rule out rheumatoid arthritis if associated joint symptoms  negative in Behçet syndrome.  Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs):  to rule out autoimmune diseases  negative in Behçet syndrome.  Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs):  to rule out necrotising vasculitis  negative in Behçet syndrome.  HLA-B51:  strongly associated genetic factor in Behçet syndrome  positive in Behçet syndrome.  Lumbar puncture:  to rule out tuberculosis (TB), herpes simplex or listeriosis if neurological involvement  may find lymphocytosis or polymorphonuclear cells.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain:  may find white matter changes if CNS involvement suspected.  Colonoscopy/endoscopy:  to rule out inflammatory bowel disease if GI symptoms  may find inflammation and aphthous-type ulcers in Behçet syndrome.  Computed tomography (CT) chest/pulmonary angiography:  indicated if haemoptysis to rule out pulmonary aneurysm.  Management  Mucocutaneous ulcers:  first line – topical corticosteroids, eg triamcinolone – used for mild symptoms  second line – colchicine, oral corticosteroids, eg prednisolone, or immunosuppressive therapy, eg azathioprine – used for 1–2 years for active lesions resistant to topical treatment  third line – TNF-α inhibitors, eg infliximab – used for 1–2 years for disease resistant to corticosteroids or oral immunosuppressant drugs.  Eye involvement:  mild/moderate – prednisolone + azathioprine  severe – prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab or adalimumab).  GI involvement:  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab).  CNS involvement:  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg infliximab).  Major vascular involvement:

DR  prednisolone + immunosuppressant therapy (eg ciclosporin).  Prognosis  Remission often occurs with treatment over 1–2 years.  If symptoms are controlled during this time doses can be tapered down.  Involvement of ocular, major vascular and GI systems carries a poorer prognosis.  Behçet eye disease can lead to blindness.  Other  Monitoring:  patients are likely to require monitoring every 2–3 months when using immunosuppressants  includes blood tests such as full blood count, liver function tests, urea and electrolytes and annual ophthalmological examinations. Bursitis Bursitis is the acute or chronic inflammation of a bursa – a small, synovial fluid-filled sac, between a tendon and skin or bone.  Overview Key Facts  Bursitis is the acute or chronic inflammation of a bursa – a small, synovial fluid-filled sac, between a tendon and skin or bone.  In bursitis, there is thickening and proliferation of the synovial lining, bursal adhesions, villus formation, tags and chalky deposits.  Bursitis occurs as a result of:  repetitive stress  infection  autoimmune disease  trauma.  Common areas for Bursitis:  olecranon  knee  shoulder  trochanteric bursitis.  The condition usually causes localised pain and tenderness, there may be swelling if the bursa is superficially sited.  Treatment for non-septic bursitis usually involves modification of physical activity, rest and analgesia. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Corticosteroid injections are reserved for cases that are unresponsive to conservative management.  First-line treatment for septic bursitis is aspiration and antibiotic therapy, it may also require surgical debridement and lavage. Epidemiology  The epidemiology is unclear, however some studies have found it affects around 1.8 in 1 000 patients per year. Aetiology The exact aetiology is unknown, however, the inflammation may be caused by:  Repetitive injury or acute trauma  any repetitive pattern of movement that puts pressure on a bursa  certain professions are thought to be more at risk of certain types of bursitis due to the repetitive action of their daily work eg infrapatellar bursitis = ‘clergyman’s knee’ (kneeling to pray).  Crystal deposition  secondary to gout or pseudogout  crystal arthropathy can result in crystal deposition within the bursa, this leads to inflammation of the synovial lining.  Autoimmune disease eg rheumatoid arthritis (RA).  Infection:  this may be acute or chronic and may follow a penetrating injury from a foreign body.  Osteoarthritis of the hip has been implicated as a cause of trochanteric bursitis through osteophyte deposition. Risk factors include:  occupations that cause mechanical stress on bursae eg carpet layers, RA  gout/pseudogout  penetrating injury (infective bursitis)  OA of the hip (trochanteric bursitis)  infection of a nearby joint  lower limb length discrepancy (trochanteric bursitis)  iliotibial band contracture (trochanteric bursitis)  valgus knee deformity (anserine bursitis). Pathophysiology  A bursa is a sac containing a small amount of synovial fluid, it lies between a tendon and either skin or bone and acts as a friction buffer.  There are > 150 bursae in the body, these can be either superficial eg subacromial bursa or deep eg olecranon bursa.

DR  In bursitis, there is thickening and proliferation of the synovial lining, bursal adhesions, villus formation, tags and chalky deposits.  Bursitis may be described according to the site of the affected bursa, the most commonly encountered are:  prepatellar bursitis (‘housemaid’s knee’)  infrapatellar bursitis (‘clergyman’s knee)  anserine bursitis (swollen bursa being restrained by the three overlying tendons of the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus muscles)  olecranon bursitis (‘student’s elbow’)  retrocalcaneal bursitis  trochanteric bursitis  subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis.  Clinical Presentation Key diagnostic factors are:  Pain at the site of the bursa.  Tenderness to palpation at bursa site.  Decreased active range of movement. Bursitis Acute Bursitis Pain (localised to bursa site, especially on movement) Swelling and erythema in superficial bursae Penetrating injury/foreign body may lead to infection There may be a Hx of trauma/repetitive occupational activity/ autoimmune disease Chronic Bursitis May last for several months and may frequently flare-up The patient is likely to have a limited range of active movement if the inflammation persists near a joint The passive range of movement is usually preserved Septic Bursitis Affects Superficial Bursae - Prepatellar and olecranon bursae Signs include a low-grade temperature, local erythema, swelling, warmth and sometimes local cellulitis Subacromial Bursitis Patient complains of a painful arc on abduction of the arm (due to impingement of the bursa under the coracoacromial arch) Trochanteric Bursitis Lateral hip pain + tenderness around greater trochanter plus 1 of the following: pain at the extremes of rotation/abduction/adduction pain of contraction of the hip abductors against resistance Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI pseudoradiculopathy (pain radiating down the lateral aspect of the thigh) Bursae of the Knee Tenderness on the upper medical tibia (3-5cm distal to the medial knee joint line) May have a valgus deformity Prepatellar/Infrapatellar Bursitis Swelling and erythema Patella may be impalpable if a lot of fluid is present Olecranon Bursitis A superficial bursa, susceptible to infection and usually accompanied by significant swelling May have a Hx of direct trauma to the elbow Retrocalcaneal Bursitis Tenderness along the distal portion of the Achilles tendon Associated with swelling May have a palpable bump Poorly fitting shoes may play a role Olecranon bursitis:  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  l meniscopathy  l compartment OA  Baker’s cyst  l collateral ligament damage  Soft tissue infection  Localised bone tumour  Osteoarthritis/Osteonecrosis of the hip  Stress fracture  Rotator cuff tendinopathy/lesion.

DR  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical, and imaging is rarely required.  If septic bursitis is suspected, then the fluid should be aspirated and sent for Gram staining and culture. It should also be sent for crystal analysis.  An X-ray of the affected region may be useful in some cases to exclude other differentials such as bone tumours.  Magnetic resonance imaging may be helpful if associated pathology such as a rotator cuff tear is suspected.  Management Non-pharmacological  Secondary prevention: activity modification and avoiding repetitive activities that are likely to cause chronic stress on a bursa.  The use of walking aids and protective padding may be helpful. Non-septic Bursitis  Activity and lifestyle modification to minimise mechanical stress on the bursa eg avoiding aggravating activities and protecting the area eg knee pads.  Rest the affected area to allow the inflammation to settle.  Physiotherapy has also been shown to be beneficial.  Identifying any predisposing risk factors and correcting them where possible.  Ice in the first 24 hours to reduce the swelling.  Simple analgesia eg paracetamol/NSAIDs. Pharmacological Non-septic bursitis  Corticosteroid injections are a second-line treatment when conservative management has not controlled symptoms.  Done under US-guidance if the bursa is deep.  An aseptic technique is essential to prevent secondary infection (steroid injections are not recommended in septic bursitis). Septic bursitis  Needle aspiration and appropriate Abx therapy.  Repeat aspiration may be needed if swelling, erythema and tenderness recur.  Oral Abx is usually sufficient for a systemically well patient.  Intravenous (IV) therapy is recommended if the patient is systemically unwell or has other comorbidities.  Initial antimicrobial therapy should cover staphylococci and streptococci. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Duration of Abx ranges from 1-4 weeks and 1st line agents include dicloxacillin or cefazolin, second-line options include clarithromycin or erythromycin. Surgical  Surgical removal of a bursa (bursectomy) may be considered if the above treatments are ineffective.  Subacromial: subacromial decompression.  Trochanteric: endoscopic approach.  Retrocalcaneal: considered after 3-6 months of conservative Mx has failed to control Sx, debridement of the calcific or diseased portion of the Achilles tendon, excision of the retrocalcaneal bursa and resection of Haglund’s deformity if indicated.  Prognosis  Complications of bursitis include:  infection secondary to aspiration or corticosteroid injection  tendon rupture secondary to corticosteroid injection  septic arthritis.  Most patients respond well to conservative management and recover completely. Charcot Arthropathy Charcot arthropathy (also called Charcot joint) is the degeneration and bony destruction of a joint leading to deformity, in people with peripheral neuropathy.  Overview Key Facts  Charcot arthropathy (also called Charcot joint) is the degeneration and bony destruction of a joint leading to deformity, in people with peripheral neuropathy.  It most commonly affects the foot and ankle in patients with diabetes.  Diabetes is the most common cause in Western society.  It can be a consequence of other conditions that cause peripheral neuropathy.  Pathophysiology is still incompletely understood but thought to be a combination of two processes:  repeated or acute trauma is unrecognised by the patient due to peripheral neuropathy and continued mobilisation leads to fractures and deformity  autonomic dysfunction leads to increased blood supply to the bone which causes increased activity of osteoclasts.

DR  Symptoms include swelling, erythema and warmth of the affected joint. Pain is not always present due to peripheral neuropathy and deformity it may be a late sign.  It is commonly misdiagnosed and treated as osteomyelitis, septic joint, cellulitis, gout or an acute fracture.  Diagnosis is with a weight-bearing X-ray of the affected joint and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is required only if this is inconclusive and suspicion is still high.  Patients should be managed by a specialist foot service.  The mainstay of treatment is offloading devices to avoid weight-bearing on the affected joint.  Early treatment can significantly decrease morbidity associated with Charcot’s arthropathy, such as ulcers, infection, gangrene and amputation. Epidemiology  It most commonly affects the foot and ankle but can affect the knee, hip and shoulder (very rare).  It may be bilateral in up to 30% of patients with diabetes.  It is thought to affect approximately 1% of patients with neuropathy. Aetiology  Peripheral neuropathy caused by diabetes is by far the most common cause in Western society.  It can be a consequence of other conditions causing peripheral neuropathy, such as:  spinal cord injury  peripheral nerve injury  alcoholic neuropathy  congenital insensitivity to pain  leprosy  tabes dorsalis  syringomyelia (most common cause of upper limb Charcot)  myelomeningocele  spina bifida  vitamin deficiencies (B1 and B12). Pathophysiology  There are two main theories regarding the pathophysiology of Charcot arthropathy, which are known as ‘neurotrauma’ and ‘neurovascular’. It is likely that the process is a combination of both and possibly other processes as yet unrecognised.  Neurotrauma: repetitive or acute trauma to the joint is unrecognised by the patient due to peripheral neuropathy; progressive wear of the joint leads to fractures which cause joint destruction and deformity.  Neurovascular: autonomic neuropathy may cause vasodilatation in arterial smooth muscle and an increased blood supply to the bone; this causes an increase in osteoclasts at the affected site, which leads to bone resorption, osteopenia and fractures. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  Presentation includes:  erythema  warmth  swelling  joint deformity (not always present, usually a late sign)  pain (not always reported due to peripheral neuropathy).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  septic joint  osteomyelitis  cellulitis  gout  ankle sprain or fracture.  Diagnosis/Investigation  For Charcot arthropathy of the foot and ankle:  weight-bearing X-ray of the affected joint: may show a joint effusion, calcification and joint space narrowing in the initial stages; later findings include subluxation and collapse of the joint  MRI, only if X-ray is inconclusive and symptoms are highly suggestive.  Management  For Charcot arthropathy of the foot and ankle:  the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) Guidance states that patients with suspected acute diabetic Charcot arthropathy should be referred within 1 day to the multidisciplinary foot care service and triaged within 1 day.  offloading devices should be used to take weight off of the affected joint; non-removable casts are preferable and the average length of casting in the United Kingdom is 9 months  monitoring of treatment through serial X-rays and measuring foot-skin temperature difference; a sustained temperature difference of less than 2 °C between both feet and no further progression on X-ray shows a high likelihood of resolution  patient education is very important to ensure that patients remain vigilant for new joint symptoms, protect their joints from trauma and continue to engage with the foot service  orthotics may be required if the joint is deformed.

DR  Prognosis  Failure to identify and treat Charcot arthropathy early can lead to complications.  Joint deformity may lead to ulceration which in turn may lead to infection or gangrene, the need for amputation and increased morbidity and mortality. Dermatomyositis Dermatomyositis is a rare inflammatory myopathy of voluntary muscles with associated characteristic skin rash.  Overview Key Facts  Dermatomyositis is a rare inflammatory myopathy of voluntary muscles with associated characteristic skin rash.  Dermatomyositis is most commonly found in women between 50 and 70 years.  When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one-third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma, most commonly of the lung.  Typical features include:  a red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema  violaceous ‘Gottron’s papules' over the knuckles  linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers  nail fold inflammation with dilated capillaries  the ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck  weakness of the major proximal muscle groups, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’).  Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing.  Diagnostic investigations include creatine kinase, anti-nuclear antibody and skin biopsy; electromyography and/or muscle biopsy.  Anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-cytoplasmic antibodies may both be associated with dermatomyositis,  Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are specific for dermatomyositis but are only found in around 30% of individuals with the condition.  Screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases.  Treatment is dictated by symptoms, not necessarily by antibody subtype positivity:  corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  azathioprine or ciclosporin can be added in poorly responding patients.  The prognosis is relatively good, with most patients reaching remission after 2–3 years.  An exception is where the condition is associated with an underlying malignancy.  Older patients with dermatomyositis and polymyositis have a higher prevalence of malignancy than expected by chance, and this is most pronounced in dermatomyositis.  Many types of malignancy have been reported in association with dermatomyositis, including lung, oesophageal, breast, colon and ovarian tumours.  Among women with dermatomyositis, the risk of ovarian cancer is as much as 20 times greater than that of the general population. Epidemiology  Dermatomyositis is a relatively rare condition:  it can be found in both adults and children  it occurs more commonly in women between 50 and 70 years. Aetiology  Dermatomyositis is associated with cancer, drugs such as penicillamine and toxins:  many types of malignancy have been reported in association with dermatomyositis, including lung, oesophageal, breast, colon and ovarian tumours  among women with dermatomyositis, the risk of ovarian cancer is as much as 20 times greater than that of the general population.  Clinical Presentation  Dermatomyositis and polymyositis present with muscle disease such as proximal weakness and muscle swelling and tenderness, as well as characteristic skin rashes.  Typical features include:  a red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema  violaceous ‘Gottron’s papules' over the knuckles  linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers  Gottron’s sign – erythema over knees and elbows  nail fold inflammation with dilated capillaries  nail-fold infarcts  the ‘shawl sign’ – erythema over the upper back and posterior neck  weakness of the major proximal muscle groups, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’).  Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing.

DR  Calcification can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis but is uncommon in adults. Heliotrope rash around the eyes: Gottron’s papules on the hands:  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  atopic dermatitis  contact dermatitis  photosensitivity  periorbital/orbital cellulitis  polymyositis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  Diagnosis/Investigation  In both dermatomyositis and polymyositis, anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) may be present and muscle enzymes will be elevated. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Blood tests should be carried out to check for:  raised creatine kinase, aspartate transaminase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)  autoantibodies (ANA/anti-mi-2/anti-Jo-1):  anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-cytoplasmic antibodies may both be associated with dermatomyositis  anti-Jo-1 is more likely to be associated with the subtype of polymyositis in which pulmonary fibrosis is also found  anti-Mi-2 antibodies are specific for dermatomyositis but are only found in around 30% of individuals with the condition.  Muscle biopsy and electromyography can help confirm the diagnosis – muscle biopsy will reveal inflammation, muscle fibre necrosis and regeneration.  It is also important to rule out underlying malignancy (in adults):  screening for underlying neoplasia (such as computed tomography (CT) chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases.  Management  Treatment is dictated by symptoms, not necessarily by antibody subtype positivity:  corticosteroids (high-dose prednisolone) are the mainstay of treatment – this dose can then be tapered down  azathioprine or ciclosporin can be added in poorly responding patients or in those with flare-ups when steroids are tapered  corticosteroids allow a rapid fall in creatine kinase, but muscle power may take many weeks to improve.  Prognosis  The prognosis is relatively good, with most patients reaching remission after 2–3 years.  An exception to this is where the condition is associated with an underlying malignancy.  Older patients with dermatomyositis and polymyositis have a higher prevalence of malignancy than expected by chance and this is most pronounced in dermatomyositis.  Many types of malignancy have been reported in association with dermatomyositis, including lung, oesophageal, breast, colon and ovarian tumours.  Among women with dermatomyositis, the risk of ovarian cancer is as much as 20 times greater than that of the general population.

DR Fibromyalgia Fibromyalgia is a syndrome of chronic pain, characterised by chronic widespread pain on both side of the body and above and below the waist for at least 3 months.  Overview Key Facts  Fibromyalgia is a syndrome of chronic pain, characterised by chronic widespread pain on both side of the body and above and below the waist for at least 3 months.  It is accompanied by other symptoms such as sleep disturbance and excessive tiredness, but there may also be depression/anxiety and GI symptoms.  It is mostly a clinical diagnosis, other potential causes of symptoms should be excluded.  Management aims are supportive and symptomatic, as there is no cure, but exercise, CBT, pain relief, and antidepressants can be helpful. Epidemiology  The condition is far more common in women than in men (1 : 10).  The absolute prevalence of fibromyalgia stands between 0.73.3% based on gender.  Studies have shown the significant prevalence of comorbidities in those with fibromyalgia, which indicates a serious burden for health economies and also for the patient. Aetiology  The aetiology of fibromyalgia is poorly understood, but generally it is thought there is an interplay of the following:  It is thought that central sensitisation of the CNS is the major mechanism involved, coupled with an increased excitability of spinal cord neurones, leading to hyperalgesia.  Serotonin is thought to be one of the neurotransmitters involved, especially as serotonin plays a big role in sleep and pain modulation, which are commonly affected in those with fibromyalgia.  Genetic predisposition is thought to be an important factor, with a suspected polygenic method of transmission. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  A patient with fibromyalgia is likely to present with widespread pain along with the two major characteristics associated with fibromyalgia:  fatigue  sleep disturbance.  There may also be issues with cognition as well as anxiety and depression which may be secondary to the pain and reduced quality of life.  Differential Diagnosis  Polymyalgia rheumatica.  Hypothyroidism.  Chronic fatigue syndrome.  Polymyositis.  Anaemia.  Psychiatric conditions such as anxiety, depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).  Multiple sclerosis.  Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is achieved clinically, however some blood tests are important to rule out other causes:  full blood count (FBC) for anaemia  thyroid studies to exclude hypothyroidism  erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)/ c-reactive protein (CRP) to rule out inflammatory arthritis.  Diagnosis should be made on the basis of two diagnostic criteria:  widespread pain on both sides of the body, both above and below the waist, for a period of at least 3 months  11 tender points among the 18 points which have been recognised as areas of extreme tenderness in those with fibromyalgia (9 sites symmetrically as seen in the diagram below).  Tenderness should be assessed using digital palpation (using the thumb); the pressure applied should be just about enough to cause blanching of the fingernail of the examiner.  It is vital to take a social, family, and psychological history in order to assess to see if stress, psychosocial experiences, or sociocultural factors are contributing to fibromyalgia.
