DR  Management  On a general note, management is intended to reduce symptoms and improve patient quality of life. Non-pharmacological  Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has shown efficacy in improving overall function and wellbeing in recent studies.  Exercise programmes are likely to be helpful; aerobic, strengthening, and aquatic exercises are recommended.  These are helpful as research suggests that exercise in those with fibromyalgia promotes wellness, reduces symptoms, and overall physical function.  Physiotherapy may be helpful depending on the patient’s presentation. Pharmacological:  Pharmacological management is split into two main domains for the management of fibromyalgia.  Pain relief should be used for symptomatic relief.  this includes paracetamol, weak opioids, and tramadol.  it is important to be careful with the use of tramadol in patients with a prior history of drug dependence as there is a potential for abuse  Antidepressants may be used to reduce pain and improve overall wellbeing.  The main indications for the use of antidepressants include poor sleep, depressed mood, poor quality of life scores, and pain:  studies have shown tricyclic antidepressants to be the best as adjuvants for pain relief, and selective-seretonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) to be the best for low mood.  Prognosis  As it stands, there is currently no cure for fibromyalgia.  Fibromyalgia does not confer any absolute increase in mortality, as much as it has an impact on the quality of life of a patient and leads to significant emotional burden. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Giant Cell Arteritis Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  Overview Key Facts  Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the second most common vasculitis, with the most common type being polymyalgia rheumatica.  The condition should be treated as a medical emergency.  The mean age of onset is 70 years; the condition is very rarely found in patients under 50.  GCA typically presents with an abrupt-onset unilateral headache and scalp pain, as well as jaw or tongue claudication.  There may be temporal artery thickening or tenderness on palpation.  The condition is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.  Treatment is urgently required with high-dose steroids to avoid the immediate complication of sight loss.  Steroid treatment is slowly tapered down, often over months or even years.  With rapid treatment, prognosis is good; however, relapses can occur in up to 50% of cases. Epidemiology  GCA is the second most common vasculitis, with the most common type being polymyalgia rheumatica:  mean age of onset 70 years  rare before age 50 years  more common in White people  women : men ratio 3 : 1. Aetiology  Infections, malignancy and drugs may all lead to vasculitis illness, but in many cases the trigger for endothelial injury is unknown.  T-cell mediated endothelial cell injury is a proposed mechanism. Pathophysiology  The Chapel Hill Classification for Vasculitis (2012) classifies vasculitis according to the predominant vessel involved; however, it is important to note the underlying pathology is similar in all disease states:  large vessel vasculitis – includes Takayasu’s arteritis and giant cell arteritis (GCA)

DR  medium vessel vasculitis – includes polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease  small vessel vasculitis – includes ANCA-associated vasculitis, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis/Churg–Strauss and immune-complex vasculitis anti-GBM disease, IgA vasculitis  variable vessel vasculitis  single-organ vasculitis – includes cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis and cutaneous arteritis  vasculitis associated with systemic disease – includes lupus vasculitis, rheumatoid vasculitis and sarcoidosis vasculitis.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms:  abrupt-onset headache (usually unilateral)  scalp pain, difﬁculty in combing hair  jaw or tongue claudication  visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax/diplopia)  constitutional symptoms (fever,weight loss,anorexia)  there may be a history of polymyalgia rheumatica.  Examination:  temporal artery tender, thickened or beaded with reduced pulsation  scalp tenderness  reduction in visual acuity  visual ﬁeld defect  afferent pupillary defect  pale, swollen optic disc with haemorrhages  unilateral or bilateral central retinal artery occlusion  upper cranial nerve palsies  large-vessel GCA – asymmetrical pulses and bruits.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  migraine  tension-like headache  cluster headache  trigeminal cephalgia and/or neuralgia  optic neuritis  medication overuse headache  substance exposure or withdrawal  intracranial disorders and/or neoplasms  head/neck injury Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  infection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The American College of (ACR) classiﬁcation criteria for GCA require three of the following to be present:  age at disease onset ≥ 50 years  new headache  temporal artery abnormality – tenderness or decreased pulsation  elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  positive temporal artery biopsy.  However, treatment should not be delayed by waiting for results if there is strong clinical suspicion.  A biopsy of the temporal artery can confirm the diagnosis.  A positron emission tomography (PET) scan can be useful in cases where the biopsy is non diagnostic.  Management  Early and urgent intervention with high-dose corticosteroids is required to prevent complications such as blindness occurring:  a dose of 40–60 mg per day is indicated  the first dose may be initiated in primary care before the patient is seen on an urgent (same-day) basis in secondary care (usually by an ophthalmologist)  the steroid dose can be gradually tapered down over months, and in some cases, years.  Methotrexate as adjunctive therapy for relapsing disease.  Low-dose aspirin may be indicated (to reduce the risk of stroke).  Prognosis  Most patients respond rapidly to treatment with glucocorticoids with timely intervention.  Relapses of GCA are common and occur in up to 50% despite appropriate treatment.  In general, treatment with glucocorticoids is usually needed for 1–2 years, and sometimes even longer.  Complications may be broken down into:  early (visual loss, stroke)  late (aortic aneurysm, dissection)  treatment-related (corticosteroid side-effects).

DR Gonococcal Arthritis Gonococcal arthritis is a bacterial arthritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gram-negative diplococcus).  Overview Key Facts  Gonococcal arthritis is a bacterial arthritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gram-negative diplococcus).  Manifests as localised septic arthritis or as a syndrome of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and migratory polyarthritis.  Requires intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy in the first instance with a switch to oral antibiotics; joint drainage may be required.  Prognosis is good with adequate treatment. Complications can include meningitis, hepatitis, endocarditis and long-term joint damage. Epidemiology  Lower incidence in Europe than North America.  Common in developing countries due to limited access to health care.  The highest rates of infection occur in young people < 25 years of age.  Most common in African American ethnicities. Aetiology  Risk factors for disseminated infection causing gonococcal arthritis include:  host-related:  female sex  pregnancy  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  complement deficiency  low socioeconomic status  IV drug use  HIV infection  multiple sexual partners.  organism related:  antigenic variation of pili  protein P or B1A on the outer membrane which makes host complement cascade less effective  strains with nutritional requirements for arginine  colony opacity protein-independent invasion. Pathophysiology  Gonococcal arthritis is caused by infection with N gonorrhoeae which is a gram-negative diplococcus. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  It is highly infectious in humans with common sites of infection being the urethra, cervix and pharynx.  Dissemination of infection is thought to cause gonococcal arthritis and is more likely in those whose immune systems are unable to control the infection.  Clinical Presentation  Time from initial infection to disease manifestation ranges from 1 day to 3 months.  Bacteraemic form:  Forty per cent of patients with disseminated gonococcal infection present with arthritis dermatitis syndrome which is a triad of polyarthritis, tenosynovitis and dermatitis  symptoms usually appear 3–5 days before a diagnosis is made  usually presents as polyarticular migratory arthralgias affecting the wrist, elbows and knees  pain can be present due to tenosynovitis which occurs at the wrist, hand, ankles and knees most commonly  a non-pruritic and painless rash consisting of small popular, pustular or vesicular lesions may also be present  other systemic symptoms that may be present include myalgias, fever and malaise.  Septic arthritis form:  joint symptoms start within days to weeks of infection  pain, redness and swelling in one or more joints most commonly knee, wrist, ankle and elbow.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  reactive arthritis  septic arthritis  syphilis  rheumatic fever  meningococcaemia  Lyme disease  hepatitis B/C.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full blood count – leukocytosis.  ESR – raised.  Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) – detects small amounts of DNA or rRNA.  Cultures (blood, cervix, rectum, urethra, pharynx, joint aspirate) – growth of N. gonorrhoea.  Ultrasound of affected joint – can identify tenosynovitis and exclude arthritis.  Skin biopsy of lesions – dermal vasculitis with perivascular neutrophils.

DR  Management  IV antibiotics – ceftriaxone, cefotaxime.  Oral antibiotics – azithromycin.  Arthrocentesis.  Surgical drainage of joint.  Prognosis  Prompt treatment with antibiotics and joint drainage for gonococcal arthritis is usually all that is necessary for a full recovery. Goodpasture Syndrome Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease where antibodies are produced against the GBM (glomerular basement membrane) and the alveolar basement membrane.  Overview Key Facts  Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease where antibodies are produced against the GBM (glomerular basement membrane) and the alveolar basement membrane.  The newer terminology for Goodpasture syndrome and Goodpasture disease is anti-GBM (glomerular basement membrane) disease.  Antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.  It can present as glomerulonephritis alone or as a pulmonaryrenal syndrome and is more common in men.  Pulmonary involvement in people with anti-GBM antibodies may be more likely with environmental triggers such as smoking, inhalation of cocaine, respiratory infections or exposure to hydrocarbons.  Associated with HLA-DR15 and HLA-DRB1.  Symptoms include haematuria, frothy urine (proteinuria), decreased urine output, peripheral oedema, haemoptysis and dyspnoea.  The presence of anti-GBM antibodies on blood tests differentiates Goodpasture’s from other diseases that cause renal and pulmonary symptoms.  Other investigations include urinalysis (haematuria and proteinuria), renal function tests, renal biopsy (lung biopsy if not possible) and chest X-ray.  Treatment is with plasma exchange (plasmapheresis), prednisolone and cyclophosphamide.  1-year survival is 70–90% if appropriate treatment commenced early. The most common cause of death is respiratory failure following pulmonary haemorrhage. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  It is not known what first triggers the production of anti-GBM antibodies.  In patients with anti-GBM antibodies, it is thought that pulmonary involvement may have environmental triggers:  smoking  inhalation of cocaine  exposure to hydrocarbons  lung infections such as influenza.  Damage to the lungs caused by the above may expose the alveolar basement membrane to circulating anti-GBM antibodies.  There is a strong genetic association between HLA-DR15 and HLA-DRB1. Pathophysiology  Anti-GBM antibodies are produced which form an antigenantibody complex at the glomerular basement membrane.  Complement is activated which leads to tissue injury.  This results in ‘crescentic glomerulonephritis.  The alveolar and glomerular basement membrane comprise type IV collagen.  Anti-GBM antibodies target the alpha 3 subunits of type IV collagen.  Not all patients present with pulmonary involvement and it is thought that environmental factors may make pulmonary disease more likely.  Clinical Presentation  80%–90% of patients present with features of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.  40–60% will also have haemoptysis/pulmonary haemorrhage.  Only a small minority will have isolated pulmonary involvement.  Symptoms:  fever, nausea and vomiting, weight loss  haematuria  frothy urine (proteinuria)  decreased urine output  peripheral oedema due to renal failure  haemoptysis (can present with massive pulmonary haemorrhage)  dyspnoea.

DR  Differential Diagnosis  Anti-GBM antibodies are the key finding to differentiate Goodpasture syndrome from other conditions which can present with renal and pulmonary involvement:  IgA nephropathy  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  microscopic polyangiitis  granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis)  Henoch–Schönlein purpura.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Anti-GBM antibodies on blood testing are diagnostic.  Urinalysis:  haematuria  proteinuria.  ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) is usually normal in Goodpasture syndrome, which can help differentiate from vasculitides.  Renal function tests:  acute kidney injury.  Chest X-ray:  bilateral, patchy consolidation.  Renal biopsy:  crescentic glomerulonephritis  linear deposition of complement (C3) and IgG along the basement membrane.  Lung biopsy (if renal biopsy not possible):  pulmonary haemorrhage  haemosiderin-laden macrophages.  Renal biopsy showing crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear deposition of IgG: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Management  Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) – to remove anti-GBM antibodies:  daily for at least 14 days or until anti-GBM antibodies are undetectable.  Prednisolone and cyclophosphamide – to stop production of further anti-GBM antibodies:  duration of therapy varies.  Haemodialysis:  may be necessary if significant damage to the kidneys has already occurred.  Prognosis  The most common cause of death is respiratory failure following pulmonary haemorrhage.  Patients are at risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia due to immunosuppressive treatment, which can be a lifethreatening complication.  1-year survival is 70–90% if treated promptly with plasma exchange and immunosuppression. Gout Gout is the most common crystal arthropathy, and is characterised by the deposition of uric acid crystals in joints (of the big toe most commonly) due to high levels of blood uric acid.  Overview Key Facts  Gout is the most common crystal arthropathy, and is characterised by the deposition of uric acid crystals in joints (of

DR the big toe most commonly) due to high levels of blood uric acid.  It commonly affects the joints, but crystals can accumulate within the kidneys.  Gout has associations with other comorbidities such as hypertension, obesity, glucose intolerance, and hyperlipidaemia – it is often described as a disease of the western world given the rising rates of obesity.  It is managed through conservative measures to improve diet and lifestyle and then through urate lowering therapies with the aim of preventing tophi and acute gout attacks. Epidemiology  Gout is now the most common inflammatory arthritis in men and in women aged over 60.  Gout has an absolute prevalence of 2.49%, and has been increasing in recent years.  It is thought that incidence is rising as a result of increasing obesity. Aetiology  Gout is the most common crystal arthropathy, and is characterised by formation of uric acid crystals in joints or soft tissues, leading to a variety of diseases.  Uric acid is a breakdown product of purine nucleotides (found in meat).  Purines can be synthesised from precursors, but significant amounts are ingested in normal diets and released during cell death.  Hyperuricaemia (high levels of uric acid in the blood) arise from an imbalance in uric acid production/ingestion and excretion with increasing levels in the blood leading to increased deposition within tissues. Pathophysiology  Gout can be primary or secondary:  primary gout is mostly idiopathic (90%), but the other 10% is due to rare enzyme deficiencies that cause high levels of uric acid to accumulate within the blood.  secondary hyperuricaemia can be sub classified into those causes, which increase uric acid production or intake, and those causes which reduce the excretion of uric acid.  Increased uric acid production:  myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disorders  a high-purine diet, such as purines in beer and meat  acidosis, such as in DKA  cytolytic therapy  tumour lysis syndrome.  Decreased uric acid excretion:  renal failure  drugs, such as diuretics, low dose aspirin, and cyclosporin  lead intoxication. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation  The presentation of gout depends on the tissues impacted by uric acid.  Acute crystal arthritis:  this presents with small feet joint involvement, and is usually recurrent  the most commonly affected joint is the first metatarsophalangeal joint, and is often recurrently affected  the joint will be painful, red, and swollen.  Gouty nephropathy:  tubulointerstitial disease which arises as a result of renal parenchymal crystal deposits  it may present as acute renal failure and is likely to present with some element of haematuria  urate stones may form, which will be radiolucent on imaging.  Chronic tophaceous arthritis:  these are aggregates of urate crystals which affect articular, peri-articular, and non-articular cartilage, such as that in ears and can be felt as hard limps with a raised point.  Differential Diagnosis  Pseudogout.  Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPDD).  Septic arthritis.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Cellulitis.  Bursitis.  Reactive arthritis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is made by microscopy of joint fluid, which reveals negatively bifringent, needle-shaped crystals; positively birefringent brick-shade crystals would be an indication of CPDD.  Plain film radiographs are usually normal, however there may be signs of gout in severe disease, including such signs as bone erosion.  In chronic tophaceous gout, the plain film X-ray appearance may be helpful as it includes large, punched out erosions distant from the joint margin, and these are characteristic changes.  It is helpful to assess serum uric acid 4-6 weeks after an acute attack, as this is an accurate reflection of general levels of uric acid; this can confirm hyperuricaemia if levels are constantly greater than 380 micromol/l.  As gout is associated with some other comorbidities, this is a relevant stage during which to screen for any cardiovascular disease and renal disease, which may include urea and electrolytes (U&Es) as a blood test and checking blood pressure, lipid levels, and HbA1-c.

DR  Management Non-pharmacological:  Weight loss is advised, as well as reducing alcohol and meat intake.  It is advisable to reduce dietary purine intake.  Increase in physical activity levels.  Identify and treat associated factors, such as hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, and hyperglycaemia.  Withdraw drugs which may cause hyperuricaemia such as diuretics.  In order to avoid acute gout attacks, it is advised to avoid dehydration, reducing alcohol intake, and reducing weight if obese/overweight. Pharmacological:  In acute attacks, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), colchicine, or prednisolone can be used.  Urate lowering drugs are used as maintenance treatments, to promote and maintain low levels of uric acid in the blood.  These include allopurinol (1st line) and febuxostat (which are both xanthine oxidase inhibitors).  These drugs should be used under the following indications:  attacks recur within a year of the first attack  after the first attack if:  there are visible tophi  there is renal impairment  there are uric acid stones  it is not possible to stop diuretics  the patient is very young at diagnosis.  The aim with the urate-lowering therapies is to reduce serum urate to below 300 micromol/l.  Acute attacks can also be precipitated by the use of pharmacological or medical management that leads to a reduction in urate levels, so it is advisable to use colchicine during the first 6 months of urate lowering in order to prevent this.  Allopurinol should not be used during an acute event as it can exacerbate or prolong an attack.  It is usually started 1–2 weeks after inflammation has settled  The dose is titrated every few weeks until the serum uric acid level is below 300 micromol/L.  The starting dose is 100mg slowly built up to 300mg or more.  Prognosis  Gout attacks are painful but resolve with time, as treatment is symptomatic.  62% of those who have a gout attack have a reoccurring gout attack within a year. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Overall, recurring disease and ongoing gout leads to progressive joint damage.  Gout also has an independent association with CKD, MI, CVD and raised mortality.  Tophi are common in those with gout, and these subcutaneous deposits of uric acid can interfere with daily activities and become inflamed or infected, having an impact on quality of life. An image to show gouty tophi in the helix of the ear of a young man: Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  Overview Key Facts  Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  Symptoms of lung involvement include cough and haemoptysis.  Symptoms of renal tract involvement include haematuria and proteinuria.  Symptoms of upper respiratory tract involvement include nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, ‘saddle nose’ deformity and subglottic stenosis.

DR  Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss and myalgia are common.  There may also be skin, eye, ear, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms.  There is no single diagnostic test, but cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCAs), a biopsy of affected organs showing necrotising granulomas and vasculitis and imaging are used to aid diagnosis.  The mainstay of treatment is with steroids and cyclophosphamide.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases.  Once symptoms have improved, cyclophosphamide may be replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine, and treatment with steroids may continue for several years.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission, although relapses are common. Epidemiology  It affects men and women equally.  It is more common in middle-aged and older people but can present in childhood. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown, but approximately 90% of patients are positive for c-ANCA. Pathophysiology  GPA is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  It is an immune-mediated vasculitis, but the exact pathophysiology is unknown.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms depend on the organs involved; granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a multisystem disease with a diverse range of clinical features.  The most commonly affected organs are:  lungs (95% of cases) – cough, haemoptysis  kidneys (80%) – haematuria, proteinuria  upper respiratory tract (75–90%) – nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, 'saddle nose' deformity, subglottic stenosis.  Many patients have constitutional symptoms, such as:  fever  weight loss  myalgia.  Other symptoms include:  skin involvement – rashes and ulcers  eye involvement – scleritis, episcleritis, conjunctivitis  ear involvement – chronic ear infections, hearing loss Rheumatology Key points R. This includes but is not limited to the following conditions.  Other vasculitides:  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  If there is lung involvement, chest X-ray changes may be mistaken for:  lung cancer  tuberculosis  pneumonia.  Other conditions:  Goodpasture syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  rheumatoid arthritis with vasculitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There is no single diagnostic test.  Bloods:  c-ANCA is positive in approximately 90% of cases in patients with renal impairment  however, in patients without renal impairment, c-ANCA may be negative in up to 50% of patients

DR  renal function tests may be deranged if there is renal involvement  ESR – typically elevated, but non-specific finding.  Urine sample:  haematuria  proteinuria  casts.  Biopsy of affected organ (not always possible):  necrotising granulomas with associated vasculitis.  Chest X-ray:  the most common findings are nodules and/or cavitation and pulmonary haemorrhage.  CT imaging:  findings are highly variable  may include nodules, consolidation, ground-glass changes, atelectasis and pleural effusions.  Management Stage 1  Once the disease is recognised, it is treated aggressively with:  high-dose steroids  cyclophosphamide –in some cases, cyclophosphamide may be substituted with methotrexate, rituximab or mycophenolate mofetil.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases.  Stage 2 (may last 2–5 years)  Once the symptoms have improved and the disease is under control, cyclophosphamide is usually stopped and replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine.  Steroids are continued.  Stage 3  If the symptoms return, it may be necessary to:  continue steroids longer-term or  start treatment with rituximab or  restart cyclophosphamide or  consider plasma exchange.  Or a combination of the above. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Without treatment, 2-year survival may be as low as 10%.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission although relapses are common.
