JAMIL ALRAJHI Henoch–Schönlein Purpura Henoch–Schönlein purpura is the most common cause of autoimmune hypersensitive vasculitis in children.  Overview Key Facts  Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) is the most common cause of autoimmune hypersensitive vasculitis in children.  Its aetiology is unknown, but certain medications and infections are responsible for its development.  Underlying malignancy is also responsible for HSP in adults.  A classical tetrad of symptoms is helpful in the diagnosis of HSP: palpable rash, joint pain, renal involvement and gastrointestinal involvement.  Palpable purpura must be present which is not due to thrombocytopenia.  There is no definitive test for its diagnosis.  Treatment is usually symptomatic and supportive. Epidemiology  HSP is the most common autoimmune systemic vasculitis in children.  It is a rare, but most common, disease in children and 90% of affected children are aged under ten years.  Peak incidence of the disease is between four and six years of age.  It occasionally occurs in adults and adolescents but is rare in infants.  It usually affects 10–20/100 000 children per year, and the estimated annual incidence is 6–20 cases/100 000 population.  White people are commonly affected.  It mostly occurs in autumn and winter. Aetiology  The cause of HSP is unknown; however, a combination of deranged immune, genetic and environmental factors are responsible for its development.  Pathogens causing respiratory tract infections are responsible for its progression:  group A streptococci  Mycoplasma pneumoniae  Epstein–Barr virus  Coxsackie virus  parvovirus B19  hepatitis A and B viruses  Campylobacter jejuni  adenovirus  varicella–zoster virus.

DR  HSP is also associated with malignancy and vaccination.  In adults, solid tumours are responsible for HSP, not haematological malignancies (lymphomas, leukaemias). Pathophysiology  Although the pathophysiology of HSP is not fully understood yet, it is known that immunoglobulin A (IgA) plays an important role in this disorder.  IgA antibodies are produced as a result of antigenic exposure from an infection or medication and are deposited in the skin, joints, kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.  The deposition of IgA antibodies causes an influx of mediators such as prostaglandins. Complement C3 receptor-bearing lymphocytes bind to the immune complexes and deposit in vessels, causing a hyperinflammatory response.  In the gastrointestinal tract, deposition of immune complexes manifests as haemorrhage.  Mild proliferative and crescentic glomerulonephritis may result if these complexes deposit in the kidneys.  In the skin, deposition of these complexes manifests as palpable purpura and petechiae.  Clinical Presentation Henoch–Schönlein purpura:  The child is usually aged 4–6 years, most commonly presenting with symptoms of upper respiratory tract infections such as cough, runny nose and high-grade fever.  There are symmetrical erythematous and macular rashes on the ulnar side of the arms, back of the legs and buttocks. These rashes are present on both sides of the body and also around the waistline.  Purpura is present, which is slightly raised and palpable.  Abdominal pain is associated with bloody diarrhoea.  There are tender and swollen joints.  Headaches are present, associated with seizures.  If there is renal involvement, the patient will also have other findings such as microscopic haematuria and proteinuria. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Scrotal involvement, with features of acute scrotal swelling and pain, may mimic testicular torsion.  Differential Diagnosis  Intussusception when it is associated with typical purpura.  Connective tissue disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus.  Other diseases presenting with purpuric rash such as thrombocytopenia and meningococcal meningitis.  Glomerulonephropathies.  Acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical.  There are no definitive tests; however, some tests may be helpful in the diagnosis of HSP such as:  urinalysis, which may show haematuria and proteinuria  full blood count showing an increased white blood cell count with eosinophilia – some patients will have normal or increased platelets  erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) – will be raised  renal function tests – show raised creatinine level  serum IgA level may be measured and is increased – this is not diagnostic  autoantibody screening such as antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (dsDNA) – connective tissue diseases  barium enema for intussusception  abdominal ultrasound for gastrointestinal problems (to rule out intestinal obstruction/intussusception as a complication)  testicular ultrasound for testicular torsion  renal biopsy – if persistent nephrotic syndrome  skin biopsy  stool test for detection of any blood loss  screening for older patients having HSP associated with malignancy with no preceding infection.  Management  It is usually self-limiting, and treatment is usually supportive and symptomatic.  Painkillers such as paracetamol and non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen are used for joint pain.  Resting with the legs raised may reduce the severity of rashes.  Steroids.  Hospital admission is necessary when renal and gastrointestinal complications develop.  Plasma exchange is used for idiopathic, rapidly progressive hepatitis and vasculitis.

DR  Prognosis  HSP is a self-limited disease and resolves without treatment.  Recurrence of this disease is quite common and it mostly comes back after six months of initial infection.  Chronic kidney disease may develop after ten years of initial infection.  Prognosis usually depends on the severity of renal involvement.  Adult patients having HSP are more prone to developing renal impairment than children.  Other Complications include:  nephritic and nephrotic syndrome leading to chronic kidney disease  myocardial infarction  pulmonary haemorrhages  pleural effusion  gastrointestinal bleeding  intussusception  bowel infarction  testicular torsion  mononeuropathies. Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most commonly found synovial joint disease.  Overview Key Facts  Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most commonly found synovial joint disease (SJD).  This is most commonly due to obesity or age related degeneration causing by wear and tear damage to the joint.  It is characterised by softening and degradation of articular cartilage and secondary changes in adjacent bone, leading to long term arthralgia an ongoing destruction of the joint.  Commonly affects the following joints:  distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden’s nodes)  proximal interphalangeal joints (Bouchard’s nodes)  base of thumb (first carpometacarpal joint)  weight bearing joints such as the hips, knees, and spine.  OA can be broadly categorised into primary and secondary. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Within primary OA, there is a sub-classification of localised (one principal site, eg hip) or generalised (eg hands, knees, spine).  Within secondary OA, there are a variety of causes, including inherited dysplastic disorders, mechanical damage, metabolic causes, or previous inflammation such as that seen in gout or rheumatoid arthritis.  Osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically without investigations if a person:  is aged 45 years or more  has activity-related joint pain  has morning joint stiffness that lasts up to 30 minutes (or no stiffness).  Alternatively, diagnosis can be made via imaging; X-ray is the investigation of choice as it shows the typical features of osteoarthritis:  loss of articulating cartilage is seen through narrowing of the joint space  osteophytes may be seen  subchondral bone thickening occurs due to remodelling following injury.  Management includes lifestyle advice (such as weight loss) and analgesia; intra-articular corticosteroid injections can be added if symptoms persist, and joint replacement may be necessary if medical management fails to alleviate symptoms. Epidemiology  The prevalence of OA on X-ray rises with age and affects 70% of 70-year-olds.  OA is more common in women than men.  Many individuals who possess radiological OA are asymptomatic, however those who are overweight or have played high impact sports etc may report pain symptoms. Aetiology  Osteoarthritis is a change that comes about due to wear-and-tear of weight-bearing joints.  As a result, any factors that increase wear on these joints or the weight borne by these joints are likely to cause OA.  This is most often due to obesity and age related degeneration.  Alternatively, damage to bone or surrounding tissues can increase the risk of developing OA.  This occurs because the injury to the joint is a form of accelerated wear, such as that seen in septic arthritis. Pathophysiology  The basic premise is that repair processes intended to repair damage lead to structural changes within a joint.  Excessive weight-bearing and stress on a joint is the cause of this.  Cartilage is lost on the site that undergoes this stressful contact.  Adjacent bone undergoes secondary changes including remodelling and osteophyte formation.

DR  Clinical Presentation  The patient is likely to present with joint pain which is typically related to activity, and has developed over months or years.  Morning stiffness may possibly be absent, or if present, does not last longer than 30 minutes – joint pain persisting much longer is suggestive of other joint conditions eg rheumatoid arthritis (RA).  There may be associated functional restriction in some cases too.  On examination, it is possible to see some signs of OA including:  joint deformities  joint effusions (especially so in the knee)  joint warmth or tenderness, eg in synovitis  crepitus may be felt on passive joint movement. Osteoarthritis diagram:  Differential Diagnosis  Reactive arthritis.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Ankylosing spondylitis.  Gout.  Pseudogout.  Psoriatic arthritis.  Septic arthritis.  Bursitis.  Bakers cyst.  Popliteal DVT.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically without investigations if a person: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  is aged 45 years or more  has activity-related joint pain  has morning joint stiffness that lasts up to 30 minutes (or no stiffness).  Diagnosis requires a careful history to be taken, along with an examination of the affected joint.  Body Mass Index (BMI) measurements may be helpful in order to correlate risk profile for developing OA.  Alternatively, diagnosis can be made via imaging.  A plain film X-ray is the investigation of choice as it shows the typical features of osteoarthritis:  loss of articulating cartilage is seen through narrowing of the joint space  osteophytes may be seen  subchondral bone thickening occurs due to remodelling following injury. Hip osteoarthritis:  Management Non-pharmacological:  2018 National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) guidance makes it clear that information on sources of advice and support are very important, and can be delivered from a variety of useful resources, such as Arthritis Research UK and NHS information leaflets.  As obesity is the major cause, weight loss of overweight patients is key.  Exercise has the benefits of strengthening surrounding muscles and promoting aerobic fitness, but can also have the effect of further joint damage.  Pain relief can be non-pharmacological, such as transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS).  It is important to consider functional restriction and the likely impact of this condition on their quality of life.  Advice regarding appropriate footwear is important for those with OA in the knees and hips to maximise symptomatic relief.

DR  Walking devices such as frames and sticks should be considered to aid mobility. Pharmacological:  Analgesia: This can be topical or oral, for example non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), paracetamol, or codeine.  It may be necessary to manage any comorbidities.  If weight loss is refractory to lifestyle changes, medical treatment may be required for this purpose.  Intra-articular corticosteroid injections may be required and last for several weeks following the injection. Surgical:  It may eventually be necessary to carry out a joint replacement.  This should be seen as an option only if there has been inadequate management through medical treatment.  Prognosis  OA can be restrictive and progression can vary, but is not usually disabling.  Joint deformities can lead to functional restriction especially in later life.  For example, in hand OA, fine actions are likely to cause trouble, such as opening jars or writing.  There is likely to be an impact on the patient’s psychosocial health, as bony deformities and functional restriction are likely to affect self-confidence, sleep, and mood. Osteomalacia And Rickets Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) are presentations of extreme vitamin D deficiency in children and adults respectively.  Overview Key Facts  Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) are presentations of extreme vitamin D deficiency in children and adults respectively.  Both conditions are characterised by poor mineralisation of bony matrix with calcium and phosphate; however, in rickets, this poor mineralisation occurs in children before closure of growth plates.  Vitamin D is mostly gained from sunlight (90%) and less so from dietary intake (10%), however, the majority of the UK population is deficient.  Whilst rickets and osteomalacia are presentations of extreme deficiency, there is also simple, uncomplicated deficiency of vitamin D which is easily reversible by vitamin D replenishment (calciferol). Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  In children, there is bony deformity such as bow legging in rickets, whereas in adults there is pain and weakness of proximal muscles (osteomalacia).  General management principals are focused around increasing dietary and environmental consumption of Vitamin D. Epidemiology  It is estimated that Vitamin D deficiency has a prevalence of 1 billion people worldwide, and it is the commonest nutritional deficiency in the world, particularly in Scandinavia.  More than half of the UK population are Vitamin D deficient, with the highest rates of deficiency found in Scotland, Northern Ireland, and North England.  Vitamin D deficiency is greater in those with risk factors, such as malabsorption and highly pigmented skin. Aetiology  Vitamin D deficiency underpins the development of osteomalacia and rickets.  Vitamin D determines plasma calcium and phosphate levels, and this determines the extent of bone mineralisation.  Vitamin D deficiency can come about through issues in the two methods of its intake:  production from a precursor in the skin (90% of Vitamin D is obtained this way)  dietary intake.  Vitamin D undergoes processing (hydroxylation) within the body in the liver and then the kidneys to form active 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D3. Metabolic pathway of 1.25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 precursors into the active form: Pathophysiology  Low vitamin D levels can come about by reduced absorption of ultraviolet B light through the skin, which is the commonest cause in the UK.

DR  This absorption is reduced in those with darker skin and those who routinely cover their skin, as well as those who do not spend much time outdoors/institutionalised.  In the months of autumn and winter, the majority of the Great British public struggles to get enough ultraviolet B light for enough vitamin D synthesis.  High levels of vitamin D levels are found in foods such as oily fish, egg yolk, and fortified foods such as margarine and cereals, however dietary sources of vitamin D are not enough in isolation.  On some occasions, vitamin D deficiency is due to an underlying disease, such as malabsorption, liver disease, or renal disease causing defective hydroxylation.  Clinical Presentation  Generally, there are likely to be some non-specific symptoms alongside particular symptoms specific to children and adults.  Children from the age of 6 months onwards can present with bony deformity, which is known as rickets.  Legs may be bowed or there may be knock knees.  There may also be a soft, deformable skull, along with delayed fontanelle closure.  Generally, children may be unhappy to weight-bear, and may show reduced/stunted growth, including a later walking milestone than expected.  In severe cases of vitamin D deficiency, there may be seizures due to hypocalcaemia.  In adults, initially there is progressive fatigue and widespread pain, especially in the hips and lower back), as well as muscular aches, and as the condition progresses, there may be proximal muscle weakness.  pain is commonly felt in the lower back, ribs, hips, thighs, pelvis and feet  muscle weakness may exist alongside muscle aches  there may be signs of an underlying disease process, such as chronic kidney disease (CKD)  there may be signs of hypocalcaemia such as tetany. Normal alignment, as well as bowed legs (genu varum) and knock knees (genu valgum): Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  Osteoporosis.  Hyperparathyroidism.  Multiple myeloma.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Osteoarthritis.  Fibromyalgia.  Polymyalgia rheumatica.  Hypothyroidism.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  Full blood count (FBC) – to assess for anaemia which may suggest malabsorption.  Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) – to look at calcium and phosphate levels.  Renal function – to assess for CKD.  Levels of parathyroid hormone may be raised.  Liver function tests (LFTs).  Thyroid function tests (TFTs).  Vitamin D levels through 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) serum assay  deficiency: < 25nmol/l  insufficiency: 25-50nmol/l  healthy: > 50nmol/l  Bedside tests:  Urine dipstick – to assess for gross kidney disease.  Imaging:  A child with low levels of Vitamin D will require an Xray of the wrist for diagnosis as there must be radiographic evidence of a long bone showing typical radiographical features of rickets

DR  In adults, plain film radiography may not be necessary, but may show features such as pseudo fractures and osteopenia  There will be a lower density on DEXA scanning.  Special tests:  Urine microscopy to assess for any signs of CKD.  Management Non-pharmacological:  General management principals are focused around increasing dietary and environmental consumption of Vitamin D.  Encourage safe exposure to sunlight.  Dietary advice – this may include referral to a dietician.  Foods rich in vitamin D include egg yolks, oily fish, and fortified margarines/cereals. Pharmacological:  In painful presentations, there may be a need for analgesia.  Treatment of any underlying conditions.  Loading doses of vitamin D can be given weekly or as split daily doses, with a follow up maintenance treatment of approximately 800 international units.  Higher doses may be required for those with malabsorption disorders.  It is important to calculate dietary calcium intake and increase this, if it is low, through dietary advice.  It may be sensible to offer the patient a combined calcium and vitamin D preparation on the basis of this daily calcium intake calculation.  Prognosis  Generally, prognosis is good as long as vitamin D is replenished.  In those with a simple and uncomplicated deficiency of vitamin D, medical provision of vitamin D supplementation and lifestyle advice is likely to have a big impact.  Those with rickets and osteomalacia should also show a good response to vitamin D supplementation, with increased mobility usually showing the first response to treatment, despite a transient and short-lived initial increase in bone pain.  Within a few weeks, bone healing will begin, and healing should be complete within 6 months. Osteomyelitis Osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of a bone. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Overview Key Facts  Osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of a bone.  In children, it mostly affects the long bones of the limbs.  In adults it mostly affects:  feet  spine  hips.  Osteomyelitis can be classified by the route of spread  haematogenous (by blood)  post-traumatic (via an open wound)  contiguous (from local soft-tissue infection).  It may present acutely with pain and features of sepsis, or chronically with established infection and radiographic changes.  Chronic osteomyelitis arises from acute osteomyelitis, open fractures or local soft-tissue infection (contiguous osteomyelitis).  Infections can also result from open fractures or after joint replacement surgery.  Diagnosis is usually based on symptoms and is backed up with investigations such as blood cultures and radiographs.  Treatment involves resuscitation, intravenous (IV) antibiotics, splintage, aspiration or surgical debridement, and rehabilitation. Epidemiology  Osteomyelitis typically affects 2.4 per 100 000 people per year.  The condition is more common in children and older adults.  Men are more commonly affected than women. Aetiology Acute Chronic S. aureus common in all ages H. influenzae and haemolytic strep in neonates and infants Salmonella spp. in those with sickle cell disease Entry from UTIs, infected IV access sites or ENT sepsis Risk factors include: Very young/old IVDU Immunocompromise Diabetes Sickle cell disease S. aureus (most common) Anaerobes Gram-negative bacilli Risk factors include: Smoking Malnutrition Immunocompromise Diabetes Steroids Vascular disease (arterial and venous) Multiple medical comorbidities Pathogen categorisation according to age-group:

DR  Infants: S. aureus, Group B strep, gram-negative bacilli, Enterobacter spp.  Children < 4yrs: S. aureus, S. pyogenes, H. influenzae  Older children and adults: S. aureus (80%)  Patients with intravascular devices: S. aureus, Candida spp.  Sickle cell anaemia: Salmonella  IVDU: Pseudomonas Pathophysiology Haematogenous osteomyelitis  Organisms reach the bone via the bloodstream from a septic focus elsewhere.  Most common aetiology in children.  They invade the bone and the body initiates a response, however, the effectiveness is lessened due to the inability of the bone to swell, so pus collects below the periosteum.  The metaphysis is the major site of infection, with the epiphysis acting as a barrier to spread, if the metaphysis is in the joint capsule then septic arthritis can occur.  Most commonly affects the tibia, femur and humerus. Osteomyelitis following an open fracture or surgical operation (direct inoculation or contiguous spread)  Pus discharges through the wound rather than collecting below the periosteum.  Visible pus and erythema with less severe pain (no build-up of pressure).  Mx involves ensuring adequate drainage of pus and Abx.  The Cierny-Mader classification system is used in chronic osteomyelitis, it considers the anatomy of infection, local and systemic factors eg smoking and vascular disease.  Classification based on anatomical stage:  medullary = confined to the medullary cavity  superficial = periosteum and cortex  localised = medulla and periosteum, with the formation of draining sinus and cloacae  diffuse = through-and-through infection.  The formation of sequestrum (devitalised bone) and involucrum (formation of new bone around an area of bony necrosis) is followed by the formation of an encasing layer of scar tissue.  this results in a hypovascular area, which is poorly penetrated by the patient’s immune system or Abx  the encapsulated necrotic and infected material cannot be resorbed and provides a continuing focus of infection  the infection will not resolve until this material is excised. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation Acute Chronic Pain that increases in severity (may have difficulty weight-bearing or moving limb) Localised bony tenderness Systemic toxicity and pyrexia Joint effusion Adjacent joints may contain an effusion, but the joint itself will not be tender and some movement is possible This is in contrast to septic arthritis in which even small movements are painful Commonly metaphyseal in infants and vertebral in adults History indicating spread: Coinciding infection Open wound/recent surgery Local soft tissue infection Intermittent tenderness over the bone Pyrexia May have a sinus track leading to the skin surface  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for osteomyelitis are as follows:  acute suppurative arthritis  acute rheumatoid arthritis  subperiosteal haematoma  bone infarct secondary to sickle crisis  Ewing’s tumour  benign or malignant tumour.  Diagnosis/Investigation Acute Osteomyelitis Radiograph No abnormal radiological signs in the first 10–14 days Periosteal elevation plus new bone deposition may be seen after 10 days Isotope Bone Scans Useful in areas of difficult localisation eg vertebral infection Do not show abscess formation and given no information on collections that may require drainage USS May show a soft tissue or subperiosteal collection, which can be aspirated under USS or drained in an open procedure MRI Gives information on size and position of the bone infection Will show bone and soft-tissue oedema in osteomyelitis T2 sequences best CT Can be used to guide needle aspiration of collections

DR Blood Cultures Must be taken before Abx are commenced, positive blood cultures are seen in 60% Other Investigations Bone and tissue cultures FBC U&Es CRP (raised in 90%) PV/ESR (ESR is most sensitive and is raised in 97% of cases) Chronic Osteomyelitis Plain Radiograph Diagnostic changes are usually well established in haematogenous chronic osteomyelitis Dense bone with patchy sclerosis giving a honeycomb appearance The appearance may lag 10-14 days behind In contiguous osteomyelitis the radiographic changes may be more subtle and difficult to distinguish from the disuse changes associated with longstanding soft-tissue infection MRI Useful for differentiating soft-tissue infection from osteomyelitis Will show bone and soft-tissue oedema in osteomyelitis T2 sequences best CT Can identify necrotic bone Isotope Bone Scan Useful to localise infection in difficult areas eg vertebral column CRP, PV, ESR Inflammatory markers that are useful for monitoring the response to treatment Blood Culture Positive blood cultures with radiographic changes of osteomyelitis are sufficient to commence treatment Bone Biopsy Indicated if blood cultures are negative, or if the infection does not respond to initial treatment The gold standard for identifying Abx therapy, however used infrequently Swab from Sinus Tract Rarely indicated Osteomyelitis of toe: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Osteomyelitis bone scan:  Management Acute Osteomyelitis Chronic Osteomyelitis The priority is to obtain samples for culture and prescribe the correct Abx Resuscitation IV Abx (usually 10-14 days IV followed by 46 weeks PO) Initially flucloxacillin and fusidic acid or vancomycin and cefotaxime until organism identified Early discussion with Microbiology needed Splintage of the affected limb to prevent soft tissue contracture The aim is to arrest the infection and restore function Identify the organism IV Abx IV for two weeks then four weeks of PO from the start of treatment or the last surgery to treat the infection Improve general patient factors eg stopping smoking, correct malnutrition, give hyperbaric oxygen, revascularisation of any ischaemic limbs by vascular team if necessary Bone and soft-tissue Mx Eradicate dead material (surgical debridement of bone, scar tissue and implants) Reduce soft-tissue space (eg local flaps, free flaps, Abx-impregnated

DR Radiographically guided aspiration or surgical evacuation of soft-tissue or subperiosteal collections Surgical evacuation is preferred for large collections All devitalised tissue may be excised, and the procedure can be repeated if required Rehabilitation of the patient and affected limb beads or cement, vacuum-assisted closure) Stabilise the skeleton (internal or external fixation) Promote fracture union and bone regeneration (Ilizarov frame can provide stability and fine control of movement, as well as achieving compression, angular correction or distraction, resulting in the formation of new bone) If there is ongoing infection after the end of the cycle, or if there is no response to treatment, repeat cultures and debridement, and administer Abx for another six weeks. Other options such as amputation should also be considered if there is chronic infection with pervasive wound or bone damage that is unable to be salvaged  Prognosis Acute Osteomyelitis Chronic Osteomyelitis Most patients with acute osteomyelitis recover with no long-term complications if the osteomyelitis is diagnosed promptly and treated adequately In 5% there are long-term sequelae: recurrence chronic osteomyelitis septic arthritis pathological fractures through devascularised bone (will heal if the infection is successfully treated and the fracture is reduced and stabilised) damage to the growth plate causing either complete growth arrest, or an angular deformity as part of the physis continues to grow. Despite surgical debridement and longterm Abx, the recurrence rate in chronic osteomyelitis is 30%. Recurrence of infection may be early or late Early relapse is usually seen shortly after stopping Abx and can be treated by repeated surgery The success of treatment depends largely on the type of host (the causative pathogen) Other complications include: pathological fractures amyloid disease.  Other  Brodie’s Abscess  Subacute abscess in the metaphysis of any long bone  Presents with pain  Typically seen in the distal tibia of patients < 25 years  Cultures may be negative  Curettage and appropriate Abx are generally successful. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Osteoporosis And Osteoporotic Fractures Osteoporosis is the increased porosity of bone leading to decreased bone density of normally mineralised bone matrix, this leads to an increased risk of fractures.  Overview Key Facts  Osteoporosis is the increased porosity of bone leading to decreased bone density of normally mineralised bone matrix, this leads to an increased risk of fractures.  Osteoporosis is usually asymptomatic and often remains undiagnosed until a fragility fracture occurs.  An osteoporotic fracture is a fragility fracture that occurs as a consequence of osteoporosis, they typically occur in the wrist, spine and hip  A fragility fracture is defined as a fracture following a fall from standing height or less.  A 10-year fragility fracture risk score should be calculated prior to a DXA scan using QFracture or FRAX.  Osteoporosis is defined as a bone mineral density (BMD) of 2.5 standard deviations below the mean peak mass (average of young healthy adults) as measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) applied to the femoral neck.  It can be primary or secondary.  Risk factors for osteoporosis include:  female gender  increasing age  menopause  oral corticosteroids use  smoking  alcohol  family history of OP  BMI < 18.5  rheumatological conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA).  Treatment involves:  risk factor reduction  a bisphosphonate should be offered to people with a bone mineral density T-score < -2.5  Hormone replacement therapy should be offered to women who have experienced premature menopause. Epidemiology  Osteoporosis is very common in the elderly population.  Approximately 50% of women > 80 years and 25% of men > 80 years have the condition.

DR  The lifetime risk of an osteoporotic fracture is 60% for women and 30% for men.  There are around 180 000 fractures annually in the United Kingdom as a result of osteoporosis. Aetiology Primary (Type I) Postmenopausal Affects women 10-20yrs after the menopause (due to increased osteoclastic activity) Secondary (Type II) Neoplasia Multiple myeloma Carcinomatosis Leukaemia Drugs Anticoagulants (heparin) Chemotherapy Corticosteroids (30-50% of pts on longterm glucocorticoids will have a fracture) Anticonvulsants Alcohol Endocrine disorders Hyperparathyroidism Thyroid disorders Hypogonadism Pituitary tumours Addison’s disease Type I diabetes mellitus Gastrointestinal Malnutrition/Malabsorption Vitamin C or D deficiency Disease RA Ankylosing spondylitis Tuberculosis Chronic renal disease Mechanical Disuse Immobilisation Haematological Thalassaemia Sickle cell disease Risk factors for osteoporosis include:  Age  Female gender  Reduced physical activity or sedentary lifestyle  mechanical forces are stimuli for normal bone remodelling.  Smoking (increases risk)  Glucocorticoid use  Nutritional state, low weight or alcohol  low BMI correlates with a higher incidence of OP  alcohol directly reduces osteoblast function.  Hormonal influences, early menopause  decreased oestrogen levels result in increased production of IL-1, IL-6 and TNFα by monocytes and bone marrow cells  these cells are potent stimulators of osteoclast activity.  Genetic factors Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  genetic variability resulting in differences in the vitamin D receptor molecule accounts for ~75% of the peak bone mass achieved. The FRAX score (used to calculate the risk of further fractures), takes into account many of these risk factors to stratify risk score appropriately. Pathophysiology  Osteoporosis is a disease characterised by low bone mass and structural deterioration of bone tissue, with a consequent increase in bone fragility and susceptibility to fracture.  Osteoporosis is defined as a BMD of 2.5 standard deviations below the mean peak mass (average of young healthy adults) as measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) applied to the femoral neck.  Peak bone mass is achieved in early adulthood and is determined by:  nutritional state  levels of physical activity  hormonal status (sex hormone levels).  At the start of the fourth decade, the amount of bone resorbed exceeds that which has been formed, so there is a steady decrease in skeletal mass.  Osteoporosis is the end result of an imbalance in the normal process of bone remodelling by osteoclasts and osteoblasts. During normal ageing, bone breakdown by osteoclasts increases and is not balanced by new bone formation by osteoblasts.  Elderly individuals have impaired reproductive and biosynthetic potential of osteoblasts they cannot lay down bone as efficiently, non-collagenous proteins bound to the ECM eg growth factors also lose their full impact.  This results in a combination of reduced BMD and changes in bone composition, architecture, size and geometry. Age-related changes in bone mass:

DR  Clinical Presentation  Osteoporosis itself is asymptomatic and often remains undiagnosed until a fragility fracture occurs.  Symptomatic presentation is with low trauma fractures.  Commonly vertebral fracture in the thoracic and lumbar spine – pain, loss of height and kyphosis.  Other common fractures:  fractured neck of the femur  pelvis (Pubic Rami)  Colles’ fracture of the distal radius. Osteoporotic vertebral wedge fracture:  Differential Diagnosis  Metastatic bone disease  Multiple myeloma  Osteomalacia  Paget’s disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Osteoporosis cannot be reliably detected on plain radiographs until 40-50% of the bone mass is lost.  It is difficult to diagnose accurately because it is asymptomatic until advanced skeletal fragility manifests itself in the form of a pathological fracture.  Diagnosis is confirmed by either:  T score <-2.5 on DEXA scan  fragility fracture (low-impact fracture from standing height that would otherwise not be expected to cause a fracture)  only bone densitometry is diagnostic (DXA scan). Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  For all people with risk factors for osteoporosis, calculate the 10-year fragility fracture risk prior to arranging a DXA scan to measure BMD, this can be done using online risk calculators eg QFracture or FRAX.  A 10-year fracture risk of 10% is considered to be the threshold for arranging a DXA scan.  There also needs to be an assessment for vitamin D deficiency and adequate calcium intake (calcium intake of at least 1000 mg/day is recommended for people at increased risk of fragility fractures).  Investigations also need to exclude non-osteoporotic causes of fragility fractures eg metastatic bone disease, multiple myeloma as well as excluding secondary causes of osteoporosis eg endocrine and rheumatological conditions. X-ray Can only detect osteoporosis once > 40% of bone has been lost Can be useful to detect wedge fractures of the spine (if the fracture is shown, perform a DEXA scan) Bloods Often show low vitamin D, however calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH are often normal TFTs may show thyroid problems DEXA scan (dualenergy X-ray absorptiometry) This measures the bone density in multiple locations (usually spine and femoral neck) Gold standard is femoral neck density T score = no. of standard deviations from the mean bone density of a 30-year-old adult eg -2.5 represents 2.5 SD below the young adult mean > 1.0 = normal -1 to -2.5 = osteopenia <-2.5 = osteoporosis Treatment is initiated if the T score is <-2.5. Z score = no. of standard deviations from the mean bone density of age and gender-matched controls useful when suspecting osteoporosis in younger patients ie 50-year-old patient’s BMD is compared to that of other 50-yearolds, not 30-year-olds. Bone biopsy Loss of normal bony trabecular pattern When to perform a DEXA scan:  All women > 65 years and all men > 75 years with suspected Osteoporosis.  All women 50–64 years and men 50–74 years who have any of the following:  previous osteoporotic fragility fracture  current or frequent use of oral corticosteroids  Hx of falls  BMI < 18.5

DR  smoker  alcohol intake > 14 units per week  secondary cause of osteoporosis  Hypogonadism, endocrine conditions, malabsorptive conditions, RA, haematological conditions, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic liver or kidney disease.  People < 50 years who have current/frequent use of corticosteroids, untreated premature menopause or a previous fragility fracture.  Consider assessing fracture risk in those taking certain medications eg SSRIs, antiepileptics, PPIs, thiazolidinediones, aromatase inhibitors.  DEXA scans can be performed every 2 years after a diagnosis of osteoporosis. The average loss of bone density without treatment is equivalent to a decline in T-score of around 0.1 per year.  Management  The main aim of treatment is to reduce the risk of fracture by preventing further bone loss. Management involves:  Prevention: maximise peak skeletal mass by exercise, diet, calcium supplementation and/or HRT in the perimenopausal period  Exclude secondary cause  Quantitative assessment of bone density to establish a diagnosis and provide a baseline to monitor response  Treatment of fractures. Initiate treatment when there is any of the following:  Minimal trauma hip or vertebral fracture  Minimal trauma fracture at any other site and a T-score <-1.5  Risk assessed and DEXA scan performed  T-score <-2.5  T-score <-1.5 and hip fracture risk score > 3% or fracture risk score > 20%.  If the T-score is greater than -2.5 then try to modify risk factors where possible, treat any underlying conditions, and repeat the scan within 2 years. Non-pharmacological  Exercise  regular exercise to improve muscle strength  including high-intensity exercise, strength training, flexibility and balance exercises, stretching and endurance  in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, there is good evidence to show that exercise increases bone density.  Smoking cessation Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Limiting alcohol intake  Keeping weight BMI > 18  Falls prevention  If calcium intake is adequate (1000mg/day) then prescribe 10 micrograms of Vitamin D (without calcium) for people not exposed to much sunlight. Calcium supplementation is recommended in all post-menopausal women.  If calcium intake is inadequate, then prescribe 10 micrograms of vitamin D with at least 1000 mg of calcium daily, in the elderly who are housebound or living in a nursing home, prescribe 20 mg. Pharmacological  The most effective osteoporosis treatment is HRT, however long-term use is not recommended.  First-line treatment is bisphosphonates eg alendronate 10 mg OD or 70 mg weekly.  Accumulate at sites of bone remodelling and are released and taken up by osteoclasts, this decreases osteoclastic bone resorption and increases osteoclastic apoptosis.  Side effects can include:  osteonecrosis of the jaw (very rare)  oesophagitis.  Contraindicated in hypocalcaemia, uveitis and disorders which delay oesophageal emptying.  Oral agents eg alendronate must be taken first thing in the morning on an empty stomach the patient must not eat for 30 mins afterwards and must remain upright or standing for 2 hours.  Intravenous (IV) agents are easier to administer eg zoledronic acid and only need to be administered once a year.  Alendronate can reduce the rate of hip, spine and wrist fractures by 50%.  IV zoledronic acid reduces the rate of spine fractures by 70%, and hip fractures by 40% over 3 years.  If bisphosphonates are not tolerated, then specialist treatments include strontium or anabolic agents such as calcitonin or teriparatide.  Denosumab – monoclonal antibody given SC every six months, usually given for 3 years, only given when calcium and vitamin D levels are adequate, risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.  Strontium – dissociates bone resorption and formation, taken daily before bed, can cause vascular complications, VTE and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.  Teriparatide – synthetic PTH that increases bone formation, given SC daily. Surgical  Surgical management of fragility fractures if appropriate.  Prognosis  Hip fracture complications – about 50% of people with an osteoporotic fragility fracture of the hip can no longer live independently, and around 35% of the deaths

DR following hip fractures are directly or indirectly related to the fracture.  Vertebral fracture complications – can lead to back pain, loss of height and kyphosis, around 30% of deaths following vertebral fractures are directly or indirectly related to the fracture.  Other  Osteopenia is a condition in which bone mineral density is low, some people may go on to develop osteoporosis.  It is usually diagnosed when there is a BMD of between -1.0 and -2.5.  It is usually treated with lifestyle modifications and treatment of risk factors eg regular exercise, stopping smoking, adequate calcium and vitamin D intake.  If it progresses to osteoporosis, then pharmacological management involving the use of bisphosphonates may be required.  Osteopenia is not usually treated pharmacologically until the BMD is 2.5 standard deviations below the healthy adult value. Paget’s Disease Paget’s disease (osteitis deformans) is essentially an accelerated rate of bone turnover, with subsequent rapid new bone formation.  Overview Key Facts  Paget’s disease (osteitis deformans) is essentially an accelerated rate of bone turnover, with subsequent rapid new bone formation.  This bone does not have a normal matrix and is disorganised.  The bones increase in size but are more brittle and prone to fracture.  Comprised of three stages, these may all co-exist in the same bone:  osteolytic (initial)  reparative phase  inactive phase.  The condition usually presents in mid-adulthood.  It is typically discovered incidentally, either on blood tests with a raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) or on X-ray.  Paget’s disease most commonly affects:  skull  spine  pelvis  long bones of the legs. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Symptomatic patients or those at high risk of fracture are usually treated with bisphosphonates, this achieves remission in 90% of patients. Epidemiology  Paget’s disease is the second most common degenerative bone disorder after OA.  Usually presents in mid-adulthood (40s), with a 4% prevalence in those > 40 years and 10% in those > 90 years.  It affects slightly more men than women.  It is more common in White people. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown.  There is a genetic predisposition in 25%.  It has also been suggested to have a viral origin eg respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Pathophysiology  Accelerated rate of bone turnover, with subsequent rapid new bone formation.  This results in coarse trabeculae in weakened, hypervascularised bone which is prone to pathological fractures.  Commonly occurs in the pelvis, lumbar and thoracic spine, femur, skull, sacrum, tibia and humerus. Comprised of three stages:  Osteolytic (initial) stage:  mediated by osteoclasts, with bone resorption causing osteolytic lesions  the number of osteoclasts is increased, and they are often large  the osteoblasts are normal but are often overactive due to increased release of factors from osteoclasts.  Reparative phase:  rapid bone formation is mediated by an osteoclastic or osteoblastic stage that ends with predominance of osteoblastic activity  this results in a gain of bone mass (the newly formed bone is disordered and structurally unsound).  Inactive phase:  a burnt-out quiescent osteosclerotic stage (dense bone mosaic but little cellular activity).  Clinical Presentation  Many patients are asymptomatic (only 15–40% have signs/symptoms).  Often detected incidentally with raised ALP or on X-ray.  Any bone can be affected, it usually affects more than one bone (85%).

DR  The axial skeleton or proximal femur is involved in up to 80% of cases. Skeletal effects Painful affected bone seen in 40% due to impingement on other localised structures typically a deep, constant aching pain that is worse with weightbearing consider Paget’s disease in elderly patients presenting with persistent back pain Fractures – seen in 15% as the bones are more brittle Anterior bowing of the femur and tibia – can lead to altered gait and joint pain Overgrowth of craniofacial skeleton leading to leontiasis posse and a cranium that is so heavy it becomes difficult to hold the head erect Invagination of the base of the skull secondary to increased weight with compression of posterior fossa structures Distortion of the femoral head leads to severe OA Long bones of lower limbs are affected leading to ‘chalk-stick’ fractures (transverse fractures) Compression fractures in the spine may result in deformity (kyphosis) and spinal cord injury Secondary OA Neurological effects Bone overgrowth can compress spinal and cranial nerve roots (entrapment syndromes, paraplegia, paresis) Headache and dizziness Altered mental status (platybasia) Deafness or headaches due to compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve Cardiovascular and metabolic effects Hypervascularity of pagetic bone leads to increased blood flow, this acts as an AV shunt and leads to high-output cardiac failure or exacerbation of underlying cardiac disease (rare) Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria Tumours Benign Giant-cell reparative granuloma Malignant Sarcoma (5–10% with severe polyostotic disease) Osteosarcoma Malignant fibrous histiocytoma Chondrosarcoma Giant-cell tumour Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for Paget's disease are as follows:  bony malignancy  osteoarthritis  osteoporosis  osteopetrosis  osteomalacia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is usually made radiologically, but blood tests may support X-ray findings.  Once a diagnosis is confirmed, a radionuclide scan is often performed to check for other areas of involvement. Biochemical markers  Increased ALP.  Normal Calcium/Phosphate/PTH  calcium may be elevated in Polyostotic disease.  ALP can be an indicator of osteoblastic activity, need BONE SPECIFIC ALP, the ALP level correlates with the severity of the disease.  Increased urinary excretion of hydroxy-proline (collagen breakdown marker).  Vitamin D levels are normally tested to help rule out another cause for the raised ALP and to ensure levels are sufficient to allow bisphosphonate therapy. Radiological appearance  Widening of the cortical region (the hollow cortex at the centre of the bone is wider).  Mixed areas of sclerosis and lysis are seen in early disease.  Bone thickening and enlargement seen in later disease.  Bony deformities eg anterior bowing of the tibia and lateral bowing of the femur.  Osteoporosis circumscripta – areas of very high osteoclastic activity in the skull (cotton wool exudates). Cotton wool spots are seen as part of Paget’s disease of the skull:

DR Paget’s disease of the right innominate bone: Technetium isotope scanning  Allows visualisation of the entire skeleton, and demonstration of early lesions.  There is increased isotope uptake in affected bones.  Often performed after the initial lesions have been diagnosed to assess the extent of the disease.  Management  Treatment aims to reduce pain and slow the rate of bone remodelling. Asymptomatic disease often does not require treatment. Treatment may be indicated if there is:  severe pain  nerve compression from expanding bone or other neurological complications Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  fractures  asymptomatic disease with significant biochemical abnormalities eg ALP > 2 × normal. Non-pharmacological  Simple analgesia eg paracetamol, ibuprofen  Orthoses eg braces to support and protect a bone  Orthotics  Education  Treat any complications eg joint replacements, hearing aids, physiotherapy. Pharmacological  Bisphosphonates are the mainstay of treatment.  They inhibit osteoclast activity and cause osteoclast apoptosis.  They are often able to induce disease remission. Zoledronic acid Given via IV infusion and are usually the first-line agent Induces remission for up to 2-3 years after a single dose, 90% remission rate Can cause flu-like symptoms after the first dose Much more expensive than oral therapy Oral therapy eg alendronate Considered in younger patients or those with less severe disease 60% remission rate Usually given daily for 3-6 months however must be taken very carefully: Must be taken with a glass of water No food should be taken for at least 30 minutes afterwards The patient must not lie down for 2 hours afterwards to avoid any oesophageal irritation or reflux In rare instances, they can lead to osteonecrosis of the jaw Calcitonin Used in patients who cannot tolerate bisphosphonates Causes osteoclasts to shrink and decreases their resorptive activity Given SC or IM Teriparatide contraindicated due to the risk of secondary osteosarcoma Surgical  Surgical intervention may be required in cases of neurological compression, fracture or tumour.  Total hip or knee replacement in patients with degenerative joint disease. Patients are treated with pharmacologic agents prior to arthroplasty to reduce bleeding.  Metaphyseal osteotomy and plate fixation may be indicated in patients with fractures through pathological bowing of long bones.

DR  Prognosis  Ongoing management involves repeating the ALP levels after 3–6 months to assess the effectiveness of treatment, this is then repeated annually.  Increased risk of bone tumours, particularly osteosarcoma, this is seen in up to 1% of patients.  If osteosarcoma develops, it is often advanced and fatal. Polyarteritis Nodosa Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic, necrotising vasculitis, targeting medium-sized arteries and leading to aneurysm formation.  Overview Key Facts  Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic, necrotising vasculitis, targeting medium-sized arteries and leading to aneurysm formation.  More common in middle age and in men.  Associated with hepatitis B infection (and HIV and hepatitis C to a lesser extent).  Most cases are idiopathic.  A transmural inflammation of arteries leads to the formation of an aneurysm.  Necrosis of vessels may lead to thrombosis, which causes infarction or ischaemia of the tissues or organs supplied.  Symptoms relate to ischaemia or infarction of tissues supplied by affected blood vessels.  Non-specific symptoms include fever, myalgia and weight loss.  Symptoms can affect the skin, heart, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, brain and kidneys.  Classic symptoms include subcutaneous nodules, livedo reticularis, necrotic ulcers, hypertension, ischaemic abdominal pain, haematuria and mononeuritis multiplex.  PAN is classically anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) negative which helps to differentiate it from other causes of vasculitis.  Biopsy may be taken from affected arteries or muscle/skin and will show necrotising inflammation.  Angiography shows microaneurysms, known as the ‘rosary sign’, as the aneurysms look like a string of beads on a rosary necklace.  Treatment is usually with steroids and cyclophosphamide (or azathioprine).  If hepatitis B positive, patients are treated with antiviral medications and/or plasma exchange. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Can be fatal if left untreated.  Causes of death include myocardial infarction, bowel perforation and stroke. Epidemiology  Most common in middle age.  More common in men.  May present in childhood.  Associated with hepatitis B infection, therefore more common where hepatitis B is endemic. Aetiology  Most cases are idiopathic.  May be triggered by viral infections, most commonly hepatitis B and less commonly HIV or hepatitis C. Pathophysiology  It is not known how hepatitis B triggers vasculitis or what triggers the disease in other cases.  Thought to be due to the deposition of immune complexes.  Polyarteritis nodosa causes a transmural, necrotising inflammation of medium-sized arteries which leads to aneurysm formation.  Necrosis of vessels may lead to thrombosis, which causes infarction or ischaemia of the tissues or organs supplied.  Symptoms are the result of ischaemia or infarction of organs or tissues supplied by affected vessels.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms relate to ischaemia or infarction of tissues supplied by affected blood vessels.  Presentation will vary depending upon which organs are affected. Symptoms  General:  fever  weight loss  myalgia.  Skin:  livedo reticularis  cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules  purpura  necrotic ulcers.  Cardiovascular:  pericarditis  myocardial infarction and heart failure (caused by coronary arteritis)  hypertension.

DR  Gastrointestinal:  postprandial abdominal pain (due to ischaemia)  bowel necrosis or perforation.  Renal (most common organ involved):  acute or chronic kidney injury  haematuria  proteinuria.  Neurological:  mononeuritis multiplex  stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Polyarteritis nodosa is characteristically ANCA-negative, which can help to distinguish it from several other causes of vasculitis.  Other causes of vasculitis include:  microscopic polyangiitis  eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)  granulomatosis with polyangiitis  Kawasaki disease  Henoch–Schönlein purpura  immunoglobin A vasculitis  drug-induced vasculitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation Bloods  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are commonly elevated.  Bloods may show anaemia and leukocytosis.  ANCA is negative.  Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAG) is positive in approximately 30%. Biopsy  Lesions of varying stages are typically found from the same specimen.  Necrotising inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis and fibrosis will be seen on biopsy of affected arteries.  Muscle and skin biopsies are generally preferred as they are less invasive. Imaging  Angiography:  multiple microaneurysms  often called the ‘rosary sign’, as the small aneurysms look like a string of beads on a rosary necklace. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Polyarteritis nodosa:  Management  Oral corticosteroids for mild disease.  Add cyclophosphamide (or azathioprine) for moderate disease.  Antiviral treatment and/or plasma exchange if concurrent hepatitis B.  For the management of hypertension, prefer angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs).  Prognosis  Can be fatal if left untreated, but the prognosis is generally good with treatment.  Complications that can lead to death include:  myocardial infarction  heart failure  bowel perforation  stroke. Polymyalgia Rheumatica Polymyalgia rheumatica is a rheumatological condition with inflammation causing pain and morning stiffness. It is the commonest inflammatory arthritis in older people.  Overview Key Facts  Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a rheumatological condition with inflammation causing pain and morning stiffness. It is the commonest inflammatory arthritis in older people.

DR  Clinical presentation is commonly shoulder and pelvic girdle pain associated with morning stiffness (> 45 minutes).  Acute in ‘flare-up’ onset, chronic in disease nature.  Diagnosis is normally made through typical clinical history being supported by laboratory findings suggesting inflammation (raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)).  First-line treatment is oral corticosteroids (possible long-term).  PMR usually responds quickly to corticosteroid therapy; however, around 50% of PMR patients’ relapse, normally within two years.  Complications are commonly related to long-term corticosteroid use.  PMR is associated with giant cell/temporal arteritis and patients should be informed of the warning signs of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Epidemiology  PMR is the commonest inflammatory arthritis in older people.  Incidence – approximately 100 per 100 000 people.  Prevalence – just under 1%.  More common in women than men.  Increased incidence with age (most common age > 50 years).  Race – most common in northern Europeans.  Link to giant cell arteritis (GCA, also known as temporal arteritis). Approximately 25% of those with PMR have GCA and approximately 50% of those with GCA have PMR. Aetiology  Cause is unknown.  It may be linked to concurrent infection – PMR occurs more in the winter, older people and has been associated with infections such as parvovirus B19 and mycoplasma.  There are theories of autoimmunity involvement, with some HLA alleles being linked to PMR development. Pathophysiology  Unknown cause leading to ‘typical joints’ developing inflammation, pain and potential articular damage.  Clinical Presentation  Oligoarthritis – bilateral with a rapid onset, lasting > 2 weeks.  Morning stiffness (ie > 45 minutes).  Site pain – neck, shoulder girdle and/or pelvic girdle pain (especially in older patients, > 50 years).  Difficulty standing from seated or prone positions.  Muscle tenderness (patients describe a range of pain severities).  Episodes may be associated with other systemic features (eg low-grade pyrexia, anorexia and/or weight loss, low mood, tiredness).  Manifestations may include shoulder/hip bursitis.  Peripheral involvement may occur. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Muscle strength is normal (but of course, pain can make this hard to examine).  Shoulder pain in 70–95%, whereas hip and neck pain is the main complaint in 50–70%.  Systemic features coexist in roughly half of those with PMR.  Peripheral involvement coexists in roughly half of those with PMR (eg, carpal tunnel syndrome, asymmetric peripheral arthritis).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  rheumatoid arthritis  gout/pseudogout  fibromyalgia  chronic fatigue syndrome  hypo/hyperthyroidism  rotator cuff problems or adhesive capsulitis  multiple myeloma  adverse drug effects, eg statins  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis  Diagnosis is normally made through typical clinical history being supported by laboratory findings suggesting inflammation.  Other differentials need to be excluded.  Rapid response to prednisolone confirms diagnostic accuracy. Investigations  Bloods including: full blood count (FBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), liver function tests (LFTs), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), bone profile, thyroid function tests (TFTs), rheumatoid factor (bloods suggesting active inflammation include raised ESR + raised CRP).  Urinalysis.  Ultrasound of affected joints (will show synovitis and maybe others, eg gout).  Consider further joint imaging (eg MRI), joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis, serum protein electrophoresis, chest Xray.  Management  PMR can normally be managed in the community.  Treatment is only started once diagnosis is confirmed.

DR  The treatment is mainly pharmacological, including prevention of the medication side-effects.  Factors for rheumatology referral include diagnostic uncertainty, poor response to oral corticosteroids, difficulty reducing steroids without relapse, or needing steroid treatment for more than two years. Non-pharmacological  Patient information especially including:  symptoms of GCA, that it is an emergency and that they are at higher risk of developing it  relapse is common  ‘Blue Steroid Card’ and information on steroid risks (ie not to stop them abruptly, that they will effectively be immunocompromised)  support often needed through physical therapy/occupational therapy. Pharmacological  Stepwise pharmacological prescribing is used with NSAIDs used as an adjunct (eg ibuprofen PO 600 mg TDS + gastric protection with PPI) 1. Low-dose oral prednisolone (eg 12.5–25 mg OD, then reduced very slowly over months) + calcium supplementation + vitamin D supplementation + bisphosphonate (for bone protection) 2. Methotrexate + folic acid supplementation 3. Biologics, eg tocilizumab  There is normally fast (1–3 days) improvement with low-dose PO prednisolone.  Treatment needs regular monitoring – normally done at week one and at around one month (including repeat bloods and consideration of trialling medication reduction).  Treatment success can be seen through:  symptom resolution  reduced synovitis  normalisation of ESR/CRP (if treatment working it happens within four weeks).  Treatment may be needed for up to two years to control a PMR episode.  With glucocorticoid resistance or disease recurrence – prednisolone dosing may be increased or combined with methotrexate therapy and biologics may be started sooner. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Prognosis  Around 50% of PMR patients relapse, normally within two years.  PMR normally responds quickly to oral steroid treatment.  Strong link between PMR and GCA.  Risk of complications due to long-term corticosteroid and other immunotherapy treatments.  Psychosocial consequences may be great as PMR may reduce independence.  PMR is not directly linked to increased mortality. Polymyositis Polymyositis is a very rare inflammatory disorder of skeletal muscle.  Overview Key Facts  Polymyositis is a very rare inflammatory disorder of skeletal muscle.  It causes an autoimmune-mediated striated muscle inflammation, associated with progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness with myalgia and arthralgia.  The condition can lead to dysphagia and in severe cases can affect the respiratory muscles.  The term dermatomyositis is used when polymyositis symptoms are associated with characteristic cutaneous lesions (heliotropic rash/Gottron's papules).  Polymyositis is associated with an increased risk of malignancy (threefold).  Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) are positive in one-third of patients with polymyositis.  Anti-Jo antibodies are also commonly described as being positive in myositis, although they are more commonly seen in patients with features such as pulmonary fibrosis, arthritis and Raynaud’s phenomenon.  The diagnosis is established by electromyography and is confirmed by muscle biopsy.  Patients may also have a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), a normocytic and normochromic anaemia, and positive rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibodies.  Muscle enzymes (creatine phosphokinase and aldolase) are raised and can also be used to monitor the disease.  Autoantibody testing for myositis-specific antibody (MSA) and myositis-associated autoantibodies (MAA) may be useful in differentiating patients who have an underlying malignancy.  Treatment includes high-dose corticosteroids, adding diseasemodifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as azathioprine or ciclosporin in poorly responding patients:

DR  physiotherapy to restore muscle strength can be helpful, and biologics may also be considered as a treatment option.  The prognosis is variable; many patients will experience a chronic, relapsing pattern of disease, whereas a number may experience complete remission.  The prognosis is worse in those with associated malignancy. Epidemiology  Polymyositis most commonly presents between 30 and 60 years of age, with a smaller peak at about 15 years of age.  The condition is twice as common in women. Aetiology  Polymyositis a may be associated with other autoimmune diseases including:  myasthenia gravis  Raynaud's phenomenon  Hashimoto's thyroiditis  systemic sclerosis. Pathophysiology  Polymyositis is a disorder of the muscles characterised by necrosis of muscle fibres, together with regeneration and inflammation.  Clinical Presentation  The typical presentation is symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, usually affecting the lower extremities first.  The condition often develops over weeks or months with steady progression – although there may be fluctuations in weakness.  Muscle pain and tenderness can occur in up to 50% of patients, but weakness is the main symptom.  Arthralgia affecting the small joints of the hands can occur in about half of all patients, pre-dating the muscle weakness.  Dysphagia due to oesophageal muscle spasm occurs in up to 50%.  Raynaud’s phenomenon is a common association.  Respiratory muscles are affected in severe disease (especially those patients with anti-Jo-1 antibodies).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  dermatomyositis  polymyalgia rheumatica  inclusion body myositis  motor neurone disease  drug-induced myopathy. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  In both dermatomyositis and polymyositis, anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) may be present, and muscle enzymes will be elevated.  Blood tests should be carried out to check for:  raised creatine kinase, aspartate transaminase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); muscle enzyme levels can also be used to monitor the condition  autoantibodies (ANA/anti-Mi-2/anti-Jo-1)  ANAs and anti-cytoplasmic antibodies may both be associated with polymyositis  anti-Jo antibodies are also commonly described as being positive in myositis, although they are more commonly seen in patients who also have other features such as pulmonary fibrosis, arthritis and Raynaud’s phenomenon  raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)  a normocytic and normochromic anaemia (full blood count)  positive rheumatoid factor.  Muscle biopsy and electromyography (EMG) can help confirm diagnosis:  muscle biopsy will reveal inflammation, muscle fibre necrosis and regeneration.  EMG shows short polyphasic motor potentials, spontaneous fibrillation and high-frequency repetitive discharges  It is also important to rule out underlying malignancy (in adults):  screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases  ANA is positive in one-third of patients with polymyositis  autoantibody testing for myositis-specific antibody (MSA) and myositis-associated autoantibody (MAA) may be useful in differentiating patients who have an underlying malignancy  screening blood tests for underlying malignancy may include CA-125 or CA19-9 levels.  Management  Treatment is dictated by symptoms, not necessarily by antibody subtype positivity:  corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment  azathioprine or ciclosporin can be added in poorly responding patients  patients should be treated with prednisolone at a dose of 60 mg daily, reducing to a smaller maintenance dose and a maintenance DMARD such as methotrexate or azathioprine  physiotherapy to restore muscle strength can be helpful  patients with anti-Jo-1 antibodies require long-term immunosuppression

DR  for lung disease, aggressive treatment with combination regimens, including ciclosporin or tacrolimus with cyclophosphamide, is recommended to be added to corticosteroids  Biologics such as ritixumab and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may also be helpful.  Prognosis  The prognosis is variable; many patients will experience a chronic relapsing pattern of disease. whereas a number may experience complete remission.  Polymyositis is associated with an increased risk of malignancy (threefold).  The prognosis is worse in those with associated malignancy.  Complications of polymyositis include:  interstitial lung disease  aspiration pneumonia  cardiac conditions, inlcuding heart block, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, pericarditis, myocardial infarction  dysphagia  malabsorption  infection  complications of long-term steroid therapy. Pseudogout Pseudogout (also called calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease) is an acute, painful seronegative acute synovitis that mimics gout.  Overview Key Facts  Pseudogout (also called calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease) is an acute, painful seronegative acute synovitis that mimics gout.  It is characterised by joint deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals.  Clinical presentation is an acute mono- or oligoarthritis commonly affecting knee, ankle, wrist or shoulder.  Diagnosis made clinically, with X-ray, ultrasound and bloods and synovial fluid analysis is also used to differentiate from other causes.  It is usually self-limiting within a fortnight.  Treatment is mainly supportive, but steroids or joint aspiration may be useful.  Some patients may develop permanent joint damage and reduced function. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  It is more common in the elderly, especially women. Aetiology  Unknown.  It can occur secondary to other conditions, such as: hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism and haemochromatosis.  Risk of pseudogout is increased by: any other form of arthritis, dehydration, concurrent disease, dialysis, trauma including surgery, and decrease in magnesium. Pathophysiology  Calcium pyrophosphate crystals become deposited in articular cartilage and periarticular spaces.  Inflammation occurs when the crystals are in a joint space.  Treatment with oral colchicine reduces inflammation by reducing leukocyte mitotic rates; it is used when NSAIDs and steroids are contraindicated.  Clinical Presentation Similar Presentation to Osteoarthritis and Gout  Acute mono- and oligoarthritic pain and/or temporary loss of function and/or range of movement.  May occur in any joint.  Common sites: knee, ankle, wrist, shoulder  Pain: palpation and movement. On joint examination:  swelling  effusion  warmth.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses include:  gout, regular  trauma  pre-patellar bursitis  septic arthritis  osteoarthritis  single joint presentation of inflammatory arthritis eg rheumatoid, psoriatic  transient synovitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is based on clinical examination, investigation and ruling out other differentials and/or associated conditions.

DR  Typical Bloods:  normal Ca2+  high white cell count (WCC)  negative rheumatoid factor.  Investigations to be considered:  ultrasound  joint X-ray  joint aspiration  bloods: full blood count, bone profile, thyroid function tests, rheumatoid factor.  Synovial fluid analysis through aspiration has the potential benefit of reducing symptomology. Due to fluid often appearing purulent, it needs to be sent to the microbiology laboratory to rule out septic arthritis. Synovial Fluid ↑ WCC (mainly neutrophils) Normal glucose Positive birefringence Often appears purulent  Management Non-pharmacological  The main treatment is supportive:  joint rest  cooling of the area (eg ice)  pain relief with NSAIDs.  If not improving or high severity, other options include:  joint aspiration  steroids via articular injection or orally  oral colchicine. Pharmacological  Pain relief with NSAIDs.  Steroids via articular injection or orally.  Oral colchicine.  Prognosis  Usually resolves within two weeks from onset.  Acute inflammation may lead to future and permanent joint damage.  Other  Birefringence: a term used to describe the refraction of light off a surface. It is microscopically analysed in synovial fluid by shining a polarised light onto the sample and having a filter placed over it. If the light is seen through the filter it is deemed ‘positive’. Rheumatology Key points R.
