DR Soft tissue swelling Treatmen t Rest ✓ ✓ NSAIDs ✓ ✓ Joint aspiratio n ✓ ✗ Steroids ✓ ✓ Colchici ne ✓ ✓ In Chronic Situation Allopurin ol ✗ ✓ Psoriatic Arthritis Psoriatic arthritis is an autoimmune-mediated seronegative spondyloarthritis that is associated with psoriasis.  Overview Key Facts  Psoriatic arthritis (PA) is an autoimmune-mediated seronegative spondyloarthritis that is associated with psoriasis.  It typically presents with nail changes, distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint arthritis, dactylitis and paravertebral calcification.  males and females are equally affected  most patients will have psoriasis preceding onset of arthritis  arthritis may present before the diagnosis of psoriasis in some patients with underlying psoriasis (around 1 in 6 cases)  diagnosis is through a score of > 3 in a patient with inflammatory arthritis or spondylitis using the Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR).  There is a genetic association with HLA-B27.  Treatment involves the use of:  symptom-modifying drugs (analgesics such as NSAIDs)  disease-modifying drugs (DMARDS) such as:  leﬂunomide  sulfasalazine  methotrexate  ciclosporin.  anti-TNF-α therapy for disease refractory to DMARDs.  The condition is chronic and often progressive.  Aggressive treatment of the progressive disease may reduce progression to severe deformity and improve prognosis. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  The condition is thought to affect between 5% and 25% of all patients with psoriasis.  Psoriasis is already present in around 80% of patients when psoriatic arthritis develops.  Prevalence is equal in men and women. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown, but risk is increased in the West.  There is an association with HLA subtypes. Pathophysiology  There is inflammation of the sites of insertion of tendons and ligaments into bone (enthesitis) in many of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.  It is thought that cytokines enhance the inflammatory process, including tumour necrosis factor; this is targeted by TNF-α monoclonal antibodies in the management of seronegative spondyloarthropathy, which is refractory to disease-modifying drugs and steroid management.  There is a growing body of thought that ‘microtrauma’ from bodily stress may cause inflammation at the site of enthesitis, leading to bony changes and pathological new bone formation.  Clinical Presentation  Psoriatic arthritis (PA) typically presents with:  nail changes (pitting and onycholysis)  distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint arthritis  dactylitis  paravertebral calcification.  Men and women are equally affected.  Often the patient will already have a diagnosis of psoriasis (or will have psoriasis even if undiagnosed).  Arthritis may less commonly present before the diagnosis of psoriasis in some patients with underlying psoriasis.  Diagnosis is through a score of > 3 in a patient with inflammatory arthritis or spondylitis using the Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR):  psoriasis or a family history of psoriasis – 2 points  typical psoriatic nail dystrophy – 1 point  negative rheumatoid factor – 1 point  dactylitis – 1 point  radiographic evidence of new bone formation – 1 point. Patterns of psoriatic arthritis  Polyarthritis similar to rheumatoid arthritis (most common type).  Distal interphalangeal joints (5–10%).

DR  Sacroiliitis and spondylitis (20–40%).  Asymmetric oligoarthritis (20–40%.).  Arthritis mutilans (<5%).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  ankylosing spondylitis  reactive arthritis  rheumatoid arthritis  osteoarthritis  septic arthritis  lupus (SLE)  gout  psoriasis  inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  infection, eg tuberculosis  malignancy, such as metastasis or lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is often clinical, based on the Classiﬁcation Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR):  psoriasis or a family history of psoriasis – 2 points  typical psoriatic nail dystrophy – 1 point  negative rheumatoid factor – 1 point  dactylitis – 1 point  radiographic evidence of new bone formation – 1 point.  A score of > 3 in a patient with inﬂammatory arthritis or spondylitis conﬁrms a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.  Other initial investigations include:  blood tests such as inflammatory markers, full blood count (FBC) for anaemia, and alkaline phosphate (ALP) which may be elevated  serology for rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibodies  HLA-B27 testing is not a reliable diagnostic method for any of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, although it can increase suspicion in some cases; it is, however, only positive in around 20% of cases of psoriatic arthritis.  Management Non-pharmacological  Generally, physiotherapy is likely to be helpful for most seronegative spondyloarthropathies and regular exercise helps maintain dependence and improves symptoms in the long term.  Heat treatment may also be effective in providing relief. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Pharmacological  Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a good analgesic for symptomatic pain relief.  If the disease is refractory to NSAIDs, disease-modifying drugs or steroids can be used:  leflunomide, sulfasalazine, ciclosporin and methotrexate.  Anti-TNF-α therapy for disease refractory to DMARDs:  options include adalimumab, etanercept, golimumab and infliximab. Surgical  Severe deformative disease may require surgical treatments such as joint replacement.  Prognosis  The condition is chronic and often follows a progressive course.  The prognosis is worse with arthritis multilans form of the condition.  Severity may range from mild synovitis to severe progressive erosive arthropathy.  Over half of patients develop erosive or deforming joint disease and up to 10% may need surgical intervention.  Aggressive treatment of progressive disease in early stages improves prognosis. Raynauds Disease Raynaud's disease (Raynaud's phenomenon) is characterised by a paroxysmal episodes of vasospasm followed by vasodilation of peripheral arterioles.  Overview Key Facts  Raynaud's disease (Raynaud's phenomenon) is characterised by a paroxysmal episodes of vasospasm followed by vasodilation of peripheral arterioles.  The condition predominantly affects the digits of the hand and feet.  Triggers include exposure to cold and emotional turmoil.  The condition may occur as a primary condition (unrelated to any other condition, or occur secondarily to other disease processes.  Primary Raynaud's is more common, symptoms tend to be less severe and there is usually no associated long term tissue damage such as ulceration or necrosis.  Secondary Raynaud's is more prone to being problematic, and is often the first presentation of underlying connective tissue disorders.

DR Epidemiology  Primary Raynaud's is more commonly found in younger females, and is far more common than secondary Raynauds.  Secondary Raynaud's is less common, and can occur at any age but usually found in those over 30. Aetiology  Connective tissue disorders linked to secondary Raynaud's include:  systemic sclerosis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  rheumatoid arthritis  polymyositis  dermatomyositis.  Mechanical/environmental causes  Tobacco smoking  Trauma  Vibration  Frostbite  Exposure to heavy metals such as lead, arsenic  Vinyl chloride exposure  Other causes include drugs (beta-blockers) malignancy, infection, endocrine disorders and haematological conditions.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms are precipitated by cold or stress  The patient experiences the typical triphasic colour changes that are seen with Raynaud’s -  Pallor followed by numbness, cyanosis (bluing of the digit), which is then followed by hyperaemia as reperfusion occurs.  There is often pain on rewarming/reperfusion.  The thumb is often spared.  There may be a history of digital ulcers.  Check for symptoms of underlying connective tissue disorders, these may include:  rashes  alopecia  mouth ulcers  presence of dysphagia/reflux/symptoms of malabsorption;  joint pain  evidence of previous serositis  dyspnoea (interstitial lung disease and/or pulmonary hypertension) Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is predominately based on history.  In a young otherwise healthy female, further investigations may not be required.  Testing for associated conditions may be indicated based on clinical suspicion and may include:  Bloods tests including:  ANA  ENA  dsDNA  complement levels  CRP  ESR  Urine dipstick to assess for any proteinuria or heamaturia  Capillaroscopy  ECG  Chest X-Ray  Lung function tests  Echocardiogram  Management  Ask the patient to stop smoking.  Advice regarding the use of gloves, particularly heated gloves, and socks.  Advice re avoidance of cold precipitant.  Consider vasodilators such as calcium channel blockers eg nifedipine  Topical nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil)  Prostaglandins (such as iloprost) is reserved for incipient gangrene.  Alternatively, inhibitors of vasoconstriction such as endothelin receptor antagonists (eg bosentan) may be considered for extreme cases.  Aspirin may also be indicated. Reactive Arthritis Reactive arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that occurs as a reaction to an infection in another part of the body, typically involving joint pain, swelling, and stiffness.

DR  Overview Key Facts  Seronegative spondyloarthropathies comprise a group of disorders characterised by seronegative inflammatory arthritis or spondylitis, and they include:  ankylosing spondylitis (AS)  reactive arthritis (RA)  psoriatic arthritis (PA).  Reactive arthritis usually follows infection, which may be a respiratory, urinary, sexually transmitted (especially chlamydia) or due to gastroenteritis (eg due to Shigella spp., Salmonella spp. or Campylobacter spp.).  It most commonly affects young men carrying the HLA-B27 antigen.  Presentation typically includes musculoskeletal features of spondylitis, arthritis and enthesitis, but also has extra-articular features such as uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).  Joint symptoms usually post-date the initial infection by some weeks (typically 4–8 weeks).  The arthritis can affect various joints but is typically an oligoarthritis that involves the knees and ankles.  Enthesitis can lead to heel and foot pain.  Inflammatory eye disease and mucocutaneous manifestations are common.  Conjunctivitis may be followed by uveitis (around 30% of patients).  Some patients (around 10%) develop skin lesions – psoriasiform changes on the soles (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) present as tender, keratotic plaques; palmar involvement may be present and more typical psoriasis-like plaques may occur elsewhere.  An annular or serpiginous eruption known as circinate balanitis may be present on the glans penis.  Rare complications include heart block, aortic incompetence and pericarditis.  Management involves identification and treatment of the precipitating infection, symptomatic treatment such as with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), injection of corticosteroids into affected joints and topical treatments akin to those used in psoriasis.  Prolonged disease may require disease-modifying agents. Epidemiology  Most of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, including reactive arthritis, present between 15 and 40 years of age.  It is estimated to be five times more prevalent in men than women. Aetiology  The aetiology of seronegative spondyloarthropathies is poorly understood, but it is thought to have a strong association with the presence of the HLA-B27 genotype. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  In reactive arthritis, a preceding infection is responsible for the arthritis; this is usually enteric, urogenital or respiratory in nature:  enteric infections include Yersinia spp., Salmonella spp., Shigella s pp., Campylobacter spp. and Escherichia coli.  urogenital causes: Chlamydia trachomatis  upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) include group A streptococci and Chlamydia pneumoniae. Pathophysiology  Reactive arthritis is an immune-mediated syndrome that is triggered by a recent infection.  There is inflammation of the sites of insertion of tendons and ligaments into bone (enthesitis) in many of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.  It is thought that T lymphocytes are activated by bacterial fragments when invasive bacteria reach the systemic circulation, which then attack the synovium.  It is believed that the antibacterial cytokine response is also impaired in reactive arthritis, resulting in the decreased elimination of the bacteria.  It is, however, unclear why such localisation of inflammation occurs.  The presence of HLA-B27 in patients with reactive arthritis may potentiate reactive arthritis by numerous mechanisms including:  presenting bacterial antigens to T cells  altering self-tolerance of the host immune system  increased TNF-α production  promoting the invasion of microbes in the gut  delayed clearance of causative organisms.  Clinical Presentation  Presentation typically includes musculoskeletal features of spondylitis, arthritis and enthesitis, but also extra-articular features such as uveitis, aphthous ulcers, erythema nodosum and symptoms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).  Reactive arthritis (typically presents a number of weeks after infection at a distant site, such as enteric, urinary or upper respiratory) and is characterised by a triad of symptoms:  arthritis  conjunctivitis  urethritis.  It is estimated to be five times more prevalent in men than women and usually presents between 15 and 40 years of age.  The arthritis can affect various joints but typically involves the knees and ankles.  Enthesitis can lead to heel and foot pain.  Inflammatory eye disease and mucocutaneous manifestations are common:

Keratoderma blennorrhagicum: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Keratoderma_blennorrhagi ca.jpg Circinate balanitis: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Balanitis_circinata.png Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI The HERO model – Healthy and Resilient Organisations: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65/chapter/recommendations  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  ankylosing spondylitis  psoriatic arthritis  septic arthritis  rheumatoid arthritis  osteoarthritis  lupus (SLE)  gout  inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)  infection, eg tuberculosis  malignancy, such as metastasis or lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Each type of seronegative spondyloarthropathy will require a different diagnostic method, but some investigations are commonly done for each type.  These include blood tests such as inflammatory markers, full blood count (FBC) for anaemia and alkaline phosphate (ALP) which may be elevated.  An initial set of investigations would also include blood tests for rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibodies.  HLA-B27 testing is not a reliable diagnostic method for any of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, but it increases the suspicion of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy if positive.  In reactive arthritis, it is useful to carry out serological testing to assess for related bacterial infection.

DR  If there are any suspicions of a sexually transmitted infection, then urine and genital swab testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia, in particular, would be indicated.  There are no specific findings on plain X-rays in acute reactive arthritis that can confirm the diagnosis, so these would not be helpful unless to rule out other potential diagnoses.  If there is any effusion, then joint aspiration would be appropriate for cell count, crystals, culture and sensitivity.  Management  Reactive arthritis is usually self-limiting.  Management involves:  identification and treatment of precipitating infection  rest  symptomatic treatment such as with non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  injection of corticosteroids into affected joints, and topical treatments akin to those used in psoriasis in prolonged or chronic cases  physiotherapy may benefit patients with ongoing symptoms.  Most patients will not require steroids or disease-modifying anti-rheumatic agents to control inflammation or to prevent erosive joint changes.  Prominent systemic symptoms may also require corticosteroid treatment.  Prognosis  Reactive arthritis completely resolves in 50% of cases but may recur in 35% of patients after an initial resolution.  Chronic persistent disease develops in about 15% of cases.  Rare complications include heart block, aortic incompetence and pericarditis.  Reactive arthritis is more likely to recur or be persistent in those with HLA-B27. Rheumatoid Arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis.  Overview Key Facts  Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis.  The cause is not clearly understood, but both genetic and environmental factors are thought to play a role. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  RA characteristically involves small joints, but may also involve soft tissues and extra-articular structures.  Symmetrical (metacarpophalangeal) MCP, (proximal interphalangeal) PIP and wrist joint synovitis are characteristic features.  Diagnosis is primarily based on history and examination:  rheumatoid factor (RhF) is positive in 70% of patients  X-ray changes are more apparent as the disease progresses.  Medical treatments broadly fall into two categories, symptom modifying and disease modifying.  Prognosis varies markedly between individuals; up to 25% may have mild disease whereas 50% may be impacted so severely at 10 years that they are unable to work.  Overall mortality rates are also increased when compared to the general population, this is mostly attributed to increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Epidemiology  RA is prevalent in 1-3% of the population.  It is more common in females (3 : 1).  It has a peak onset in middle age. Aetiology  The cause is not known, but it is thought that both genetic and environmental factors play a part leading to long term low level inflammation, with an evolving disease process occurring over many years.  Genetic factors account for 10-30% of the risk of developing RA.  There is an association with HLA-DR4.  The strongest environmental risk factor is smoking, and both HLA-DR4 and smoking are associated with more severe disease. Pathophysiology  Rheumatoid arthritis is a disease of exclusively synovial joints.  There is inflammation of the synovial membranes due to the presence of immune complexes in these joints, which leads to activation of the immune system and synovitis.  Clinical Presentation  The onset of disease may take several forms:  insidious (weeks to months) – 55-70%  intermediate – 15-20%  acute (days) – 8-15%.  Symmetrical MCP, PIP, and wrist joint synovitis is characteristic but any synovial joint may be involved.  This presents as symptoms such as joint pain and stiffness, swelling of joints, and erythema/hotness.  There may be cervical spine involvement in 30%.  There may be some characteristic deformities, such as:

DR  ulnar deviation of MCP joints  boutnonniére deformities of fingers  swan-neck deformities of fingers  Z-deformity of thumbs.  There may be extra-articular features such as true extra-articular manifestations of the rheumatoid process, as well as systemic effects of inflammation.  True extra-articular manifestations of RA are present in approximately 30% and is usually present in those with more severe RA.  an example is rheumatoid nodules which may be subcutaneous or visceral  eye involvement is common, including episcleritis. The common features of rheumatoid arthritis in the hand: Rheumatoid arthritis deformity of the hand:  Differential Diagnosis  Fibromyalgia.  Gout. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Reactive arthritis.  Polymyalgia rheumatica.  Septic arthritis.  Sarcoidosis.  Lupus.  Seronegative spondyloarthropathies.  Diagnosis/Investigation  RA diagnosis is based primarily on the history and examination.  Laboratory tests and X-rays may be helpful but are rarely diagnostic in early disease.  Radiology:  early changes:  may be no identifiable changes in early disease  soft-tissue swelling  juxta-articular osteoporosis  osteopenia  intermediate changes:  joint space narrowing due to loss of cartilage.  late changes:  bone and joint destruction  subluxation.  Laboratory studies:  rheumatoid factor (RhF) is positive in 70% of patients  antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) have high specificity for RA, and hence are particularly useful in those who are RF-negative  it is important to remember that neagative RhF and antiCCP test do not rule out RA  erythrocyte sedimentation ratio (ESR) and c-reactive protein (CRP) may reflect disease activity, CRP especially can be used to track the severity of disease flare ups  anaemia is common and there may be iron deficiency or normochromic anaemia.  The ACR/EULAR 2011 classification criteria can be used to provide RA management if they score more than 6 points.  Patients receive the highest point score they fulfil within each domain, for example, a patient with 5 small joints and 4 large joints involved would score 3 points.  Low titre serology means more than the upper limit of normal (ULN).  High titre serology is more than 3 times the ULN. Feature Score available Joint involvement 1 large joint 0 points 2-10 large joints 1 point 1-3 small joints 2 points 4-10 small joints 3 points > 10 joints (including at least 1 small joint) 5 points

DR Serology Not positive for either RF or antiCCP 0 points At least one of these is positive at low titre 2 points At least one test is positive at high titre 3 points Duration of synovitis < 6 weeks 0 points > 6 weeks 1 point Acute phase reactants Neither CRP nor ESR are raised 0 points Abnormal ESR/CRP 1 point  Management Non-pharmacological:  As this is a chronic and autoimmune mediated disease, it is important to provide education about the disease, its course, and the importance of stopping smoking if a patient presents as a smoker. Pharmacological:  Medical treatments broadly fall into two categories: symptom modifying and disease modifying.  Symptom-modifying drugs reduce pain, stiffness, and swelling (inflammatory changes), and include drugs such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  long-term use of NSAIDS can lead to poor renal function, which can also be a result of concomitant autoimmune disease.  Disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) have additional actions and will:  reduce pain, swelling, and stiffness, as well as the number of swollen and tender joints  reduce ESR and CRP (inflammatory markers)  correct the anaemia of chronic disease sometimes seen in RA patients  slow disease progression.  Methotrexate is the DMARD of choice in RA, and may be used alone, or in combination with, other DMARDs.  The aim is to begin treatment with DMARDs as soon as RA is diagnosed in order to achieve control of inflammation as soon as is possible.  The aim underlying this is to reduce disease activity to remission or low disease-activity levels; these are associated with better outcomes.  DMARDs take several weeks to become effective, so corticosteroids are employed during this period, which may be given intra-articularly, parenterally, or orally.  If DMARDs fail, biological DMARD agents may be used, which include examples such as infliximab and adalimumab (TNF alpha antagonists) Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Surgical:  Surgery is rarely used as part of normal management, however surgical approaches may be necessitated in the case of orthopaedic complications which may arise in RA.  Such complications include carpal tunnel syndrome, tendon rupture, and cervical myelopathy.  Rarely, joint replacement may be indicated in severe joint destruction.  Prognosis  Prognosis is variable and difficult to predict in individual cases:  50% are unable to work by 10 years after diagnosis of the disease.  25% have relatively mild disease.  there is an increased mortality risk compared to the general population, which is mostly cardiovascular in origin.  The following factors are associated with a poorer prognosis:  rheumatoid factor  anti-CCP antibodies  smoking  extra-articular features  HLA-DR4 genotype  female gender  early erosions  severe disability at presentation. Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  Overview Key Facts  Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  90% of patients have intrathoracic involvement, known as pulmonary sarcoidosis.  Chest examination is frequently normal and finger clubbing is rare.  Incidence in the UK is 7 per 100 000 a year.  The skin is the second most commonly affected organ. Other organs such as the eyes, brain, nervous system, liver, and heart may also be affected.  Patients may have no respiratory symptoms or complain of dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, malaise, and weight loss.

DR  Diffuse parenchymal lung involvement may progress to irreversible fibrosis; the mid- and upper zones of the lungs are most frequently affected.  In chronic disease, the lung parenchyma and hilar nodes can calcify.  The characteristic histological lesion is the granuloma composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells.  The disease may present acutely with respiratory difficulty or insidiously with multi-organ involvement.  Treatment, when necessary, involves the use of corticosteroids. Epidemiology  Though sarcoidosis can occur at any age, it commonly affects adults in their 30s or 40s and uncommon in childhood.  The incidence of sarcoidosis is 7 cases per 100 000 in the UK, with both men and women affected equally. Aetiology  Mechanism not fully understood: it is thought that in sarcoidosis the immune system in impaired, and so attacks health tissue unnecessarily.  There may be a genetic component, though this has yet to be fully discovered.  There is no evidence that is it infectious. Pathophysiology  Granulomas composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells develop.  Most commonly found in the lungs and the lymph glands which drain the lungs. However, they can develop anywhere including: the skin, heart, nervous system, liver, spleen, muscles, nose, sinuses, and eyes.  An abundance of granulomas in one area will result in the progression of symptoms as it hampers the organs ability to work effectively.  Clinical Presentation  Lymphadenopathy:  painless, rubbery lymph node enlargement is more common in Black patients;  cervical and scalene lymph nodes are most frequently affected.  Splenomegaly (25%).  Liver involvement:  common but often subclinical (ie derangement of liver function tests) unless an enlarged liver can be felt  liver biopsy is of diagnostic value in 90% (typical sarcoid granulomas).  Skin:  erythema nodosum (most commonly in White females) in disease with BHL; Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  skin plaques  subcutaneous nodules  lupus pernio (violaceous lesions on the nose, cheeks, and ears) seen in chronic disease.  Acute anterior uveitis (25%).  Heerfordt–Waldenstrom syndrome:  parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, fever, and cranial nerve palsies.  Neurological manifestations:  cranial nerve palsies (usually facial nerve), meningitis, hydrocephalus, space-occupying lesions, and spinal cord involvement;  granulomas infiltrating the posterior pituitary may produce diabetes insipidus, hypothalamic hypothyroidism, or hypopituitarism.  Cardiac sarcoid:  cardiac muscle/conducting system dysfunction, resulting in arrhythmias, bundle-branch block, or complete heart block.  Renal involvement:  hypercalcaemia  granulomatous interstitial nephritis.  Bone cysts:  with overlying soft-tissue swelling, bone cysts occur most often in the phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, and nasal bones;  arthritis is common.  Hypercalcaemia: due to excess production of vitamin D and gut activity causing calcium reabsorption, a lower proportion will develop renal calculi.  Eyes: dry itchy eyes - keratoconjunctivitis sicca.  Differential Diagnosis  Tuberculosis.  Lymphoma. Also consider:  Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)  Histoplasmosis.  Berryliosis.  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The combination of bi-hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) with erythema nodosum (EN) in a young adult is highly suggestive of sarcoidosis.  When bi-hilar lymphadenopathy and erythema nodosum are in association with fever and arthralgia, it is known as Lofgren syndrome.

DR Imaging:  CT appearances are often characteristic, showing hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, nodules along bronchi, vessels and, in subpleural regions, ground-glass shadowing, parenchymal bands, cysts, and fibrosis.  Chest X-ray - changes are graded:  stage 0: clear chest radiograph  stage 1: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)  stage 2: BHL and pulmonary infiltration  stage 3: diffuse pulmonary infiltration  stage 4: pulmonary fibrosis. This radiograph shows upper zone fibrosis, which has caused the hilar to be pulled superiorly bilaterally as shown by the arrows: The arrows on this radiograph point to enlarged bi-hilar lymph nodes: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Tissue biopsies (transbronchial and endobronchial biopsy) can demonstrate non-caseating granulomas in 85–90% of cases with respiratory involvement. Bloods:  Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and calcium are consistent with the diagnosis, but are non-specific. May show anaemia and leukopenia due to splenic/bone marrow involvement.  Raised serum urea and creatinine due to kidney involvement.  Deranged LFTs may be present.  The 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is often raised.  Pulmonary function tests – pattern may be restrictive, obstructive, or mixed. Used for disease monitoring as the transfer factor (usually reduced in patients with sarcoidosis) is sensitive to disease exacerbations and treatment.  ECG – may show conduction/rhythm defects.  Bronchoalveolar lavage – CD4 : CD8 ratio is typically raised.  Management Pharmacological:  The recommended first-line treatment is usually corticosteroids. They are indicated in:  patients with persistent hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria despite dietary calcium restriction  ophthalmological complications  neurological complications.  Methotrexate or azathioprine may be used as an adjunct or alone if steroid-sparing agents are required.  If prednisolone is prescribed, the dose should be gradually reduced after four weeks of treatment to the lowest maintenance dose possible for disease control.  Immunosuppressive or anti-inflammatory treatments have only a limited role:  can consider if corticosteroids do not provide adequate control/have intolerable side effects.  use of infliximab for treating sarcoidosis is off-label.  Prognosis  The prognosis is generally good, with the resolution in most people within 2 to 5 years.  25% of people will develop residual fibrosis in the lungs or elsewhere.  Common causes of disease-related mortality are lung, cardiac, and neurological disease that is non-responsive to therapy.

DR Septic Arthritis Septic arthritis (infective arthritis) is the infection of one or more joints which causes inflammation, rapid destruction of the joint, and even death if left untreated.  Overview Key Facts  Septic arthritis (infective arthritis) is the infection of one or more joints which causes inflammation, rapid destruction of the joint, and even death if left untreated.  The most common cause is S. aureus infection and the knee joint is involved in over 50% of cases.  Infection of the joint can occur through direct inoculation or through haematogenous spread.  The affect joint is likely to be warm, erythematous, swollen and tender; systemic symptoms such as fever may also be found.  A third of patients are left with significant morbidity.  Early empirical treatment is useful and improves outcomes.  The treatment of choice is high-dose intravenous antibiotics and possibly surgical aspiration and drainage of the synovial fluid. Epidemiology  Septic arthritis is most common in the elderly and the very young.  Previous joint pathologies increase the risk of infective arthritis, as does procedure on the joint.  Septic arthritis incidence stands at 4-10 per 100 000 patient years per year, according to the latest data for Western Europe. Aetiology  Infection of a joint usually occurs by one of two methods; direct inoculation through iatrogenic methods (eg arthroscopy or arthroplasty), or through haematogenous spread, ie those with systemic bacteraemia.  Direct inoculation can occur during intra-articular injection, however this cause of infectious arthritis is rarer than that caused by haematogenous spread.  Bacteraemia is common in those with immunosuppression and invasive devices such as catheters.  The most common cause of infective arthritis is S. aureus bacterial infection; infections caused by Neisseria gonococcus, streptococci, and gram negative bacilli are also common. Pathophysiology  The synovium is a highly vascularised tissue; resultantly, haematogenous spread through the circulation can cause seeding.  Current understanding of infective arthritis is based on animal models, but the general picture is that the inflammatory process Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI that follows infection leads to joint destruction through destruction of cartilage and then bone erosion.  This process is promoted by inflammatory cytokines, proteases, and toxins. Common causes of infective arthritis in the commonest affected:  Clinical Presentation  The classic presentation involves one affected joint (most commonly the knee) which presents with signs of inflammation including pain, swelling, and erythema.  It is, however, possible, that patients will present with polyarticular pain, although this is far less likely.  Most patients will also present with signs of fever and may have bacteraemia.  The joint may be warm, swollen, and sore at rest.  There will be severe pain when undergoing active or passive movement.  Whilst the knee is the commonest affected joint, less commonly affected joints include the hips, shoulders, wrists, and ankles. DR  Differential Diagnosis  Gout.  Pseudogout.  Osteoarthritis.  Rheumatoid arthritis.  Reactive arthritis.  Infective endocarditis.  Lyme disease.  Ruptured Barkers Cyst.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A good history and examination are key, but should be supported by a variety of investigations in order to direct medical therapy.  Laboratory investigations.  bloods should include full blood count (FBC) and inflammatory markers, as an inflammatory/infectious picture is usually seen in infective arthritis, cultures may identify the causative organism in bacteraemia  these bloods will also be useful in monitoring response to treatment  further bloods include blood cultures to look for bacteraemia  synovial fluid should be examined if it is possible to aspirate it:  gram staining and leukocyte count are useful to direct medical management  polarising microscopy can help to rule out crystal arthropathies  synovial fluid can be cultured to determine appropriate antibiotic use for anti microbial stewardship.  synovial tissue should be cultured if there is a strong suspicion of fungal or mycobacterium infection Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  if there is a suspicion that this may be a presentation of rheumatological arthropathy, the relevant immunology tests should be undertaken.  Imaging investigations:  plain film radiography has limited use in early disease, however it may be useful to show some features seen in infective arthritis, including fat pad displacement, widening of joint space, and in later disease, cartilage destruction which has caused narrowing of joint spaces  ultrasound may be useful to see early effusions and guide aspiration of synovial fluid  CT and MRI are not usually used but are the best investigations to detect abscesses, and joint effusions.  Management Pharmacological:  Empirical antibiotics should be started on the basis of a clinical picture of infective arthritis, and gram staining results.  The choice of antibiotics should then be refined on the basis of culture results.  Antibiotics should be delivered intravenously at first, and then after 3-4 weeks should be changed to oral delivery as long as treatment is seen to be working.  First line choice of antibiotics are flucloxacillin for 4-6 weeks.  Pain relief should be delivered according to the WHO pain ladder. Surgical:  Joint drainage may be required if the infection is refractory to medical treatment.  Certain joints, such as the shoulder will require ultrasound guidance for needle aspiration, or even open arthrotomy.  If occurring post arthroplasty, the foreign body (joint) may need to be removed.  Prognosis  Infective arthritis carries a mortality rate between 10-20%, depending on other factors such as comorbidities and immunosuppression.  A third of patients with bacterial arthritis may suffer postinfectious morbidity such as amputation, prosthetic surgery, or severe functional impact.  Prolonged arthralgia is not uncommon following septic arthritis. DR  Overview Key Facts  Still’s disease is also classified under the umbrella of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) with the term ‘systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis’.  Clinical features include polyarthritis, rash and intermittent fever.  Diagnosis is clinical, with investigations for confirmation, assessment of complications and management.  Management aims to halt the inflammatory process and reduce complications. referral is required.  Main treatment options include NSAIDs, systemic steroids, methotrexate and tocilizumab.  Severe complications include uveitis, serositis and macrophage activation syndrome.  Outcomes of chronic arthritis or resolution all may impact a child’s development. Epidemiology  JIA, itself, is the most common chronic paediatric illness, with a prevalence of approximately 1–2 per 1000 children.  Approximately 4–15% of JIA cases are Still’s disease.  Boys and girls are equally affected.  Onset is usually in the under 5s. Aetiology  Unknown cause, but thought to be due to autoimmunity.  The aetiology of autoimmunity is unknown; it is linked to the loss of ‘self-tolerance’, genetic predisposition (eg HLA allele variations), infection, hormones (women > men) and other factors.  Triggers to autoimmune ‘flare-ups’ may include burns, stress, pregnancy, vaccination, sun/UV light and drugs (eg rifampicin, penicillamine).  It is not known why there are differences in the progression of disease process (ie why some ‘recover’, some develop extraarticular complications and some never recover). Pathophysiology  In Still’s, there is a process of intra-articular and systemic inflammation.  Thought to be driven by innate immunity abnormalities.  Active monocytes and neutrophils are the main cause of articular inflammation and damage.  In synovitis, thickening of the synovium occurs due to an increased number of cells and cytokines arriving at the site.  Joint effusion is a direct result of increased vascular permeability.  Cartilage damage and resulting bone exposure can occur not only from cytokine presence but also the thickened synovium directly blocking its nutrient supply. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Osteoporosis can occur through reduced joint use, cytokine action on the bone and fibroblasts growing beyond the synovium and into the bone.  The main pro-inflammatory components in Still’s are thought to be the cytokines IL-1 and IL-6. Treatments targeting these specifically are highly effective.  ANA (anti-nuclear antibody) positivity is correlated to the development of uveitis; the reason for this is unknown.  Clinical Presentation  Most common clinical presentation:  age < 5 years  spiking fever + rash (‘salmon pink’ and macular), often appearing and disappearing quickly together and nightly  symmetrical polyarthritis (only at onset in one-third, otherwise within months of onset)  pain (tends to be severe)  tiredness  anorexia.  Uveitis is the most common extra-articular manifestation of JIA. Features include pain, redness, photophobia and visual blurring. Often unilateral.  Approximately 1 in 10 with Still’s develop serious macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).  Much rarer presentation is adult-onset Still’s disease, seen mostly in ages 16–35. Other aspects of the disease are remarkably similar. MAS  Clinical presentation:  fever  organomegaly  cytopenias  ↑ ferritin  ↑ triglycerides  ↓ fibrinogen  coagulopathy.  Examination:  main examinations needed – musculoskeletal, dermatological and eye  other examination would be to exclude other diagnoses.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  Lyme disease  other causes pyrexia of unknown origin  septic arthritis  osteomyelitis

DR  trauma/mechanical pain  inflammatory bowel disease  malignancy  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  other forms of JIA.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Still’s disease is a clinical diagnosis and, as with all types of JIA, other causes of arthritis need to be eliminated.  All suspected cases need rheumatology referral for confirmation of diagnosis and management. Diagnostic criteria for systemic JIA (American College of , ACR) < 16 years old + Arthritis (≥ 1 joint for at least six weeks) + / preceded by > 39 °C fever spikes (≥ 2 weeks duration, daily for at least 3 days) + ≥ 1 of these features: typical rash lymph node enlargement hepato- and/or splenomegaly evidence of serositis (pericarditis and/or pleuritis and/or peritonitis) Investigation  Investigations are normally used for ruling out other differentials as well as optimising management.  Common tests:  Bloods:  FBC  CRP  ESR  U&Es  LFTs  clotting  lipids  ferritin  ANA  rheumatoid factor (RF)  ultrasound scan (USS)  joint X-ray.  Blood findings: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  ↓Hb (normocytic), →/↑WCC, mild ↑platelets  ↑ESR/CRP  typically, antibody negative.  Imaging:  X-ray – baseline in case of future deformity and to exclude other diagnoses; joint erosions might be seen within few months of arthritis  Ultrasound scan – highlighting the synovial fluid (eg looking for synovitis, synovial hypertrophy and joint erosions).  Less common:  joint aspiration + synovial fluid analysis (often used to rule out infection).  Management  Treatment aims to halt the inflammatory process and reduce complications.  Fast rheumatology referral needed (ie within six weeks).  If very severe, or MAS is suspected, hospitalisation is needed. Ophthalmology referral  If evidence of uveitis, referral needs to be urgent (same day or < 1 week).  Otherwise, regular assessment essential for detecting uveitis (reviews normally occur 6–12 monthly unless classed as ‘higher risk’).  Treatment monitoring for – fever (aiming < 37.5 °C), rash resolution, degree of arthralgia, CRP, Hb, platelets and WCC.  JIA ACR scoring, or child health questionnaires (CHQ) could also be used for treatment monitoring. Non-pharmacological  Full paediatric-specific multidisciplinary team (MDT) management is coordinated through rheumatology (eg physiotherapy, occupational therapy, hydrotherapy).  Patient, caring and repeated advice/discussion is needed for the families.  Treatment decisions need to involve full holistic discussion between the families of the child and the clinical team.  Treatments/consultations should be performed in an ‘ageappropriate’ environment.

DR  Involvement of schools (possibly employers) following diagnosis and if any adjustments need to be made (eg aids, equipment modifications, time off for appointments).  Possible direction of families to social services to assist with financial aid that might be available (eg for home modifications, if parents stop working for care needs).  If needed, a clear ‘transfer of care pathway’ must be established for transition into adult services.  Examples of support organisations to direct families too – Children’s Chronic Arthritis Association and Arthritis Care. Pharmacological  Stepwise approach: 1. NSAIDs for pain/stiffness 2. Systemic corticosteroids mainly PO, sometimes IV 3. SC/PO methotrexate always + folic acid 4. Failure to respond to NSAIDs, systemic steroids and methotrexate(or to limit long-term steroid effects in systemic corticosteroid + methotrexate combo) consider:  Anti-tumour necrosis factor(Anti-TNF) therapies (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) or  Anakinra (Il-1 inhibitor) / Tocilizumab - IL-6 inhibitor (this is the only licensed biological therapy in Still’s Disease, and is licensed for those > 2 years of age). Surgical  Arthroplasty, if severe joint damage.  Prognosis  Estimates of disease progression:  1 in 10 have only one episode and stay in remission  3–4 in 10 have relapsing/remitting disease that lasts several years  5–6 in 10 remain with chronic disease.  Complications include:  joint deformity  uveitis  joint destruction  osteoporosis  growth restriction  pubertal delay Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  restrictions of learning, movement, daily living  mortality in MAS approximately 6%  if associated uveitis is severe, approximately 50–70% develop permanent visual impairment  estimated that 7–28% need arthroplasty.  Potential impact on education, behaviour, family and social life, with possible continued ramifications into adulthood (eg level of educational attainment, employment).  Treatment complications:  potential long-term consequences of systemic steroids, eg approximately 10–20% have growth impairment as a result  monitoring for methotrexate side-effects, eg chest X-ray, 3-monthly bloods.  regular monitoring for side-effects of tocilizumab; ≥ 5 in 100 people develop adverse reactions (eg URTI infections, hypertension, headache, abnormal LFTs).  Other  Still’s Disease is also known as systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.  Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, itself, is defined by: Joint inflammation with: Age: <16 years + Duration: ≥ 6 weeks + No other possible diagnosis.  The full seven JIA categories are:  oligoarticular JIA  polyarticular JIA (-ve RF)  polyarticular JIA (+ve RF)  systemic-onset JIA (Still’s disease)  juvenile psoriatic arthritis  enthesitis-related arthritis  undifferentiated arthritis.

DR Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Systemic lupus erythematosus is a multisystem inflammatory connective tissue disease with small-vessel vasculitis and non-organspecific antibodies.  Overview Key Facts  Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem inflammatory connective tissue disease with small-vessel vasculitis and non-organ-specific antibodies.  It is characterised by skin rashes, arthralgia and antibodies against double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).  SLE is more common in younger women, with a men to women ration of 1 : 10.  There is also significant geographical variation, with it being more common in West Indian populations.  Treatment includes disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as hydroxychloroquine, corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, as well as analgesia.  There is signiﬁcant morbidity associated with cardiovascular disease in SLE, so risk factor reduction (blood pressure, smoking, obesity, lipids, exercise) is an important aspect of treatment.  10-year survival has improved significantly in recent years and now exceeds 90%.  Lupus variants  Drug-induced lupus is more common in men than in women:  it is usually mild and always resolves on stopping the drug  CNS and renal disease are rare  ANA is positive but antibodies to dsDNA are not usually present  the pathogenesis is not known and antibodies to the drug do not occur  the drugs commonly implicated (procainamide, isoniazid and hydralazine) all have active amido groups.  Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome (Hughes syndrome):  characterised by recurrent venous or arterial thromboses, fetal loss and thrombocytopenia  Libman– Sacks endocarditis and focal neurological lesions (such as cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or transient ischaemic attack (TIA)) in lupus are usually due to antiphospholipid antibodies. Epidemiology  SLE is more common in women, with a men to women ratio of 1 : 10 and is more common in West Indian populations.  Prevalence in the United Kingdom (UK) is estimated to be around 1 in 1000 population. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  Broadly speaking, connective tissue disorders are autoimmune conditions.  It is thought that most cases result from activation of the immune system due to environmental factors in those people with a genetic predisposition.  There is often a familial association with these diseases.  There is a significant cross-over in symptoms given the widespread distribution of non-specific antibodies (this can lead to misdiagnosis).  Geographic variation can be seen with these conditions.  Autoimmune diseases are thought to involve both a genetic predisposition and an environmental trigger (eg viral illness).  A small percentage of the general population may have autoantibodies present in their blood but display no signs or symptoms of the disease.  Conversely, people may have signs and symptoms of disease with no positive findings of autoantibodies until the disorder progresses. Pathophysiology  The exact cause of SLE is unknown, however, it is classed as a type III hypersensitivity reaction (immune-complex-mediated reaction).  When antibodies react with an antigen they form a complex that is usually phagocytosed rapidly.  If these complexes are not destroyed adequately they are able to accumulate in smaller blood vessels and are subsequently attacked by neutrophils and complement proteins.  The reactions that then ensue can damage the endothelium of blood vessels eventually compromising the circulatory supply to the specific organ.  Clinical Presentation  Connective tissue disorders often manifest with skin-based presentations and often bony involvement with widespread arthralgia.  SLE can affect multiple organs and is often challenging to diagnose.  Signs and symptoms may vary from person to person and may have different time courses; they can be progressive or relapsing and remitting.  Most common presentations in SLE ( > 80% of cases):  arthralgia or non-erosive arthritis  rash (malar, discoid or photosensitive)  fever.  Other symptoms include:  serositis (30–60%) – pericarditis, pleurisy, effusions  renal – proteinuria (30–60%), nephrotic syndrome less common, glomerulonephritis (15–20%)  neuropsychiatric (10–60%) – psychosis, seizures  haematological (up to 50%) – leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, haemolysis

DR  alopecia (up to 50%)  Raynaud’s phenomenon (10–40%)  oral or nasal ulcers (10–40%)  respiratory (10%) – pneumonitis, shrinking lung syndrome  cardiac (10%) – myocarditis, endocarditis (Libman– Sacks)  weight loss.  Lupus erythematosus skin manifestations:  cutaneous discoid lupus erythematosus – associated with scaly erythematous plaques with follicular plugging on sun-exposed sites, these tend to heal with scarring  malar rash  photosensitivity  vasculitis  Raynaud’s phenomenon  alopecia  oropharyngeal ulceration.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  mixed connective tissue disorder  amyloidosis  polymyositis  dermatomyositis  rheumatoid arthritis  sarcoidosis  tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis requires a combination of clinical features and the presence of at least one relevant immunological abnormality.  If there is clinical suspicion, blood tests including serological markers should be checked.  A full blood count (FBC) may show numerous abnormalities:  anaemia of chronic disease (normal mean cell volume (MCV))  neutropenia/leukopenia  thrombocytopenia  haemolytic anaemia ( high MCV reticulocytosis)  lymphopenia  aplastic anaemia (rare).  Serology:  anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs) are present in about 95% of patients with the condition:  a negative test indicates a low probability of SLE.  anti-dsDNA antibodies, low complement levels or antiSmith (Sm) antibodies are also highly predictive of a Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI diagnosis of SLE in patients with clinical features of the condition  anti-Ro/La and anti-RNP antibodies may be positive but are also found in other autoimmune conditions  anti-phospholipid antibodies should be tested in all patients with SLE  C-reactive protein (CRP) rises with active disease of the joints or serositis (eg pleurisy and pericarditis), but in active lupus of other organ systems, it may not rise; this may help differentiate between a ﬂare of SLE and intercurrent infection  low C3 and C4 may suggest lupus nephritis.  Urinalysis – to check for proteinuria and haematuria.  Other investigations will depend on clinical features of systemic involvement.  Management  Management will depend on the system and organs affected.  Treatment can do the following:  relieve symptoms:  such as pain, anxiety, fatigue and rashes.  suppress the immune system:  such as chemotherapy agents or anti-TNF medications to control inflammation and preserve organ function. Non-pharmacological  Treatment of SLE involves high SPF factor sunscreen use, as sunburn can provoke a generalised flare in disease in around two-thirds of patients (UV rays are what trigger the flare in disease).  SLE is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), so risk factor reduction is important and should focus on promoting a healthy lifestyle to improve blood pressure, obesity, lipids and to reduce/stop smoking. Pharmacological  DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs), eg hydroxychloroquine, will suppress inflammatory arthritis and reduce the risk of flares, but can also reduce the need for steroid treatment in SLE.  Analgesia such as NSAIDs should be prescribed for arthritis.  Corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs (eg methotrexate or azathioprine) are used if there is vital organ involvement.  Plasma exchange and biological agents such as rituximab are used in disease which is refractory to standard treatment.  Prognosis  Mortality and morbidity in SLE have improved drastically with improved treatment of SLE itself, through reductions in drugassociated problems by limiting corticosteroid use and treatment of comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease.  10-year survival in SLE is now approaching 90%.

DR  The main causes of death in the ﬁrst five years of disease are active SLE and infection, with thrombotic diseases becoming the predominant causes in later disease. Systemic Sclerosis Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ?brosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Overview Key Facts  Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ﬁbrosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Fibrosis may occur in:  skin tissues  the gastrointestinal (GI) tract  the heart and lungs and other vital organs.  Vascular damage may lead to:  secondary Raynaud's phenomenon  ischaemia of extremities  pulmonary arterial hypertension  renal disease.  Systemic sclerosis can be divided into two types depending on the extent of skin involvement – limited or diffuse scleroderma.  It is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups, with an incidence of 4–12 per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age.  Management focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications:  this may include immunosuppressants, corticosteroids and supportive therapies.  Mortality rates in people with the condition are up to eight times higher than in people without it. Epidemiology  Systemic sclerosis is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups.  Incidence is estimated to be between 4–12 cases per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age. Aetiology  The cause is not clearly understood. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Genetic, infectious and environmental factors all appear to play a role.  Some cases may be due to or triggered by exposure to substances such as vinyl chloride.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical features of systemic sclerosis  Raynaud’s phenomenon:  the initial complaint in 70%  associated digital ulcers and calcinosis (very unusual in primary Raynaud’s phenomenon).  Musculoskeletal:  arthralgia  erosive arthritis in about 30%  myositis (usually mild, often asymptomatic with raised creatine kinase, CK)  flexion deformities of ﬁngers due to skin ﬁbrosis.  Pulmonary:  fibrotic interstitial lung disease  pulmonary hypertension.  Renal:  scleroderma renal crisis (malignant hypertension, rapid renal impairment with ‘onion skin’ intrarenal vasculature).  Scleroderma:  early oedematous phase  later indurated and hidebound  affected areas may become pigmented and lose hair.  Gastrointestinal:  motility can be impaired at any level (smooth muscle atrophy and ﬁbrosis)  oesophagus (reﬂux, dysphagia, peptic strictures)  gastric dilatation  intestine (bacterial overgrowth, malabsorption, steatorrhoea, pseudo-obstruction)  colon (constipation).  Disease patterns  Limited scleroderma with systemic involvement (previously known as CREST):  scleroderma limited to the face, neck and limbs distal to the elbow and knee  usually begins with Raynaud’s phenomenon  CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia)  anti-centromere antibody-positive in most patients  renal crisis rare, pulmonary hypertension more common.  Diffuse scleroderma with limited involvement:

DR  scleroderma involving the trunk and proximal limbs as well as face and distal limbs  usually begins with swelling of ﬁngers and arthritis  anti-Scl70 antibodies 20–40%  pulmonary hypertension rare, renal crisis more common.  Scleroderma without internal organ disease:  plaques – morphoea  linear – coup de sabre.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diganoses include:  Raynaud's phenomenon  vibration injury  amyloidosis  polymyositis  dermatomyositis  rheumatoid arthritis  mixed connective tissue disorders  sarcoidosis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation Laboratory tests  Elevated ESR or CRP.  Urinalysis and renal function tests.  Autoantibodies:  rheumatoid factor positive in 30%  anti-nuclear factor positive in 90% (homogeneous, speckled or nucleolar staining)  anti-centromere and anti-Scl70 are quite speciﬁc  anti-centromere positive in 50–90% of limited and 10% of diffuse scleroderma  anti-Scl70 (anti-topoisomerase l) positive in 20–40%.  Further investigation will depend on symptomology.  Management  Management of systemic sclerosis includes:  screening for pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary ﬁbrosis (annual echocardiography and pulmonary function tests)  monitoring for renal involvement (blood pressure and creatinine)  corticosteroids – increase the risk of renal crisis and are avoided except where essential (eg pulmonary ﬁbrosis, myositis). Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Supportive treatment:  proton pump inhibitors for reﬂux  intermittent antibiotics for smallbowel bacterial overgrowth  vasodilators for Raynaud’s phenomenon  iloprost infusions for severe digital ischaemia.  Speciﬁc:  immunosuppressants (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide) for rapidly progressive skin disease  cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids for pulmonary ﬁbrosis  angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors for scleroderma renal crisis  iloprost, bosentan, sildenaﬁl for pulmonary hypertension.  Prognosis  Both diffuse and limited forms of the disease are associated with increased mortality, 5–8 times higher than the general population.  Diffuse disease has a worse outcome.  Prognosis is also dependent on early detection and intervention to prevent complications of disease progression. Takayasu Arteritis Takayasu arteritis is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory condition involving large and medium-sized arteries (aorta and its main branches).  Overview Key Facts  Takayasu arteritis is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory condition involving large and medium-sized arteries (aorta and its main branches).  The progressive inflammation of the arteries causes transmural fibrosis with consequent stenosis and occlusion, which if severe in upper or lower limbs can show the signs of a diminished or absent pulse.  this is why it is also given the name of ‘pulseless disease’.  Weakening of the arterial wall with subsequent pseudoaneurysm formation may also be seen. Epidemiology  The disease is quite rare worldwide with some studies reporting a rate of 1 to 2 cases per million; however, comparatively, the

DR incidence is predominantly found in young women of Asian origin.  The affected age is usually less than 40 years.  with advanced techniques, women in their late teens and early twenties are increasingly being diagnosed shifting the focus to an even younger age group.  More than 90% of the patients are women. Aetiology  No known cause has been identified.  It has a higher prevalence in women of a specific descent, however, suggests a genetic predisposition. Pathophysiology  Not much is known about the pathogenesis of Takayasu’s arteritis.  Essentially, it is an autoimmune condition where cell-mediated immunity plays an essential role.  CD4+ and CD8+ cells aid in the inflammatory process forming granulomas and promoting the chronic gradual process of inflammation.  Transmural fibrosis as a result of this inflammation causes widespread areas of vascular obstruction, which ultimately leads to ischaemia.  Inflammation of the vessels causes damage to the smooth muscles of the vessel wall and results in decreased elasticity, thus forming alternating areas of dilatations called pseudoaneurysms.  Clinical Presentation  Early signs and symptoms are nonspecific and include constitutional inflammatory features of systemic illness such as fever, malaise, joint pains and weight loss.  As the inflammation causes occlusion of the vessels, clinical presentation indicative of arterial insufficiency and ischemia becomes prominent. This may also be referred to as the ‘pulseless’ or the ‘occlusive’ phase.  Manifestation of the disease depends on the site involved:  renal artery stenosis presents with hypertension  carotid artery involvement can cause neurological features of stroke, dizziness or headaches  coronary artery occlusion may result in angina  jaw claudication, mesenteric ischaemia or heart failure may also be the consequences of Takayasu’s arteritis.  Examination findings in a patient with Takayasu’s arteritis may include:  difference of more than 10 mmHg in the systolic blood pressure of both arms  diminished or absent peripheral pulses  arterial bruits. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Differential Diagnosis  A significant differential diagnosis is Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). The key differentiating factor between Takayasu’s arteritis and GCA is the age of the patient. Patients affected with GCA are generally aged 50 or over.  Another major difference is the initial presentation. Where Takayasu’s arteritis has a more nonspecific presentation with pulselessness, GCA patients typically present with temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and/or vision abnormalities.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is made on clinical grounds (for example, if the characteristic features are present for more than a month) and imaging such as computed tomography (CT) angiography (CTA).  CTA is also performed for staging the disease based on the thickness of the arterial wall and the degree of stenosis.  The disease can be classified into types depending on the arteries involved based on the CTA findings.  An ESR value of > 20 mm/hour also supports the diagnosis.  Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging scanning are also used in some cases.  Management  Since the aetiology is autoimmune, immunosuppressive drugs such as steroids or the more conventional types, including azathioprine or methotrexate, may be used.  Cases resistant to steroids may then be considered for treatment with biological agents such as rituximab.  Management catering to an individual’s specific presentation is also carried out; hypertension with antihypertensive drugs, antiplatelet drugs to prevent stroke.  After the acute inflammatory phase, endovascular intervention procedures for revascularization may be considered in the late stage.  Prognosis  The prognosis varies widely depending on several factors such as the specific clinical presentation, ESR and CRP levels, major complications that may result and the level of care offered. As a reflection of this variability, the mortality rate can range anywhere from as low as 2% to up to more than 30%.  The majority of the patients face relapses (at least one). Tendonitis Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon resulting in pain and swelling and may lead to impaired function.

DR  Overview Key Facts  Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon resulting in pain and swelling and may lead to impaired function.  Clinical features depend on the tendon affected.  Common presentations include lateral epicondylitis (‘tennis elbow’), medial epicondylitis (‘golfer’s elbow’), Achilles tendinopathy, patellar tendonitis and rotator cuff tendinitis.  Symptoms are usually worse during movement and weightbearing exercise.  Tendonitis is usually self-resolving with a good prognosis through self-care, physical therapy and analgesics. Epidemiology  Up to 30% of consultations to orthopaedic doctors and sports medicine doctors are tendonitis. Aetiology  Commonly caused by repetitive activities of a particular movement and strain on that joint.  Constant repetitive movement causes inflammation of the tendon and joint, especially if not undertaken correctly in the right form. Pathophysiology  Still poorly understood but inflammation and release of inflammatory cytokines are involved.  It also involves intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms that lead to inflammation.  Clinical Presentation  Tendonitis typically presents with pain on movement. The surrounding skin may be warm and erythematous. The affected joint may be weak, stiff or painful.  Lateral epicondylitis (‘tennis elbow’):  elbow pain  worse during gripping  reduced grip strength  tenderness over insertion of extensor carpi radialis brevis into lateral epicondyle.  l epicondylitis (‘golfer’s elbow’):  less common than lateral epicondylitis  pain over the medial epicondyle, worse with movement of forearm and wrist.  Achilles tendinopathy:  heel pain  pain on dorsiflexion.  Patellar tendonitis:  ‘jumper’s tendonitis’  pain and swelling over patella tendon, worse with activity. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Rotator cuff tendinitis:  a common cause of shoulder pain  worse on use of the shoulder (eg overhead reaching).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  compartment syndrome  soft tissue injury  bursitis  arthritis  gout.  Diagnosis/Investigation  This is usually a clinical diagnosis upon physical examination and moving of the joint.  Other investigations to rule out differentials can include:  ultrasound  MRI  X-ray (fractures)  blood tests (infection).  Management Non-pharmacological  Self-care:  rest – avoid moving it for a few days  ice – up to 20 minutes every 2–3 hours  support – use a soft brace or elastic bandage around the affected joint  once the injured area can be moved, it is best to try to move it to prevent it from stiffening.  Prevention:  avoid playing sports that will trigger the joint  avoid heavy lifting or sudden actions that will trigger the joint.  Physiotherapy could help if the pain is severe or for a prolonged amount of time. Pharmacological  Analgesia:  paracetamol  oral and topical NSAIDs. Surgical  There are surgical treatment options if the patient is suffering from severe tendonitis or causing limited mobility.  Steroid injections for temporary pain relief.  Shockwave therapy to help with healing.

DR  Surgery to remove any damaged tissue or to repair a ruptured tendon.  Prognosis  Prognosis is usually good with most tendonitis self-resolving within a few months. Thromboangiitis Obliterans Thromboangitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a debilitating vasculitic condition resulting in progressive obliteration of distal small- and medium-sized arteries of upper and lower limbs.  Overview Key Facts  Thromboangitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a debilitating vasculitic condition resulting in progressive obliteration of distal small- and medium-sized arteries of upper and lower limbs.  It affects mainly young men who smoke heavily but can affect women too.  Prevalence is highest in South Asian people and Ashkenazi Jews (associated with HLA-B5 and anti-collagen antibodies in about 50%)  The condition presents with pain in the affected areas, digital gangrene/ischaemia and may also present with acute limb ischaemia.  Management includes smoking cessation, sympathectomy, antibiotics, foot care and analgesia.  Amputations are often required in cases of gangrene and ulceration. Epidemiology  Occurs mainly young men (age < 30 years) who smoke heavily but can affect women too (prevalence is increasing in women due to changing smoking habits).  Most commonly occurs in South Asian people and Ashkenazi Jews. Aetiology  The exact cause of the disease remains unknown, but smoking is associated with occurrence of the condition. Risk factors  Smoking  Male sex  Age < 30 years  Certain ethnic groups Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Genetic component: associated with HLA-B5 and anti-collagen antibodies in about 50%. Pathophysiology  Inflammatory changes in the walls of the arteries and veins occur leads to thrombosis of small- and medium-sized vessels.  Medium-sized arteries show transmural inflammation, intimal proliferation and thrombosis, with surrounding deposition of collagen.  Clinical Presentation Presents with one or two manifestations of the following:  symptoms and complications of occlusive disease of the distal arteries: usually severe rest pain and tissue loss in the feet and hands  other signs and symptoms include:  intermittent claudication  digital gangrene/ischaemia  autoamputation  acute limb ischaemia.  thrombophlebitis of the superficial and deep veins  Raynaud syndrome. Digital gangrene and autoamputation of the middle digit's distal phalanx:  Differential Diagnosis  Thoracic outlet syndrome  Subclavian steal syndrome  Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  Scleroderma  Diabetes mellitus and other causes of peripheral arterial disease.

DR  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis is predominantly a clinical diagnosis based on the patient’s history of characteristic symptoms, alongside a positive smoking history.  There are no specific investigation but diagnosis can be supported with results of:  CT/MRI angiography  tissue biopsy  genetic testing.  Laboratory investigations to exclude other vascular disease are recommended.  Management Non-pharmacological  Smoking cessation is the primary intervention – slows progression and reduces the severity of amputation.  Light to moderate exercise.  Wound care. Pharmacological:  Analgesia for pain relief.  Low-dose aspirin.  Antibiotics for infection.  Vasodilation drugs may be effective in acute episodes, such as prostaglandins.  Stem cell therapy is an emerging method of possible treatment which is still being investigated. Surgical  Lumbar sympathectomy – may be useful in chronic cases.  Surgical revisualisation.  Debridement – necrotic ulcers.  Amputations are often required, especially for gangrenous digits.  Prognosis  Disease is progressive with continuous smoking.  The condition is associated with a poor prognosis and often amputations are required (amputation rate is doubled in those who continue to smoke).  Smoking cessation slows progression and markedly improves prognosis but does not reverse the condition.  The prognosis is better when the condition affects women. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Vasculitis Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  Overview Key Facts  Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  The Chapel Hill Classification for vasculitis (2012) classifies vasculitis according to the predominant vessel involved, however it is important to note the underlying pathology is similar in all disease states:  large vessel vasculitis, includes Takayasu’s arteritis and giant cell arteritis (GCA)  medium vessel vasculitis (includes polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease)  small vessel vasculitis (includes ANCA-associated vasculitis Microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and eosinophilia granulomatosis with polyangiitis/Churg-Strauss and immune-complex vasculitis Anti-GBM disease, IgA vasculitis)  variable vessel vasculitis  single-organ vasculitis (includes cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis and cutaneous arteritis)  vasculitis associated with systemic disease (includes lupus vasculitis, rheumatoid vasculitis, and sarcoidosis vasculitis). Epidemiology  Vasculitis is a rare condition – it has an combined incidence of 14 000 cases a year.  Higher incidence is noted in smokers, Hep B/C positive patients, and those with concomitant autoimmune disease.  The most common vasculitis is polymyalgia rheumatica, followed by giant cell arteritis.

DR Aetiology  Infections, malignancy, and drugs may all lead to vasculitis illness, but in many cases, the trigger for endothelial injury is unknown.  The following mechanisms of endothelial cell injury have been proposed:  immune complex deposition: Hepatitis B-associated polyarteritis nodosa  direct endothelial cell infection: HIV  anti-endothelial cell antibodies: Kawasaki disease and Behcet syndrome  ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis  T-cell dependent injury: Giant cell arteritis. Pathophysiology  Inflammation of the blood vessel occurs due to immune complex deposition, leading to damage to the vessel wall.  This inflammation can be secondary to autoimmune disease and connective tissue disease.  Current thinking suggests that the inflammatory process leads to accelerated atherosclerosis, which is part of the reason for increased risk of cardiovascular disease and events.  Each type of vasculitis follows a slightly different pathogenesis, however many of them are united by the autoantibodies that case inflammation.  For example, in ANCA-related vasculitis, autoantibodies are directed against enzymes which are contained within white blood cells.  Clinical Presentation  As vasculitis can affect many different organs, it can present with a large variety of symptoms.  Initially this includes unspecific symptoms such as arthralgia and fatigue – the size of the vessel affected reflects the level of end organ damage; the larger the vessel, the larger the region of tissue/organ that is compromised.  Small vessel vasculitides often present as skin changes such as purpuric rashes, urticaria, vesicles, and splinter haemorrhages.  Medium-sized vessel vasculitides present with ulcers, digital infarcts, nodules, and hypertension due to renal damage.  Large vessel vasculitis can lead to end organ ischaemia such as TIAs, as well as hypertension and dissection.  Symptoms can broadly be classified as either general or related to the specific organ involved. General symptoms include:  Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, fatigue, and anorexia.  Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia, myalgia, and arthritis. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI Specific organ-related symptoms include:  Kidney – glomerulonephritis, which is seen clinically as acute kidney injury (AKI) with proteinuria and/or haematuria.  Respiratory – alveolitis, haemorrhage, sinusitis.  Peripheral neuropathies.  Gastrointestinal – diarrhoea, abdominal pain, perforation, haemorrhage.  Cardiovascular – jaw or extremity claudication, angina, myocardial infarction (MI).  Central Nervous System (CNS) – headache, visual loss, stroke, seizures.  Skin – Livedo reticularis, urticaria, vasculitis lesions including purpura, and erythema multiforme.  Particular types of vasculitis also have characteristic presentations:  giant cell arteritis typically presents with an abrupt-onset unilateral headache and scalp pain, as well as jaw or tongue claudication. Often there is visual disturbance too. Temporal vessels are often hard when palpated  polymyalgia rheumatica typically presents with bilateral shoulder or pelvic girdle aching, along with morning stiffness with a duration of more than 45 minutes  takayasu’s arteritis typically presents with arm claudication and absent pulses and bruits due to its aortic vasculitic involvement.  Differential Diagnosis  Most of the differential diagnoses are related to the dermatological manifestations of other blood/vessel disorders.  This includes purpura, trauma, and disseminated intravascullar coagulation (DIC).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is generally based on a combination of clinical and laboratory findings, and is usually confirmed by biopsy and/or angiography.  Bloods should include:  full blood count (FBC)  urea and electrolytes (U&Es) - renal function  liver function tests (LFTs)  inflammatory markers (especially for GCA), including erythrocyte sedimenation rate (ESR) and c-reactive protein (CRP).  hepatitis serology (as HBV and HCV are associated with some vasculitic disorders)  complement levels  RhF levels  cryoglobulins  ANAs  urine dip for haematuria or myoglobinuria.
