DR  There are also some specific investigations that are pertinent in a vasculitic work-up:  anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) are found in a number of inflammatory disorders including vasculitides, UC, AIH, and connective tissue disorders.  immunofluorescence reveals two major staining patterns:  cytoplasmic (cANCA): associated with anti-PR3 antibodies  perinuclear (pANCA): associated with anti-MPO antibodies.  anti-PR3 and anti-MPO titres can reflect disease activity, so are helpful in monitoring responses to treatment and recognising relapse.  although ANCAs may be positive in non-vasculitic diseases, they are unlikely to be positive for anti-PR3 or anti-MPO, whereas the predominant associations for vasculitis diseases are as follows:  microscopic polyangiitis: 70% ANCA-positive, usually anti-PR3  eosinophilia granulomatosis with polyangiitis: 50% ANCA-positive, and mostly anti-MPO.  Imaging: CT/MRI can identify vessel damage and occlusion.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoidance of the precipitating factor, such as a causative drug. Pharmacological  In general, steroid-based treatment is used to control symptoms in the acute setting; steroids are then slowly tapered off.  Oftentimes, immunosuppressive treatment is used, including cyclophosphamide and methotrexate.  Certain vasculitides require specific interventions, as mentioned below.  ANCA-positive vasculitides:  the aim is to initially achieve induction with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, followed by a maintenance programme involving azathioprine or mycophenolate.  PMR and GCA:  corticosteroids are used to control both PMR and GCA  immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and azathioprine may be used as steroid-sparers if the corticosteroid dose cannot be tapered  low dose aspirin is recommended in GCA due to the increased risk of stroke.  Takayasu’s arteritis:  usually treated with combined corticosteroids and immunosuppressants  may need arterial reconstruction or bypass in up to 70% of cases.  Kawasaki arteritis: Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  corticosteroids are contraindicated as they increase the number of coronary aneurysms  aspirin is used initially during the fever stage and then antiplatelet doses are given. Surgical  Surgery may have a variety of different aims, including opening up a blood vessel, taking a biopsy, or balloon dilation, eg in subglottic stenosis.  Prognosis  Despite treatment with immunosuppressants and corticosteroids, up to 20% of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis or PAN will die within five years.  Some complications of vasculitis include renal disease, arterial/venous thrombosis, digital infarction and subsequent gangrene, amongst many others. Amyloidosis Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  Overview Key Facts  Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  It is a rare but fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the United Kindom (UK).  The main classifications are AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis (the most common) and ATTR amyloidosis – classified by the type of amyloid fibril deposition.  AL amyloidosis is of unknown cause and also called ‘primary amyloidosis’. It has associations with myeloma.  Clinical presentation depends on the site of deposition but can range from nephrotic syndrome to heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination with Congo red stain classically showing green birefringence under polarised light. Immunoglobulins and serum or urine immunofixation show the presence of monoclonal protein.  Treatment of AL amyloidosis is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant if eligible.  AA amyloidosis is associated with inflammatory arthropathies and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The mainstay of treatment is controlling the underlying condition.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator.

DR Epidemiology  Amyloidosis is a rare disease but the specific incidence is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  It is a fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the UK.  AL amyloidosis is the most common, with an incidence of nine cases per million per year.  Age of diagnosis is around 65 years and less than 10% of patients are under 50.  Men have a higher prevalence and incidence than women. Aetiology  Dependent on the type of amyloidosis  AL amyloidosis – unknown cause but has associations with myeloma. No genetic, occupation or environmental risk factors have been identified for AL amyloidosis.  AA amyloidosis – 60% are secondary to inflammatory polyarthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis and other types of arthritis.  Other causes include other inflammatory conditions such as IBD, chronic infections, etc.  The risk of developing AA amyloidosis without a background of an inflammatory disorder is very unlikely. Pathophysiology  There are around 23 different proteins that can form amyloid fibrils.  Amyloid diseases are classified chemically by the fibril protein – AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis, transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), described below.  Classification AA amyloidosis:  Mainly an acute phase reactant.  Only a small number develop amyloidosis with elevated serum amyloid A levels – usually the kidney, liver and spleen are the main sites for deposition.  Systemic AA amyloidosis is a complication of chronic inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn’s disease, malignancies, etc.  Treatment of these reduces the incidence of AA amyloidosis.  It will often present with nephrotic syndrome or renal dysfunction.  If not adequately treated, then AA amyloidosis end-stage renal failure (ESRF) can develop and dialysis is required.  Prognosis is overall poor even with treatment. AL amyloidosis:  Previously called ‘primary amyloidosis’. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Extracellular fibril-forming monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains accumulate in organs such as the heart, kidney, nervous system, lungs, colon.  Majority of patients have monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or asymptomatic myeloma.  Clinical presentation is variable – dyspnoea, weakness, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, impaired renal function, cardiomyopathy and heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination and Congo-redpositive stain of the amyloid deposits, with classic green birefringence under polarised light.  Treatment is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant.  Amyloid cardiac disease should be treated supportively. Amiodarone and pacemakers may be required for arrhythmias. A heart transplant can be considered.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator. Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR)  An autosomal dominant disease that is associated with a large number of mutations.  Each variant involves a different organ – eg peripheral neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, renal impairment and proteinuria.  The requirement of dialysis is a poor prognostic indicator. Other types of amyloidosis:  These include heavy chain amyloidosis, beta-microglobulin amyloidosis (associated with CKD), hereditary renal amyloidosis, central nervous system amyloidosis (eg in Alzheimer's disease or prion proteins in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). Other classifications of amyloidosis:  Localised.  Systemic.  Familial periodic fever syndromes – familial Mediterranean fever, Muckle–Wells syndrome, hyper IgD.  Inherited forms of amyloidosis – TTR amyloidosis, fibrinogen amyloidosis, gelsolin amyloidosis, apolipoprotein amyloidosis.  Senile systemic amyloidosis.  Dialysis amyloidosis.

DR  Clinical Presentation  Variable clinical presentations dependent on which system is involved.  Symptoms:  fatigue  weight loss  easy bruising  breathlessness  oedema  peripheral neuropathy  autonomic symptoms.  Signs:  proteinuria  signs of heart failure – raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, murmurs  hepatomegaly, jaundice and ascites  glove and stocking neuropathy  autonomic disturbance – postural hypotension  GI bleeding  skin lesions – orbital purpura, enlarged goitre.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  chronic kidney disease (CKD)  other causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy  MGUS-associated nephropathy  membranous glomerulopathy  multiple myeloma  sarcoidosis  diabetes  lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Amyloidosis is suspected on the basis of symptoms and diagnosed with biopsy.  Serum immunofixation – positive in 60% – shows the presence of monoclonal protein.  Urine immunofixation – positive in 80% with AL.  Immunoglobulin free light chain assay – very sensitive for diagnosing AL – with raised kappa lambda ratio.  Bone marrow aspirate should be done on all patients and will show clonal plasma cells.  Beta-2 microglobulin can help predict prognosis.  Biopsy of the affected organ will stain red with Congo red.  Any organ-specific investigations may be helpful such as an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI. Rheumatology Key points R. JAMIL ALRAJHI  Management  Treatment of amyloidosis is dependent on the type.  Generally, the goal of treatment is to reduce the plasma cell clone which is responsible for the production of the immunoglobulin light chain. By reducing production, this means deposition is also reduced, in an attempt to halt progressive organ failure. Treatment of AL  Any patient who has biopsy-proven amyloidosis within any organs should be considered for chemotherapy or stem cell transplant.  Those who are candidates for stem cell transplant can be offered chemotherapy. Monitoring of immunoglobulin free light chains is used to assess response to treatment. Treatment of AA  The aim of the treatment of AA is to control the underlying inflammatory process.  Colchicine has been shown to be useful in reducing the development of AA in patients with familial Mediterranean fever.  Prognosis  Again, this is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  The prognosis of AL amyloidosis is dependent on the response to therapy for suppression of light chain synthesis.  7-year survival rate sits around 80% in those who completely respond; this reduces to 57% for a partial response.  In patients who fail to respond, the survival at 7 years is around 30%.  The main predictor of mortality is the severity of cardiac involvement, which is now used as part of severity staging.  Prognosis of AA amyloidosis is hugely variable on the extent of the underlying disease.

stem: A 39-year-old woman complains of swelling, stiffness and pain in her fingers. She also tells her doctor that in winter her fingers often turn dark in colour. Her autoimmune screen shows the presence of anticentromere antibody. Which one of the following is she most likely to have?
explanation:
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
This patient is likely to have limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis . Antibodies to centromere are a subset of antinuclear antibodies, which most commonly occur in the limited form of scleroderma. She may have with skin changes involving the face and limited to below the elbows and knees.

Diffuse systemic sclerosis
Diffuse systemic sclerosis is incorrect. Anti-centromere autoantibodies are uncommon in the diffuse form of scleroderma, which is more likely to show anti-SCL-70 antibodies.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Anti-centromere antibodies are rarely present in polyarteritis nodosa.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is incorrect. Anti-centromere antibodies are rarely present in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

stem: A 35-year-old patient complains of feeling unwell for the last 6 months. He has noticed a malar rash and weakness of his proximal muscles. On examination there is an erythematous scaly eruption over the extensor surfaces of his knuckles. His creatine kinase is elevated. What is the best test to obtain the diagnosis and guide treatment?
explanation:
Muscle biopsy
In cases of possible polymyositis or dermatomyositis confirmation of the diagnosis by muscle biopsy is essential.

Electromyography
Electromyography is incorrect. Investigations such as electromyography are adjuncts to diagnosis but do not supplant tissue biopsy.

MRI muscles
MRI muscles is incorrect. Other investigations such as magnetic resonance imaging are adjuncts to diagnosis but do not supplant tissue biopsy. An MRI of the muscles is often performed to direct the site of the biopsy.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is incorrect. Skin biopsy of the erythematous, scaly skin eruption overlying the knuckles would confirm the presence of Gottron's papules, which would confirm the diagnosis, but the diagnostic yield of a muscle biopsy is higher and confirmation of muscle involvement would be useful to guide treatment, as treatment is often more intensive when the muscles are involved.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who has longstanding systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents to the Emergency Department with deterioration in her condition. She takes low-dose prednisolone (5 mg daily) and hydroxychloroquine. Over the past few days, she has felt increasingly tired with night sweats and a cough productive of small amounts of yellow sputum. Her General Practitioner has started amoxicillin for a presumed respiratory tract infection. On examination, her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg; pulse is 88 bpm and regular. There are signs of consolidation at the left lung base. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 119 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 12.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 129 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 180 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Chest X-ray Left lower lobe pneumonia Which of the following is the most important step with respect to her management?
explanation:
C IV hydrocortisone Given the patient’s long-term steroid usage, hypotension and electrolyte disturbances, IV hydrocortisone is essential. This patient most likely has acute adrenal insufﬁciency secondary to pneumonia, and corticosteroids are essential to the treatment of these patients. D IV normal saline Although important in the management of acute adrenal insufﬁciency, it is not the most essential treatment option. IV hydrocortisone is more important with respect to treatment, as with IV ﬂuid replacement alone, underlying cortisol deﬁciency won’t be corrected.

A Fluid restriction This patient most likely has acute adrenal insufﬁciency secondary to pneumonia, given her long-term steroid use, hypotension and low sodium level. Fluid restriction would worsen her clinical condition and therefore is not clinically indicated. Corticosteroids and IV ﬂuids are essential. Fluid restriction is useful in the setting of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). B Intravenous (IV) furosemide IV furosemide is contraindicated, as this patient most likely has acute adrenal insufﬁciency secondary to pneumonia, given her long-term steroid use. These patients require ﬂuid resuscitation and therefore IV furosemide would clinically worsen the patient’s condition. E Oral demeclocycline Demeclocycline is used in patients with SIADH and has no role in the treatment of acute adrenal insufﬁciency. Therefore, it is not clinically indicated.

stem: A 72-year-old man with temporal headaches, hip and shoulder girdle pain presents to the Emergency Department with sudden loss of vision in his right eye. He also reports pain in his jaw on eating. He has a past history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. On examination he appears to have no vision in his right eye and he has 6/12 vision in his left eye. There is tenderness to palpation over both temples. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 115 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 10.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 321 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 79 mm/h 0–10 mm in the 1st hour ECG Slow AF, ventricular rate 65/min Which of the following is the most likely cause of his loss of vision?
explanation: D Vasculitis This man has temporal arteritis, as evidenced by his clinical history, examination and raised ESR. Management of temporal arteritis involves the use of high-dose steroids and, if successful, symptoms usually improve signiﬁcantly within a few days of starting therapy. In patients who fail to respond to treatment, another diagnosis should be suspected. The jaw pain on eating seen here most likely represents claudication due to maxillary artery involvement. C Thromboembolic disease Given the marked temporal artery tenderness consistent with temporal arteritis, AF as a cause of the symptoms here is less likely to be responsible. A Right carotid artery stenosis The symptoms ﬁt more with temporal arteritis here, although ipsilateral visual ﬁeld disturbance is seen, other symptoms such as contralateral weakness or sensory disturbance. B Right inﬂammatory optic neuritis Right inﬂammatory optic neuritis is more usually associated with ocular pain, with either a pale optic disc in patients with established disease or the potential for the optic disc to be oedematous in patients with acute disease. E Mastoiditis Although mastoiditis may result in jaw tenderness on eating, it wouldn’t result in the temporal artery tenderness or visual ﬁeld loss seen here.

stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of skin thickening on her hands with subcutaneous calcinosis, and leathery skin elsewhere. She also feels that her fingers feel particularly cold and very painful when she goes out, to the extent that she has started to wear gloves even in the summer. She also suffers from reflux oesophagitis and was started on omeprazole a few months ago. On examination, her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, she has sclerodactyly and calcification in her hands, and you notice multiple telangiectasia. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 x 10 9/l Platelets 142 × 10 9/l 150–400 x 10 9/l Anti-centromere antibodies Positive Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 162 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely cause of mortality related to her underlying disease?
explanation:
Pulmonary fibrosis
Two causes of death are particularly prominent in systemic sclerosis, these are death due toChat progressive with pulmonary fibrosis and death due to kidney disease.

stem: A 62-year-old retired carpet fitter presents with a 2-month history of pain and stiffness in both knees. You suspect early osteoarthritis as other joints appear to be unaffected and there are no other symptoms of connective tissue disease. His BMI is 32 and he has a history of hypertension but there is nil else of note. Which one of the following clinical findings is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Limitation of range of movement
One of the earliest symptoms of osteoarthritis is joint stiffness and pain after immobility. Limitation of range of movement may be noted in early, symptomatic osteoarthritis.

Crepitus on movement
Crepitus on movement is incorrect. Crepitus on movement is a later feature.

Joint instability
Joint instability is incorrect. Joint instability is a later feature.

Joint swelling
Joint swelling is incorrect. Joint swelling is not a common feature of osteoarthritis.

Muscle weakness
Muscle weakness is incorrect. Muscle weakness is a later feature.

stem: A 35-year-old woman who suffers from rheumatoid arthritis attends the Rheumatology Clinic complaining of marked episodic pain in her right hand. Physical examination reveals a loss of pinprick sensation in the hand. There is tingling and numbness involving the thumb, index and middle fingers. You suspect median nerve compression. Which one of the following clinical findings is most commonly associated with this condition?
options: Loss of sensation in the lateral palmar aspect
Swelling on the back of the hand
Wasting of the interosseous and hypothenar muscles
explanation:
Positive Tinel’s sign
This woman most probably has carpal tunnel syndrome, which is due to compression of the median nerve as it passes under the flexor retinaculum. Pregnancy, the oral contraceptive pill, myxedema (hypothyroidism) and rheumatoid arthritis can all exacerbate compression. Tapping the median nerve in the carpal tunnel reproduces tingling and pain – known as Tinel’s sign. Prolonged flexion of the wrists (in the inverse prayer position) can also reproduce the symptoms – known as Phalen’s sign. Lateral palmar sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome, as its supply, the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve, does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

Wasting of the interosseous and hypothenar muscles
Wasting of the interosseous and hypothenar muscles is incorrect. Wasting of the interosseous and hypothenar muscles occurs in ulnar neuritis This can occur following a childhood supracondylar fracture that results in severe cubitus valgus and consequent friction of the ulnar nerve.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with left hip pain. He reports pain over the lateral aspect of the hip, and this pain is reproduced when you examine him with the hip flexed, and then ask him to abduct it against resistance. He has no significant past medical history apart from mild hypertension, and enjoys walking the family dog. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Trochanteric bursitis
The lateral hip pain, coupled with pain on resisted abduction, is typical of that seen in trochanteric bursitis. Trochanteric bursitis, now termed greater trochanteric pain syndrome, is due to gluteus medius or minimus tendinopathy with some involvement of regional bursae. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the mainstay of management of trochanteric bursitis, with appropriate physiotherapy to maintain joint mobility.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative disease of joints characterised clinically by chronic pain which is worse with activity. Osteoarthritis is more likely to be associated with limitation of the range of hip movements, including external rotation, and pain deeper within the joint, making it an unlikely diagnosis for this patient.

Lumbosacral radiculopathy
Lumbosacral radiculopathy is incorrect. Lumbosacral radiculopathy is pathology affecting the nerve roots of one or more of the lumbosacral nerves. This can occur through a variety of mechanisms but is commonly compressive in nature. Lumbosacral radiculopathy is characterised by nerve pain radiating in a dermatomal distribution, which this patient does not have.

stem: A 65-year-old woman complains of increased morning stiffness, particularly in her shoulder girdle, so that she can’t get up and has to roll out of bed. The stiffness lasts approximately 2 hours. She also complains of fatigue and of being depressed. Investigation Result Normal Value Rheumatoid Factor Weakly positive Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 67 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 48 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Her CRP and ESR are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia occurs commonly in patients between 60-70 years, presenting with morning stiffness and proximal muscle pain with constitutional upset (fatigue) and raised CRP and ESR. PMR: Initial symptoms are seldom seen before 50 years or after 80 years of age. The male to female ratio is 1:2. The onset can be acute and dramatic or gradual, and in most cases it is fully developed within a month. The onset is most common in the shoulder girdle, spreading to involve both shoulders, the pelvic girdle and proximal muscles with striking symmetry. Involvement of distal muscles is unusual. Immobility is most severe on waking; a characteristic complaint is the need to roll out of bed, often with the aid of a partner. This morning stiffness can persist for hours. Most patients complain of general malaise, fatigue and depression. Anorexia and weight loss with fever are frequent and are occasionally the presenting feature. Diagnosis is usually made on the presence of a symptomatic response to steroid therapy and raised inflammatory markers, in the absence of other significant underlying pathology.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with a three-month history of pain and stiffness in her hands, particularly in the morning for more than one hour. She also reports swelling in her wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, along with occasional fatigue. Her symptoms improve slightly with movement throughout the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory joint disease that often affects the small joints of the hands and wrists symmetrically. This patient's history includes the hallmark features of RA: morning stiffness lasting more than one hour, improvement with activity, and symmetrical joint swelling. Due to its autoimmune nature, fatigue is also a common systemic symptom associated with RA. This presentation fits well within the typical clinical picture of RA.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can indeed cause arthralgia or polyarthritis but usually comes accompanied by other systemic manifestations like malar rash, photosensitivity or serositis, making it less likely given the lack of specific supportive signs suggestive of SLE over another connective tissue disorder, particularly presenting symmetric inflammatory arthropathy predominant hand/wrist involvement fitting classic rheumatoid profile.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to the Medical Assessment Unit with recurrent episodes of a swollen, red hot right ankle. She has a past medical history of alcohol excess. Renal function is normal. Aspiration of the joint reveals negatively birefringent crystals. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Monosodium urate monohydrate arthropathy
This patient has acute attacks of gouty arthritis affecting her ankle. Secondary gout due to alcohol or drug intake mainly affects people over the age of 65 and is the form most commonly seen in women. MSUM crystals appear strongly negatively birefringent under polarised light. Acute gout attacks normally last 5–7 days, with a hot, swollen affected joint with severe pain. Management of symptoms include non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with gastroprotection. Alternatively, colchicine can be used. The use of corticosteroids for acute gout is off-label.

Calcium oxalate arthropathy
Calcium oxalate arthropathy is typically seen in patients with hyperoxaluria (excess oxalate loss in the urine) who usually have kidney disease. Hyperoxaluria can be divided into primary and secondary causes. Primary causes include genetic conditions that lead to overproduction of oxalate. Secondary conditions include fat malabsorption and increased absorption of dietary oxalate. Oxalate is renally excreted and accumulates in chronic renal failure.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a swollen right knee. Three weeks ago, he had an episode of food poisoning after attending a wedding. He feels well now, but reports red eyes that have persisted for a few days. On examination, there is an effusion in the right knee and bilateral conjunctival injection. His temperature is normal. Blood tests show an ESR of 47 mm/hr and CRP of 99 mg/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Corticosteroid injection following a negative microscopy and culture of a single joint aspirate
explanation:
Corticosteroid injection following a negative microscopy and culture of a single joint aspirate
This man has a seronegative reactive arthritis, presumably due to an enteropathic infection with Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter. If it is a single joint that is affected it will probably respond to intra-articular steroid. Synovial fluid should be sent off for microbial analysis first as a precaution, as septic arthritis should always be considered with a monoarthritis.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. The gastrointestinal (GI) infection causing a reactive arthritis is usually self-limiting, so does not need to be treated with antibiotics. Genitourinary infections will always need to be treated, as per standard medical practice.

Sulfasalazine
Sulfasalazine is incorrect. One affected joint usually responds to an intra-articular steroid. If the reactive arthritis is chronic or recurrent then sulfasalazine may be tried.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of severe pain and swelling of the left wrist. She now describes difficulty in moving her wrist, and getting dressed is extremely difficult. Her past medical history includes rheumatoid arthritis and hypertension. On examination, she has a temperature of 38 ºC. There are visible rheumatoid nodules over her right hand. Her left wrist is erythematous and swollen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Joint aspiration
Septic arthritis should always be considered in cases of monoarthritis. Joint aspiration is essential and fluid should be sent for urgent Gram staining and culture. This should be followed by prompt treatment with antibiotics, as waiting for investigation reports can result in permanent joint destruction. Formal surgical treatment is required where there is evidence of osteomyelitis. The most common cause of septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, although seeding from respiratory infections caused by streptococci can also occur. Other causative organisms, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Haemophilus influenzae, can cause septic arthritis in children. Opportunistic pathogens, such as Salmonella, may be responsible in sickle cell disease.

Serum urate level
The urate level can be normal in 40% of cases of acute gout, therefore is not overtly helpful, even in cases of suspected gout.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to Medical Outpatients with fever, headache, body aches and a weight loss of 6 kg over 3 months. On questioning, he tells of a recent onset of jaw pain while chewing food. Physical examination reveals normal temporal arteries. Fundus examination shows a pale, swollen optic disc on the right side and perimetry reveals an altitudinal field defect. Blood examination reveals mild normocytic anaemia, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 98 mm/hour, C-reactive protein (CRP) 56 mg/L and a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Which of the following is the next best step in his management?
options: Immediate temporal artery biopsy and concurrent initiation of treatment
Immediate temporal artery biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment subsequently
Schedule another visit in 2 weeks to follow up on the eye findings/ESR
Treatment as soon as possible after biopsy
explanation:
Immediate temporal artery biopsy and concurrent initiation of treatment
In cases of suspected temporal arteritis, steroid therapy should be started and an urgent temporal artery biopsy arranged. The most dreaded complication of temporal arteritis is irreversible blindness, primarily due to ischaemic optic neuropathy. The patient may have visual defects or even develop sudden blindness. A biopsy is imperative to establish the diagnosis, but GCA is still possible if there is a negative biopsy due to skip lesions.

Immediate temporal artery biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment subsequently
Immediate temporal artery biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment subsequently is incorrect. Steroid therapy should not be delayed pending the results of a biopsy

Schedule another visit in 2 weeks to follow up on the eye findings/ESR
Schedule another visit in 2 weeks to follow up on the eye findings/ESR is incorrect. Immediate management is needed to prevent irreversible ocular complications.

stem: A 22-year-old man gives a history of high-grade fever associated with pustules on his hands and severe joint pain 4 weeks ago. His left knee is now swollen and red. Cultures from blood and joint aspirate are negative. His urethral discharge shows the presence of gonococci. Investigation Result Normal value White Cell Count (WCC) 13.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets 395 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 68 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 50 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Which drug would be most suitable in this condition?
explanation:
Ceftriaxone
This man has gonococcal arthritis. First line therapy would usually be IM Ceftriaxone as a single dose (usually provided in a specialist genito-urinary clinic setting). If sensitivites are known and the organism is sensitive to ciprofloxacin, this would be an alternative choice.

Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. Whilst gonococcus was historically sensitive to quinolones, there is now significant resistance.

stem: A 44-year-old man with coeliac disease presents with pain in his hips and thighs. Blood tests performed in primary care show a normal FBC (aside from a mild anaemia), U&Es, CRP and ESR. Calcium is 2.15 mmol/l, phosphate is low, the alkaline phosphatase is 1.5x the upper limit of normal with the rest of his LFTs being normal. A hip X-ray shows linear areas of low density surrounded by sclerotic borders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has coeliac disease, which is associated with malabsorption, and malabsorption of vitamin D can lead to osteomalacia. Osteomalacia occurs when there is inadequate mineralisation of the bone matrix, typically due to vitamin D deficiency. The characteristic X-ray finding of Looser’s zones (linear areas of low density surrounded by sclerotic borders) is often seen in osteomalacia and is indicative of areas of weakened bone that are at risk of fracture. The patient’s low phosphate and mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase further support this diagnosis.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis typically develops after an infection, such as a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, and is characterised by a sterile synovitis. This patient has no history of recent infection, which is a key feature that would help rule out reactive arthritis. The X-ray findings in reactive arthritis are generally normal or show only mild joint changes, which is not the case here. The patient's pain in the hips and thighs, along with the specific X-ray findings of Looser’s zones, is more consistent with osteomalacia than with the features of reactive arthritis.

stem: A 22-year-old man who suffers from inflammatory bowel disease has developed pain and stiffness in his lower back with buttock pain over the past 6 months. His pain tends to get better after he plays squash on Saturdays. He tests positive for HLA-B27. His blood tests, including CRP and ESR are normal, apart from a mild hypochromic microcytic anemia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis most commonly involves the sacroiliac joints causing pain and stiffness, which classically improves with exercise. Up to half the patients have inflammation of the colon or ileum. Although this may be asymptomatic, frank inflammatory bowel disease may develop in 5–10% of cases. The HLA-B27 gene is present in nearly 90% of White patients with ankylosing spondylitis. It is the distribution, with particularly the sacroiliac joints (indicated by buttock pain) being affected and the absence of a peripheral small joint arthropathy, which fits better with ankylosing spondylitis rather than enteropathic arthritis. N.B. inflammatory markers may be normal in ankylosing spondylitis.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is usually associated with an acute episode of GI illness or a sexually transmitted infection and is associated with arthritis, a psoriatic type rash and conjunctivitis.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis seldom involves the sacroiliac joints as the primary site.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is sent by the Emergency Department with a fractured neck of femur. She has a past medical history of unprovoked pulmonary embolism (PE) and is an ex-smoker. She undergoes surgical repair of her fracture and bone densitometry of the lumbar spine and femoral neck on the non-replaced side reveal a T score of –3 and –2.8, respectively. Three months later you review her in the clinic. Which of the following long-term interventions would be most appropriate for her?
options: Observe and repeat the densitometry in 12 months
Initiate calcium and vitamin D therapy
explanation:
Initiate bisphosphonate therapy
This woman has osteoporosis and a fracture and should begin treatment. This should be used in conjunction with intakes of at least 1000 mg/day of calcium, 800 IU of vitamin D and 1 g/kg body weight of protein, either through diet or supplements.

Observe and repeat the densitometry in 12 months
Observe and repeat the densitometry in 12 months is incorrect as she has established osteoporosis and a fracture, which merits immediate treatment.

Initiate calcium and vitamin D therapy
Initiate calcium and vitamin D therapy is incorrect as although she should indeed take sufficient calcium and vitamin D, this will not treat her existing osteoporosis.

Initiate hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
Initiate hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is incorrect as she has had an unprovoked PE, which would be a contraindication to the use of HRT, which carries an increased venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk.

stem: A 62-year-old, previously fit man presents with a 2-month history of fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and abdominal pain. He also has evidence of severe pain in his hands (but no swelling) and progressive numbness of his feet. On examination, livedo reticularis and nodules are noted on the extensor surfaces of his lower limbs. An X-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly. What diagnosis is best suggested by these findings?
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa
This man has polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), which may present with all these features. PAN is a necrotising vasculitis that causes aneurysms of medium-sized arteries. Abdominal pain due to mesenteric vasculitis infarction of a viscus, dyspnoea due to pulmonary infiltrates and cardiomegaly, arthralgia (not arthritis, ie joint pain without swelling), neuropathy and purpuric spots can all occur in this condition.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is incorrect. Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness resulting from muscle inflammation is seen in polymyositis. Some 25% of patients have a purple (heliotrope) rash on the cheeks, eyelids and light- exposed areas (dermatomyositis).

Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica is incorrect. Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) occurs commonly in older women and presents as aching and morning stiffness in the proximal muscles

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He complains of pain over the medial aspect of his elbow, radiating into the forearm, aggravated by pronation and flexion of the wrist. There is no past medical history of note; he tells you, however, that he has recently taken up golf. On examination pain is localised over the insertion of the wrist flexors on the medial side of the elbow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Medial epicondylitis
The clue here is the taking up of golf as a hobby, which is well recognised as a cause of medial epicondylitis. The point tenderness over the medial epicondyle and pain on pronation and flexion of the wrist confirm the diagnosis. Treatment with NSAIDS and physiotherapy is the mainstay of therapy, and he should of course be advised to stop golf for a while. Medial tendon release may be of value in patients who fail to respond to conservative management.

Brachioradialis tendonitis
Brachioradialis tendonitis is overuse tendinopathy characterised by chronic pain and tendon thickening. Clinical presentation is with pain over the upper lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and the lateral intermuscular septum.

De Quervain’s tenosynovitis
De Quervain’s tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis within the extensor compartment. It is characterised by pain at the base of the thumb. It is thought to be caused by repetitive thumb extension and abduction. Pain can occur with holding or gripping objects with the affected side. Chat Treatment with is with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and splinting. Steroid injections are also an option.

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with a chronic infected foot ulcer on the ball of his left foot. He has had it for some 6 weeks and completed one course of flucloxacillin and two of co-amoxiclav. On examination, you find a 1.5 cm diameter ulcer with surrounding erythema and soft tissue swelling. You probe it and the probe extends to the bone. He has no pain, since he has a pre-existing neuropathy. Which of the following is the most likely finding on X-ray to suggest osteomyelitis?
explanation:
Periosteal reaction
Osteomyelitis can occur as a result of contiguous spread of infection into bone from soft tissue, direct traumatic infection or from haematogenous spread. The latter is usually monomicrobial, whilst the former two are usually polymicrobial. Periosteal reaction cannot be seen until about 7 days into osteomyelitis.

Joint space calcification
Joint space calcification is incorrect. Joint space calcification is a manifestation of osteoarthritis.

New bone formation
New bone formation is incorrect. As periosteal blood flow is interrupted and necrosis occurs, dead bone can be separated and new bone formation can occur in its space. This is termed sequestrum and can occur if osteomyelitis leads to bone necrosis. It is a feature of chronic osteomyelitis but rather a later feature, and therefore not a sensitive marker for early cases.

stem: A 59-year-old woman complains of left knee pain. On examination, no abnormality is found except that her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m 2. An X-ray of the knee joint shows narrowing of the joint space and subchondral sclerosis. What is the possible cause of her condition?
explanation:
Obesity
Obesity is one of the commonest causes for the early appearance of osteoarthritis, which is confirmed by the X- ray. A body mass index (BMI) of 32 kg/m 2 indicates that she is obese (a BMI of > 30 kg/m 2 is classified as obesity). Weight loss and physiotherapy (quadriceps strengthening) would be key to the management of this lady’s pain.

Ageing
Ageing is incorrect. Although ageing is a risk factor for osteoarthritis, she is only 59 years old and her weight is likely to be the most significant contributing factor.

Gout
Gout is incorrect. The X-ray changes are of osteoarthritis and gout usually presents as a monoarthritis – red, hot swollen joint.

Pyrophosphate arthropathy
Pyrophosphate arthropathy is incorrect. The radiographic appearance of pyrophosphate arthropathy (pseudogout) is chondrocalcinosis (calcified cartilage in the articular space).

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of gradually progressive swelling and pain below the right knee. On examination, the knee joint appears normal. An X-ray shows a lytic lesion with sclerotic margins in the upper tibial metaphysis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Brodie’s abscess
This patient has a Brodie’s abscess, as demonstrated by the insidious onset and the classic X-ray features. This is a form of chronic osteomyelitis that arises insidiously. A localised abscess is present within the bone, often near the site of the metaphysis. Deep ‘boring’ pain is often the predominant symptom. The X-ray is usually characteristic.

Classical osteomyelitis
Classical osteomyelitis is incorrect. In chronic osteomyelitis the bone is thickened and generally denser than normal. Sequestra are commonly present within cavities in the bone. There might be a sinus track leading to the skin surface discharging pus. X-rays show thickened bone with irregular and patchy sclerosis that gives a honeycombed appearance. Sequestra are seen as dense loose fragments lying within a cavity in the bone. Chronic osteomyelitis is nearly always a sequel to acute osteomyelitis.

Ewing's sarcoma
Ewing's sarcoma is incorrect. This patient does not have radiographic features of a Ewing’s sarcoma. This is a highly malignant tumour that arises in bone marrow. The tumour is therefore common in the shafts of the femur, tibia or humerus. It arises in the diaphysis rather than the metaphysis of the bone. Radiographs Chatshow with destruction of bone and concentric layers of subperiosteal new bone (an ‘onion peel’ appearance).

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with pain in the lower back that has been increasing in severity over the past six months. He says that when he gets out of bed in the morning, he can hardly move, although this improves throughout the day. He has also suffered from plantar fasciitis on two occasions over the past three years. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 103 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 62 mm/first hour 0–10 mm in the first hour Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to request?
explanation:
Pelvis X-ray
Chronic lumbar back pain, coupled with other evidence of enthesitis (plantar fasciitis) is suggestive of a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). The modified New York criteria utilise the presence of sacroiliitis on X- ray as part of the diagnostic criteria. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be useful in determining the extent of inflammation (which is not required for diagnosis) and, given the slightly higher sensitivity for early changes, when the X-ray is negative for sacroiliitis.

stem: A 22-year-old man complains of having low back pain for the past 3 months. He has also noticed a swelling of his right second toe and has pain in his heels when he walks. He was treated for red eyes 6 months earlier. Which investigation would most likely lead to a diagnosis of his symptoms?
options: Joint aspirate and microscopy for uric acid crystals
explanation:
MRI of the sacroiliac joint
This patient has ankylosing spondylitis (AS). The main lesion is spinal ankylosis with sacroiliac joint involvement. The earliest changes (such as bone marrow oedema) are visible on MRI, which is more sensitive than X-ray. Hence X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is incorrect. Imaging of the sacroiliac joints may show squaring of the vertebrae, erosions of the apophyseal joints and obliteration of the sacroiliac joints. Uveitis is common and may occur in 25% of patients with AS.

HLA testing
HLA testing is incorrect. Imaging the sacroiliac joints is most likely to be diagnostic. Although Human leucocyte antigen (HLA) testing is part of the diagnostic criteria, it is not very helpful because of the high frequency of HLA B27 in the population.

X-ray of the sacroiliac joints
X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is incorrect. The earliest changes (such as bone marrow oedema) are visible on MRI, which is more sensitive than X-ray.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is treated with pulsed monthly intravenous cyclophosphamide for grade 4 nephropathy. She presents in the Emergency Department with a dry cough, shortness of breath and fever. Her last cyclophosphamide dose was 10 days ago. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 2.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Lymphocytes 0.7 × 10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 10 9/l Platelets 81 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 56 in 1 hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour C-reactive protein (CRP) 43 mg/l 0–10 mg/l The blood gases after walking up and down the department show: Investigation Result Normal Value P o2 7.2 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa P co2 3.6 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa A plain chest X-ray shows some patchy pulmonary infiltration. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
This patient is immunosuppressed and has pancytopenia. She has exercised-induced hypoxia. The most likely opportunist infection is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

Pericarditis
Pericarditis is incorrect. Her CRP is elevated, indicating infection, she has patchy changes on her chest X-ray, and she is significantly hypoxic after exercise.

Pleuritis
Pleuritis is incorrect. Her CRP is elevated, indicating infection, she has patchy changes on her chest X-ray and she is significantly hypoxic after exercise.

Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolus is incorrect. Her CRP is elevated, and the desaturation on exercise is more consistent with infection.

TB
TB is incorrect. It is less likely to be tuberculosis because the chest X-ray appeared relatively normal.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with sickle cell disease complains of severe right hip pain for the past week; she has had milder pain in the same hip for up to 3 months. She walks with a limp and has a positive Trendelenburg’s sign. There is a tendency for the hip to twist into internal rotation during passive flexion. Blood culture is negative. An X-ray of the hip appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Pathological fracture of the femur neck
explanation:
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
This patient most probably has avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Avascular necrosis is death of subchondral bone due to a compromised arterial blood supply.The femoral head is the commonest site of avascular necrosis because its peculiar blood supply that makes it vulnerable to ischaemia, as it is supplied by an end-artery. Sickle cell disease is a risk factor for avascular necrosis. MRI changes are seen before X-ray changes.

Osteoarthritis of the hip
Osteoarthritis of the hip is incorrect. Osteoarthritis of the hip is uncommon in women at this age, unless the hip has been damaged due to rheumatoid arthritis or ankylosing spondylitis.

Pathological fracture of the femur neck
Pathological fracture of the femur neck is incorrect. A pathological fracture of the femoral head usually occurs after a fall, rarely spontaneously unless there is severe osteoporosis. Weight bearing is painful or impossible and the leg is usually shortened and externally rotated. The fracture might be evident on X-ray.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with an acutely red and swollen right great toe, with no history of trauma. He is treated with thiazide diuretics for hypertension. He also has hypertriglyceridaemia. Which one of the following findings is most useful for making a diagnosis of gout in this patient?
options: Radiograph showing joint erosion of the first right metatarsophalangeal joint
explanation:
Good response to colchicine
It is rare for a patient with other diagnoses apart from gout to respond to a trial of colchicine. The most specific way to diagnose gout is to aspirate the involved joint and to identify negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals under polarised light. In this case it's quite possible he may have raised urate without gout, particularly given his use of thiazides, hence urate may not be particularly useful.

An associated right ankle effusion
An associated right ankle effusion is incorrect. The presence of synovial fluid is non-specific.

Elevation of serum uric acid
Elevation of serum uric acid is incorrect. Some patients (such as those on diuretics) may have asymptomatic hyperuricaemia. Note that the serum urate can be normal in 40% of cases of acute gout.

Radiograph showing joint erosion of the first right metatarsophalangeal joint
Radiograph showing joint erosion of the first right metatarsophalangeal joint is incorrect. Erosions are non- specific and can occur in gout, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with a 10-week history of pain affecting the cervical spine, both shoulders, lumbar spine and both hips. Early morning stiffness lasts until lunchtime and she feels markedly tired. She has lost 5kg of weight over the last 12 weeks. She has a low-grade pyrexia of 37.4 °C, bilateral knee effusions and a right carpal tunnel syndrome. Investigations reveal: normochromic normocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 101 g/l, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 81 mm in 1 st hour, C-reactive protein (CRP) 27 mg/l, weakly positive rheumatoid factor, serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis show a polyclonal increase in gammaglobulins and elevated α1- and α2-globulins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) usually affects elderly white females (female to male ratio 2:1, average age at presentation 70 years). The arthritis is symmetrical and accompanied by an acute-phase response.. The polyclonal increase in globulins is a marker of inflammation associated with PMR. Early morning stiffness, particularly of the hip and shoulder girdle with associated fatigue can be pronounced and may last for up to 2–3 hours each morning. Transient synovitis can occur in PMR and this is the most likely cause of the knee effusions here. Carpal tunnel may be associated in up to 15% of cases.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. The most prominent symptoms are proximal pain, which fits with PMR. Although she has joint involvement, she does not have a small joint polyarthritis which is seen in RA. A weakly positive rheumatoid factor is negligible in an elderly patient, as we are all likely to accrue antibodies as we age (immunosenesence).

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of pain and stiffness in both knees. You suspect osteoarthritis. Which one of the following clinical findings would be most important in deciding how best to manage his condition?
options: Crepitus elicited on movement of the joints
Fissuring and surface erosion of cartilage seen on arthroscopy
Presence of subchondral sclerosis in radiographs
Severity of pain and stiffness in the knees
explanation:
Severity of pain and stiffness in the knees
The guiding principle in the management of osteoarthritis is to treat the symptoms and disability, not the clinical or radiological appearances. Educating the individual about the disease and its effects reduces pain, distress and disability and increases compliance with treatment. Psychological or social factors alter the impact of the disease.

Crepitus elicited on movement of the joints
Crepitus elicited on movement of the joints is incorrect. Management is guided by the patient’s degree of pain and function, not by clinical or radiological features.

Fissuring and surface erosion of cartilage seen on arthroscopy
Fissuring and surface erosion of cartilage seen on arthroscopy is incorrect. Management is guided by the patient’s degree of pain and function, not by clinical or radiological features.

Fixed-flexion deformity
Fixed-flexion deformity is incorrect. Management is guided by the patient’s degree of pain and function, not by clinical or radiological features.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents in the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of a painful and swollen left knee. He is pyrexial, with a temperature of 38.5 °C. Examination of his cardiovascular and respiratory system is normal. An abdominal examination is normal. He also mentions that he developed a painful right ear and saw his doctor 5 days ago, who told him he had an infected ear and prescribed antibiotics. His left knee is swollen, red, tender and slightly flexed. A diagnosis of septic arthritis is made. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Septic arthritis results from infection of the joints with pyogenic organisms, of which Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest. The organisms reach the joint via the bloodstream, sometimes from known sites of infection such as boils or otitis media (such as in this case). Less commonly, it may spread from osteomyelitis adjacent to the joint or it may be introduced into the joint as a result of trauma. In septic arthritis, clinically, the patient complains of a single painful joint, which appears red, warm and swollen. Diagnosis: Aspirating the joint and examining and culturing the fluid should establish diagnosis. Treatment should be started immediately with appropriate antibiotics as delays can result in destruction of the cartilage. The joint should be immobilised. The joint should be drained by needle aspiration. Inaccessible joints such as the hip may require surgical drainage.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is incorrect. It is far less likely in adults (without specific risk factors) to cause septic arthritis. Other organisms responsible are streptococci, Neisseria spp. and Gram-negative bacilli.

stem: A 38-year-old woman complains of generalised body pain. Her sleep is poor, but even when she sleeps well, she does not feel refreshed in the morning. She is unable to exercise or work because she feels tired all the time and feels that her mood is low. To investigate her you send off lots of blood tests, including antibody profiles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is a syndrome that covers a multitude of symptoms, including chronic fatigue, widespread pain, sleep disorders (non-restorative sleep) and mood disturbances. In many cases the symptoms are severe, persistent and disabling and cause considerable personal, social and healthcare costs. There is no obvious medical disease or major psychiatric illness. This is a diagnosis of exclusion as there is no diagnostic test. Investigations are usually entirely normal. Management involves supervised exercise programmes (taking people’s needs and preferences into account), encouraging physical activity and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) using behavioural techniques to gradually and consistently increase activity, reduce avoidance behaviour and improve confidence and illness control. NICE guidelines for Chronic Pain (April 2021) incorporate patients with fibromyalgia symptoms.

Hypochondriasis
Hypochondriasis is incorrect. In hypochondriasis, the person’s preoccupation is with the fear that they have a physical disease. Reassurance is unhelpful in these cases and they require some form of CBT.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. Polymyositis is a condition of proximal symmetrical muscle weakness.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has become disabled by pain and tightness behind the right knee. Physical examination reveals a cystic swelling over the popliteal fossa and semimembranosus tendon. Which of the following would confirm the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right knee
Synovial biopsy of the right knee
Ultrasound study of the right knee popliteal fossa
explanation:
Ultrasound study of the right knee popliteal fossa
The physical examination is suggestive of a distended Baker's cyst, but physical examination alone is not diagnostic, particularly if there has been a dissection or rupture. Ultrasonography has been found to be very useful in making a diagnosis of popliteal cyst, with or without dissection, and is likely to be more readily available than magnetic resonance imaging. The radiologist can also inject the Baker’s cyst under ultrasound guidance.

Arthroscopy of the right knee
Arthroscopy of the right knee is incorrect. An arthrogram could also demonstrate a popliteal cyst but is less desirable because it is an invasive procedure.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right knee
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right knee is incorrect. An ultrasound will suffice and is usually faster and cheaper than an MRI. Furthermore the ultrasound may allow the radiologist to inject the Baker’s cyst, hence being diagnostic and therapeutic

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with lateral swelling and tenderness of both forearms. There is severe induration of the skin (peau d’orange) and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome with flexion contractions of the fingers. He denies having Raynaud’s phenomenon. Investigations show: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets 360 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l White cell count (WCC) 7.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Neutrophils 4.3 × 10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 10 9/l Lymphocytes 2.0 × 10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 1.5 × 10 9/l 0–0.4 × 10 9/l Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates hypergammaglobulinaemia. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Eosinophilic fasciitis
This patient has features of eosiniophilic fasciitis. The characteristic findings in eosinophilic fasciitis are: Swelling and tenderness of the forearms, with induration of the skin (peau d’orange) Carpal tunnel syndrome Flexion contractions of the fingers

stem: A 44-year-old man complaining of bone and joint pains is found to have osteopenia. His doctor feels that his present condition may be due to the lack of attainment of peak bone mass at around 30 years of age. What is the most important influence on peak bone mass attainment in an individual?
explanation:
Genetic factors
Genetic factors are the single most significant influencing factor for peak bone mass. Studies including the Hertfordshire Cohort Study suggest that birth weight is closely correlated to risk of osteoporosis, and body morphology including fat mass have a strong genetic component. After a peak at around 30 years of age there is a gradual decline in bone mass in men. In contrast, accelerated loss occurs in the 10 years following the menopause in women, because estrogen is protective.

Calcium deficiency
Calcium deficiency is incorrect. Calcium deficiency is a factor influencing bone mass, but the most important for peak bone mass is genetics.

Physical activity
Physical activity is incorrect. Physical activity is a factor influencing bone mass, but the most important for peak bone mass is genetics.

Sex hormone status
Sex hormone status is incorrect. Sex hormone status is a factor influencing bone mass, but the most important for peak bone mass is genetics.

stem: A 35-year-old Turkish man is referred with a suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT) to the Emergency Department by his General Practitioner (GP). He recently returned to the United Kingdom after a 1-year break in Turkey. While away, he was admitted once to the hospital with diarrhoea and abdominal pain, which was accompanied by multiple painful lesions in his mouth. A few days after discharge from the hospital, he presented again to the Emergency Department with an acute red and painful eye. He was sent home with eye drops for suspected conjunctivitis. A few months afterwards, the mouth lesions reappeared, but this time with similar lesions on his scrotum. At the same time, his ankle and wrist joints were swollen and painful. The lesions resolved after a few weeks, as well as the joint problems. He has no past medical history. On examination, he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38 °C. The left calf is swollen and tender, and there are several painful lesions on the extensor surface of both legs. The wrists and ankles are swollen and tender, and there are two well-demarcated ulcers on the roof of his mouth that are tender to touch. Investigation Result Normal value RF Negative Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) Negative (Hb) 88 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 14.0 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Platelets (PLT) 350 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 98 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 120 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 210 g/l < 10 g/l Doppler ultrasound (US) Popliteal deep vein thrombosis (DVT) RHEUMATO Given the likely diagnosis, what is the best management option for this patient?
options: Adalimumab 80 mg initially, with 40-mg dose after two weeks
Apixaban 10 mg twice a day for seven days, followed by 5 mg twice a day
explanation:
D Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day and azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day This man has orogenital ulceration, likely uveitis, inﬂammation in his bowels, erythema nodosum and a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), unprovoked as the ﬂight to Turkey is not long-haul. Behçet syndrome is characterised predominantly by inﬂammation of small blood vessels, leading to recurrent ulceration, especially in the oral and genital mucosa. It persists for many years, with characteristic painful oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, seronegative arthritis, thrombophlebitis, DVT and erythema nodosum. Venous thrombotic events are managed in Behçet syndrome by controlling inﬂammation with a combination of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide or ciclosporin. This is therefore the correct option from those listed. A Rheumatology specialist should be involved in this case to guide immunosuppressant choice and the need for anticoagulation treatment. B Apixaban 10 mg twice a day for seven days, followed by 5 mg twice a day Venous thrombotic events are managed in Behçet syndrome by controlling inﬂammation with a combination of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide or ciclosporin. A Adalimumab 80 mg initially, with 40-mg dose after two weeks Tumour necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors can be considered for severe Behçet syndrome and refractory venous thrombosis. However, they would be given in combination with corticosteroids, and therefore, this does not represent the best treatment option. C Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg/day Anticoagulants may be used in some patients, if the overall bleeding risk is low and coexisting pulmonary artery aneurysms are ruled out; however, they are not part of the standard treatment approach.

A specialist consultation should be completed for the choice of anticoagulant therapy in patients with Behçet syndrome. E Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day Steroid therapy alone is not the recommended management. A specialist consultation should be completed to guide the choice of immunosuppressant in combination with prednisolone

stem: A 43-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Her GP had observed Raynaud’s phenomenon, calcinosis and thickening of the skin affecting her ﬁngers, and telangiectasiae around her mouth and over her upper body. Her provisional diagnosis was systemic sclerosis. You conﬁrm the clinical features on examination, and her BP is 155/82 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 199 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ANA + Anti-RNA polymerase III antibody + Urine Protein+ Which of the following is she at risk of developing?
explanation: E Scleroderma renal crisis Different auto-antibody patterns are associated with differing patterns of disease associated with systemic sclerosis. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) tests positive in approximately 95% of patients with SSc, and therefore a negative test should prompt consideration of other ﬁbrosing illnesses. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are found in patients with diffuse disease, and are associated with rapidly progressive skin involvement as well as an increased risk for scleroderma renal crisis. These patients may also be at increased risk for cancer. D Pulmonary ﬁbrosis RHEUMATO Anti-Scl-70 antibody is generally associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and a higher risk of severe interstitial lung disease. A CREST syndrome CREST syndrome is a term no longer used, as not all patients fulﬁl the entire mnemonic. Rather, the ‘limited cutaneous’ terminology is preferred. B Features of rheumatoid arthritis Even if she had a rheumatoid factor (RF), this is non-speciﬁc and does not indicate propensity to develop features of rheumatoid arthritis. C Limited cutaneous disease only Anti-centromere antibodies are usually associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, and these patients are more likely to have pulmonary hypertension and gastrointestinal involvement.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with complaints of a non-productive cough and exertional dyspnoea that has been progressive over the past two years. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and consumes alcohol occasionally. He reports normal bowel activity but has had to urinate more frequently and has felt increasingly thirsty over the past six months. The patient also has back pain, with difﬁculty bending forward for the past four months. On examination, bilateral crepitations were present in the apical region of both lung ﬁelds. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 104 bpm. Oximetry revealed an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Which of the following investigations would conﬁrm the diagnosis in this patient?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of hip and spine with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 testing
explanation:
E Transbronchial lung biopsy A lung biopsy forms the mainstay of diagnosis of Langerhans cell

histiocytosis. Identiﬁcation of Langerhans cells, which are moderately sized with an irregular convoluted nucleus, is typical. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen and positivity for CD1a and S100 are conﬁrmatory. Additionally, electron microscopy may be useful for conﬁrmation by identiﬁcation of Birbeck granules. C High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) thorax While HRCT thorax would be useful in delineating the underlying pulmonary pathology, it is not useful in conﬁrming the diagnosis. In this patient who is a young smoker with interstitial lung disease, vertebral involvement and features of diabetes insipidus, the likely diagnosis is Langerhans cell histiocytosis. In these patients, HRCT thorax may show multiple apical cystic lesions, nodules, cavitating nodules and, in late stages, honeycombing of the lung. A Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage can help in the diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. However, its main utility lies in eliminating infections and other inﬁltrating disorders that can be seen in young adults. B Cytology for malignant cells Cytology for malignancy is neither sensitive nor speciﬁc and cannot be used for the diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. D Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of hip and spine with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 testing Hip and spine MRI will be helpful in the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis, which can also present with apical lung ﬁbrosis and cause back pain. However, the patient’s polyuria and polydipsia likely indicate diabetes insipidus and this is not likely to be caused by ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of diabetes presented to the clinic with bilateral knee pain. He works as an insurance salesman; he is a non-smoker but drinks on most weekends. He is on insulin for the diabetes and also takes sildenaﬁl occasionally for erectile dysfunction. On examination, he appeared suntanned with sparse body hair. The knees were swollen and tender, with limited range of movement. Investigation Result Normal values Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Albumin 35 g/l 35 - 55 g/l RHEUMATO Bilirubin 1.75 mg/dl 0.2 - 1.2 mg/dl ALT 75 u/l 7 - 55 u/l AST 65 u/l 10 - 40 u/l GGT 160 u/l < 50 u/l Glucose 14 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l LH 0.6 u/l 1.25 - 7.80 u/l (male) FSH 0.5 u/l 1.0 - 7.0 u/l Testosterone 6.8 nmol/l 9.0 - 35.0 nmol/l X-ray of the knees Calciﬁcation present What is the most likely cause of the joint abnormality?
explanation:
D Chondrocalcinosis Hereditary haemochromatosis should be suspected in patients with liver cirrhosis (liver function tests can often be normal), diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism and impotence, skin hyperpigmentation, fatigue and arthropathy. Biochemical ﬁndings include high serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation, and liver biopsy shows staining for excess iron. Arthropathy in hereditary haemochromatosis is due to calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition and can include pseudo-gout, chondrocalcinosis and chronic arthropathy. A Osteomalacia Bilateral knee joint pain is not a common presentation of osteomalacia, which is often asymptomatic. Bone pain and tenderness, fragility fractures, waddling gait and osteopenia on X-ray may be features. B Ochronosis Ochronosis describes the pigment deposition that occurs in the connective tissues of patients with alkaptonuria, an autosomal recessive disorder. Brown or blue–grey discoloration of the skin can be seen in the axillary and inguinal areas, face, palms or soles. The bronze appearance of the skin in this patient with the associated signs is not typical for alkaptonuria. C Cystinosis Cystinosis is a metabolic disease caused by the accumulation of cysteine, characteristically causing end-stage renal function. E Gout Bilateral knee involvement would be unusual for gout, which would present with hot, tender, swollen joints. Imaging ﬁndings

could include subcortical bone cysts. Monosodium urate crystal deposition is not associated with hereditary haemochromatosis.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with bony pain affecting his right hip and pelvis. He has a past history of prostatism, for which he received a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) some three years earlier. On examination, there is pain on right hip ﬂexion and internal and external rotation. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 121 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 191 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.3 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Prostate-speciﬁc antigen (PSA) 2.0 μg/l ALP 360 u/l 30 - 150 u/l X- ray of the pelvis is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Paget’s disease of bone RHEUMATO The X-ray shows severe degenerative disease in the right hip, along with cortical thickening. As is most common in the general population, these changes are found more so in the right hip than the left. The site described is a typical one for Paget’s disease, and the combination of raised alkaline phosphatase and normal calcium level also ﬁts with this. A radionucleotide bone scan may be useful at a later stage to determine the extent of disease. Both a prolonged oral course of bisphosphonates and intermittent intravenous courses are used for the treatment of Paget’s disease. These inhibit osteolysis and, as such, lead to a reduction in serum ALP levels (which can be used for serial measurements of treatment response) and reduce the pain associated with Paget’s disease. For patients who fail to respond to bisphosphonates or cannot tolerate them, calcitonin may be a suitable alternative. B Osteoarthritis of the right hip X-rays of osteoarthritis show sclerosis, without areas of osteolysis. The isolated elevated ALP level also ﬁts with Paget’s disease. A Metastatic prostatic carcinoma It is likely that his previous TURP was for benign prostatic hypertrophy. His PSA level now does not give any cause for concern and his calcium level is normal. C Myeloma His calcium level is normal; the ALP level is elevated, and there are areas of increased bone density on the X- ray, a picture that does not ﬁt with myeloma. E Hyperparathyroidism His calcium level is normal.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with a long history of asthma comes to the clinic for review. She previously had a myocardial infarction, aged 51. She is currently taking 500 μg ﬂuticasone inhaled bd and salbutamol prn. She complains of a further exacerbation and you prescribe her oral prednisolone. This is her eighth course of oral steroids over the past 3 years. Other past medical history of note includes vertebral fractures diagnosed after an episode of acute pain some 3 months ago. On auscultation of her chest you can hear wheeze throughout both lung ﬁelds. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l eGFR T score – 2.6 Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her osteoporosis?
explanation: C Alendronate Guidelines for osteoporosis recommend prescription of a weekly generic bisphosphonate in the ﬁrst instance. For patients who fail to tolerate a weekly preparation, monthly oral or more intermittent IV preparations may be appropriate. Strontium and teriparatide are reserved for patients with more severe osteoporosis. Her asthma therapy should be reviewed, with consideration of a long acting beta agonist. See also SIGN guideline on osteoporosis. E Calcium and vitamin D This patient is on glucocorticoids and has a fragility fracture (vertebral) and is osteoporotic on her DEXA scan (T score <–2.5). She therefore does need therapy and bone protection and calcium and vitamin D is insufﬁcient on its own. A Teriparatide While teriparatide does have some evidence for osteoporotic vertebral fractures, current NICE guidelines recommend bisphonates ﬁrst and teriparatide is reserved for more severe osteoporosis. B Ibandronate Guidelines recommend a weekly oral bisphosphonate ﬁrst, before an alternative of a different frequency. Ibandronate is given intravenously every 3 months. D Strontium Strontium is relatively contraindicated in patients with previous myocardial infarctions, or other thromboembolic diseases (eg pulmonary emboli) as it can increase the thrombotic risk.

stem: A 45-year-old Asian woman presents with 3-month history of difﬁculty climbing stairs. She also described non-speciﬁc pain all over her joints, the lower legs and upper arms. She has been seeing her general practitioner for her symptoms, and several analgesics have been tried, but her symptoms are not improving. She is on insulin for diabetes and bendroﬂumethiazide for mild hypertension. On examination there is slight tenderness on the upper arms and the lower legs but not at multiple trigger points. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/l 50–120 mol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.08 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Phosphate(PO43) 0.69 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Creatinine kinase (CK) 200 U/l 23–175 IU/l ALP 150 mmol/l 30–130 IU/l X-ray of the lower legs shows coarsened trabecular bone, no fracture. What diagnosis will you consider the most likely in her case?
