explanation: E Osteomalacia The patient has slightly low calcium, low phosphate and high ALP. Osteomalacia results from inadequate mineralisation of bone due to deﬁciency in vitamin D. Inadequate sunlight exposure (particularly in some Asian women who wear protective long clothing), in combination with dietary deﬁciency is often seen as a cause. Other causes of osteomalacia are chronic kidney disease, renal osteodystrophy, malabsorption and renal tubular defects etc. Osteomalacia may result in symptoms such as skeletal pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness and spontaneous fractures. X-ray of long bone is often normal but may show defective mineralisation, with the characteristic ‘Looser’s zone’ (pseudofractures). Biochemistry shows low calcium, phosphate, vitamin D levels and raised ALP. D Osteoporosis Osteoporosis is associated with normal bone proﬁle. A Fibromyalgia The patient has an abnormal bone proﬁle and does not have tenderness at multiple trigger points on examination. Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion. B Polymyositis RHEUMATO The patient’s main symptoms are generalised bony pain, she has an abnormal bone proﬁle and her CK is only mildly elevated. Osteomalacia can cause a proximal myopathy. C Osteoarthritis The patient’s bone proﬁle and her clinical features of generalised bone pain are suggestive of osteomalacia and she is too young for generalised osteoarthritis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue and difﬁculty sleeping, which have been ongoing for over a year. She describes her pain as 'aching all over' and notes that it often worsens with stress. She has been evaluated by multiple specialists, and extensive testing has ruled out other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and hypothyroidism. She has tried over-the-counter analgesics with minimal relief. Physical examination reveals multiple tender points, but no signs of joint inﬂammation or swelling. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 240 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l (TSH) 2.1 mIU/l 0.4–4.0 mIU/l ESR 10 mm/hour < 20 mm/hour Given this patient's diagnosis of ﬁbromyalgia, what is the best way to manage her symptoms?
options: Start high-dose NSAIDs on a daily basis
Refer to Rheumatology for immune-modulating therapy
Prescribe high-dose opioids for pain relief
Recommend a structured exercise programme combined with cognitive behavioural therapy
Initiate corticosteroid therapy to reduce inﬂammation
explanation:
D Recommend a structured exercise programme combined with cognitive behavioural therapy Exercise, particularly aerobic activity, has been shown to improve physical function and decrease pain in ﬁbromyalgia. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is also effective in helping patients manage the psychological aspects of chronic pain. Together, these non-pharmacological therapies form the basis of ﬁbromyalgia management, as per guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. A Start high-dose NSAIDs on a daily basis

NSAIDs have limited efﬁcacy in ﬁbromyalgia, as the pain is not primarily due to inﬂammation. They may provide some relief for mild musculoskeletal discomfort but should not be used as a primary treatment. B Refer to Rheumatology for immune-modulating therapy Immune-modulating therapies are unnecessary, as ﬁbromyalgia is not an autoimmune condition. Management should focus on lifestyle interventions, non-pharmacological therapies and, if needed, medications that target pain perception rather than immune function. C Prescribe high-dose opioids for pain relief Opioids are not recommended for managing ﬁbromyalgia due to their limited efﬁcacy in chronic pain syndromes and a high risk of dependency. Non-pharmacological strategies, such as exercise and CBT, have shown greater long-term beneﬁts for symptom control in ﬁbromyalgia patients. E Initiate corticosteroid therapy to reduce inﬂammation Corticosteroids are not indicated in ﬁbromyalgia, as it is a noninﬂammatory condition. This therapy would be ineffective and expose the patient to unnecessary side-effects.

stem: A 33-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents with a history of hair loss on her scalp without any regrowth. She is systemically well and denies any other symptoms. RHEUMATO Clinical examination revealed several patches of alopecia associated with scarring. There is no loss of hair anywhere else on her body but some erythematous plaques are also noted on the patient’s ears and cheeks. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Discoid lupus erythematosus In scarring alopecia destruction of the hair follicles has occurred and therefore hair loss is permanent. Common causes include discoid lupus erythematosus, lichen planus/frontal ﬁbrosing alopecia, and kerion from fungal infection. D Female-pattern alopecia Female-pattern (androgen-dependant) alopecia is associated with diffuse thinning of hair on the scalp due to increased hair shedding or a reduction in hair volume, or both. A Alopecia areata Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition associated with nonscarring, localised hair loss in circular patterns. Alopecia totalis describes widespread involvement of the same process with loss of all scalp hair and eyebrows, while alopecia universalis describes complete loss of all body hair. B Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism is a cause of sparse and brittle hair and nails, and is also linked to hair loss in the lateral third of the eyebrows. C Trichotillomania Trichotillomania describes a psychological disorder where patients are compelled to pull their own hair, resulting in alopecia. It is typically encountered in teenage females, leading to irregular patches of alopecia that are not commonly associated with a scarring process unless encountered in chronic, severe forms.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with acute gout. He has a history of type II diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and atrial ﬁbrillation. Medication of note includes ramipril, furosemide, digoxin, atorvastatin and insulin. He is also warfarinised. On examination, his BP is 142/82 mmHg and his heart rate is 78 bpm in atrial ﬁbrillation. He has obvious gout affecting his right ankle. Investigations: Investigation Results Hb 110 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l PLT 220 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l Creatinine 285 µmol/l Estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR) Which of the following therapies for gout would be the best choice taking into account he is warfarinised, although it may not currently be licensed for all forms of acute gout?
explanation: E Intrarticular steroid injection This is the best option, provided infection has been excluded, as a localised steroid injection into the affected joint will alleviate the symptoms from the acute attack and not upset the renal function but may upset his glycaemic control for short period. If done correctly, and in a patient with an INR below 5.0 (usual range is 2-3 or 3-4 if higher target), there is little to almost no risk of bleeding in a patient on warfarin over and above the usual population. C Prednisolone Although systemic steroids (prednisolone) will be effective and will not worsen his renal function directly, it might worsen his glucose control. A Colchicine There is some evidence that colchicine increases the INR and his eGFR is less than 30, therefore colchicine is ideally best avoided, if possible even at a 500 μg bd dosage. B Allopurinol Allopurinol should not be started in the acute attack of gout and can worsen the acute episode. Furthermore his renal function is very poor. D Naproxen RHEUMATO NSAIDs should not be used with this degree of renal impairment.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of lower back pain, particularly over the lateral lower spine on bending forward. The pain is worse in the morning; he was signed off from his job as a builder 6 months earlier due to an episode of plantar fasciitis. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 126 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 198 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.9 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 2.8 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 15 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 7.0 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 28 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 101 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 25 IU/l 5–30 IU/l (Anti-CCP) < 20 Rheumatoid factor (RF) Negative (ANA) Negative What is the best initial therapy in this case?
explanation:
C Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents and physiotherapy This man’s presentation is highly suspicious of spondyloarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis, ie. back pain onset < 40 years, morning stiffness and associated plantar fasciitis. Adequate pain relief and physiotherapy have a crucial role to play in the maintenance of function when the disease is diagnosed early. A Rest for a further 1 month Minimising activity, i.e. rest, is the worst thing this gentleman could do. Mobilising and exercise have a critical role in the management of spondyloarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis. B Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents NSAIDs, in combination with physiotherapy have been shown to have the best outcomes in ankylosing spondylitis.

D Sulphasalazine DMARDs, such as sulfasalazine, are used when patients have peripheral joint arthritis (eg a swollen knee), which this man does not. E Etanercept TNF-a antagonists such as etanercept are recommended by NICE if disease is still active despite two NSAIDs for at least four weeks.

stem: You review a 24-year-old man who has recently returned from a holiday in Spain. He complains of fever and malaise with associated myalgia and joint pain affecting his lower back, knees, ankles, and feet. He has burning and itching affecting his eyes and urethral discharge. On examination, he has balanitis and a psoriatic-type rash affecting his feet. You prescribe a course of antibiotics and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs. Which of the following is associated with an increased risk of the arthropathy described in this scenario?
explanation: E HLA-B27-positive status This man has the typical picture of reactive arthritis, most likely related to non-speciﬁc urethritis acquired while on holiday in Spain. Reactive arthritis should always be considered whenever a young adult presents with acute arthritis affecting the knees, ankles or feet. Reactive arthritis is a systemic inﬂammatory disorder characterised by an aseptic arthritis triggered by infections arising most commonly from the genitourinary and gastrointestinal site. Peak onset of reactive arthritis occurs in the 15–35-year-old age group. Reactive arthritis post-chlamydial infection is much more common in men, while the sex ratio of reactive arthritis post-dysentery is roughly equal between men and women. HLAB27 patients have been described as up to 50 times more likely to develop reactive arthritis than the rest of the population (Aho K. et al., HLA-B27 in reactive arthritis). In general, symptoms last from a few weeks to around 6 months in RHEUMATO total. However, recurrent arthritis is said to occur in 15–50% of reactive arthritis patients, and chronic persistent arthritis or sacroiliitis occurs in 15–30%. In HLA-B27-positive patients, ankylosing spondylitis may develop in up to 50% of patients who have suffered an episode of reactive arthritis. Rarer long-term complications include urethral stricture, cataracts and aortic root necrosis. Prognosis with respect to long-term complications is better when dysenteric infection is the precipitant factor rather than chlamydial infection. D Candida infection Candida infection is not linked with reactive arthritis, Chlamydia trachomatis is often indicated in sexually acquired cases of reactive arthritis. A Female sex Recurrent arthritis is more usually found in men, where it is approximately three times more common. B Age >50 years The peak onset of reactive arthritis occurs in the 15–35-year-old age group. C Coeliac disease Enteric-acquired reactive arthritis can occur up to 4 weeks after an acute episode of diarrhoea. However, there is no clear association with coeliac disease.

stem: A 60-year-old woman who is being treated with methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis has misunderstood the directions for therapy and presents to the surgery with glossitis, severe mouth ulcers and megaloblastic anaemia. On further questioning, it transpires she has been taking a dose of 40 mg per week, rather than 10 mg per week. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 98 g/l 115–155 g/l (MCV) 107 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 2.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Which of the following is the most appropriate rescue medication?
explanation:
B Folinic acid

The answer is Folinic acid (Option B). Unfortunately, medication errors with respect to rheumatoid arthritis are not uncommon. Patients occasionally ﬁnd it difﬁcult to understand that they must take their medication weekly, as opposed to daily. Calcium folinate is a potent antagonist for the effects of methotrexate on the haematopoietic system, given by intravenous (IV) infusion at doses of up to 75 mg in the ﬁrst 12 hours. This can then be followed by doses of 6–12 mg every 4 hours. Blood transfusion may also be required in exceptional circumstances. Where a massive overdose of methotrexate has occurred, hydration and urinary alkalinisation may be an option. Standard dialysis is ineffective in removing methotrexate, although intermittent high-ﬂux dialysis may be of value. A Vitamin B12 Vitamin B12 (Option A) is incorrect. Vitamin B12 deﬁciency can occur with decreased intake, eg veganism, decreased absorption, eg Crohn’s disease, coeliac disease, pancreatic insufﬁciency, pernicious anaemia, or with drugs that interfere with absorption such as metformin, antihistamines and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). Vitamin B12 deﬁciency causes macrocytic anaemia, jaundice, mental sluggishness and a shufﬂing gait. This is similar to the presentation of folate deﬁciency, but it is worth noting vitamin B12 deﬁciency occurs over years, while folate deﬁciency develops over months. The history of high dose of methotrexate makes vitamin B12 deﬁciency less likely than folate deﬁciency. C Vitamin C Vitamin C (Option C) is incorrect. Vitamin C, or ascorbic acid, deﬁciency causes scurvy. This is characterised by primarily cutaneous ﬁndings, including petechiae, bruising, perifollicular bleeding, gingivitis and arthralgia. Deﬁciency is primarily to a dietary lack of fruits and vegetables. It is primarily seen in patients with drug or alcohol dependence or in severe malnourishment. D Iron sulfate Iron sulfate (Option D) is incorrect. Iron deﬁciency can occur primarily due to decreased dietary intake, reduced absorption and blood loss. Presentation can include symptoms of anaemia, eg fatigue, weakness and angina pectoris, and signs such as pallor, cheilosis and koilonychia. There is no particular cause for the loss in this patient, and anaemia would be far more likely to be microcytic, rather than macrocytic, in nature. E Niacin Niacin (Option E) is incorrect. Niacin, or vitamin B3, deﬁciency causes a condition called pellagra. RHEUMATO This is characterised by photosensitive pigmented dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. Pellagra tends to occur in patients with malabsorption and in those with alcohol dependence. The absence of such clinical ﬁndings makes this an unlikely diagnosis and treatment.

stem: A 54-year-old man is admitted via the medical take. He has been seen on a number of occasions over the past few months by his general practitioner (GP) complaining of nasal stufﬁness. On this occasion, he presented with worsening cough, and two episodes of haemoptysis. Laboratory testing reveals a creatinine of 285 µmol/l, markedly raised ESR and positive c-ANCA. Chest X-ray reveals diffuse shadowing. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following options would you give as a component of initial therapy in this patient?
explanation: A IV methylprednisolone This patient has strong evidence pointing towards a diagnosis of Granulomatosis with polyangitis (GPA). This is a systemic vasculitis of mainly medium- and small-calibre vessels, and is associated with of systemic necrotising angiitis, necrotising granulomatous inﬂammation of the respiratory tract, and necrotising glomerulonephritis. This patient has evidence of lung involvement and established renal damage, and warrants intravenous therapy to establish remission. The gold-standard choice for intravenous induction is pulsed therapy with IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. Rituximab has been shown to be non-inferior to cyclophosphamide as the induction agent in recent clinical trials. IV steroids are later converted to oral prednisolone and a suitable steroid-sparing agent, such as methotrexate or azathioprine. It should be noted that patients on high-dose prednisolone and cyclophosphamide are at increased risk of pneumocystis pneumonia, and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be considered. Good prognosis in GPA is very RHEUMATO closely linked to early aggressive intervention, with over 90% of patients improving on cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone in combination; remission however is only achieved in 75%. E Azathioprine Steroid-sparing agents like methotrexate and azathioprine take 8–12 weeks before exerting any beneﬁt, and therefore are far too slow for an induction agent. They are used as maintenance of remission agents. B Prednisolone This patient has life- and organ- threatening vasculitis and needs steroids fast. The most effective route of administration, with the most rapid onset of action, is intravenous methylprednisolone, not oral prednisolone. C Hydrocortisone This patient has life- and organ-threatening vasculitis and needs steroids fast. The most effective route of administration, with the most rapid onset of action, is intravenous methylprednisolone, not intravenous hydrocortisone. D Methotrexate Steroid-sparing agents like methotrexate and azathioprine take 8–12 weeks before exerting any beneﬁt, and therefore are far too slow for an induction agent. They are used as maintenance of remission agents.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with painful and itchy swellings on her knuckles. These are worse after exposure to sunlight and have been problematic for her for several weeks. She has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes, two pregnancies, one miscarriage and hypertension. She currently takes metformin and ramipril. Apart from the changes on her knuckles, she has not noticed any other changes. She denies any other rashes, joint stiffness or breathing problems.
explanation:
B Dermatomyositis The photograph shows Gottron’s papules on the patient’s right hand. This is a clinical sign pathognomonic for dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is a chronic, autoimmune condition which affects proximal muscles and skin primarily, but can also cause cardiac, pulmonary and rheumatological complications. Peak onset is at 50 years old with a slow but steady progression, causing diffuse weakness in proximal muscles, fatigue and myalgia. Distal muscles are spared. There can be systemic upset with fever, malaise and weight loss. A heliotrope rash is pathognomonic, and there can be also a photosensitive rash. Investigation is with autoantibodies: ANA, anti-Mi and anti-Jo antibodies can help establish diagnosis, but muscle biopsy may be necessary as a diagnostic investigation. Steroid treatment may be successful, but immunosuppressive therapy can be used as secondary treatment. C Atopic dermatitis Atopic dermatitis is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, dry and red skin, which comes out in ﬂares of acutely inﬂamed, red and sometimes blistered skin. It affects particularly the ﬂexural surfaces. It does not cause plaques as this patient has, except in very chronic cases. The association with sun exposure also makes this less likely. A Psoriasis Psoriasis is chronic inﬂammatory dermatological condition deﬁned by salmon-red rash with silvery plaques. It has several types. The most common pattern of presentation affects extensor areas over limbs with involvement of scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft and groin. The pattern of this patient’s rash is different in distribution and the appearance is not consistent with psoriasis. D Lichen planus Lichen planus is a pruritic skin condition with polygon-shaped purple plaques on the lower back, wrists and ankles, as well as evidence of Wickham striae, white lines near sites of erosion. The location of this patient’s lesions does not match this diagnosis. Also, lichen planus is not worsened by sunlight. The mainstay of treatment for lichen planus is topical steroid treatment but can also include retinoids and UV light therapy.

E Dermatitis herpetiformis Dermatitis herpetiformis is a persistent immunobullous disease linked to coeliac disease and characterised by pruritic clustering blisters symmetrically distributed on scalp, shoulders, buttocks, elbows and knees. Management is with a gluten-free diet, and dapsone can be useful to reduce itch.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to his doctor for review. He has been suffering particularly from increased bony pain around his lower back and pelvic region over the past few months. Some degree of hearing loss was diagnosed two years ago. Blood testing reveals normal calcium levels but alkaline phosphatase is raised. X-rays reveal skull features consistent with Paget’s disease, and increased activity on bone scanning is seen in the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis. You commence bisphosphonate treatment. Which of the following represents the most appropriate way to monitor disease activity in this man?
explanation: B 6-monthly alkaline phosphatase levels The goals of therapy in Paget’s disease are to normalise bone turnover and achieve an alkaline phosphatase as a marker of this, in the normal range if possible. Bisphosphonates have become the mainstay of therapy, with daily, weekly, monthly and intravenous intermittent formulations now all possibilities for treatment. It appears that the more aggressive initial therapy is, then the longer a period of remission may be achieved. Alkaline phosphatase, as a non-invasive method, appears to be the best way to monitor disease activity. Levels should be checked at 6 months, and subsequently every 6-12 months. D 6-monthly calcium levels Calcium is normal in Paget’s disease. A 3-monthly alkaline phosphatase levels Alkaline phosphatase levels can take 3-4 months to normalise following treatment. C 6-monthly acid phosphatase levels Serum total acid phosphatase is an osteoclastic enzyme that may be elevated in active Paget’s disease, but is not as reliable in males as it can also be raised in prostate cancer. E Yearly isotope bone scan It is unclear whether normalisation of appearances on isotope bone scan correlates to clinical outcome. It is therefore difﬁcult to justify the use of serial bone scans to monitor treatment in view of the radiation dose involved.

stem: A 34-year-old woman complains of severe pain and aching in her ﬁngers and toes on going out into cold weather. She reports a triad of initial whitening of the ﬁngers resulting from vasospasm, followed by blue discoloration and then reddening and pain. She is currently taking atenolol 50 mg po daily for hypertension and takes methysergide for intermittent migraine. She has a history of reﬂux nephropathy and her creatinine is 180 μg/l. Her methysergide is discontinued. Which other intervention would be most appropriate for this patient?
options: Stop atenolol and start ramipril RHEUMATO
explanation: B Stop atenolol and start ramipril Both methysergide and atenolol are possible causes of Raynaud’s phenomenon, or can exacerbate existing Raynaud’s as described here. Other causes include ergotamine, vinblastine, bleomycin and oral contraceptives. ACE inhibitors also have the best evidence for reno-protection where there is underlying autoimmune pathology. Calcium channel antagonists such as nifedipine may be of value in improving symptoms. D Start diclofenac 50 mg po tds NSAIDs are contraindicated given her kidney disease and would not improve her Raynaud’s symptoms in any case. A Start isosorbide dinitrate There is no evidence for nitrates in improving Raynaud’s symptoms. C Start prednisolone 40 mg po daily There are no features of underlying connective tissue disease and this may well be primary Raynaud’s or related to medications. Raynaud’s phenomenon has many causes, including systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, polycythemia and thromboangiitis obliterans. E Start verapamil Although verapamil is a calcium channel blocker it is not used for Raynaud’s, unlike nifedipine (and even amlodipine).

stem: A 34-year old woman is due to be discharged after being admitted for iloprost infusion for systemic sclerosis. She was admitted due to poorly controlled digital ulceration.
explanation: C Pulmonary function tests and echocardiogram This patient has systemic sclerosis and is at risk of developing complications. Complications of systemic sclerosis include: • respiratory: pulmonary ﬁbrosis, pulmonary hypertension, aspiration pneumonia and pulmonary haemorrhage • gastrointestinal: gastroesophageal reﬂux disease (GORD), peptic strictures, dysphagia, bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption • renal: malignant hypertension, angiopathic haemolytic anaemia and intermittent renal crisis. Systemic sclerosis should be monitored in terms of skin and complications. Skin monitoring is done by measuring skin tightness and interlabial distance which can be combined into the Rodnan skin score. Annual monitoring for internal organ pathology includes screening for interstitial lung disease and pulmonary artery hypertension, and therefore requires pulmonary function tests, transthoracic echocardiogram and ECG on an annual basis. A Oesophageal manometry Patients with systemic sclerosis may develop oesophageal reﬂux and swallowing problems. If the patient develops symptoms then they should be investigated with oesophageal manometry to assess dysphagia, and they may also need barium swallow to further assess them. Without symptoms, these investigations are not needed. B High-resolution computed tomography (HR CT) chest HR CT scan of the chest is indicated in patients with systemic sclerosis if pulmonary function tests demonstrate a restrictive picture. HR CT can then help diagnose and characterise the extent of pulmonary ﬁbrosis. D Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Cardiac MRI can be useful in the assessment of cardiac scleroderma, which is cardiomyopathy of the heart in the context of systemic sclerosis. This can present with shortness of breath, decreased exercise tolerance, chest pain and palpitations. Cardiac MRI is useful for patients presenting with these symptoms in the context of systemic sclerosis but is not generally used as annual monitoring. E Right heart catheterisation Right heart catheterisation is the gold-standard investigation to assess pulmonary arterial hypertension, a complication of systemic sclerosis. However, echocardiogram is done to screen for pulmonary hypertension and then patients who are suspected of pulmonary hypertension are further investigated with right heart catheterisation. RHEUMATO

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness over the past two months, primarily affecting her shoulders and hips. She ﬁnds it increasingly difﬁcult to lift objects and rise from a seated position. She denies any recent infections, respiratory symptoms or rashes. On examination, there is symmetrical proximal muscle weakness in the upper and lower limbs. There is no muscle tenderness or joint swelling. Her vital signs are normal, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 148 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 350 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 40 mm/hour Less than 20 mm/hour Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Which investigation would best conﬁrm a diagnosis of polymyositis in this patient?
explanation:
B Muscle biopsy Muscle biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing polymyositis, as it can conﬁrm muscle inﬂammation, ﬁbre necrosis and the presence of inﬂammatory inﬁltrates, all of which are characteristic of polymyositis. Muscle biopsy is essential for distinguishing polymyositis from other inﬂammatory and non-inﬂammatory muscle disorders. C Antinuclear antibody testing Antinuclear antibody testing can be positive in polymyositis but is non-speciﬁc, as it is also positive in various autoimmune diseases. It does not conﬁrm polymyositis speciﬁcally and is typically used to assess associated connective tissue diseases. A Electromyography Electromyography (EMG) can detect muscle abnormalities typical of inﬂammatory myopathies such as short- duration, low-amplitude polyphasic potentials and spontaneous ﬁbrillations. However, EMG ﬁndings are not speciﬁc to polymyositis and cannot alone conﬁrm the diagnosis without histopathological evidence. D MRI of the muscles MRI can reveal muscle oedema and inﬂammation, which may support the diagnosis of an inﬂammatory myopathy. However, it does not provide the deﬁnitive histopathological evidence needed to

conﬁrm polymyositis and is often used to guide the biopsy site rather than for diagnosis alone. E Rheumatoid factor test Rheumatoid factor is not typically associated with polymyositis. Its level may be elevated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or other rheumatological diseases, but it does not contribute to a diagnosis of polymyositis.

stem: A 44-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with an 8-hour history of chest pain. She reports the pain to have gradually worsened as the day continues and she is struggling to take deep breaths. The pain radiates across the front of her chest and is worsened on breathing and coughing. She has taken paracetamol for the pain which has provided only some relief. Her past medical history includes irritable bowel syndrome and ﬁbromyalgia. She takes regular duloxetine and recently started over-the-counter vitamin supplementation after recently recovering from inﬂuenza. On examination, she is afebrile. Her heart rate is 66 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 123/77 mmHg. She is warm peripherally and her calves are soft and non-tender bilaterally, with no evidence of oedema. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal and chest sounds are clear, with oxygen saturations of 98% on room air. Palpation of her anterior chest wall causes severe discomfort. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen. Chest X-ray: clear lung ﬁelds Electrocardiogram (ECG): normal sinus rhythm Bloods: pending Assuming the likely diagnosis, what is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
explanation: D Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) This patient has costochondritis characterised by tenderness of the costochondral and chondrosternal joints of the anterior chest wall. Pain may have an acute or gradual onset and can be described as sharp, aching or like a pressure sensation. Exacerbating symptoms include coughing, deep inspiration and physical activity. Before the onset of symptoms, there is often a history of recent illness or strenuous exercise. This patient’s symptoms started shortly after an illness with inﬂuenza and is reproducible on chest wall palpation, RHEUMATO suggesting a diagnosis of costochondritis. Treatment of choice includes regular analgesia, particularly NSAIDs like ibuprofen. A Corticosteroids Corticosteroid injections may play a role in reducing inﬂammation in costochondritis. However, they are not the ﬁrst-line recommended treatment. B Lidocaine 1% patch Lidocaine patches are not frequently used to treat costochondritis. First-line measures such as oral analgesia should be trialled initially. Adding to this, this patient seems to have chest pain across her entire anterior chest wall requiring the need for several patches. C Low-molecular weight heparin Low-molecular-weight heparin is used in the treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE) such as pulmonary embolism (PE). PE can cause pleuritic chest pain and should be considered as a differential diagnosis. From the clinical history and examination, a Wells score should be calculated for any patient with a potential diagnosis of PE. There are some missing criteria to accurately calculate a Wells score in this patient. However, the lack of hypoxia and tachycardia and the presence of soft and non-tender calves, along with reproducible chest wall pain, make the diagnosis of PE less likely. E Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) plays a role in the treatment of chronic pain syndromes such as ﬁbromyalgia. Fibromyalgia is characterised by widespread pain that can frequently fail to improve with regular analgesia. Other illnesses often coexist with ﬁbromyalgia such as irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache and atypical chest pain. However, the onset of chest pain after a recent viral illness is less likely to be ﬁbromyalgia and regular analgesics should be trialled before referral for CBT.

stem: A 24-year-old White woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-day history of left-knee swelling and pain. She denies trauma and has never had issues with her joints before. On further questioning, she reports feeling feverish and nauseated with lower abdominal discomfort but puts that down to menstrual cramps. Her past medical history includes coeliac disease and hypothyroidism. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 80 bpm and a BP of 125/75 mmHg. Auscultation of her chest is clear with oxygen saturations of 98% in air. Her left knee is erythematous and warm to the touch. It is swollen and immobile due to both pain and swelling. Her abdomen is mildly tender in the right upper quadrant and suprapubic regions, but there is no guarding. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: A Neisseria gonorrhoeae This patient likely has disseminated gonococcal disease, given the history of acute-onset left-knee swelling associated with fever, swelling and reduced mobility. The additional symptoms of abdominal discomfort, particularly in the suprapubic and right upper quadrant, are also suggestive of gonococcal arthritis and other complications of N. gonorrhoeae infection, such as Fitz–Hugh–Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis). Disseminated gonococcal arthritis is caused by the Gram-negative organism N. gonorrhoeae for which the treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone. Gonococcal arthritis tends to affect young, healthy adults who are sexually active, and women are more frequently affected than men. B Salmonella enterica S. enterica is a much rarer cause of septic arthritis, and osteomyelitis and is mostly associated with patients with sickle cell anaemia. It is unlikely to be the causative organism in this patient. C Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common organism associated with non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Non-gonococcal arthritis is more common in the elderly population, particularly those with co-existing joint disease or prosthetic joints. In contrast, this patient is a young female making other organisms, such as N. gonorrhoeae, more likely to be the cause. D Staphylococcus epidermidis S. epidermidis is a commensal organism and is less likely to be the cause of septic arthritis. It is more commonly seen in patients who are immunocompromised. Nevertheless, the presentation of a young woman with symptoms and signs of an infected joint along with a history of abdominal pain is more suggestive of N. gonorrhoeae. E Streptococcus pyogenes S. pyogenes (group A streptococcus) is another common cause of non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Patients infected with group A streptococcus are usually very acutely unwell with signs of septic shock. It is less likely to be the causative organism in this patient. RHEUMATO

stem: A 49-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of painful mouth ulcers. He also mentions intermittent diarrhoea, and occasional colicky abdominal pain. Until a year ago, his general health had been good, but he has felt generally unwell recently with diffuse aches and pains. Six months ago, he required ophthalmological investigation and treatment for anterior uveitis. At this time, he also developed superﬁcial venous thrombophlebitis at two different venepuncture sites. Oral lesions noted on examination are shown in the photograph below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Behçet’s disease Recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers are the most common lesions associated with Behçet’s disease and occur in 99.3% of cases. Genital ulcers may also be present. At least 50% of patients who have Behçet’s disease also develop gastrointestinal erosions and ulcers that may cause abdominal pain, melaena, and even perforation. This constellation of intestinal signs and symptoms may simulate Crohn’s disease and other inﬂammatory bowel disorders. However, a distinguishing feature between the two conditions is the phenomenon of pathergy (a condition in which minor trauma can lead to the development of further blistering lesions), which is characteristic of Behçet’s syndrome. Ocular involvement is seen in about 70% of patients; most often in

the form of anterior or posterior uveitis. Other manifestations include musculoskeletal (arthralgias/arthritis in 50%); skin (erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions, thrombophlebitis, and cutaneous hypersensitivity); central and peripheral nervous system lesions; and vascular lesions. Behçet’s syndrome can involve both the arterial and venous systems, and typically presents as superﬁcial thrombophlebitis or deep venous thrombosis. The cause and pathogenesis of Behçet’s disease remain unknown, but the tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) pathway is likely implicated. E Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disorder that can affect multiple organs. Common manifestations include: fatigue, loss of weight, interstitial lung disease, erythema nodosum, lupus pernio, conductive cardiac abnormalities, and uveitis. B Crohn’s disease Extraintestinal involvement of Crohn’s could lead to similar symptoms; however bowel symptoms would be the predominant feature and superﬁcial thrombophlebitis would not be typical. C Ulcerative colitis As with Crohn’s disease, the symptoms of ulcerative colitis (UC) may be similar but are usually intestine predominant. Additional commonly encountered extraintestinal symptoms of UC and Crohn’s disease include arthritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum. D Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is associated with diarrhoea, abdominal cramping and bloating. The commonest cutaneous manifestation is of dermatitis herpetiformis.

stem: A 69-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe tiredness, temporal headaches and jaw claudication when she tries to eat. She has a history of hypertension, for which she takes ramipril, but is otherwise well. Examination reveals a BP of 155/95 mmHg; her heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally and visual ﬁelds are full to confrontation. She is tender over the temporal arteries bilaterally. Her weight is 98 kg. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 101 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythromycin 75 mm/1sthour 0–10 mm/1sthour RHEUMATO sedimentation rate (ESR) Steroids are to be commenced. What dose of steroids is recommended?
explanation:
B 60 mg prednisolone daily The lethargy, temporal headaches and jaw claudication in combination with a raised ESR indicate possible giant cell arteritis. Treatment should be prompt and response is usually seen in the ﬁrst 48 hours, sometimes taking up to seven days. In the absence of visual symptoms, guidelines recommend oral prednisolone at a dose of 40-60 mg daily with a slow taper. The usual treatment duration is between 12- 18 months with careful observation for relapses. A 1g intravenous methylprednisolone for 3 days Patients with suspected or conﬁrmed giant cell arteritis with visual manifestations require urgent corticosteroid therapy. No trials have been conducted in these patients with threatened vision, but it is recommended that either intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500mg-1g daily for three days followed by oral prednisolone therapy or oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg (or between 60-100 mg daily) with a taper thereafter. Here, as no visual symptoms or signs are reported, such high-dose steroids are not required. C 8 mg hydrocortisone twice daily Hydrocortisone has a much shorter half-life than prednisolone. The approximate equivalent dose of prednisolone 60mg is 240 mg of hydrocortisone daily, usually split into 3 or 4 doses. Such a prescription would only be warranted in an IV form as a temporary measure if the patient was nil by mouth or unable to eat or drink for an alternate pathology. A dose of 8mg of hydrocortisone twice daily is a huge underdosing of corticosteroids and is unlikely to control the patient’s symptoms. D 20 mg prednisolone daily Giant cell arteritis has a high level of morbidity. Complications include ischaemic visual failure, stroke and polymyalgia rheumatica. Although no randomised controlled trials of therapy exist, the standard dosing of patients with suspected giant cell arteritis without threatened vision is 40-60 mg prednisolone initially. A long

slow taper is then undertaken. 20 mg prednisolone is unlikely to control symptoms and may result in complications. E 1mg/kg prednisolone daily Where vision is threatened in giant cell arteritis a larger dose of corticosteroids is urgently warranted. This is usually given in the form of pulsed methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone starting at 60 mg. Where pulsed methylprednisolone cannot be given, then 60-100mg of oral prednisolone is recommended in current guidelines. With no sign of visual symptoms or signs here, this is not required.

stem: A 65-year-old woman, known to have stable rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years, has been re-referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with symptoms of chronic foul-smelling diarrhoea. She says she has lost 10 kg in weight in last 6 months. Her general appetite is quite poor as well. She ﬁnds herself quite lethargic and has noticed peripheral oedema early in the mornings. According to her, her joints have not troubled her for a long time. She is currently on methotrexate and folic acid. On examination, she has waxy skin, with plaques clustered in the axillary folds, and multiple bruises are seen. No lymph nodes are palpable. Joint examination showed no evidence of synovitis. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm, blood pressure (BP) 140/90 mmHg and respiratory rate (RR) 16 breaths/min. Heart sounds are normal, and she has good air entry bilaterally, with no added sounds. Abdominal examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. There is no ascites, and no other masses are felt. Central nervous system examination shows evidence of peripheral neuropathy. Investigation Result Normal values Sodium (Na+) 143 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.8 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Liver function tests Normal Thyroid function tests Normal CRP 20 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 9 mm/h 1 - 22 mm/h 24-h urinary analysis Shows 5 g of proteinuria Chest X–ray Shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette Electrocardiogram (ECG) Shows low-voltage QRS complexes Which one of the following will be of most diagnostic value?
options: Serial sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis (TB) culture
explanation: C Rectal biopsy This patient has many of the hallmarks of systemic amyloidosis. An abdominal fat biopsy or a rectal biopsy is the best way to make the diagnosis. A positive Congo red histological stain helps to establish diagnosis. The AA type of amyloid is seen secondary to a host of chronic inﬂammatory conditions, including long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, familial Mediterranean fever, and leprosy. Amyloidosis should be suspected in any patient with an underlying chronic inﬂammatory disease who develops hepatosplenomegaly, malabsorption, cardiac disease or proteinuria. Cardiac disease usually consists of congestive heart failure with low QRS-complex voltage and exquisite sensitivity to digitalis. Echocardiography shows a characteristic speckled appearance and may also be helpful in contributing to the diagnostic process. Waxy papules in the axillary folds may signal the deposition of amyloid in the skin; purpura after minor skin trauma is not uncommon. In addition to amyloid-induced synovitis, peripheral neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome may be seen. B Serial sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis (TB) culture Given respiratory examination is normal and there are no symptoms of cough, TB is unlikely as the cause of her current symptoms. A Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy Bone marrow aspirate may reveal amyloid deposits, but it is signiﬁcantly more invasive, when compared to a rectal biopsy, and is therefore not the preferred option. RHEUMATO D Nerve conduction studies Although nerve conduction studies are likely to be abnormal as a result of amyloidosis, they will not provide a histological diagnosis. E Faecal elastase Faecal elastase is used as a screening test for pancreatic insufﬁciency, and although malabsorption is suspected, there may be other reasons for it to occur here such as bacterial overgrowth due to gut dysmotility.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He complains of multiple joint pains, particularly affecting his back, wrists, ankles and feet, with clear distal interphalangeal joint involvement. On examination, he has psoriatic patches on his elbows. There is onycholysis, transverse ridging and pitting on examination of his nails. DIP swelling, pain and restricted movement is noted. He is started on and methotrexate but on return to the clinic there is no improvement. You elect to treat him with adalimumab. The mode of action of adalimumab is mediated through which of the following?
explanation:
D TNF-α Adalimumab is anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody. Adalimumab, etanercept and inﬂiximab are anti-TNF agents which show some degree of efﬁcacy as second-line agents in the management of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. TNF-α is thought to play an important role as a cytokine leading to worsening of joint inﬂammation and destruction. C IL-23 Ustekinumab has recently been approved by NICE for the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, and is an IL-12/23 antagonist. A CRP While CRP and ESR may well fall in response to anti-TNF therapy, they are more non-speciﬁc markers of inﬂammation.

B ESR While CRP and ESR may well fall in response to anti-TNF therapy, they are more non-speciﬁc markers of inﬂammation. E IL-12 Ustekinumab has recently been approved by NICE for the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, and is an IL-12/23 antagonist.

stem: You are seeing a 54-year-old woman in the clinic. She has had rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for the past 4 years and is on treatment with methotrexate 20 mg per week. She complains of pain in the joints of the bothhands with tingling/numbness over the thumb and lateral two ﬁngers, these being present for the last 6 months. The pain in her joints is present all the time and is worse in the mornings. Paraesthesia occurs intermittently and awakens her in the night. Examination reveals mild swelling and tenderness over the small joints of the hands and wrists. There is no motor or sensory deﬁcit on neurological examination. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 114 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 234 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 38 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 11 mg/l < 0 mg/l What would be the most appropriate further investigation at this stage?
options: Urgent magnetic resonance (MR) scan of the cervical spine
Routine MR of the cervical spine
explanation: E Electromyogram (EMG)/nerve conduction studies This patient has carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), as evident by paraesthesia in the hands especially at night. CTS occurs as a result of compression of the median nerve at the wrist and characteristically affects the thumb and lateral two ﬁngers. It is seen commonly in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), most often due to entrapment of the median nerve by synovial swelling. Treatment includes the use of resting hand splints, local corticosteroid injections or median nerve release surgery. An electromyogram (EMG)/nerve conduction study is useful for conﬁrming clinical diagnosis prior to actual surgery. RHEUMATO B Routine MR of the cervical spine This lady has carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is usually compressed at the wrist. Cervical spine imaging is not indicated. A Urgent magnetic resonance (MR) scan of the cervical spine This lady has carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is usually compressed at the wrist. Cervical spine imaging is not indicated. C X-ray of the hands X-rays are not helpful in the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome or assessing RA disease activity, but may be useful in detecting damage resulting from RA. D MR of the hands MRI imaging of the hands may not show median nerve compression. It is very expensive and an insensitive method for detection of carpal tunnel syndrome. MR imaging may be helpful in looking for RA disease activity,although an ultrasound is cheaper and faster (but less sensitive).

stem: A 28-year-old white man presented with a 2-week history of fever and chills followed by a widespread papular rash over his body. One week ago, he noticed that his wrist and ankle were swollen and tender. The inﬂammation resolved a few days later, but now his right knee is very swollen and tender and he can barely weight-bear on it. He works as a computer salesman and he was in Thailand until 2 weeks ago on a business trip. On examination, his right knee is hot and swollen and there are a few pustular lesions on his trunk. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 136 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 13.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 88 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Rheumatoid factor (RF) Negative ANA Absent Synovial ﬂuid white cells > 20 000/μl What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
C Gonococcal arthritis Disseminated gonococcal infection is caused by the bacteraemic spread of the sexually transmitted bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The syndrome described in this patient is the dermatitis– polyarthritis–tenosynovitis syndrome, symptoms including fever, symmetrical polyarthralgia (small or large joints), tenosynovitis and dermatitis (painless vesiculopustular lesions). Diagnosis is made by culture of synovial ﬂuid, skin lesions and specimens from urethral swabs. Treatment includes symptomatic relief with NSAIDs and ceftriaxone and azithromycin. B Reactive arthritis Reactive arthritis would be in the differential diagnosis, but the pres-

ence of white cells in the synovial ﬂuid indicates joint infection rather than an inﬂammatory response to remote infection, as is the case in reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis also typically presents with the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis. A Acute gout The age, social history and associated signs are not typical for acute gout, which usually presents as a mono- arthritis. D Tuberculous arthritis TB arthritis tends to occur in the knee and hip, which is subacute in onset. It is uncommon in developed countries and would not explain the associated signs. E Pseudo-gout The age, social history and associated signs are not typical for pseudo-gout, which usually presents as a mono- arthritis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with episodic discoloration of the ﬁngers of both hands – white followed by a bluish tinge – ﬁrst noticed 2 years ago. She has otherwise been ﬁt and healthy and denies any previous medical problems. Which of the following investigations would be most useful in determining whether the Raynaud’s is related to vasculitis?
explanation: E Nail fold capillaroscopy This young woman has symptoms of Raynaud’s syndrome. It will be important to differentiate between primary and Raynaud’s secondary to connective tissue disease (CTD). The most useful initial assessment must include nail fold capillary loop examination, ideally by capillaroscopy or, if not available, by ophthalmoscope using magniﬁcation. Patients with CTD such as systemic sclerosis most RHEUMATO often will show a positive ANA and dilated, distorted, missed nail fold capillary loops (i.e. with gaps – areas of drop-out). A RFtesting The RF is non-speciﬁc and is found in multiple conditions, including infections. B Antinuclear antibody testing A close second to nail fold capillaroscopy. Measurement of anti-nuclear antibodies, whilst being non-speciﬁc, may provide additional clariﬁcation for Raynauds. C X-ray of the hands X-rays are likely to be completely normal, even in secondary Rayaud’s associated with connective tissue disease. D X-ray of the chest X- ray of the chest is useful to determine whether cervical ribs are present, as a cause of Raynauds, but not to determine any other causes.

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Over the past few months, she has developed a photosensitive rash, which is particularly prominent on her face, and small joint polyarthritis which is affecting her job as a data operator. You note evidence of active arthritis affecting her ﬁngers, wrists, both elbows, and her feet. Urine is positive for both blood and protein.
explanation:
B Anti-nuclear antibody The rash seen here is suggestive of the erythematous changes seen in patients with active SLE, as is the evidence of arthritis and renal vasculitis. Anti-nuclear antibody testing has a sensitivity of 95% for SLE, but the titre is not closely related to disease activity. As such, other measures, such as complement testing, are more useful in assessing this. A Anti-CCP Anti-CCP antibodies are a marker of disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis. Although that may be a reasonable alternative diagnosis, the facial rash is a stronger pointer towards systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) here. C Anti-Scl 70 Scl 70 positivity is a marker of diffuse systemic sclerosis, which is not suggested here because of the absence of other features such as sclerodactyly and peripheral calcinosis. D c-ANCA c-ANCA positivity is most associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, in which pulmonary and renal vasculitis is seen, often with evidence of chronic sinusitis. There is no evidence of pulmonary vasculitis here. E p-ANCA p- ANCA positivity is seen in around half of patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is usually

associated with symptoms of poorly controlled asthma. It is also seen in patients suffering from primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem: A 76-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with progressively worsening joint pain and mobility. She is struggling to get dressed in the morning and to achieve small tasks such as carrying a cup of tea. The pain is constant throughout the day, although it improves with rest and paracetamol. Her past medical history includes hypothyroidism, for which she takes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. On examination, her observations are recorded within normal limits. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. She has crepitus over the hip and knee joints. There is a visible deformity to her proximal (PIPJs) and distal interphalangeal joints (DIPJs) (shown below). There are no skin or nail changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Osteoarthritis (OA) OA is a degenerative arthritis affecting multiple joints. The pathological basis of the disease is characterised by loss of cartilage and signiﬁcant articular and periarticular inﬂammation. No single cause RHEUMATO has been identiﬁed, but risk factors for OA include obesity, trauma, repetitive injury (eg in extreme sport) and certain diseases leading to secondary OA such as pre-existing joint disease and metabolic disease (eg haemochromatosis). Symptoms of OA include joint pain with clear functional limitation. Unlike inﬂammatory arthritis, OA does not have a typical pattern of early morning joint stiffness that improves throughout the day. Restricted movement, joint effusions and crepitus are all signs of OA. OA of weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees, as well as OA of the hands, are common. DIPJs are more often involved than PIPJs. This photograph shows a patient with bony swellings at the DIPJs (Heberden’s nodes) and PIPJs (Bouchard’s nodes), which are commonly seen in OA. C Psoriatic arthritis Psoriatic arthritis belongs to a group of spondyloarthropathies associated with the HLA-B27 antigen. Skin changes may or may not be seen. A common pattern of joint disease is distal interphalangeal arthritis with adjacent nail dystrophy. In approximately 5% of patients with psoriatic arthritis, severe deformity, known as arthritis mutilans, secondary to severe periarticular osteolysis and bone shortening may occur. The pattern of joint disease in this patient, combined with the clinical history, is more suggestive of OA. A Gout Gout is a crystal arthropathy associated with hyperuricaemia. Causes of hyperuricaemia include chronic kidney disease, a purinerich diet and drug therapy, including thiazide diuretics. Gout presents as an acutely painful joint, typically in the ﬁrst metatarsal joint. Men are more commonly affected than women. The clinical history does not suggest that this patient has hyperuricaemia and the pattern of joint involvement does not reﬂect gout, making it an incorrect answer. D Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a symmetrical, polyarticular inﬂammatory arthritis associated with synovial inﬂammation. It is more common in women. Early morning stiffness is a common complaint, with joint pain and stiffness improving throughout the day. Hand disease in RA commonly involves the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCPJs), causing a subluxation deformity referred to as ulnar deviation. RA of the PIPJs can cause ﬁxed ﬂexion deformities (Boutonnière deformity) or ﬁxed hyperextension (swan neck deformity). These are not the changes seen in this patient. That, combined with the clinical history of progressive pain that fails to improve throughout the day, is more suggestive of osteoarthritis. E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an inﬂammatory autoimmune disorder affecting multiple organ systems, including the car-

diovascular, renal and nervous systems. The disease commonly involves the skin and joints, causing arthralgia and distinctive rashes such as the ‘butterﬂy rash’ across the face. Although it is more common in women, SLE is usually diagnosed between 20 and 40 years of age. It is less likely for this patient to be presenting with her ﬁrst symptoms of SLE at 76 years of age.

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of feeling lethargic and feverish with a loss of appetite. He also reports aching joints starting with his upper limbs and now affecting his lower limbs, particularly his left knee, which he reports to have become very tender and swollen in the last 24 hours. There is no history of trauma, and he has no past medical history of note. However, he did visit his General Practitioner earlier in the week due to experiencing burning on micturition. On examination, his left knee is erythematous, swollen and warm to the touch. He is reluctant to extend his knee due to pain. There are multiple vesicular lesions over these extremities which he reports to be new. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation: A Ceftriaxone This patient likely has disseminated gonococcal arthritis, given the history of polyarthritis and acute-onset knee pain, swelling and erythema. It is not uncommon for patients with gonococcal arthritis to experience extra- articular features such as urethritis, tenosynovitis and cutaneous symptoms, including a papular or vesicular rash, most commonly on the extremities. The history of burning on micturition is suggestive of underlying urethritis in this scenario. Disseminated gonococcal arthritis is caused by the Gram-negative organism Neisseria gonorrhoeae for which the treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone. C Flucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is used in the treatment of non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Non-gonococcal arthritis is more common in the elderly population, particularly those with co-existing joint disease or prosthetic joints. Men are more likely to be affected than women and RHEUMATO the causative organisms also differ with the most common being Staphylococcus aureus, followed by streptococcal species and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Given the young age, history of dysuria, and a vesicular rash gonococcal arthritis secondary to N. gonorrhoeae should be expected. B Colchicine Colchicine is used in the treatment of gout and Behçet syndrome. Key features of Behçet syndrome include oral and genital ulceration, uveitis and musculoskeletal involvement. Meanwhile, gout presents with acute-onset inﬂammation of a joint (mostly the ﬁrst metatarsal joint) with risk factors including male sex, age over 40 years and dietary habits including high red meat, seafood and alcohol intake. Neither of these conditions matches the presentation of this patient, making colchicine a less appropriate management option. D Naproxen Naproxen and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs are the ﬁrst line of choice for osteoarthritis and reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis is a sterile synovitis triggered by an infectious agent outside of the joint. The most common examples include sexually transmitted diseases, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and dysenteric infections such as Salmonella, Shigella, Clostridium and Yersinia species. However, the systemic upset, along with the history of polyarthritis, vesicular rash and dysuria make gonococcal arthritis the more likely diagnosis. E Prednisolone Prednisolone is used in the treatment of inﬂammatory arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis. However, it is uncommon for inﬂammatory arthropathies to cause fever, reduced appetite and dysuria, and these symptoms suggest an underlying infective cause.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chest pain to the Emergency Department. She smokes approximately 30 cigarettes per day. There is no history of hypersensitivity to non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents. There is pain with coughing and deep breathing, with tenderness of the 2nd to 5th costochondral junctions with the sternum. Chest X-ray is unremarkable and electrocardiogram (ECG) shows no acute changes; saturations are 98% on air. Which of the following would be the most appropriate intervention in this case?
explanation: C Naproxen 250 mg qds This patient has costochondritis (Tietze syndrome), which has a higher prevalence in women and is commoner over the age of 40 years. It is associated with tenderness over the costochondral junctions and/or sternum, pain on coughing and deep breathing, and equal involvement with both sides of the chest. Non-steroidals would be an appropriate ﬁrst-line intervention for pain relief. It is of course an ideal opportunity to reinforce advice about smoking cessation. D Amoxicillin 500 mg po tds This lady does not have productive cough, fever, raised CRP or crackles on examination, and therefore antibiotics in this case are inappropriate and may perpetuate antibiotic resistance. A Low-molecular weight heparin A pulmonary embolism is very unlikely given the normal ECG, lack of tachycardia, normal oxygen saturations on room air and tenderness on palpation of the chest wall. B Aspirin 75 mg po Aspirin 75 mg would be inadequate to treat acute coronary syndrome, which is unlikely in any case given her lack of ECG changes and no mention of cardiac enzymes being elevated. E Fluticasone 50 μg inhaler bd There is no suggestion that this is an exacerbation of asthma – she has no wheeze or dyspnoea, but does have pain on palpation of her chest wall at the costochondral junction.

stem: A 67-year-old man, who has previously been given a diagnosis of osteoarthritis, presents to the Acute Medical Assessment Unit with pain in his ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. He has a past history of hypertension, for which he takes bendroﬂumethiazide 5 mg/day. On examination, the joint is hot and red and has a knobbly appearance. The X-ray is shown below: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient?
options: Stop bendroﬂumethiazide and substitute a calcium antagonist
Advise dietary restriction of rich foods
explanation: C Stop bendroﬂumethiazide and substitute a calcium antagonist The X-ray shows erosive changes in the ﬁrst MTP joint, with wellmaintained joint space and coexisting soft tissue swelling. This, along with the presentation, demonstrates that the patient has chronic tophaceous gout, which is usually associated with chronic renal impairment and long-term use of diuretic therapy. Deposits of sodium urate occur in the skin and around joints; larger deposits are unsightly and may ulcerate. Diuretics should be substituted for another medication where the condition is associated with diuretic use. B Start ibuprofen Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs are beneﬁcial as a shortterm therapy in ﬂares but should not be continued long-term due to their implication on renal function. A Start allopurinol This patient has chronic tophaceous gout. If a patient is already receiving urate-lowering therapy, then there is no value in suspending RHEUMATO it during an acute ﬂare, and subsequent reintroduction may precipitate an attack. In the absence of any urate-lowering attack, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend the use of xanthine-oxidase inhibitors, such as allopurinol or febuxostat, ﬁrst line. Uricosuric drugs, such as sulﬁnpyrazone or benzbromarone, can be used second line where prescribed by a specialist. D Start ﬂucloxacillin The description and radiological ﬁndings are not consistent with septic arthritis, and ﬂucloxacillin is not an appropriate empirical antibiotic for this indication. E Advise dietary restriction of rich foods The NICE guidelines recommend eating a healthy, balanced diet rather than following any speciﬁc diet. There is not enough evidence that speciﬁc diets sufﬁciently lower urate levels.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the General Medical Clinic. He is concerned as his wife has pointed out that his ears look different. He has a past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, recurrent joint pain and steatohepatitis. Aside from the joint pain, he has not noticed anything abnormal in terms of pain or itch. He has otherwise been feeling well, without any other pain or systemic problems. He currently takes ramipril, atorvastatin and amlodipine.
options: Staging computed tomography (CT) scan of head and neck
explanation: D Allopurinol This patient has gouty tophi on his ears. It is likely given this that he has undiagnosed recurrent gout given his history of recurrent joint pain. Gouty tophi are nodular masses of monosodium urate crystals deposited in soft tissue and are a sign of chronic hyperuricaemia. Starting urate-lowering treatment would be appropriate to prevent further attacks of gout. Measuring serum urate would be appropriate to ensure adequate response. As allopurinol is started, he should also be given treatment for acute gout as allopurinol can, in the ﬁrst instance, precipitate an acute attack. A Excision biopsy of lesion The lesions presents are not consistent with malignancy. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can arise on the ears as they are in a sun-exposed area. These lesions are hyperkeratotic lesions which often develop a central ulcer which can bleed and are often itchy. There is also usually only one lesion. B Staging computed tomography (CT) scan of head and neck RHEUMATO Staging scanning is appropriate when a malignant melanoma has been conﬁrmed. Melanomas are usually characterised by ﬂat, irregular, multichromatic lesions with changing appearance. They are also usually pigmented. If these features were present, the initial step would still be to do a biopsy to conﬁrm the nature of the lesion. C Prednisolone Systemic steroid therapy would be an option for acute gout, not for chronic gout. E Stop ramipril In most patients with gout, the excess or urate arises from failure of excretion. It is important to stop thiazide diuretics for these patients, but not ramipril. Ramipril is important to maintain renal function by preventing hypertensive nephropathy.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of type II diabetes returns to the Foot Clinic for review one week after beginning coamoxiclav for an ulcer on his left heel. He and the chiropodists feel that it is not improving signiﬁcantly. Examination reveals a 2-cm diameter lesion affecting the left heel. There is fresh pus and exudate around the edge of the lesion, and your probe easily reaches the bone. CRP is still elevated at 170 mg/l (185 at presentation). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Osteomyelitis is a possibility and should be excluded as soon as possible with MRI. In the event there is evidence of osteomyelitis, then surgical review for possible debridement is the most appropriate next step. At this point, further blind antibiotic therapy without imaging evidence is not advised. C Admit for intravenous (IV) vancomycin Vancomycin IV is effective against staphylococcal infection. However, with the possibility of mixed infection here, coupled with possible osteomyelitis, MRI scanning is a more appropriate next step.

A Add rifampicin Adding rifampicin may be useful in the event of deep-seated staphylococcal infection, although it will not achieve clearance in the event there is signiﬁcant osteomyelitis, and this must be ruled out ﬁrst. B Add clindamycin Although clindamycin achieves very good tissue penetration and has good activity against staphylococcal infection, it is most important to rule out osteomyelitis, which may require surgical resection ﬁrst. D Continue co-amoxiclav This is the least appropriate option here. It is clear that infection is not improving with co-amoxiclav, and both investigation for osteomyelitis and a change of antibiotic therapy are likely to be required. While adding rifampicin, clindamycin and vancomycin could all be considered for deep-seated staphylococcal infection, they should only be considered as part of a treatment strategy which includes MRI and orthopaedic review. Continuing co-amoxiclav alone is not an option.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of a painful right knee. He reports that he is now unable to bear weight on his knee due to pain despite taking regular paracetamol. During this time, he also complains of lethargy and reduced appetite. He has a past medical history of Crohn’s disease which is well-controlled with azathioprine. On examination, he has a temperature of 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 110 bpm and regular, with a BP of 105/65 mmHg. His right knee is swollen and erythematous with a ﬁxed-ﬂexion deformity. There is a papular rash over the extremities. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 145 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 14.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 255 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 45 mm/h < 15 mm/h What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Gonococcal arthritis This patient likely has gonococcal arthritis given the history of acute-onset knee pain, swelling and erythema with low-grade fevers and raised inﬂammatory markers. A ﬁxed-ﬂexion deformity is highly suggestive of a septic joint, like in gonococcal arthritis. Furthermore, it is not uncommon for patients with gonococcal arthritis to experience extra-articular features such as urethritis, tenosynovitis and cutaneous symptoms, including a papular or vesicular rash, most commonly on the extremities. Gonococcal arthritis tends to affect young, healthy adults who are sexually active, and women are more frequently affected than men. B Gout Gout is caused by the deposition of urate crystals, causing attacks of acute inﬂammatory arthritis. The most affected joint is the ﬁrst metatarsal, although the knee, ankle, wrist and hand can also be affected. Risk factors for gout include male sex, age over 40 years and dietary habits, including high red meat, seafood and alcohol intake. This patient is unlikely to have gout based on the lack of these features. A Behçet syndrome Behçet syndrome is a chronic multisystem inﬂammatory disorder that classically presents as recurrent oral ulceration. The onset of symptoms is typically between the ages of 30 and 40 years with men and women being equally likely of developing the disease. Key features of Behçet syndrome include oral and genital ulceration, uveitis and musculoskeletal involvement. This does not completely ﬁt with this patient’s presentation, making it unlikely here. D Pseudogout Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate deposition, causing an acute inﬂammatory arthritis. Many different joints can be affected by pseudogout, including the knees. Generally, pseudogout affects older people or those with certain metabolic conditions such as haemochromatosis or hyperparathyroidism. The presence of low-grade fever and systemic symptoms makes pseudogout very unlikely. E Reactive arthritis Reactive arthritis is a sterile synovitis triggered by an infectious agent outside of the joint. The most common examples include sexually transmitted disease, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and dysenteric infections such as Salmonella, Shigella, Clostridium and Yersinia species. The post-sexually transmitted disease form is approximately ten times more common in men, while post-dysenteric disease affects men and women equally. Not all infections will go

on to produce reactive arthritis, but it is an important consideration to have when a person presents with acute joint pain, especially young and healthy adults. Features of reactive arthritis include arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis. Mucocutaneous symptoms include circinate balanitis (erythematous and ulcerative lesions on the glans penis), keratoderma blennorrhagia, and nail involvement is also seen, including thickening and onycholysis. It is uncommon for reactive arthritis to cause a systemic upset, as seen in this scenario, making gonococcal arthritis more likely to be the diagnosis.

stem: A 58-year-old self-employed man presents with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnoea and fatigue. He complains of a painful rash on the backs of his hands. He also reports redness on the face and the central upper chest. The rash worsens after sun exposure. He has not noticed any blisters. On further questioning, he has noticed a signiﬁcant weight loss with reduced appetite. He takes regular analgesics for migraines. He is allergic to penicillin. He is a non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 100 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 490 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CRP 40 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 30 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Liver enzymes Normal Creatine kinase (CK) 860 IU/l 23–175 IU/l Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) + Chest examination Unremarkable Abdomen examination Unremarkable Central nervous system (CNS) examination reveals the following: RHEUMATO Investigation Result Cranial nerves Intact Tone Normal throughout Reﬂexes Intact Power 5/5 except hip ﬂexors 4/5 Other Downgoing plantars bilaterally; no sensation deﬁcits What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Dermatomyositis Clues include the violaceous eruption and nail-fold inﬂammation seen in the image, history of photosensitivity, positive ANA and elevated CK. Dermatomyositis is a rare disease in which a characteristic rash is associated with myositis. When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma. It is more common in females. Typical features include: • A red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema. • Violaceous ‘Gottron’s papules’ over the knuckles. • Linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the ﬁngers. Nail-fold inﬂammation with dilated capillaries. • The ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck. • Weakness of the major proximal muscle groups, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’). • Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difﬁculties in swallowing or breathing. • Calciﬁcation can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis, but is uncommon in adults. • Investigations should include creatine kinase, antinuclear antibody and skin biopsy; electromyography and/or muscle biopsy can conﬁrm myositis.

Screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases. C Polymyalgia rheumatica This causes muscle pains and stiffness, but is not associated with rash. A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Although ANA positivity and photosensitivity would ﬁt with this, and SLE frequently involves the skin, the eruption in the photograph is very suggestive of dermatomyositis. B Porphyria cutanea tarda This is another photosensitive disorder, but it typically leads to blistering at sun-exposed sites. There is usually a history of chronic liver disease. ANA positivity and raised inﬂammatory markers would not be expected. D Guillain–Barré syndrome This is a disorder of the peripheral nervous system which presents with weakness and paraesthesia, usually beginning in the legs. It usually follows an infection and is not associated with a rash.

stem: A 59-year-old man presents with an acute pain and effusion in his right knee. He is on haemodialysis for chronic kidney disease related to type 1 diabetes and takes a number of medications including vitamin D and cinacalcet. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/89 mmHg, his pulse is 80 bpm regular, his temperature is 37.6 °C. He does not appear to be ﬂuid overloaded. He has psoriatic plaques on knees and elbows. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.7 × 10 /l 4–11 × 10 /l Platelets 179 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Corrected Ca 2.15 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Creatinine 540 µmol/l (pre-dialysis) 50–120 µmol/l Knee effusion Neutrophils and rhomboid crystals identified,weakly positively birefringent Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
