explanation: C Pseudogout This man has end-stage kidney disease and hyperparathyroidism, as evidenced by his cinacalcet prescription, and his low normal calcium. Hyperparathyroidism is associated with pseudogout (chondrocalcinosis) which may present acutely as an oligoarthritis, similar to gout, in shoulders, elbows or ankles or knees. Diagnosis is based on negative culture, and non- or weakly positively birefringent rhomboid or rod-shaped crystals. NSAIDs are used in patients without renal dysfunction, but may worsen salt and water retention and blood pressure in this patient, so colchicine may be a more appropriate choice. B Hydroxyapatite arthritis Hydroxyapatite crystals are associated with a very destructive type of arthritis, usually in the shoulders of elderly women; heavily blood stained ﬂuid is usually found. A Gout Gouty crystals are needle shaped and negatively birefringent. D Psoriatic arthritis Although this patient has psoriasis, the presence of crystals in the synovial ﬂuid make a crystal arthritis far more likely. E Osteoarthritis The history is too acute for osteoarthritis and the synovial ﬂuid ﬁndings crystalize the diagnosis of pseudogout.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with a 10-day history of feeling unwell. She describes fever, a rash on her body that has now cleared, and currently has pain in her left knee. She tells you that she has had a few eye infections in the past that cleared up and often gets swollen joints, as she is a keen gymnast. She takes no regular medications and has no allergies. She has not been abroad recently. She has previously had similar episodes in the past affecting both her knees and has felt that other joints were involved too. These have been episodic in nature over the last 2 years. She had seen her GP at the time who wanted to investigate with blood tests, but she declined due to needle-phobia and managed her pain with over the counter ibuprofen. On examination she is thin. Her temperature is 38.7 °C. She has cervical lymphadenopathy. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mm/Hg; pulse 106 bpm regular. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Auscultation of the chest is unremarkable. There is a splenic tip palpable on abdominal examination. Her left knee is swollen and tender and there is evidence of a small effusion. Investigations are as follows: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 118 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 13 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 190 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ESR 90 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Blood ﬁlm NAD Joint aspirate Microscopy, Culture & Sensitivity No growth after 48 h Urine microscopy and culture Paul–Bunnell test No abnormality detected Negative Three days later, while in hospital, she develops painful wrists and pain on neck movement. Cardiovascular examination reveals a new friction rub but no evidence of cardiac failure. Which diagnosis should be considered?
explanation: C Juvenile idiopathic arthritis The initial presentation with fever, pain and swelling of the left knee with a prodromal history makes a diagnosis of infective arthritis important to exclude. Occasionally acute leukaemia can cause a pyogenic arthritis but the normal blood ﬁlm excludes this. The progression of symptoms suggests a systemic disease. The most important differentials to consider are therefore rheumatic fever, juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and rheumatoid arthritis. The history of similar joint problems with a chronic relapsing course starting before the age of 16 makes missed JIA a strong possibility. Cervical spine involvement is more common in JIA. D Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease working in multiple immunological ways including immune complex formation and deposition and complement activation. It is relapsing-remitting with variable symptoms including fatigue, malaise, fever with lymphadenopathy, weight loss Raynaud’s and migraine. It is often associated with a malar rash and a discoid rash, as well as non-erosive arthritis of peripheral joints. However, the presentation is very early for this diagnosis and the joint involvement is far more likely to be of small joints and symmetrical. A Lyme's Disease RHEUMATO Lyme disease is a tick-borne infection of Borrelia burgdorferi causing erythema migrans at the site of infection, which expands. It causes systemic features as well, including fatigue, myalgia, myocarditis, arthralgia and fever. The absence of a tick bite and erythema migrans makes this diagnosis unlikely, and it would also not explain the joint effusion. B Rubella This is a very unlikely diagnosis in general due to vaccination, and also does not explain the presence of pericarditis or joint effusion. E Infectious mononucleosis Mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and following 4-5 weeks incubation causes symptoms in adolescents. It is commonly contracted in early childhood and causes no symptoms there. It can a cause fever, sore throat and lymphadenopathy, as well as splenomegaly. A negative Paul–Bunnell test makes infectious mononucleosis unlikely. It would also not explain cardiac or arthritic involvement.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents to Rheumatology Clinic after noticing a new swelling on the side of his ﬁnger. He has noticed that the swelling has been worsening over the past several months. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He normally takes methotrexate, paracetamol, ramipril, atorvastatin and aspirin.
explanation: B Rheumatoid nodule This patient has developed a rheumatoid nodule. These are ﬁrm swellings in subcutaneous tissue, often occurring over bony prominences, but also in the lungs. A quarter of patients with RA develop nodules which are usually asymptomatic. They consist of ﬁbrous layers. Methotrexate can make nodules worse, while rituximab can make them better. Surgical removal is often successful. C Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) BCCs are slow growing and locally invasive epidermal tumours of the skin. They occur in sun-exposed areas. They are small and have a pearly or translucent appearance with telangiectasia. The absence of such features makes this an unlikely diagnosis. A Xanthoma Xanthomas are ﬂat, yellow plaques appearing in the 30s or 40s, typically in women. The lesions tend to become static and do not regress. They are associated with high cholesterol-rich beta-lipoproteins (LDLs). This nodule, however, is not ﬂat and does not have the typical yellowish colour. D Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) SCCs are malignant tumours arising from keratinising cells of the epidermis and can be locally invasive and sometimes metastatic. Presentation is as an individual nodular keratinising or crusting lesion which can ulcerate. There is some variety in presentation, but typically it is a small nodule which progressively grows, becomes RHEUMATO necrotic and sloughs. The absence of such features makes this an unlikely diagnosis. E Keratoacanthoma Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing squamous lesions that appear over months and spontaneously resolve. They are solitary, round and skin coloured or reddish papules which may project like a horn. The absence of a centre keratin horn-like structure makes this unlikely.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic. He has suffered from arthritis for many years but is now ﬁnding it very difﬁcult to manage at home, particularly with respect to cooking food and eating. His hands have become progressively more disﬁgured. He takes thyroxine 100 µg/day and amlodipine. He is otherwise well, a scar over his neck is noted. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 126 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 151 × 109/l 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.4 mmol/l 2.2–2.7 mmol/l ESR 30 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Psoriatic arthritis This patient has long-standing arthritis with arthritis mutilans. Shortening, particularly of the distal interphalangeal joints, is consistent with psoriatic arthritis. It is likely that this patient’s active disease burnt out some time ago, given that the routine blood tests are in the normal range. B Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is associated with ﬁnger stiffness and the formation of Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes rather than bone resorption and deformity, which seem apparent here. A Hyperparathyroidism Although hyperparathyroidism does result in the shortening of the distal phalanx, it is not associated with the more proximal deformity seen in this patient, and the blood tests are all in the normal range. C Pseudohypoparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with the shortening of the ﬁfth metacarpal and hypocalcaemia, rather than the picture of arthritis mutilans seen here. E Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with arthritis mutilans in advanced diseases. However, the predominantly distal features of this patient’s disease count against rheumatoid arthritis, as opposed to psoriatic arthritis, as the cause in this patient.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of fever, lethargy and a generalised macular rash, which comes and goes. Before the episode, he was well. He had no previous medical history or recent illness and there was no recent travel abroad. On examination, temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, pulse of 100 bpm. The chest was clear and there were no heart murmurs on auscultation. A widespread non-blanching macular rash is seen over the chest and abdomen. There is swelling of the interphalangeal joints of both hands and feet with slight tenderness. Lymph nodes are palpable on the supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal regions. Examination of the abdomen also reveals a palpable mass on both right and left hypochondrium. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 135 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 14.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 380 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 89 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l RHEUMATO Rheumatoid factor (RF) Negative ANA Negative Anti-dsDNA Negative Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titre Not detected Electrocardiogram (ECG) Sinus rhythm What is the most likely underlying diagnosis from the choices listed below?
explanation: E Systemic Still’s disease Systemic Still’s disease and other forms of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) usually begin before the age of 16 years. There are different types of JRA with different presenting features. Systemic Still’s is characterised by systemic features, high fever, rashes, generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly with minor features of arthritis. Systemic features may precede the onset of arthritis. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies are absent. C Pauciarticular Still’s disease In pauciarticular Still’s disease, antinuclear antibodies are present. Large joints are affected and most patients develop classic features of seronegative spondyloarthritis. A Acute rheumatic fever The history is too long, the ASO titre is negative and there are no features of carditis with a normal ECG and PR interval. B Juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus The antinuclear antibody is negative and there are signiﬁcant systemic features (high fevers). D Reactive arthritis The history is too long, there is no infective precipitant and the generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly does not ﬁt with reactive arthritis.

stem: A local general practitioner (GP) asks you to review a 42-year-old woman who has suffered from symptoms of oesophageal reﬂux disease that have only partially responded to proton-pump inhibitors. She has recently started to complain in particular about cold weather, and may have Raynaud’s phenomenon. Routine blood testing has revealed a raised creatinine of 180 µmol/l, and she is hypertensive with a blood pressure of 170/85 mmHg. Which one of the following agents is the best treatment to ameliorate further renal impairment?
explanation: A Ramipril ACE inhibitors are seen as the treatment of choice for renal disease associated with systemic sclerosis (the diagnosis here). This lady should be seen in Casualty, as she may have scleroderma renal crisis. In systemic sclerosis, interlobular renal arteries are affected with intimal thickening, and ﬁbrinoid changes occur in afferent glomerular arterioles. The pathogenesis is unknown, and neither steroids nor immunosuppressive therapy appears to have an effect on the progression of renal disease. In contrast, treatment with ACE inhibitors has positive effects on proteinuria and appears to halt or even reverse decline in renal function in some cases. Prostacyclin infusion may be of additional beneﬁt in cases where renal function is rapidly deteriorating. D Prednisolone Steroids may provoke/trigger renal crisis and should be used sparingly or in caution with patients who have scleroderma. High-dose steroids can be useful in patients with pulmonary ﬁbrosis, pleural inﬂammation, pericarditis or other systemic manifestations of systemic sclerosis, commenced at high dose which is gradually reduced and then withdrawn. However, steroid treatment is not a valid option to ameliorate further renal impairment. B Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. ACE inhibitors are seen as the treatment of choice for renal disease associated with systemic sclerosis. Calcium channel blockers may be used in the treatment of Raynaud’s, where they reduce the frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks. Calcium channel blockers can also be useful in patients who have systemic sclerosis with lung involvement. C Bendroﬂuazide Bendroﬂuazide is a thiazide diuretic, and thiazides are moderately RHEUMATO potent diuretics. Because of their negative effects on glucose tolerance, they are no longer the recommended ﬁrst-line treatment for hypertension, but are useful in the treatment of mild to moderate heart failure. Thiazides are ineffective if eGFR is <30 ml/min/1.73 m2, and have no reno-protective beneﬁts. E IV methylprednisolone Methylprednisolone may be used in certain cases of highly active inﬂammatory disease while long-term treatment is commenced. However, steroids may provoke/trigger renal crisis and should be used sparingly in patients with scleroderma; this is therefore not the best treatment option to ameliorate further renal impairment.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents the Acute Medical Unit with an acutely swollen and sore left knee. She and several family members who attended a family BBQ experienced acute-onset abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea that lasted several days, just one week previously. She also reports a gritty sensation in her eyes. Examination reveals a swollen left knee which is warm to touch but maintaining a good range of motion. Synovial ﬂuid examination is sterile, with a raised neutrophil count. Her knee pain is uncontrolled despite the maximum dose of naproxen. What is the next most appropriate management for the knee symptoms?
explanation:
A Intra-articular steroid injection The question describes a combination of oligoarthritis with a sterile aspirate and likely conjunctivitis following GI symptoms. The most likely diagnosis is reactive arthritis, probably following Campylobacter jejuni infection acquired from undercooked poultry. Treatment consists of treating the underlying cause and symptomatic management with non-steroidal analgesia initially. For symptoms uncontrolled with NSAIDs, intra-articular glucocorticoids are indicated. Following this, systemic steroids can be used; however, they are only required in a minority of patients. C IV ﬂucloxacillin Flucloxacillin is indicated for an acutely septic joint, although the sterile aspirate indicates this is not the cause in this patient.

B Azithromycin PO Azithromycin can be used in the treatment of chlamydia and gonorrhoea but would be unhelpful in the absence of any current infective symptoms, as here. D Prednisolone PO Steroids are indicated in the management of knee pain, which does not resolve following treatment with NSAIDs in reactive arthritis. Given the possible adverse effects with systemic administration, intra-articular steroids are used preferentially to PO steroids. E Methylprednisolone IV Methylprednisolone is usually used IV for suppression of inﬂammatory disorders such as relapse of multiple sclerosis or transplant graft rejections. Given possible adverse effects with systemic administration, intra- articular steroids are used preferentially to PO steroids. If systemic steroid administration is required, then PO prednisolone would be preferred over IV methylprednisolone in this case.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has been admitted from clinic with severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA). She has symptoms of persistent synovitis, despite taking high-dose weekly methotrexate, non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatories and low-dose prednisolone. The consultant has discussed pros and cons of starting biological therapy. What of the following criteria would rule out inﬂiximab as an option for this patient?
explanation: B Coexistent multiple sclerosis Evidence from intervention trials with anti-TNF agents in inﬂammatory bowel disease and arthritis have suggested increased risk of new demyelinating diseases in patients prescribed them. The mechanism as to why this happens is unclear, as it is not consistently reﬂected in animal models of multiple sclerosis. Other contraindications for anti-TNF agents include: • Active serious infection ( invasive fungal infection or bacterial infection) • Doses >5 mg/kg in patients with moderate-to-severe heart RHEUMATO failure (NYHA Class III/IV) • Active tuberculosis (patients should also be screened for previous infection before starting therapy). Previous severe hypersensitivity reaction to inﬂiximab or known hypersensitivity to any component of inﬂiximab or to any murine proteins. It would be prudent to note that pregnancy and lactation is not absolute contraindications to inﬂiximab. Inﬂiximab products cross the placenta and can detect up to six months following birth; recommend waiting at least six months following birth before administering of any live vaccine to infants exposed in utero to inﬂiximab products. C Asthma Although TNF is not a target for patients suffering from asthma, anti-TNF agents do not worsen symptoms of asthma. A Coexistent psoriasis Psoriasis is a target disease for treatment with anti-TNF agents and data show a consistent improvement in symptoms associated with therapy. D Gout Anti-inﬂammatory agents may impact on the acute phase of gout, although anti-IL1-based agents probably have the greatest positive effect rather than anti-TNF. E Glaucoma Anti-TNF agents have no negative effect on intra-ocular pressure or symptoms of glaucoma.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She complains of increasing bony pains and proximal muscle weakness. Her Crohn’s is currently relatively under control. She is taking azathioprine only and her CRP is only just above the normal range. Her consumption of dietary calcium has been increased since her last operation nine months earlier. She opens her bowels 3–4 times per day. Past surgical history includes three small bowel resections. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg; pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, she has the scars from previous surgery, and her body mass index (BMI) is 19 kg/m2. She has proximal myopathy affecting the hips and shoulders. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 105 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 167 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 87 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 18 mg/l 0–10 mg/l ALT 41 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 195 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 29 g/l 35–55 g/l Calcium 2.0 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: E Vitamin D This patient is most likely to have malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins due to multiple previous bowel resections. The fat-soluble vitamins are vitamin A, D, E, K. Her symptoms and blood picture are consistent with osteomalacia and vitamin D supplementation will therefore improve her condition. A Calcium supplements Although calcium supplementation would help correct the low calcium, it is likely the low calcium is a result of vitamin D malabsorption. Therefore, calcium supplements would be not clinically indicated unless adequate vitamin supplementation does not correct the calcium. B Cholestyramine Cholestyramine is a treatment option for diarrhoea associated with bile acid malabsorption. It is a binding agent and does not directly affect absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. C Codeine Codeine is a treatment option for bile acid malabsorption associated diarrhoea and does not directly affect absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. D Increased Azathioprine The clinical symptoms and blood tests reﬂect a malabsorption disorder secondary to previous bowel resection, there is no value in increasing the azathioprine dose.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1day history of anterolateral chest pain. He noticed the onset of pain while cooking dinner and describes the pain as sharp in nature, made worse on taking in deep breaths. He feels slightly breathless and unable to take full breaths of air. He denies fever or coryza but has a slight residual cough from a viral infection one week ago. His past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, for which he takes amlodipine, ramipril and atorvastatin. He smokes 5– 10 cigarettes per day. On examination, his temperature is 36.2 °C. He has a heart rate of 88 bpm, with a blood pressure of 150/89 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute and oxygen saturations of 99% on room air. His heart sounds are normal, with a capillary reﬁll time of < 2 seconds. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen. There is reproducible chest pain on palpation of his sternum and anterior chest wall. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 4.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.5 × 109/l Lymphocytes 3.6 × 109/l 0.8–5.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 367 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.3 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 62 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l eGFR 69 ml/min/1.73 m2 60+ ml/min/1.73 m2 D-dimer 350 ng/l < 400 ng/l Fibrinogen 2.1 g/l 2–4 g/l Troponin 14 ng/l 0–14 ng/l CRP 9 mg/l < 10 mg/l Electrocardiogram (ECG) – sinus rhythm Chest X-ray – pending What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Costochondritis This patient has costochondritis characterised by tenderness of the costochondral and chondrosternal joints of the anterior chest wall. Pain may have an acute or gradual onset and can be described as sharp, aching or like a pressure sensation. Exacerbating symptoms include coughing, deep inspiration and physical activity. Before the onset of symptoms, there is often a history of recent illness or strenuous exercise. This patient has reproducible chest pain following a recent viral illness, in addition to normal laboratory investigations, making the diagnosis of costochondritis most likely. C Pneumonia A secondary bacterial lower respiratory tract infection may follow from a recent viral illness; pneumonia should be considered in patients presenting with chest pain and shortness of breath after a recent viral infection. This is particularly true following infection with inﬂuenza, as pneumonia secondary to Staphylococcus aureus is a well- known complication. However, the presence of normal inﬂammatory markers and normal chest sounds makes the diagnosis of pneumonia less likely. B Pericarditis Pericarditis is inﬂammation of the pericardial sac often, but not always, triggered by a viral or bacterial illness. Other causes include uraemic pericarditis and post-myocardial infarction pericarditis (Dressler syndrome). Symptoms include sharp central chest pain that is made worse when lying ﬂat and relieved by sitting forward. The ECG is diagnostic of pericarditis and often shows PR-segment depression and saddle-shaped ST-segment elevation, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads aVR and V1. Cardiac enzymes such as troponin may be normal and pericarditis and raised levels indicate damage to the myocardium. The presence of a normal ECG makes the diagnosis of pericarditis less likely. D Pneumothorax A pneumothorax, particularly secondary pneumothorax, should be considered in a patient with chest pain and shortness of breath and a history of smoking. However, the presence of equal breath sounds RHEUMATO bilaterally, makes the diagnosis of a pneumothorax less likely. E Pulmonary embolism (PE) PE is an important differential to consider for patients with pleuritic chest pain. However, the absence of tachycardia and hypoxia, along with a negative D-dimer, suggests an alternative diagnosis.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with progressive swelling of both hands and shortness of breath. She has noticed her hands becoming whiter at times for many years. More recently, she has started to experience dyspnoea on exertion of up to 400 yards, with occasional palpitations. The patient has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 20 years and drinks 14 units of alcohol a week. She currently takes lansoprazole prescribed by her General Practitioner for gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease. On examination, her hands reveal evidence of calcinosis. Autoantibodies are checked, which reveal a positive anti-centromere antibody. Which is the most likely cause of this patient’s exertional dyspnoea?
explanation:
E Pulmonary artery hypertension This patient has ﬁndings in keeping with a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Scleroderma is a rare multisystem chronic condition of unknown cause. It is characterised by tissue ﬁbrosis, small blood vessel vasculopathy (Raynaud’s phenomenon) and autoimmunity. Diffuse scleroderma is characterised by both cutaneous and visceral involvement, with rapid skin thickening on the extremities, face and trunk. Limited scleroderma has a lower risk of early visceral involvement; pulmonary artery hypertension is a signiﬁcant risk but usually appears later in the disease process, such as in this patient. The features of calcinosis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia meant that it was historically referred to as CREST. Limited scleroderma or limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is the preferred term when the patient does not have all of the features of CREST. Anticentromere antibodies are most strongly associated with

CREST (speciﬁcity > 90%) and pulmonary hypertension. Antitopoisomerase 1 antibodies are associated with interstitial lung disease and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are associated with renal and cardiac involvement, including scleroderma renal crisis. A Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease This patient’s signs, symptoms and investigation ﬁndings are in keeping with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not a feature of this condition. Although she has just under a 20 pack-year smoking history, her symptoms are most likely to be related to pulmonary hypertension, which is a common feature of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. B Chronic pulmonary emboli Although chronic small pulmonary emboli may result in pulmonary hypertension and the respiratory symptoms experienced by this patient, her other symptoms and investigation ﬁndings point towards a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. C Congestive cardiac failure Although cardiac failure may present with dyspnoea on exertion, it is unlikely to present at such a young age without any prior history of cardiac disease. The patient’s other signs and symptoms, along with her positive anti-centromere antibodies, point towards a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, of which pulmonary hypertension is a feature. D Interstitial lung disease Fibrosing interstitial lung disease is the main differential here. However, this is more commonly seen in systemic sclerosis where there are positive anti-topoisomerase 1 autoantibodies. Interstitial lung disease may cause a cough, exertional dyspnoea and fatigue but is unlikely to be associated with palpitations.

stem: A 71-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with pain over his left hip and pelvis. Previously very active, he is now limited to walking only a few hundred yards due to pain. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, which is treated with felodipine. On examination, his BP is 135/70 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. He has pain over the left hip, and ﬂexion and external rotation are limited by pain. His GP has arranged an X-ray of the hip, which reveals evidence of osteolysis and new bone formation around both the femoral head and the pelvis. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal?
explanation: B Alkaline phosphatase The X-ray appearance is typical of Paget’s disease. In patients with Paget’s, other markers of bone turnover, apart from alkaline phosphatase, are usually in the normal range. Alkaline phosphatase is a useful marker of disease activity and of response to bisphosphonates, with a fall in alkaline phosphatase correlating with a reduction in disease activity. Over the longer term, bisphosphonates may not be completely effective; one study suggested that despite the use of etidronate, disease progression occurred in 28% of individuals. D Phosphate Elevations in phosphate are seen in hypoparathyroidism and in those with renal impairment, rather than those with Paget’s. A Calcium Calcium in patients with Paget’s remains in the normal range for the majority of patients, unless there is a prolonged period of bed rest, where minor elevations may be seen. C Vitamin D Vitamin D elevation is seen in patients with sarcoidosis and symptomatic hypercalcaemia, and in those who take excess exogenous vitamin D. E Parathyroid hormone (PTH) Hyperparathyroidism is not usually associated with single joint destruction, and is normal in patients with Paget’s disease.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the general practitioner after returning from a 1-week holiday in Thailand. He complains of pain on passing urine, and cloudy urine that looks like pus on occasions. There is also joint pain predominantly affecting the knees and ankles, and itchy eyes. On examination, there appears to be a psoriatic-type rash affecting the feet. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following treatments would best ﬁt with the management of this condition?
explanation:
C Doxycycline 100 mg bd This patient has reactive arthritis, which is a form of seronegative arthritis caused by a remote gastrointestinal or urogenital infection. Pathogens include Chlamydia trachomatis, Yersinia, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli, Clostridium difﬁcile and Chlamydia pneumoniae. The social history and suggestion of keratoderma blennorrhagica would implicate Chlamydia infection. A Methotrexate 2.5 mg po weekly

This patient has reactive arthritis, which is addressed by treating the underlying infection and NSAIDs for symptomatic relief. B Azathioprine Explanation as for Methotrexate 2.5 mg po weekly. D Prednisolone 40 mg po daily Oral glucocorticoids are not suggested in the treatment of reactive arthritis, but intra-articular steroid injections can be used in those who do not respond to oral NSAIDs. E Coal tar skin creams The psoriatic-type rash in this patient is more likely keratoderma blennorrhagica, given the history. This can be treated with topical steroids or salicylates.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with an acutely red, tender, left knee joint. He has a long history of hypertension, which has been well controlled over a number of years with bendroﬂumethiazide and amlodipine. There is no history of recent injury. The pain has been severe for 2 days, and on examination, the joint is red, warm and tender. There is swelling and a small effusion. The knee joint is aspirated, and the aspirate sent to the lab for analysis. Below is an image of the aspirate when examined under a microscope using polarised light. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 140 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 14.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 180 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 10 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 70 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour Knee joint aspirate White blood cells 2000/µl What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Gout This patient has risk factors for gout (middle-aged man, on a diuretic), and therefore, gout is the most likely explanation in this scenario. The low potassium level is consistent with the use of bendroﬂumethiazide, a drug that predisposes the patient to gout (but not pseudogout), and the inﬂammatory markers support this. Bendroﬂumethiazide is not the ﬁrst-line treatment for hypertension, but the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend that patients who are already taking bendroﬂumethiazide with well- controlled hypertension continue this treatment. Gout and pseudogout cannot be reliably distinguished on purely clinical grounds. The synovial ﬂuid would be expected to show the presence of crystals. In gout, needle-shaped intracellular and extracellular crystals of monosodium urate appear. When examined with a polarising ﬁlter, these are yellow when aligned parallel to the axis of the red compensator, but they turn blue when aligned across the RHEUMATO direction of polarisation (ie they exhibit negative birefringence), as seen in the image. In pseudogout, calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals appear, these being shorter and often rhomboidal. Under a polarising ﬁlter, CPP crystals do not change colour, according to their alignment relative to the direction of the red compensator. In pseudogout, radiography may show chondrocalcinosis, which is useful in differentiating between the two conditions. However, of the ﬁve options provided, gout is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. B Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) RA is very unlikely to present as monoarthritis of the knee and is usually a small joint polyarthritis affecting the hands. A Meniscus tear A meniscal tear would cause a swollen, painful knee joint, but the patient would provide a history of recent injury to the knee, with progressive increase in swelling over a few days. With more severe injury, the patient may experience locking of the knee. This patient has no history of knee injury, and a warm, red joint is not consistent with a meniscal tear. D Septic arthritis Whenever a patient has monoarthritis, the clinician should always consider joint sepsis, as it is very important not to miss this diagnosis. However, in this case, the relatively low number of pus cells is against a diagnosis of septic arthritis; most septic joints have a WCC of > 50 000/µl, with > 75% of polymorphonuclear leukocytes. E Osteoarthritis (OA) OA is not correct, because of the acute history and very high levels of inﬂammatory markers. OA is insidious in onset and is associated with normal levels of inﬂammatory markers.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a rash on his back, face and scalp, which has appeared over the past year or so. The rash began as dry, red patches, which increased in size and became scaly. He is particularly concerned, as the rash has been associated with some hair loss on his scalp, which has not regrown. The rash has been worse over the summer months, which he has spent with family abroad. On examination, you see the rash pictured below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) This is a typical presentation of DLE, the most common type of cutaneous lupus, characterised by plaques on the face, scalp and occasionally generalised rash on the chest or back. The rash is photosensitive and classically associated with scarring alopecia, which is a major differentiating feature in this condition. C Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) PCT is the most common type of porphyria and is caused by a defective enzyme (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase), leading to a disorder in haematological production. This manifests as fragility of the skin, particularly on the back of the hands, and photosensitivity. While the rash in this question is photosensitive, PCT is more commonly associated with sores or blisters, with the formation of milia as the blisters heal. PCT does not cause scarring alopecia. B Pityriasis versicolor (PV) PV is a common yeast infection causing hypopigmented irregular patches, frequently on the chest or back. The rash in this image is hyperpigmented and associated with scarring alopecia. PV is not particularly photosensitive, though loss of pigment can become more marked when adjacent skin becomes tanned. D Psoriasis This rash does appear to form scaly plaques akin to psoriasis; how- RHEUMATO ever, the history of photosensitivity and scarring alopecia is incompatible with the diagnosis of psoriasis. E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) SLE is a multi-system disorder featuring a wide range of symptoms, including photosensitive rash. However, to seal a diagnosis, one would expect more systemic symptoms, including arthralgia, mouth ulcers, or renal impairment. Moreover, DLE is signiﬁcantly more common than SLE.

stem: A 65-year-old man who lives alone presents with right-sided shoulder pain after falling out of bed. He had a previous history of asthma, angina and poorly controlled diabetes. Upon presentation, his shoulder X-ray showed mild degenerative changes only. He was started on basic analgesia and physiotherapy. After three years, he has lost function to his right shoulder, with mild pain. He has signiﬁcant limitation to all movements in the shoulder on examination. There is unilateral swelling and erythema of the joint. He is otherwise well and apyrexial. Investigations: WCC 5.2 × 109/l (4–11 × 109/l) Joint aspiration No organisms seen An X-ray of the shoulder is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Charcot joint Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy is most frequently associated with the foot or ankle. However, it may occur in any joint, and in the upper limb, it may be associated with syringomyelia. This X-ray shows resorption of the proximal aspect of the humerus, seen in severe Charcot joint. C Osteomyelitis Osteomyelitis is an important differential in this case. However, the X-ray features of osteomyelitis include regional osteopenia and a periosteal reaction, unlike the almost complete resorption of the humerus seen in the case. Trauma is a risk factor for osteomyelitis; however, patients are classically febrile and in signiﬁcant pain, pointing away from osteomyelitis. A Adhesive capsulitis Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a common cause of shoulder pain and may happen spontaneously or following a rotator cuff injury. However, X-rays are commonly normal in this condition. Therefore, the X-ray in this case effectively rules out adhesive capsulitis. D Septic arthritis Septic arthritis is another essential diagnosis to consider in a patient with a red and swollen joint. However, in this stem, there are no organisms seen in the joint aspiration; the patient is well and afebrile, and the pain is mild. E Shoulder dislocation The X-ray in this case features almost complete resorption of the humeral head, very different to the features of shoulder dislocation.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has attended the Emergency Department with several days of bilateral shoulder weakness and pain. She smokes 10 cigarettes per day, and has suffered from a cough in the mornings over the past few months. There are no abnormalities on plain X-rays, but the Emergency Department doctor was concerned about a purplish discoloration around the eyes and prominent nail fold telangiectasia, which the patient had not really noticed before. CK is raised at 2820 U/l. Which of the following is the most important investigation for this patient?
explanation: E Malignancy screen This lady is a smoker with a cough and has features of dermatomyositis (muscle weakness, heliotrope, dilated nail fold capillaries and raised CK), which may be paraneoplastic in 15% of cases. Dermatomyositis causes a symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, and skin signs of dermatomyositis include macular ‘shawl sign’ rash over the back and shoulders, heliotrope rash on cheeks and eyelids, nail fold erythema and Gottron’s papules. Rough papules on extensor surfaces of the phalanges are pathognomonic if there is a history of weakness and elevated creatine kinase (CK). In older patients (>40 years) there is an increased risk of malignancy, which must be extensively investigated. Thorough clinical examination should include per rectum, breasts and lymph nodes; investigations should include chest X-ray, ultrasound scan of the abdomen/pelvis, mammography and prostate-speciﬁc antigen (PSA) (men). D Weekly methotrexate This patient may do well with prednisolone and treatment of the underlying cancer without any need for a DMARD. A Autoantibody proﬁle ANA can be negative (it is positive in 40–80% of cases) and only 20% have a myositis-associated antibody, of which Jo-1 is the most common. B Serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate An ESR is non-speciﬁc, not diagnostic, and may be normal in dermatomyositis. C Analgesia and physiotherapy Although analgesia and physiotherapy are part of the management, this patient may need prednisolone and treatment of the underlying cancer.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with brittle asthma presents with left hip and groin pain. It is very painful to bear weight. An X-ray of her hip reveals no evidence of a fracture. She is confused and cannot give a history. On examination, she is afebrile and there is no redness or warmth around the hip. You notice that her ﬁngers appear deformed. RHEUMATO What investigation will give the deﬁnitive diagnosis for her hip pain?
explanation: B MRI hip The most likely diagnosis is of avascular necrosis of the hip, given the clues to oral steroid use – ‘brittle’ asthma as well as rheumatoid arthritis. An MRI is the diagnostic imaging technique of choice. E X-ray knee It is always important to think of the joint below (and above if applicable), as pain may be referred. However, in this case with groin pain and likely long-term steroid use, the most likely diagnosis is avascular necrosis of the hip. The hip is a common site, as it is supplied by an end-artery. A Inﬂammatory markers Although this lady is likely to have rheumatoid arthritis, as suggested by the swan-neck deformity of the fourth and ﬁfth ﬁngers, inﬂammatory markers are unlikely to help – the history suggests a monoarthritis but dissuades you from a septic arthritis, with the absence of fever or erythema. C Auto-antibodies Auto-antibodies may help you conﬁrm a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, but would not help delineate the cause of her acute hip pain. D Arthroscopy Arthroscopy is very invasive and unnecessary in this case, to diagnose avascular necrosis.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis is referred by her general practitioner (GP) for further management. She has bilateral lower limb swelling and difﬁcult to manage hypertension. Current medication includes low dose corticosteroids, methotrexate, ramipril, aspirin and atorvastatin. On examination, her blood pressure is 149/82 mmHg, pulse is 78 bpm regular. She has bilateral pitting oedema but her chest is clear. There is hepatomegaly on abdominal examination. Investigations: Hb 110 g/l WCC 7.8 × 109/l PLT 190 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l Creatinine 199 μmol/l ESR 44 mm/hr ALT 54 U/l Alkaline phosphatase 189 U/l 24-h urinary protein 3.1g Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Systemic inﬂammatory amyloidosis The hepatomegaly, heavy proteinuria with raised alkaline phosphatase is a strong indicator towards amyloid inﬁltration. Secondary inﬂammatory amyloidosis occurs due to increased circulating levels of serum amyloid A, which is an acute phase reactant. The raised ESR seen here is an indication of ongoing inﬂammation related to her rheumatoid disease. While colchicine is of value in reducing amyloid deposition in familial Mediterranean fever, there is no evidence it has a positive effect in amyloidosis related to underlying systemic inﬂammation. Treatment should focus on intensive control of the underlying cause; her rheumatoid disease. C Rheumatoid vasculitis Rheumatoid vasculitis very rarely affects the kidneys, but usually causes cutaneous (purpuric rashes) and neurological (mononeuritis multiplex) manifestations. B Methotrexate toxicity Methotrexate toxicity can cause myelosuppression (but her FBC is ﬁne) and hepatotoxicity (her ALT is only mildly elevated). It is not associated with hepatomegaly or nephrotic syndrome. Rheumatoid arthritis drugs that may cause nephrotic syndrome include penicillamine and gold. D Minimal change disease Although minimal change disease might explain her nephrotic syndrome, it would not explain hepatomegaly. E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) This lady has known rheumatoid arthritis and therefore is unlikely to then develop an entirely different disease later. The key to knowing that she did not have an arthritis as part of SLE that evolved later on, is the ﬁnding that she had erosions, which are strongly RHEUMATO suggestive that the original diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis was correct.

stem: A 64-year-old patient with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis attends the clinic for review. She is managed on low-dose methotrexate, folic acid and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents for her disease, but has noticed a worsening in her rheumatoid nodules over the past few months and has developed dry eyes most recently. On examination, she has splenomegaly. Investigations reveal a low total white count of 3.4 × 109/l; she is also anaemic, with haemoglobin of 98 g/l and a platelet count of 105 × 109/l. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate initially in this case?
explanation:
E Pulsed corticosteroid therapy This patient has Felty syndrome, as evidenced by splenomegaly and worsening of extra-articular manifestations in a patient with a long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis. This, coupled with the low white count, is highly suggestive of Felty syndrome, which has a 60–70% female predominance and is usually recognised from the ﬁfth decade onwards in patients who have had rheumatoid arthritis for an average of 10 years or more. Pulsed corticosteroid and/or cyclophosphamide therapy may be effective in raising neutrophil counts, as may appropriate switching/intensiﬁcation of DMARD therapy for the rheumatoid. D Busulphan This patient does not have development of lymphoma, but rather Felty syndrome. A Stop methotrexate therapy This is not methotrexate toxicity but Felty syndrome. The key is the worsening of RA features and splenomegaly. B Folinic acid rescue This is not methotrexate toxicity but Felty syndrome. Folinic acid rescue is the treatment for methotrexate toxicity.

C Splenectomy Splenectomy is one option in patients with Felty syndrome who fail to respond to medical intervention.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with intensely painful ﬁngers on going outdoors during the autumn and winter months. She reports the same problem if she washes her hands in cold water. Her ﬁngers go pale and blue- tinged, and later become erythematous and are burning and prickly. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 137 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 188 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.1 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.8 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 18 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 21 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 28 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 101 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 15 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Glucose 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l TSH 2.0 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Creatine kinase (CK) 70 IU/l 23–175 IU/l Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) Negative What is the best initial medical treatment for this lady?
explanation: A Nifedipine MR Extensive screening has failed to establish an underlying cause for this lady’s Raynaud’s, so she has primary Raynaud’s phenomenon or Raynaud’s disease. Primary Raynaud’s is not usually associated with increased mortality or morbidity, although occasionally necrosis of the affected extremity may occur. Clearly, in patients presenting with this symptom picture, it is crucial to carry out an extensive screen for underlying autoimmune or metabolic disease as in this case, as therapy should be tailored to any underlying condition. Primary Raynaud’s commonly presents in the second or third decade of life, and prevalence is slightly higher in women than men – put at RHEUMATO around 5% depending on case series. Treatment of choice is with vasodilating calcium-channel antagonists such as nifedipine modiﬁed/sustained release (MR/SR) or angiotensin II receptor blockers such as losartan. D Prednisolone Steroids do not improve symptoms of Raynaud’s, and there is no indication in primary Raynaud’s. Steroids may occasionally be used in secondary Raynaud’s where there is an underlying inﬂammatory process driving the condition, e.g. in SLE. B Atenolol Beta blockers such as atenolol may precipitate a worsening of Raynaud’s symptoms, as they may cause vasoconstriction. C Ramipril There is no evidence that ACE inhibitors improve symptoms of Raynaud’s, and there is no indication in primary Raynaud’s. There is some evidence to support the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or angiotensin II–receptor blockers (ARBs), such as losartan. However, it is unclear why the mechanisms of why ARBs are advantageous over ACE inhibitors. E Aspirin There is no evidence that aspirin improves the symptoms of Raynaud’s. Multiple antithrombotic agents, including aspirin, dipyridamole, anticoagulants and thrombolytic therapy, have been used in patients with Raynaud’s phenomenon in whom ulceration and thrombosis have occurred. The beneﬁt of antiplatelet therapy is not well studied, but such therapy is often used in cases of secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon when there is a risk of thrombosis. Longterm anticoagulation in the absence of a hypercoagulable state is not recommended.

stem: A 42-year-old banker was admitted with a 2-hour history of central crushing chest pain radiating down his left arm. He admits to abusing intravenous drugs in the past and is a life-long smoker. His past medical history includes hypertension and irritable bowel syndrome. On admission, a fast-track troponin level was raised. ECG demonstrated anterolateral ST segments elevated > 2 mm. He was treated for a myocardial infarction (MI) with intravenous thrombolysis followed by intravenous heparin infusion. ST segments returned to normal. Three days later in hospital this man developed a purpuric rash over his legs. On examination, there were normal heart sounds with no added murmurs. Chest examination revealed clinically a small left-sided pleural effusion. The abdominal examination was unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed weakness of his left arm: the patient felt this has been present for a while now since sustaining an injury playing football. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm and anterolateral Q waves. Blood results at this time show: Investigation Result Normal Values Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 15.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 179 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP 150 mg/l < 10 mg/l ESR 87 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h ANA Positive ANCA Negative Hb 100 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 11.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 8.0 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Eosinophils 0.09 × 109/l 0.04 - 0.4 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 560 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l HBsAg Positive HBeAg Negative Hep B anti-core AB Positive Hep C AB Negative What is the most likely diagnosis? RHEUMATO
explanation: B Polyarteritis nodosa The American College of Rheumatology states that patients must have three of the following to have a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): weight loss >5 kg, livedo reticularis, testicular pain/tenderness, myalgia, mono/polyneuropathy, diastolic BP >90 mmHg, elevated urea/creatinine, hepatitis B virus. This man clearly has a systemic vasculitis given a history of cardiac, gastrointestinal and renal involvement. The recent neurological involvement clinches the diagnosis of PAN. A Microscopic polyangiitis In this scenario, the test for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) is negative which rules out microscopic polyangiitis. C Streptokinase-induced vasculitis A vasculitis secondary to streptokinase occurs mainly in those who have received previous streptokinase therapy and does not explain the other manifestations. It is an immune-complex phenomenon and antistreptokinase antibodies can be measured. Renal impairment can occur. D Systemic lupus erythematosus Patients with SLE tend to present with other skin manifestations and low platelets. E Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) GPA affects the respiratory tract more commonly. There is no mention of ear, nose and throat symptoms in this case.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of pain and yellowish discharge from a wound in the left foot for the past ten days. He says that it started after sustaining a puncture wound to his left foot two weeks ago. The patient says that he was not walking barefoot and had his shoes on when he sustained the injury. He did not seek medical attention at that point in time. He has no other co-morbidities. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm and temperature 37.9°C. Local examination reveals warmth, redness and tenderness over the right foot and a purulent discharge from the wound over the left ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint. An Xray of the patient's foot is taken: RHEUMATO Which of the following is the most likely pathogen implicated in the infection from which this patient is suffering?
explanation:
C Pseudomonas aeruginosa This patient’s signs and symptoms and radiological examination are suggestive of acute osteomyelitis. In a patient who is a non-diabetic who has sustained a puncture wound, studies have shown that P. aeruginosa is the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis. P. aeruginosa can also cause infection after piercing of the ear cartilage. D Staphylococcus aureus In a diabetic, the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis after a puncture wound is S. aureus. This patient is not diabetic. Overall, in patients with no history of a puncture wound, the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis is S. aureus. A Coagulase-negative staphylococci Coagulase-negative staphylococci are common pathogens isolated in implant-related infection. B Mixed anaerobic infection Mixed anaerobic infections are common in patients who have had polytrauma and have a large amount of devitalised tissue, thereby enhancing the growth of anaerobic organisms. E Streptococcus pyogenes

S. pyogenes is a common cause of skin and soft tissue infection but only infrequently causes acute osteomyelitis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman complains of pain in the right ankle that she has experienced for the past 3 weeks. Two or three days later, she notices that the ankle is also swollen. A week later, this is followed by pain and swelling in both knees. Her general practitioner (GP) started diclofenac 50 mg three times daily, which alleviated the pain to some extent. She further remembers having loose bowel movements for a few days about 10 days prior to the onset of joint symptoms. She informs you that she sometimes develops loose bowel movements after eating a takeaway. Medications other than non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) include paracetamol, which she takes for intermittent backache, and salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers, for bronchial asthma. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 137 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 188 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 2.1 × 10 9/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Lymphocytes 1.8 × 10 9/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l ESR 18 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour CRP 21 mg/l < 10 mg/l AST 28 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 101 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ALT 15 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Glucose 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Reactive arthritis This lady has an oligoarthritis following a likely gastrointestinal infection. Asymmetrical arthritis, predominantly involving large joints in lower extremities, is suggestive of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy type of arthritis. Reactive arthritis is most likely with the preceding history of diarrhoea. Her inﬂammatory markers are modestly elevated. Reactive arthritis is aseptic inﬂammatory ar- RHEUMATO thritis, usually triggered by chlamydial urethritis or cervicitis or enteric infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia in a genetically susceptible individual. HLA B27 is the major currently known genetic risk factor. The arthritis usually resolves in 3 months but can recur or become chronic. E Still's disease Still's disease is associated with fevers, a rash and small joint polyarthritis over a more prolonged period than is seen . A Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) There is a clear infective precipitant and although she has back pain, we are not given any features of inﬂammatory back pain to suggest spondyloarthritis. C Septic arthritis She has an oligoarthritis following a diarrhoeal illness. Septic arthritis may be a polyarthritis in 10% of cases, but usually patients are far more sick (with signs of systemic sepsis) with red, hot swollen joints and can barely move these affected joints. Blood results are not overtly helpful for differentiating causes here, but one might expect a higher CRP and white cell count with septic arthritis. NB: Gonococcal septic arthritides are usually associated with a pustular skin rash and red, linear areas of tenosynovitis. D Gout This lady has a spreading oligoarthritis following a diarrheal episode. Gout is usually a sudden-onset, exquisitely painful arthritis. This young female patient does not have any risk factors for gout either.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with pain in her right elbow on forearm extension and wrist extension. She is a keen gardener and has recently been planting spring bulbs. Despite rest and use of NSAIDs over the past 4 weeks, her pain has not improved and she has garden show to prepare for in 2 weeks time. On examination, the elbow is held in partial ﬂexion, pain is reproduced on resisted wrist extension and there is pain on palpation over the lateral epicondyle. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate to gain short term relief for this patient?
options: Early surgical intervention for medial tendon release
explanation:
A Local steroid/anaesthetic injection This lady has a lateral epicondylitis (i.e. tennis elbow). Local steroid/anaesthetic injection and use of non- steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents may both be of beneﬁt. D Elbow immobilisation While restricted activity may be appropriate, it would be inappropriate for this patient to have her elbow completely immobilised because her muscles are likely to waste and therefore cause more problems later. B Flexion exercise programme With a lateral epicondylitis, physiotherapy and, in particular, stretching exercises, may also be of beneﬁt, but the beneﬁts of physiotherapy occur over the longer term.

C Oral prednisolone Oral prednisolone is not appropriate for a lateral epicondylitis, which is localised inﬂammation. Systemic steroids are likely to have side effects, despite only minimal efﬁcacy. E Early surgical intervention for medial tendon release Surgical intervention for lateral tendon release may be appropriate in patients who fail to respond to medical therapy.

stem: A 40-year-old man is attending the Rheumatology Clinic because of a several months history of pain and stiffness in his hands. The patient denies any history of rash, dry mouth or dry eyes. There is also no history of unprotected intercourse. The patient does describe a tendency towards constipation recently but denies any other gastrointestinal problems. His medications include an acute prescription of co-codamol and ramipril for his well controlled hypertension. On examination, there is tenderness to the right wrist with most distal interphalangeal joints being affected with tenderness and mild swelling.
explanation: A Psoriatic arthropathy Psoriatic arthropathy most commonly presents as a poly- or oligoarthritis. There are ﬁve patterns of involvement: distal arthritis (DIP joint involvement), asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans and spondyloarthritis. The nails show pitting and onycholysis (lifting of the nail from the nailbed). The function of the hands is usually good unless the joints are severely inﬂamed. In about 75% of patients there is a preceding history of RHEUMATO psoriasis before the arthropathy; in 15%, the onset of the rash is synchronous and in 10% the arthritis precedes the rash. D Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) SLE is a chronic inﬂammatory disease that can involve any organ. Arthritis can occur in more than 90% of patients and tends to be migratory, symmetrical and polyarticular. The nail changes seen in the picture are not characteristic. B Rheumatoid arthritis RA rarely affects the DIP joints, as is the case in this patient. Furthermore, there are associated nail changes which would not be consistent with RA. C Systemic sclerosis Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is subcategorised into diffuse cutaneous SSc and limited cutaneous SSc. Limited cutaneous SSc is commonly associated with the CREST syndrome. Skin involvement is a deﬁning feature of SSc, and includes variable thickening and hardening with oedematous swelling and erythema. Fatigue, arthralgia and myalgia are common as well as Raynaud phenomenon. These features are not provided with this patient. E Arthritis of inﬂammatory bowel disease Arthritis of inﬂammatory bowel disease is a peripheral and axial arthritis which may occur in a similar pattern to psoriatic arthropathy. The nail disease and DIP joint involvement that occur here are not characteristics of arthritis associated with inﬂammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP) complaining of skin dryness with dry and gritty eyes. She also has diminished libido because of increasing vaginal dryness. You arrange for a Schirmer test to be carried out. Which of the following test results would be useful in the diagnosis of Sjögren syndrome?
options: 4 mm of ﬁlter strip wetting on Schirmer tear test
explanation: A 4 mm of ﬁlter strip wetting on Schirmer tear test The Schirmer tear test involves placement of a standard strip of ﬁlter paper on the inside of the lower eyelid. Wetting of <5 mm in 5 min indicates defective tear production. In Sjögren syndrome, Rose Bengal staining of the eyes may show punctuate or ﬁlamentary keratitis. Laboratory abnormalities include a polyclonal raised IgG and positive rheumatoid factor. Antinuclear antibodies are found in 60–70% and antimitochondrial antibodies in 10%. Anti-Ro and -La antibodies are found in 70% of patients with primary Sjögren syndrome. Treatment is with artiﬁcial tears and saliva-replacement solution. D Positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies Positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis. B Positive ANCA A positive ANCA (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) is associated with certain types of systemic vasculitis, especially Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyarteritis. It has no clinical relevance in the diagnosis of Sjögren. C Negative rheumatoid factor RHEUMATO Rheumatoid factor is non-speciﬁc and may be positive in numerous rheumatological conditions, including Sjögren where up to 70% of patients have a positive result. A negative result would not be helpful in the diagnosis of the condition. E Reduced oestrogen levels Oestrogen levels may be measured to exclude a hormonal cause for vaginal dryness, but will not be useful in the diagnosis of Sjögren. The treatment of vaginal dryness in the setting of Sjogren syndrome includes the use of vaginal moisturisers and water-soluble lubricants during sexual activity. Oestrogen creams may also be of beneﬁt.

stem: A 23-year-old, previously ﬁt and well Turkish man presents with a history of painful oral and genital ulceration. More recently he has also developed gritty eyes and a sore knee. Examination reveals areas of mucosal ulceration and scaring in addition to knee synovitis and eye erythema. He is investigated with repeated blood tests after which he develops blistering at the sites of venepuncture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Behçet’s syndrome Behçet’s syndrome is most common in young Turkish males and presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers. It is also associated with eye problems e.g. anterior and posterior uveitis and an asymmetrical migratory non- erosive oligoarthritis. Patients may also present with neurological complications, and in particular meningoencephalitis. E Primary syphilis Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacteria Treponema pallidum. Primary syphilis manifests as a painless ulcer at the site of infection, whereas secondary syphilis presents as a widespread rash associated with a ﬂu-like illness. B Reactive arthritis Reactive arthritis consists of the triad of conjunctivitis, urethritis and arthritis. Patients also develop erosions in the mouth and also on the

penis where they are known as circinate balanitis. The distinguishing feature in this history is the development of a pustule after skin puncture. This phenomenon known as pathergy is characteristic of Behçet’s syndrome. C HIV seroconversion HIV seroconversion occurs at the time that patients develop antibodies to the HIV virus and manifests as a ﬂu- like illness. D Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection Symptoms of HSV recurrence manifest as vesicles and punched-out ulcers around the mouth or genitals, whereas primary HSV infection may also be associated with fever and malaise.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a history of arthralgia affecting the small joints of her hands, feet and wrists for the past 4 months. The pain in her ﬁngers gets worse when she goes out in the cold without gloves. She has been feeling extremely tired. She has noticed an erythematous, non-pruritic rash over both legs. The examination reveals early synovitis of joints of the hands and feet and raised non-blanching erythematous purpura over the extensor aspects of both legs. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 114 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelets (PLT) 180 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l ESR 88 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h CRP 6.7 mg/l < 10 mg/l ANA + RF + C3 Normal C4 Low Results of the radiography of hands and feet are awaited. Which one of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her ﬁnger symptoms?
explanation: C Cryoglobulinaemia This lady has a purpuric rash, Raynaud’s, polyarthralgia with a positive RFand low C4, suggestive of cyroglobulinaemia with a likely underlying connective tissue disease. RHEUMATO In RA, RF is positive in 70% of patients, whereas in Sjögren syndrome and cryoglobulinaemia it is prevalent in up to 90% of cases. E Polyarteritis nodosa The rash associated with polyarteritis nodosa is livedo reticularis, and one would usually expect mesenteric ischaemia and mononeuritis multiplex, rather than this constellation of symptoms with arthritis. A Primary Raynaud’s Although this woman does have a colour change suggestive of Raynaud’s, the underlying condition driving this condition is cryoglobulinaemia, which is therefore the best ﬁt. Cryoglobulinaemia is also driving a polyarthralgia/polyarthritis. B Mixed connective tissue disease We do not know whether she has mixed connective tissue disease as we are not given her anti-RNP antibody status. Cryoglobulinaemia is usually secondary to connective tissue disease, myeloma or infection (most commonly hepatitis C). D Subacute bacterial endocarditis Although some of her symptoms could be explained by a subacute bacterial endocarditis (purpuric rash and even the RF), you would expect the history to be shorter with endocarditis, and also both C3 and C4 to be low.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with symptoms of parotid swelling, and dry eyes. She also avoids eating dry foods like cheese biscuits because her mouth is dry, and that she has recently had to have her plate from her dental implant reﬁtted because it is rubbing on her gums. Other history of note is treatment for oral candidiasis 3 months ago. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/82 mmHg, she has blepharitis and bilateral parotid enlargement. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 182 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 135 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Rheumatoid factor weakly positive Given the suspected diagnosis, which investigation would be most likely to conﬁrm this?
explanation: B Anti-Ro and Anti-La antibodies This woman has Sjögren’s syndrome. This is an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterised by the drying of mucus membranes such as conjunctivae, the buccal mucosa, and the vagina in women. AntiRo and anti-La antibodies are seen in Sjögren’s, and antinuclear antibodies/rheumatoid factor are usually positive, but they are not speciﬁc for Sjögren’s. Sjögren’s can either be primary (on its own) or secondary to other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Schirmer’s test demonstrates the reduced ﬂow of tears and involves placing a bent piece of ﬁlter paper in the corner of the eye. This patient has bilateral parotid gland and lacrimal gland swelling which is known as Mikulicz’s syndrome. Management in the ﬁrst instance involves replacing tears and saliva with lubricants; women may also require a suitable vaginal lubricant. D Anti-smooth muscle antibodies Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are found in autoimmune hepatitis. A Antinuclear antibodies Antinuclear antibodies are non-speciﬁc and found in many different conditions, as well as 10% of the asymptomatic healthy normal population. C Serum protein electrophoresis In Sjögren’s one would see a polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia (ie polyclonal raised IgG). The presentation does not sound like myeloma at all. E c-ANCA cANCA is found in Granulomatosis with polyangitis. This presentation in the clinical vignette does not sound like a vasculitis – with no upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract or renal involvement.

stem: A 55-year-old woman complains of painful, sore, erythematous, weeping skin over the right nipple and areola. She has used a potent topical steroid for 2 weeks with no improvement. On examination of both breasts and axillae, there were no lumps and the left nipple was normal. She said she recently changed her body wash and thinks it may be an allergic reaction. RHEUMATO What is the most appropriate management step?
options: Reassure her that this is contact dermatitis and she should stop using the body wash
Prescribe a soap substitute and review in 6 weeks
Take a swab for microbiology and prescribe ﬂucloxacillin
explanation: D Refer for "one-stop" breast clinic urgently A weepy, unilateral erythematous eruption affecting one nipple should raise the suspicion of Paget’s disease, i.e. direct extension of a mammary intraductal adenocarcinoma into the nipple or areola. For this reason, refer to a breast clinic as a matter of urgency. A Reassure her that this is contact dermatitis and she should stop using the body wash Unilateral nipple symptoms do not support contact dermatitis as the underlying diagnosis. B Prescribe a soap substitute and review in 6 weeks This risks a signiﬁcant delay in treating an underlying carcinoma. C Take a swab for microbiology and prescribe ﬂucloxacillin The subacute presentation is unlikely to represent an acute bacterial infection, and prescribing antibiotics, like prescribing a soap substitute, risks delay in treating an underlying carcinoma. E Refer for patch testing Patch testing is ideal for evaluating a possible type IV hypersensitivity reaction, where bilateral changes would be expected.

stem: A 21-year-old man has recently returned from a holiday in the Far East. He gives a history of symmetrical joint pain in his knees, ankles and feet and also complains of sore eyes. On further questioning, the patient informs you that he did have unprotected sexual relations on several occasions whilst away, and is now experiencing some pain on urination. His ESR is raised. A synovial ﬂuid aspirate is sterile but with a high neutrophil count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Reactive arthropathy The history of recent travel to the Far East with episodes of unprotected sexual encounters raises the possibility of venereal disease. An oligoarthritis is seen more often than symmetrical arthropathy in reactive arthritis. The history of urethritis/dysuria and conjunctivitis completes the reactive arthritis triad. A penile swab should be taken and treatment should include treatment of the probable underlying STI. D Rheumatoid arthritis The presence of conjunctivitis and evidence of urethritis steers us more towards reactive arthritis versus rheumatoid. A Ankylosing spondylitis The potential exposure to venereal pathogens makes reactive arthropathy a more likely diagnosis than ankylosing spondylitis. Furthermore, there is no history of back or buttock pain. B Septic arthritis Septic arthritis is usually a mono-arthritis, but can be a polyarthritis in approximately 10% of cases. His synovial ﬂuid aspirate is sterile, and the concurrent symptom of sore eyes suggests conjunctivitis associated with a reactive arthritis. E Still’s disease Still's presents with high spiking fevers and oligoarthritis over the course of a few weeks/months, and not usually in this age group.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of progressive pain and stiffness involving the small joints of her hands and knees. She has xanthelasmas in the periorbital areas and nodules over the hands as shown below. There is tenderness over the DIP and PIP joints, with mild instability at the occasional PIP joints. Her knees are tender and crepitus is palpable bilaterally. X-rays of the hands show preservation of the DIP joint space with erosions having clear margins. An image of the right hand is shown below: RHEUMATO Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis The characteristic nail fold nodules of multicentric reticulohistiocytosis have the appearance of ‘coral beads’. Nodules may be numerous, may grow to as large as 2 cm and may involve mucosal surfaces. The hand radiograph reported above suggests erosive changes affecting multiple DIP joints. Distal interphalangeal erosions are characteristic and may lead to pseudo-widening of the joint spaces. Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis is a rare, non-Langherhans cell histiocytosis with skin and joint involvement. Nearly all organs can be involved. Association with cancer occurs in about 25% of cases. Association with autoimmune diseases has also been recorded. Microscopic examination shows a histiocytic nodular inﬁltrate composed of giant cells with ground-glass appearance and periodic acid-schiff (PAS)-positive cytoplasm. D Xanthomata Although this lady has xanthelasma on her eyelids, the image does not look like xanthomata, which are small, yellowish-orange to reddish-brown papules. A Rheumatoid nodules Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) does not cause erosions at the DIPJs – RA usually affects MCPs and PIPs, not DIPs. B Methotrexate-induced nodules There is no history of her being on methotrexate. NB: Methotrexate may cause nodulosis or accelerated nodulosis.

E Molluscum contagiosum Molluscum lesions look like small, umbilicated, pearly iridescent papules and are caused by a pox virus.

stem: A 77-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe right-sided hip pain. He is ﬁnding the pain unbearable despite over-the-counter analgesics and is struggling to weight-bear. There is no history of recent injury. He complains of occasional pain in both knees but says this is usually well controlled. His past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination, he appears to be in discomfort. His observations are within normal limits. There is tenderness on palpation of his right hip joint. His hip is warm to touch, but there are no signs of erythema or acute swelling. There is crepitus of his right hip and knees bilaterally. The remainder of his joints and skin remain intact. An X-ray of his hip is taken: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Osteoarthritis (OA) This patient has OA, a degenerative arthritis capable of affecting multiple joints. This patient has hip OA, most commonly seen in RHEUMATO men and usually unilateral at ﬁrst presentation. OA of weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees is common. Unlike inﬂammatory arthritis, OA does not have a typical pattern of early morning joint stiffness that improves throughout the day. Restricted movement, joint effusions and crepitus are all signs of OA. Radiological features of OA include loss of joint space, osteophyte formation, subchondral cysts and subchondral sclerosis. These are seen on the X-ray of the patient’s hip. The combination of symptoms, signs and X-ray ﬁndings make OA the most likely diagnosis. A Gout Gout is a crystal arthropathy associated with hyperuricaemia. Causes of hyperuricaemia include chronic kidney disease, a purinerich diet and drug therapy, including thiazide diuretics. Gout presents as an acutely painful joint, typically in the ﬁrst metatarsal joint. Men are more commonly affected than women. The clinical history does not suggest that this patient has hyperuricaemia and the pattern of joint involvement and X-ray ﬁndings does not reﬂect gout, making it an incorrect answer. C Osteoporosis Osteoporosis is a reduction in bone mineral density and is commonly seen in post-menopausal women or those exposed to high levels or prolonged use of corticosteroids. Patients with osteoporosis are more likely to obtain a fragility fracture such as a vertebral wedge fracture or Colles’ fracture. However, severe hip pain with degenerative X-ray changes is not a feature of osteoporosis and suggests an arthritic process. D Psoriatic arthritis Psoriatic arthritis belongs to a group of spondyloarthropathies associated with the HLA-B27 antigen. It can present as mono-, oligo- or polyarthritis. Skin changes may or may not be seen. A common pattern of joint disease is distal interphalangeal arthritis with adjacent nail dystrophy.
